p.seg: 1.1 《Mèngchūn Jì》
The first month of spring:
the sun is in Yíngshì,
at dusk Cān is at its meridian,
at dawn Wěi is at its meridian.
Its days are jiǎ and yǐ.
Its帝 (dì) is Tàihào.
Its神 (shén) is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are scaly ones.
Its sound is jiǎo.
Its lǜ is Tàicù.
Its number is eight.
Its taste is sour.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to Hù.
The first offering is the spleen.
The east wind thaws the ice.
Hibernating insects begin to stir and revive.
Fish come up and cling to the ice.
Otters offer fish.
Wild geese migrate north.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of Qīngyáng,
rides in a luán-chariot,
drawn by azure dragons,
bears a blue banner,
wears blue clothes,
is adorned with blue jade,
and eats wheat and lamb.
His utensils are plain and open.
In this month,
Lìchūn is established.
Three days before Lìchūn,
the Grand Astrologer reports to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such and such a day Lìchūn occurs,
and the predominant virtue is Wood."
The Son of Heaven then observes a fast.
On the day of Lìchūn,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dūkes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials to welcome spring in the eastern suburb.
Upon returning,
he rewards the dūkes, ministers, feudal lords, and high officials at court.
He commands the Prime Minister to disseminate virtue and harmonize decrees,
to perform benevolent acts and bestow favors,
reaching down to the common people.
Rewards and gifts are distributed accordingly,
with none being inappropriate.
He then commands the Grand Astrologer
to uphold the canons and observe the laws,
to oversee the movements of the sky, sun, moon, and stars,
to ensure that the constellations and stellar mansions do not deviate,
to not miss the regular order,
and to take the beginning as the constant.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven offers prayers for grain to Shàngdì on Yuándàn.
He then selects a yuán-day,
and the Son of Heaven personally loads the plough and spade,
placing them between the imperial charioteer and the attendant,
and leads the Three Dūkes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials to personally plough the imperial fields.
The Son of Heaven pushes three times,
the Three Dūkes push five times,
and the Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials push nine times.
Upon returning,
they hold a ceremonial cup in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and the Three Dūkes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials all participate,
this is called "Láojiǔ."
In this month,
heavenly qi descends,
earthly qi ascends,
heaven and earth harmonize,
and plants and trees flourish.
The king announces agricultural tasks:
he commands the field officials in the eastern suburb
to all repair the boundaries,
to carefully straighten the paths and roads,
to skillfully assess hills, slopes, dangers, plains, and lowlands,
what land is suitable for,
and what five grains can be planted,
to instruct the people,
and to personally attend to these matters.
Once the field work is in order,
first establish straight and level lines,
then the farmers will not be confused.
In this month,
the Music Master is commanded to enter and teach dances.
The sacrificial rites are then renewed,
and sacrifices are ordered to mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
no female animals are to be used for sacrifice.
Felling trees is forbidden,
no nests are to be overturned,
no young insects, unborn dogs, premature or newly fledged birds are to be killed,
no fawns or eggs are to be taken,
no large crowds are to be gathered,
no cities or outer walls are to be built,
and exposed skeletons are to be covered and buried.
In this month,
arms must not be taken up;
taking up arms will surely bring heavenly disaster.
Military conflict should not arise;
it must not begin with us.
Do not alter the way of Heaven,
do not sever the principles of Earth,
do not disrupt the order of humanity.
If in Mèngchūn one practices the ordinances of summer,
then winds and rains will be untimely,
plants and trees will wither from drought,
and the state will face dread.
If one practices the ordinances of autumn,
then the people will suffer a great plague,
fierce winds and torrential rains will arrive frequently and successively,
and weeds and thistles will flourish.
If one practices the ordinances of winter,
then floods will cause ruin,
frost and snow will be severe,
and the first crops will not grow.
1.2 《Běnshēng》
The one who initiates life
is Heaven and Earth;
the one who nurtures it
is humanity.
One who can nurture what Heaven has brought forth without disturbing it is called the Son of Heaven.
The actions of the Son of Heaven
are undertaken with the goal of preserving Heaven's completeness.
This is the reason why offices are established.
Offices are established to preserve life.
Yet the deluded rulers of this age
multiply offices and thereby harm life,
thus losing the purpose for which they were established.
It is like someone who repairs weapons
to guard against invaders;
if he now repairs weapons and instead uses them to attack himself,
then he has also lost the purpose for which they were repaired.
The nature of water is clear,
but earth muddies it,
so it cannot remain clear.
The nature of humanity is longevity,
but external things disturb it,
so it cannot attain longevity.
External things
are for nurturing one's nature,
not for one's nature to nurture them.
Yet people of this age,
many of them deluded, use their nature to nurture external things,
thus failing to understand what is light and what is heavy.
If one does not understand what is light and what is heavy,
then what is heavy becomes light,
and what is light becomes heavy.
If this is the case,
then every action will result in failure.
With this, a ruler becomes perverse,
a minister becomes rebellious,
and a son becomes insane.
If a state has any one of these three,
it will surely perish without exception.
If there is a sound here,
and the ear listens to it with delight,
but continuous listening makes one deaf,
then one must not listen to it.
If there is a sight here,
and the eye views it with delight,
but continuous viewing makes one blind,
then one must not view it.
If there is a taste here,
and the mouth savors it with delight,
but continuous savoring makes one mute,
then one must not savor it.
Therefore, the sage, regarding sounds, sights, and tastes,
takes them if they benefit his nature,
and discards them if they harm his nature;
this is the way to preserve one's nature.
The wealthy and noble of the world,
many of them are deluded by sounds, sights, and tastes;
they seek them day and night,
and if by chance they obtain them, they become enslaved to them.
If they are enslaved,
how can their nature avoid injury?
If ten thousand men draw bows and together shoot
at a single target,
no arrow will miss.
If all things are manifest,
to harm a single life,
no life will remain unharmed;
if to benefit a single life,
no life will fail to flourish.
Thus, the sage's regulation of all things
is for the sake of preserving their heavenly completeness.
When Heaven is complete, the spirit is harmonized,
the eyes are keen,
the ears are sharp,
the nose perceives scents,
the mouth is agile,
and all three hundred and sixty joints are unimpeded.
Such a person:
believes without speaking,
acts rightly without deliberation,
and achieves without anxiety;
their essence penetrates Heaven and Earth,
their spirit covers the universe;
there is nothing among things that they do not receive,
nothing that they do not encompass,
like Heaven and Earth.
Raised to be a Son of Heaven, they are not arrogant;
reduced to a commoner, they are not dejected.
This is what is called a person of complete virtue.
To be noble and wealthy yet not know the Way
is merely enough to cause trouble;
it is not as good as being poor and humble.
It is difficult for the poor and humble to acquire things;
even if they wished to go to excess, how could they?
Going out by carriage
and entering by palanquin,
striving to indulge oneself,
is called the mechanism of stumbling and falling.
Rich meats and thick wines,
striving to strengthen oneself,
are called foods that rot the intestines.
Luxurious beauty and white teeth,
the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
striving to amuse oneself,
are called axes that cut down one's nature.
These three harms
are brought about by nobility and wealth.
Therefore, among the ancients, there were those who were unwilling to be noble and wealthy,
because they valued life,
not to boast of their name,
but for its reality.
Thus, this argument must not be left unexamined.
1.3 《Chóngjǐ》
Thirdly, Chuí was supremely skillful.
People do not cherish Chuí's fingers,
but cherish their own fingers,
because of the benefit they derive from them.
People do not cherish the jade of Kūnshān or the pearls of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
but cherish their own small, dark jade disk or tiny pearl,
because of the benefit they derive from them.
Now, our life being ours
also benefits us greatly.
Considering its value,
even the title of Son of Heaven cannot compare to it;
considering its weight,
owning the whole world cannot exchange it;
considering its safety,
to lose it in one morning
is to never regain it for a lifetime.
These three
are what those who possess the Way are cautious about.
Those who are cautious but still harm it
do not comprehend the true nature of life and destiny.
If one does not comprehend the true nature of life and destiny,
what good is caution?
It is like a teacher who loves his child
but cannot help but use chaff as a pillow for him;
it is like a deaf person raising an infant,
peeking at it from the hall during a thunderstorm.
This is no different from not knowing caution at all.
Those who do not know caution
make no distinction between life and death, survival and destruction, whether things are permissible or not.
They have never made a distinction.
For those who have never made a distinction,
what they call right has never been right,
what they call wrong has never been wrong.
They treat what is right as wrong,
and what is wrong as right.
This is called profound delusion.
Such people
are cursed by Heaven.
Using this to govern oneself
will surely lead to death and disaster;
using this to govern a state
will surely lead to ruin and destruction.
Indeed, death, disaster, ruin, and destruction
do not come on their own;
delusion summons them.
Longevity and reaching the norm are also like this.
Therefore, those who possess the Way
do not investigate what is summoned,
but investigate that which summons it;
then its arrival cannot be prevented.
This argument must be thoroughly considered.
If Wūhuò forcefully pulls a bull's tail,
the tail breaks and his strength is exhausted,
but the bull cannot move,
this is because it is contrary.
If a five-foot tall boy leads it by its nose-ring,
and the bull goes wherever it pleases, this is because it is compliant.
The rulers and noblemen of the world,
whether worthy or unworthy,
all wish for long life and lasting vision,
yet daily act contrary to their lives.
What good is such a wish?
Indeed, for life to be long
is to be compliant with it;
that which makes life non-compliant
is desire.
Therefore, the sage must first adapt to desires.
A large house has too much yin,
a high tower has too much yang.
Too much yin causes stumbling,
too much yang causes impotence.
This is the affliction of imbalanced yin and yang.
Therefore, the former kings did not reside in large houses,
nor did they build high towers.
Their food was not a multitude of delicacies,
their clothing was not excessively hot.
Excessive heat obstructs the channels,
and obstructed channels prevent qi from circulating.
A multitude of delicacies fills the stomach,
and a filled stomach causes the mid-abdomen to be greatly distended.
If the mid-abdomen is greatly distended and qi does not circulate,
can long life be obtained from this?
In ancient times, the former sage kings made parks, gardens, and ponds
only for viewing and resting the body;
they made palaces, houses, and terraces
only to avoid dryness and dampness;
they made carriages, horses, clothes, and furs
only to relax the body and warm the bones;
they made food, drink, and sweet wine
only to suit the taste and fill the emptiness;
they made music of sounds and colors
only to soothe their nature and entertain themselves.
These five
are how the sage kings nourished their nature;
it was not that they preferred frugality and disliked extravagance,
but that they regulated themselves according to nature.
1.4 《Guìgōng》
Fourthly,
when the former sage kings governed the world,
they must first be impartial.
If they were impartial, the world would be at peace.
Peace is attained through impartiality.
Let us observe the records of the past:
many have gained the world,
and they gained it through impartiality;
they lost it through partiality.
Indeed, the establishment of a ruler
originates from impartiality.
Thus, the 《Hóngfàn》 says:
"Without partiality, without partisanship,
the Kingly Way is broad and vast.
Without partiality, without bias,
follow the King's righteousness.
Do not act on personal likes,
follow the King's Way.
Do not act on personal dislikes,
follow the King's Path."
The world is not the world of one person;
it is the world of the world.
The harmony of yin and yang
does not favor one species;
sweet dew and timely rain
do not privatize to one thing.
The ruler of all people
does not show favoritism to one person.
When Bóqín was about to depart,
he asked how to govern Lǔ.
Zhōugōng said:
"Benefit them but do not seek benefit for yourself."
A person from Jīng lost a bow,
but was unwilling to search for it,
saying:
"A Jīng person lost it,
a Jīng person will find it,
so why search for it?"
Kǒngzǐ heard this and said:
"Remove the 'Jīng' and it would be acceptable."
Lǎodān heard this and said:
"Remove the 'person' and it would be acceptable."
Therefore, Lǎodān was utterly impartial.
Heaven and Earth are great indeed:
they give birth without claiming as children,
they bring to completion without possessing.
All things are covered by their beneficence and receive their benefit,
yet none know whence they originate.
This is the virtue of the Sān Huáng and Wǔ Dì.
Guǎn Zhòng had an illness.
Huán Gōng went to visit him,
and said:
"Zhòngfù's illness
is severe,
the people of the state do not avoid speaking of it,
to whom shall I entrust the state?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"In the past, when your servant exerted all his strength and exhausted all his wisdom,
he still was not sufficient to know it.
Now, with illness lingering between morning and evening,
how can your servant speak?"
Huán Gōng said:
"This is a great matter.
I wish Zhòngfù would instruct me."
Guǎn Zhòng respectfully assented,
and said:
"Whom does Your Lord wish to make prime minister?"
The Lord said:
"Is Bào Shúyá acceptable?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"No.
Yí Wú is good friends with Bào Shúyá,
but Bào Shúyá's character is
pure, honest, and upright.
He does not associate with those he deems inferior to himself,
and he does not condescend to others.
Once he hears of a person's fault,
he never forgets it throughout his life."
"If not him,
then perhaps Xí Péng is acceptable?"
"Xí Péng's character is such that
he aims high and seeks what is low.
He is ashamed of being inferior to Huáng Dì,
and grieves for those inferior to himself.
Regarding the state,
there are things he does not hear.
Regarding matters,
there are things he does not know.
Regarding people,
there are things he does not see.
If there is no other choice,
then Xí Péng is acceptable."
Indeed, a prime minister
is a high official.
Those who hold high office
should not desire petty scrutiny,
nor desire petty wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
A great craftsman does not hew,
a great cook does not dish out,
a great hero does not fight,
a great army does not raid.
Huán Gōng acted publicly and cast aside private vices,
used Guǎn Zǐ, and became the chief of the Five Hegemons.
He acted privately and indulged his favorites,
used Shù Diāo, and insects emerged from the household.
When people are young, they are foolish;
when they grow old, they are wise.
Therefore, it is better to be foolish and act publicly
than to be wise and act privately.
To be drunk daily yet adorn one's clothes,
to seek private gain yet establish public institutions,
to be greedy and violent yet seek kingship,
even Shùn could not do these things.
1.5 "Qu Sī"
Fifth:
Heaven covers without partiality,
Earth carries without partiality,
the sun and moon illuminate without partiality,
the four seasons proceed without partiality.
They carry out their virtues, and all things can grow and thrive.
Huáng Dì said:
"Sounds are forbidden to be excessive,
colors are forbidden to be excessive,
clothing is forbidden to be excessive,
fragrances are forbidden to be excessive,
flavors are forbidden to be excessive,
residences are forbidden to be excessive."
Yáo had ten sons,
but did not give the throne to his sons; instead, he bestowed it upon Shùn.
Shùn had nine sons,
but did not give the throne to his sons; instead, he bestowed it upon Yǔ.
This is ultimate impartiality.
Jìn Píng Gōng asked Qí Huángyáng:
"Nányáng has no magistrate;
who is suitable to be one?"
Qí Huángyáng replied:
"Jiě Hú is acceptable."
Píng Gōng said:
"Is Jiě Hú not your enemy?"
He replied:
"Your Lord asks who is acceptable,
not about your servant's enemy."
Píng Gōng said:
"Good."
And so, he employed him.
The people of the state praised this as good.
After a while,
Píng Gōng again asked Qí Huángyáng:
"The state has no commandant;
who is suitable to be one?"
He replied:
"Wǔ is acceptable."
Píng Gōng said:
"Is Wǔ not your son?"
He replied:
"Your Lord asks who is acceptable,
not about your servant's son."
Píng Gōng said:
"Good."
And again, he employed him.
The people of the state praised this as good.
Kǒng Zǐ heard of this and said:
"Excellent!
Qí Huángyáng's judgments
involved recommending outsiders without avoiding enemies,
and recommending insiders without avoiding his own son."
Qí Huángyáng can be called impartial.
The Mòists had a Great Master, Fù Dūn,
who resided in Qín.
His son killed a man.
Qín Huì Wáng said:
"Sir, your years are advanced,
and you have no other son.
I have already ordered the officials not to execute him.
Sir, please listen to me on this matter."
Fù Dūn replied:
"The Mòist law states:
'He who kills a man shall die;
he who injures a man shall be punished.'
This is for the purpose of prohibiting killing and injuring people.
Indeed, prohibiting killing and injuring people
is the great righteousness of the world.
Though Your Majesty grants a pardon
and orders officials not to execute him,
Fù Dūn cannot but follow the Mòist law."
He did not grant Huì Wáng's request,
and subsequently executed his son.
A son is what a person holds dear privately.
To bear to sacrifice one's private affection in order to uphold great righteousness,
the Great Master can be called impartial.
A cook seasons and harmonizes food but dares not taste it,
thus he can be a cook.
If a cook seasons and harmonizes food and then eats it,
then he cannot be a cook.
The rulers of kings and hegemons are also like this:
they punish the violent without partiality,
and enfeoff the worthy of the world.
Thus they can be kings and hegemons.
If the rulers of kings and hegemons punish the violent but do so with partiality,
then they also cannot be kings and hegemons.
2.1 "Zhòngchūn Jì"
In the month of mid-spring:
the sun is in Kuí,
at dusk the constellation Hú is at its meridian,
at dawn the constellation Jiàn Xīng is at its meridian.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its emperor is Tài Hào.
Its god is Gōu Máng.
Its creatures are the scaly ones.
Its note is Jiǎo.
The pitch-pipe is Jiāzhōng.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to Hù.
One sacrifices the spleen first.
Rainwater begins.
Peach and plum trees blossom.
The orioles sing.
Hawks transform into doves.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Qīngyáng Grand Temple,
rides in a luán-chariot,
drawn by azure dragons,
carrying green banners,
dressed in green clothes,
adorned with green jade,
eats wheat and lamb.
His vessels are sparse and permeable.
In this month,
the sprouting seeds are given peace,
the young and weak are nurtured,
and all orphans are cared for.
A propitious day is chosen,
and the people are ordered to perform the shè (社) sacrifice.
The officials are commanded
to inspect prisons,
remove fetters and shackles,
forbid plunder and pillage,
and stop lawsuits.
In this month,
the xuánniǎo (玄鳥) arrives.
On the day of its arrival,
the tàiláo (太牢) sacrifice is offered to Gāoméi (高禖).
The Tiānzǐ (天子) personally goes,
and the Hòufēi (后妃), leading the jiǔpín (九嬪) and the yù (御),
then performs the ritual for those favored by the Tiānzǐ,
who are presented with bow quivers,
and given bows and arrows before Gāoméi.
In this month,
day and night are equal.
Thunder then sends forth its sound,
and lightning begins.
Hibernating insects all stir,
opening their burrows and beginning to emerge.
Three days before the first thunder,
the officials brandish bells to instruct the common people, saying:
"Thunder is about to sound.
If anyone does not guard their demeanor and conduct,
their children will be incomplete,
and there will surely be misfortune and disaster."
When day and night are equal,
measures are standardized,
scales and weights are made uniform,
dou (斗) and tǒng (桶) measures are rectified,
and steelyards and grain scrapers are corrected.
In this month,
farmers take a short rest,
then repair doors and screens,
and ensure that the ancestral temple is fully prepared.
No major undertakings should be initiated
to avoid hindering agricultural work.
In this month,
rivers and marshes must not be drained dry,
ponds and reservoirs must not be dredged,
and mountains and forests must not be burned.
The Tiānzǐ then offers a lamb and opens the ice,
first presenting them in the ancestral temple.
On the first Dīng (丁) day,
the Yuèzhèng (樂正) is commanded to enter the dance hall to gather samples,
and the Tiānzǐ then leads the Sāngōng (三公), Jiǔqīng (九卿), and Zhūhóu (諸侯) to personally observe it.
On the middle Dīng day,
the Yuèzhèng is again commanded to enter and learn music.
In this month,
sacrifices do not use victims,
but use guī (圭) and bì (璧) jades,
and change to silk and leather currencies.
If the autumn regulations are followed in mid-spring,
then the state will suffer great floods,
cold air will arrive generally,
and invaders will come to attack.
If the winter regulations are followed,
then the yang (陽) energy will not be victorious,
wheat will not ripen,
and the people will plunder each other often.
If the summer regulations are followed,
then the state will suffer a great drought,
warm air will arrive early,
and insect pests will cause harm.
2.2 "Guìshēng" (貴生)
Second:
The Sage deeply considers the world,
and nothing is more precious than life.
Indeed, the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
are servants of life.
Although the ears desire sounds,
the eyes desire colors,
the nose desires fragrances,
and the mouth desires flavors,
if they harm life, they must stop.
Regarding the four senses,
that which is not beneficial to life should not be pursued.
From this perspective,
the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
cannot act arbitrarily;
they must be controlled.
It is like official positions:
they cannot act arbitrarily;
they must be controlled.
This is the art of valuing life.
Yáo (堯) offered the world to Zǐzhōu Zhīfù (子州支父).
Zǐzhōu Zhīfù replied:
"It would be acceptable for me to be the Tiānzǐ.
However, I happen to have a disease of profound melancholy,
which I am about to treat,
and I do not have time for the world."
The world is a weighty matter,
yet he would not let it harm his life;
how much less would he harm his life for other things?
Only one who would not harm his life for the world
can be entrusted with the world.
The Yuè (越) people had killed their ruler three times in three generations.
Wángzǐ Sōu (王子搜) was troubled by this,
and fled to Dānxué (丹穴).
The state of Yuè (越) had no ruler,
so they sought Wángzǐ Sōu but could not find him.
They followed him to Dānxué.
Wángzǐ Sōu refused to come out,
so the Yuè people smoked him out with mugwort
and carried him on the royal carriage.
Wángzǐ Sōu grasped the rope, ascended the carriage,
looked up to heaven, and cried out:
"Oh, ruler!
Could you not just leave me alone?!"
Wángzǐ Sōu did not dislike being a ruler;
he disliked the troubles of being a ruler.
Someone like Wángzǐ Sōu
can be said not to have harmed his life for the sake of the state.
This is indeed the kind of person the Yuè people desired to get as their ruler.
The ruler of Lǔ (魯) heard that Yán Hé (顏闔) was a man who had attained the Way,
and sent someone with gifts to him first.
Yán Hé guarded his gate,
dressed in coarse cloth,
and personally fed his cattle.
When the envoy from the ruler of Lǔ arrived,
Yán Hé personally responded to him.
The envoy said:
"Is this the home of Yán Hé?"
Yán Hé replied:
"This is the home of Hé."
The envoy presented the gifts.
Yán Hé replied:
"I fear I might have misheard and would cause trouble for the envoy.
It would be better to verify it."
The envoy returned to verify it,
and when he came back to seek him,
Yán Hé was no longer to be found.
Therefore, someone like Yán Hé
did not dislike wealth and nobility;
he disliked them because he valued life more.
The rulers of this generation
often use wealth and nobility to lord over those who have attained the Way.
Their failure to understand each other—
is this not tragic?
Thus it is said:
The true essence of the Way
is for upholding oneself;
its surplus
is for managing states and families;
its dregs
are for governing the world.
From this perspective,
the achievements of emperors and kings
are but the leftover matters of the Sage,
not the Way by which one perfects oneself and nurtures life.
Nowadays, the gentlemen of this generation
often endanger their bodies and abandon their lives to pursue external things.
What do they gain by this?
What do they achieve by this?
Whenever the Sage acts,
he must examine what he is going towards and what he is acting for.
Now, if there were a person here
who used a Suíhóu (隨侯) pearl to shoot a sparrow on a cliff a thousand rèn (仞) high,
the world would surely laugh at him.
Why is this?
Because what is used is valuable,
and what is sought is trivial.
Is life not even more valuable than a Suíhóu (隨侯) pearl?
Zǐhuázi (子華子) said:
"To preserve life completely is supreme;
to damage life is next;
death is next;
to coerce life is lowest."
Therefore, what is meant by "honoring life"
is to preserve life completely.
What is meant by "preserving life completely"
is that all six desires obtain their proper measure.
What is meant by "damaging life"
is that the six desires only partially obtain their proper measure.
To diminish life is to be indifferent to what one holds dear.
The more severe the diminution,
the greater the indifference.
What is called death
is to have no means of knowing,
to return to one's unborn state.
What is called a constrained life
is when none of the six desires obtain their proper gratification;
everyone receives what they intensely loathe—
servitude is this,
disgrace is this.
There is no greater disgrace than unrighteousness,
therefore unrighteousness
is a constrained life.
But a constrained life is not only unrighteousness,
therefore it is said that a constrained life is not as good as death.
How do we know this is so?
To hear what one dislikes
is not as good as hearing nothing;
to see what one dislikes
is not as good as seeing nothing.
Therefore, when it thunders, one covers one's ears;
when there is lightning, one covers one's eyes—
this is the analogy.
As for all six desires,
if one knows what one intensely dislikes
and is certainly unable to avoid it,
it is not as good as having no means of knowing.
Having no means of knowing
is what is meant by death.
Therefore, a constrained life is not as good as death.
One who enjoys meat
does not mean rotten meat.
One who enjoys wine
does not mean spoiled wine.
One who values life
does not mean a constrained life.
2.3 《Qíngyù》
The third states:
Heaven creates humans and causes them to have avarice and desires.
Desires have emotions (or natural inclinations),
emotions have limits.
Sages cultivate limits to restrain desires,
thus they do not excessively indulge their emotions.
Therefore, the ear's desire for the five sounds,
the eye's desire for the five colors,
the mouth's desire for the five flavors
are natural inclinations.
These three
are desired equally by the noble and the humble, the foolish and the wise, the worthy and the unworthy.
Even Shénnóng and Huángdì were the same in this regard as Jié and Zhòu.
The reason sages are different
is that they attain their natural inclinations.
To act from valuing life is to attain one's natural inclinations;
not to act from valuing life is to lose one's natural inclinations.
These two
are the foundation of life and death, survival and destruction.
Common rulers diminish their natural inclinations,
so every action leads to ruin and defeat.
The ears cannot be satisfied,
the eyes cannot be sated,
the mouth cannot be filled.
The body becomes entirely swollen,
muscles and bones become stagnant and heavy,
blood vessels are obstructed,
the nine orifices are hollow and depleted,
everything loses its proper function.
Even Pénzǔ
would be unable to help.
As for material things,
desiring what cannot be obtained is greed,
seeking what cannot be satisfied is craving,
greatly losing the root of life.
The people resent and criticize,
and great enemies are made.
One's spirit is easily swayed,
unstable and not firm.
One prides oneself on power and loves cleverness,
with deceit and trickery in one's heart.
Virtue and righteousness are neglected,
but evil gains are eagerly pursued.
The body is thus impoverished,
even if one regrets it later,
what good will it do?
The cunning and sycophantic are near,
the upright and honest are far.
The state is in great peril,
regretting past mistakes
cannot undo them.
Hearing words, one is startled,
unable to understand the cause.
A hundred ailments arise furiously,
chaos and difficulties arrive constantly.
To rule people in this way
is a great sorrow for oneself.
If the ears do not enjoy sounds,
the eyes do not enjoy colors,
the mouth does not relish tastes,
there is no difference from death.
Ancient people who attained the Way
lived long lives,
and could enjoy sounds, colors, and tastes for a long time.
Why?
Their principles were established early.
When principles are established early, one knows how to conserve early.
When one knows how to conserve early, one's essence does not deplete.
If autumn is cold early, winter will certainly be warm.
If spring has much rain, summer will certainly be dry.
Heaven and Earth cannot have both extremes,
how much less so humanity?
Humans are the same as Heaven and Earth;
though the forms of myriad things differ,
their essence is one body.
Therefore, those of old who governed themselves and the world
invariably modeled themselves on Heaven and Earth.
If many people drink from a precious goblet, it will quickly be exhausted.
Many people draw upon the life of the greatly noble,
therefore the lives of the greatly noble often exhaust quickly.
Not only do myriad things draw upon them,
but they also diminish their own lives to benefit the people of the world,
yet they never realize it themselves.
Although their achievements are external,
their lives are diminished internally.
The ears cannot hear,
the eyes cannot see,
the mouth cannot eat.
There is great agitation in the chest,
delusional talk and imagined sights.
Nearing death,
they are confused, astonished, and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
To use one's mind in such a way,
how could it not be sorrowful!
When people of the world serve their rulers,
they all consider Sūn Shú'áo's encounter with Jīng Zhuāngwáng to be fortunate.
However, from the perspective of one who has attained the Way, this is not so.
This was the good fortune of the state of Jīng.
Jīng Zhuāngwáng loved traveling and hunting,
galloping, shooting, and enjoying himself without restraint.
He entirely handed over the burdens within his borders and the worries of the feudal lords to Sūn Shú'áo.
Sūn Shú'áo worked day and night without rest,
unable to prioritize his own life's ease.
Thus, he enabled Zhūangwáng's achievements to be recorded on bamboo and silk,
and transmitted to later generations.
2.4 《Dāngrǎn》
The fourth states:
Mòzǐ saw someone dyeing plain silk
and sighed, saying:
"Dyed blue, it becomes blue;
dyed yellow, it becomes yellow.
What it enters changes,
its color also changes;
five times it enters and becomes five colors."
Therefore, one must be careful about what one is dyed by.
Not only is this true for dyeing silk,
but states also have their dyes.
Shùn was dyed by Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yáng.
Yǔ was dyed by Gāotáo and Bó Yì.
Tāng was dyed by Yī Yǐn and Zhòng Huǐ.
Wǔwáng was dyed by Tàigōng Wàng and Zhōu Gōngdàn.
These four kings were dyed appropriately,
therefore they ruled all under Heaven,
established themselves as Sons of Heaven.
Their merits and fame covered Heaven and Earth,
and when listing people known for benevolence and righteousness in all under Heaven, these four kings are invariably mentioned.
Xià Jié was dyed by Gān Xīn and Qí Zhǒngróng.
Yīn Zhòu was dyed by Chóng Hóu and È Lái.
Zhōu Lìwáng was dyed by Guó Gōngchángfù and Róng Yízhōng.
Yōuwáng was dyed by Guó Gōnggǔ and Jì Gōngdūn.
These four kings were not dyed appropriately,
therefore their states were ruined and their bodies perished,
becoming a scorn to all under Heaven.
When listing people known for unrighteousness and disgrace in all under Heaven, these four kings are invariably mentioned.
Qí Huán Gōng was dyed by Guǎn Zhòng and Bāo Shú.
Jìn Wén Gōng was dyed by Jiù Fàn and Xī Yǎn.
Jīng Zhuāngwáng was dyed by Sūn Shú'áo and Shěn Yǐnzhēng.
Wúwáng Hélǘ was dyed by Wǔ Yuán and Wén Zhīyí.
Yuèwáng Gōujiàn was dyed by Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhǒng.
These five rulers were dyed appropriately,
therefore they became hegemons among the feudal lords,
and their merits and fame were transmitted to later generations.
Fàn Jíshè was dyed by Zhāng Liǔshuò and Wáng Shēng.
Zhōngháng Yín was dyed by Huáng Jièqín and Gāo Qiáng.
Wúwáng Fūchā was dyed by Wángsūn Xióng and Tàizǎi Pǐ.
Zhì Bóyáo was dyed by Zhì Guó and Zhāng Wǔ.
Zhōngshān Shàng was dyed by Wèi Yì and Yǎn Cháng.
Sòng Kāngwáng was dyed by Táng Yāng and Tián Bùyīn.
The six lords mentioned were influenced inappropriately,
hence their states were all ruined and destroyed,
their persons either died in disgrace,
their ancestral temples lacked blood sacrifices,
their lines were severed,
lords and ministers were separated and scattered,
and the common people became refugees.
When speaking of the greedy, tyrannical, and shameful people in the world, these six lords are invariably cited.
The purpose of being a lord is not to gain honor,
nor is it to gain security,
but to administer governance.
Good governance arises from appropriate influences,
hence the good rulers of ancient times
labored in judging people,
and were at ease in official duties;
they understood the principle.
Those who cannot rule well
harm their bodies and exhaust their spirits,
trouble their minds and tire their ears and eyes,
making their states more perilous
and their persons more disgraced,
because they do not know the essential principle.
If one does not know the essential principle, then their influences are inappropriate.
If their influences are inappropriate,
how can good governance be achieved?
The six lords are examples of this.
The six lords
did not fail to value their states or love their persons;
it was their inappropriate influences.
Thus, survival and destruction are not unique to this;
it is also true for emperors and kings.
It is not only states that have influences.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) learned from Lǎo Dān, Mèng Sū Kuí, and Jìng Shú.
Duke Huì of Lǔ sent Zǎi Ràng to request the rites of the suburban sacrifice and ancestral temple from the Son of Heaven.
King Huán (Píng) sent Shǐ Jiǎo.
Duke Huì detained him,
and his descendants remained in Lǔ.
Mòzǐ learned from them.
These two scholars
had no official rank to make people prominent,
nor rewards or emoluments to benefit people,
yet all those who are famous and honored throughout the world invariably speak of these two scholars.
They have both been dead for a long time,
yet their followers grow ever more numerous,
their disciples ever more abundant,
filling the world.
Kings, dukes, and great men follow and honor them,
and those who love their sons and younger brothers follow and learn from them,
never ceasing.
Zǐgòng, Zǐxià, and Zēngzǐ learned from Kǒngzǐ.
Tián Zǐfāng learned from Zǐgòng.
Duàn Gānmù learned from Zǐxià.
Wú Qǐ learned from Zēngzǐ.
Qín Huálí learned from Mòzǐ.
Xǔ Fàn learned from Qín Huálí.
Tián Xì learned from Xǔ Fàn.
The later followers of Kǒng and Mò who became prominent and honored in the world are numerous,
beyond counting;
this is because their influences were appropriate.
2.5 "Gōngmíng" (Achievement and Fame)
Fifthly:
If one follows the right way,
achievement and fame cannot escape them,
just as a shadow follows a gnomon,
or an echo follows a call.
A skilled angler can catch fish from ten *rèn* below;
the bait is fragrant. A skilled archer can shoot down birds from a hundred *rèn* above;
the bow is good.
A skilled ruler
can subdue even barbarians, those with different tongues, and those with strange customs and habits;
their virtue is profound.
When a spring is deep, fish and turtles gather there.
When trees are lush, birds gather there.
When grasses are abundant, beasts gather there.
When a lord is virtuous, heroes and outstanding individuals gather there.
Therefore, the sage kings do not strive to make them gather,
but strive for that by which they gather.
A forced smile is not joyful;
forced tears are not sorrowful.
The way of compulsion,
can achieve small things,
but cannot achieve great things.
In a jar of vinegar, yellow gnats
gather because it is sour;
in plain water, they certainly will not.
To attract a rat with a wildcat,
or a fly with ice,
even a skilled person cannot.
To try to remove flies with rotten fish,
the flies will only come more, and cannot be stopped,
because you are using the method of attracting them to remove them.
Jié and Zhòu used the method of removing people to attract them.
Even if punishments were heavy and penalties severe, what good was it?
When great cold arrives,
people find warmth beneficial.
When great heat prevails,
people flee towards coolness.
Therefore, people have no fixed abode;
they gather where there is benefit,
and depart where there is none.
If one wishes to be the Son of Heaven,
they must carefully observe
where the people flee to.
In the present age,
it is extremely cold,
it is extremely hot,
yet the people have nowhere to flee,
because the policies are all similar.
If one wishes to be the Son of Heaven,
what they show to the people
must be different.
If policies are not different,
even if chaos doubles the present,
the people will still have nowhere to flee.
If the people have nowhere to flee,
then the king will be overthrown,
the tyrant will be fortunate,
and the people will lose all hope.
Therefore, in the present age,
if there is a benevolent person,
they cannot but strive for this.
If there is a worthy lord, they cannot but attend to this matter.
The worthy and the unworthy cannot but be distinguished,
just as fate cannot be changed,
and good and evil cannot be shifted.
Jié and Zhòu, though noble as Sons of Heaven and possessing all under heaven,
could harm all the people under heaven,
but could not obtain the name of worthiness.
Guān Lóngfēng and Prince Bǐgān, though they died with their heads severed
for remonstrating against the faults of their superiors,
could not share the name of worthiness with them.
Fame, by its nature, cannot be shared;
it must follow its principle.
3.1 "Jìchūn Jì" (Annals of Late Spring)
First:
In the month of late spring:
The sun is in Wèi (the Stomach constellation).
At dusk, Qī Xīng (the Seven Stars, i.e., the Big Dipper) is at its zenith.
At dawn, Qiānniú (the Herdboy, i.e., Altair) is at its zenith.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its emperor is Tàihào.
Its spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are scaly ones.
Its musical note is jué.
The pitch pipe is in Gūxǐ.
Its number is eight.
Its taste is sour.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the household gate.
The first offering is of spleen.
The phoenix tree begins to flower.
Field mice transform into quails.
Rainbows begin to appear.
Duckweed begins to grow.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right wing of Qīngyáng Palace,
rides the luán-chariot,
drawn by blue-green dragons,
bears a blue-green banner,
wears blue-green clothes,
and wears blue-green jade ornaments.
He eats wheat and lamb.
His vessels are sparse and permeable.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven offers a *júyī* (silk robe) to the former emperor.
He commands the boat master to overturn boats,
five times overturning and five times righting,
and then reports the boat preparations to the Son of Heaven,
whereupon the Son of Heaven begins to travel by boat.
He offers sturgeon to the ancestral temple
and prays for a bountiful harvest of wheat.
In this month,
the vital energy is flourishing,
the yang energy is emitted,
all living things emerge,
all buds sprout and extend,
and nothing should be kept suppressed.
The Son of Heaven extends virtue and bestows kindness,
commands officials
to open granaries and storehouses,
give to the poor,
aid the destitute,
open treasuries,
distribute silks and fabrics,
travel throughout the world,
encourage the feudal lords,
invite famous scholars,
and honor the worthy.
In this month, the Sīkōng
was ordered, saying: "Timely rains are about to fall,
and lower waters will rise.
Circulate through the national capital and cities,
inspect the plains and wilds,
repair and improve dikes and embankments,
guide and unblock ditches and conduits,
open up roads,
so that there are no obstructions.
Hunting with nets and arrows,
snares and traps,
and medicines to poison beasts,
must not leave the national gates."
In this month,
the Yěyú
was ordered not to cut down mulberry and zhe trees.
When the cuckoo flaps its wings,
and the dài-rèn descends upon the mulberry,
prepare sturdy baskets and curved trays.
The Empress and consorts observe a fast,
and personally face east
to pick mulberries.
Women are forbidden to watch.
Reduce the number of female servants,
and encourage sericulture.
Once the silk farming is complete,
distribute the cocoons and weigh the silk to evaluate the work,
to provide for the garments for the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temple.
No one dares to be lazy.
In this month,
the Gōngshī
was ordered to command the hundred artisans
to examine the stores of the five treasuries:
gold, iron, leather, sinews, horn, teeth, feathers for arrows, and animal fat, glue, vermilion, lacquer.
None must be of poor quality.
When all artisans are properly managed,
the inspecting artisans daily declare that nothing should be contrary to the season,
and no one should create excessive or elaborate crafts,
to disturb the superior's mind.
At the end of this month,
choose an auspicious day,
hold a grand music performance.
The Son of Heaven then leads the Sāngōng, Jiǔqīng, Zhūhóu, and Dàfū
to personally inspect it.
In this month,
oxen are tethered and horses released to mate and roam in the pasture.
The sacrificial animals, colts, and calves,
are counted and recorded.
The people of the capital are ordered to perform the Nuó exorcism,
and at the nine gates, sacrifices and purifications are performed,
to conclude the spring qi.
If these commands are carried out,
then timely rains will last for thirty days.
If winter commands are carried out in late spring,
then cold qi will arise at the wrong time,
plants will all wither,
and the state will experience great fear.
If summer commands are carried out,
then the people will suffer many diseases and epidemics,
timely rains will not fall,
and the mountains and hills will yield no harvest.
If autumn commands are carried out,
then the sky will be filled with heavy gloom,
excessive rains will fall early,
and military conflicts will arise simultaneously.
3.2 《Jìnshù》
Second, it says: Heaven produces Yin and Yang, cold and heat, dryness and dampness.
The transformations of the four seasons,
and the changes of myriad things,
all are beneficial,
and all are harmful.
The sage observes what is appropriate for Yin and Yang,
and discerns the benefits of myriad things to facilitate life.
Thus, the spirit is at peace in the body,
and one's lifespan can be prolonged.
Prolonged means not being cut short and then continued,
but completing its full measure.
The essential task of completing one's full measure
lies in eliminating harm.
What is meant by eliminating harm?
Great sweetness, great sourness, great bitterness, great pungency, great saltiness—
if these five fill the body, harm will arise.
Great joy, great anger, great worry, great fear, great sorrow—
if these five affect the spirit, harm will arise.
Great cold, great heat, great dryness, great dampness, great wind,
great continuous rain, great fog—
if these seven disturb the essence, harm will arise.
Therefore, in nurturing life,
nothing is better than understanding the root.
If the root is understood, illness will have no way to arrive.
When vital energy gathers, it must have an entry point.
If it gathers in feathered birds, it makes them fly.
If it gathers in running beasts, it makes them move.
If it gathers in pearls and jade, it makes them lustrous.
If it gathers in trees, it makes them grow lush.
If it gathers in a sage, it makes him profoundly enlightened.
When vital energy comes,
it lifts things that are light,
it moves things that walk,
it makes beautiful things good,
it nourishes things that grow,
it enlightens those who are wise.
Flowing water does not putrefy;
door hinges do not get worm-eaten—this is due to movement.
The body's qi is the same.
If the body does not move, essence does not flow;
if essence does not flow, qi stagnates.
If stagnation is in the head, it causes swelling and wind-related illnesses.
If in the ears, it causes ringing and deafness.
If in the eyes, it causes blurring and blindness.
If in the nose, it causes a runny nose and obstruction.
If in the abdomen, it causes distension and accumulation.
If in the feet, it causes paralysis and lameness.
Regions with light water produce many bald and goitrous people.
Regions with heavy water produce many swollen-legged and lame people.
Regions with sweet water produce many kind and beautiful people.
Regions with pungent water produce many carbuncles and boils.
Regions with bitter water produce many emaciated and hunched people.
In all eating, do not be excessively strong or rich,
and do not combine strong flavors with heavy wine.
This is what causes "sick head."
If one eats at the proper time,
the body will certainly be free from calamities.
The way of all eating is
neither hunger nor satiety.
This is called the preservation of the five zàng organs.
The mouth must enjoy sweet flavors,
harmonize the essence and maintain a proper countenance,
guiding it with spiritual qi.
All joints will be joyful,
and will receive qi fully.
When drinking, always take small sips,
straight and without deviation.
Today's world relies on divination, fortune-telling, prayers, and sacrifices,
which is why diseases increasingly arise.
It is like an archer:
if he shoots and misses,
and instead adjusts the target (or the string, 招 can mean either),
what good is it for hitting?
Trying to stop boiling water with hot water,
the boiling only increases.
Remove the fire, and it will stop.
Therefore, sorcerers, physicians, and poisonous drugs are used
to expel and treat illnesses,
which is why people of ancient times considered them base,
because they are but a branch (not the root).
3.3 《Xiānjǐ》
Third, it says: Tāng asked Yī Yǐn:
"How should one take possession of the world?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"If one wishes to take possession of the world,
the world cannot be taken possession of.
If it could be taken,
one's own person would first be taken."
The root of all matters
is necessarily to first govern oneself,
to conserve one's great treasure.
Use the new,
discard the old,
and the pores will be clear.
Vital energy will daily renew,
evil qi will be completely expelled,
and one will complete one's natural lifespan.
This is called a true person.
In ancient times, the former sage kings
perfected themselves, and the world was perfected;
governed themselves, and the world was governed.
Thus, one who is good at making echoes does not focus on the echo but on the sound;
one who is good at making shadows does not focus on the shadow but on the form;
one who acts for the world does not focus on the world but on oneself.
The 《Shī》 says: "A good and noble person,
his deportment is without fault.
His deportment without fault,
corrects the four states (regions),"
meaning correcting oneself.
Therefore, by reversing one's path, one's person becomes good;
by practicing righteousness, people become good;
by fulfilling the way of a ruler,
all officials will already be well-governed,
and the myriad people will already benefit.
The accomplishment of these three
lies in non-action (wúwéi).
righteousness is called benefiting oneself,
and the ruler's way is called selflessness.
Selflessness leads to diligent listening,
self-benefit leads to tranquility,
and triumphing over Heaven leads to according with nature.
To accord with nature leads to intelligence and longevity,
tranquility leads to advancing in one's undertakings and a joyful state,
and diligent listening leads to blocking treachery and preventing disorder.
Therefore, when the ruler loses the Way, the borders are invaded by enemies;
when internally one loses proper conduct,
one's reputation declines externally.
Thus, for a pine tree a hundred *rèn* tall,
if its root is damaged below,
its tip will wither above.
For the states of Shāng and Zhōu,
if strategy failed in their hearts,
their decrees would be ineffective there.
Therefore, if the heart gains, listening gains;
if listening gains, affairs gain;
if affairs gain, achievements and reputation gain.
The Wǔdì prioritized the Way before virtue,
hence their virtue was unsurpassed.
The Sānwáng prioritized teaching before punishment,
hence their achievements were unparalleled.
The Wǔbà prioritized affairs before military force,
hence their military power was unmatched.
In the present age,
clever schemes are pursued simultaneously,
deceptive tactics are employed in turn,
attacks and warfare are ceaseless,
and the number of ruined states and disgraced rulers increases,
for what is pursued is trivial.
Xiàhòu Xiāng
fought with Yǒuhù at Gānzé but did not win.
The Liùqīng requested to renew the battle,
and Xiàhòu Xiāng said:
"No.
Our territory is not small,
our people are not few,
yet we fought and did not win.
This means my virtue is meager and my teaching is not good."
Thereupon, he did not use layered mats for dwelling,
did not eat dishes of two flavors,
the *qín* and *sè* were not played,
the bells and drums were not repaired,
his sons and daughters were not adorned,
he treated his relatives kindly and respected his elders,
honored the worthy and employed the capable.
After a full year, the Yǒuhù clan submitted.
Therefore, those who wish to conquer others must first conquer themselves;
those who wish to judge others must first judge themselves;
those who wish to know others must first know themselves.
The *Shī* says: "Hold the reins like a woven cord."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Whoever understands this saying can govern All-under-Heaven."
Zǐgòng said:
"Why is it so impatient?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It does not refer to impatience.
It refers to acting here,
and the pattern becoming complete there.
Sages weave and cultivate themselves,
and the pattern is completed throughout All-under-Heaven."
Therefore, Zǐhuázǐ said:
"When hills and mounds are formed, those who dwell in holes are secure;
when great waters and deep abysses are formed, fish and turtles are secure;
when pine and cypress trees are formed, people on the road already find shade."
Kǒngzǐ met with Lǔ Āigōng.
Duke Āi said:
"Someone told me:
'Those who govern the state
do so from the hall, and that is all.'
I consider this circuitous talk."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is not circuitous talk.
I, Qiū, have heard: 'Those who gain it within themselves gain it in others;
those who lose it within themselves lose it in others.'
Those who govern All-under-Heaven without leaving their doors,
are surely those who know how to turn back to themselves!"
3.4 *Lúnrén*
Fourth, the ruler's Way is concise,
and the lord's observance is close.
The highest turns back to oneself;
the next seeks in others.
The further one searches,
the more distant one's influence;
the more one strives to seek,
the further one loses it.
What is meant by "turning back to oneself"?
It means to moderate the ears and eyes,
to curb appetites and desires,
to abandon wisdom and schemes,
to discard cleverness and artifice,
and to let one's mind roam in the realm of the infinite,
to serve the heart in the path of spontaneity.
If one does this, nothing will harm one's innate nature.
If nothing harms one's innate nature, then knowledge becomes subtle;
if knowledge is subtle, then it becomes spiritual.
To have spiritual knowledge is called attaining the One.
All the myriad forms
are formed after attaining the One.
Therefore, knowing the One,
one can respond to things and transform,
becoming vast, profound, and deep,
beyond measure.
Virtue shines beautifully,
comparable to the sun and moon,
and cannot be extinguished.
Heroic scholars honor him,
guests come from afar,
and cannot be obstructed.
One's spirit flows freely,
unbound,
and cannot be confined.
Therefore, knowing the One,
one returns to simplicity,
appetites and desires are easily satisfied,
taking sustenance is frugal,
and cannot be seized.
Detached from the world and self-content,
one's inner feelings are pure,
and cannot be measured.
Might cannot intimidate,
sternness cannot frighten,
and one cannot be subdued.
Therefore, knowing the One,
one's actions are always appropriate to the task,
adapting to the times,
inexhaustibly.
One's actions and policies are based on principles,
giving and taking follow reason,
and one cannot be deluded.
Words leave nothing out,
deeply ingrained,
and cannot be altered.
Slanderers are distressed and impoverished,
the worthy then prosper,
and this cannot be concealed.
Therefore, knowing the One,
one is like Heaven and Earth;
what task cannot be overcome,
what thing cannot be responded to?
It is likened to a charioteer who,
by turning back to oneself,
makes the chariot light and the horses swift,
reaching distant places and returning to eat without weariness.
In former ages, ruined rulers
regarded the fault as being in others,
thus daily killed and punished without ceasing,
until ruin came and they did not realize it.
Kings who flourished in the Three Dynasties
regarded the fault as being in themselves,
thus daily achieved merits and did not decline,
until they became kings.
What is meant by "seeking in others"?
People are of the same kind but their wisdom differs,
the worthy and unworthy are different,
all are skilled in words and eloquent in speech,
to defend themselves.
This is why unworthy rulers fall into disorder.
In general, when judging people:
When prominent, observe whom they treat with courtesy;
when noble, observe whom they promote;
when wealthy, observe whom they support;
when listened to, observe what they do;
when at rest, observe what they like;
when familiar, observe what they say;
when impoverished, observe what they refuse;
when lowly, observe what they will not do.
Delight them to test their resolve;
please them to test their biases;
anger them to test their integrity;
frighten them to test their steadfastness;
grieve them to test their humanity;
cause them hardship to test their ambition.
These eight observations and six tests
are how worthy rulers judge people.
To judge people, one must also use the six relations and four intimates.
What are the six relations?
Parents, brothers, wife, and children.
What are the four intimates?
Friends, old acquaintances, fellow villagers, and household retainers.
Internally, use the six relations and four intimates;
externally, use the eight observations and six tests.
Then people's true nature, deceit, greed, meanness, good, and evil will not be missed,
it is likened to dodging rain
and mud: there is no place where it is not revealed.
This is how the ancient sage kings understood people.
3.5 *Huándào*
Fifth: The Way of Heaven is circular;
the Way of Earth is square.
The sagely kings modeled themselves on this,
thereby establishing what is above and what is below.
How is it said that the Way of Heaven is circular?
The vital qi rises and descends,
circulating repeatedly,
never pausing.
Therefore, it is said that the Way of Heaven is circular.
How is it said that the Way of Earth is square?
The myriad things have distinct categories and forms,
each with its designated function,
unable to act for one another.
Therefore, it is said that the Way of Earth is square.
The ruler holds the circular,
the ministers occupy the square.
If the square and circular do not change,
then the state will prosper.
Day and night complete one cycle,
this is the circular Way.
The moon traverses the twenty-eight mansions,
Zhěn and Jiǎo are connected,
this is the circular Way.
The qi moves through the four seasons,
each rising and falling and meeting the others,
this is the circular Way.
When things move, they sprout;
sprouting, they are born;
born, they grow;
growing, they become large;
large, they mature;
maturing, they decline;
declining, they wither;
withering, they are stored away.
This is the circular Way.
Clouds and qi move westward,
endlessly, winter and summer;
spring water flows eastward,
unceasingly day and night;
above it does not dry up,
below it does not overflow;
the small becomes large,
the heavy becomes light;
this is the circular Way.
Huáng Dì said:
"The emperor has no fixed abode;
he who has an abode is truly without an abode."
This means not being bound or hindered,
this is the circular Way.
Man has nine orifices;
if one occupies one, then the other eight are empty.
If the eight remain empty for too long, the body will perish.
Therefore, listen exclusively,
and then stop listening;
listen and then see,
and then stop listening.
This means to speak of the one;
the one does not wish to stay fixed;
if it stays fixed, its movement fails.
This is the circular Way.
The one is most precious;
none know its source,
none know its beginning,
none know its origin,
none know its end,
yet the myriad things take it as their foundation.
The sagely kings modeled themselves on this,
to order their nature,
to fix their uprightness,
to issue decrees and commands.
Commands issue from the ruler's mouth;
officials receive and execute them,
unceasingly day and night,
spreading them thoroughly downwards,
penetrating the hearts of the people,
reaching the four directions,
then circling back
to the ruler's place.
This is the circular Way.
If commands are circular, then what is permissible and impermissible, good and not good, will have no impediments.
When there are no impediments,
the ruler's Way is unobstructed.
Therefore, commands
are what the ruler uses to establish his mandate,
and by which worthiness or unworthiness, safety or danger, are determined.
Man has a body with four limbs;
he can make them move
because he feels and necessarily knows.
If he feels but does not know,
then the body and four limbs cannot be made to move.
The same is true for ministers:
if commands are not felt,
then they cannot be made to move.
To have them and not use them is worse than not having them.
A ruler is one who uses what is not his own.
Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and Wǔ were all like this.
The former kings, when establishing high officials,
always made them square.
Being square means their divisions are fixed;
when divisions are fixed, subordinates do not hide things from each other.
Yáo and Shùn
were worthy rulers;
they all made worthy men their successors,
unwilling to give the throne to their sons and grandsons,
just as they established officials, always making them square.
Today's rulers,
all desire to keep their power for generations,
and give it to their sons and grandsons.
They cannot establish officials and make them square,
but confuse them with private desires.
Why is this?
Their long-term desires
are distant, while their knowledge is short-sighted.
Now, the five musical notes always respond
because their divisions are clear.
Gōng, Zhǐ, Shāng, Yǔ, Jiǎo,
each occupies its place,
and all sounds are well-tuned;
they cannot contradict each other.
This is why they are not rejected.
The worthy ruler's establishment of officials
is similar to this.
If all officials each occupy their posts and manage their affairs awaiting the ruler,
the ruler will have no unease.
If the state is governed with this,
the state will have no disadvantages;
if troubles are prepared against with this,
troubles will have no way to arrive.
4.1 《Mèng Xià Jì》
First: In the month of Mèng Xià:
The sun is in Bì;
at dusk, Yì is at the meridian;
at dawn, Wùnǚ is at the meridian.
Its days are bǐng and dīng.
Its Emperor is Yán Dì.
Its god is Zhù Róng.
Its creatures are feathered ones.
Its sound is zhǐ.
Its lǜ is Zhònglǚ.
Its number is seven.
Its nature is propriety.
Its affair is seeing.
Its flavor is bitter.
Its smell is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the stove.
Sacrifice the lung first.
Mántis and crickets chirp.
Earthworms emerge.
Wángpú grows.
Bitter vegetables flower.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Míngtáng,
rides in a vermilion chariot,
drives red liú horses,
carries a red banner,
wears red clothes,
adorns himself with red jade,
eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and rough.
In this month,
Lìxià is established.
Three days before Lìxià,
the Grand Historian announces to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such and such a day, Lìxià occurs,
and the flourishing virtue is of fire."
The Son of Heaven then purifies himself.
On the day of Lìxià,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Sāngōng, Jiǔqīng, and Dàfū to welcome summer in the southern suburb.
Upon returning, he bestows rewards,
grants fiefs and celebratory gifts,
and none are not joyful.
He then orders the Music Master to practice and combine rites and music.
He orders the Grand Marshal to praise the outstanding and eminent,
promote the worthy and good,
and advance the senior and experienced.
The granting of ranks and distribution of emoluments must be appropriate to their positions.
In this month,
growth continues and height increases;
there should be no destruction or collapse.
No earthworks should be started,
no large multitudes assembled,
no large trees felled.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins to wear fine linen.
He orders the Field Overseer
to go out into the fields and plains,
to commend farmers and encourage the people,
so that none miss the proper season.
He orders the Minister of Education
to inspect the counties and villages.
He orders farmers to work diligently,
and not to linger in the cities.
In this month,
animals are driven away without harming the five grains.
No great hunting expeditions are held.
Farmers then harvest wheat.
It is offered as tribute. The Son of Heaven then tastes the wheat with pork,
first offering it to the ancestral temple.
In this month, all kinds of herbs are gathered and stored.
Mí Cǎo dies.
The wheat harvest arrives.
Light punishments are cut,
minor offenses are decided,
and those lightly bound are released.
When the silkworm work is finished,
the empresses and consorts offer cocoons.
Then cocoon taxes are collected,
with mulberry trees used as a standard,
regardless of social status, age, or youth, all treated equally,
to provide sacrificial robes for the suburban and ancestral temples.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven drinks zhòu,
using ritual and music.
If this command is carried out,
sweet rain will arrive for thirty days.
If autumn commands are executed in early summer, then bitter rains will come frequently,
the five grains will not flourish,
and all four borders will enter a state of alarm.
If winter commands are executed, then grass and trees will wither early,
followed by great floods that destroy cities and walls.
If spring commands are executed, then insect plagues will cause destruction,
violent winds will come and strike,
and flourishing crops will not bear fruit.
4.2 《Quàn Xué》
Second, among the teachings of the former kings,
none is more glorious than filial piety,
none more prominent than loyalty.
Loyalty and filial piety
are what rulers and parents greatly desire.
Prominence and glory
are what sons and ministers greatly wish for.
However, if rulers and parents do not attain what they desire,
and sons and ministers do not attain what they wish for,
this arises from not understanding principles and righteousness.
Not understanding principles and righteousness
arises from not studying.
If a scholar has a knowledgeable and capable teacher,
I do not doubt that he will become a sage.
Where sages reside,
there the world is well-governed.
If they are on the right, the right is esteemed;
if they are on the left, the left is esteemed.
Therefore, among the ancient sagely kings, there were none who did not respect their teachers.
Respecting teachers means not considering their noble or humble status, nor their poverty or wealth.
If this is the case, then one's name will be prominent,
and one's virtue will be manifest.
Therefore, the teaching of a teacher
does not contend over importance, respect, humility, poverty, or wealth,
but contends over the Way.
If the person is acceptable,
then nothing he undertakes is impossible,
all he seeks will be obtained,
all he desires will be accomplished;
this arises from obtaining a sage.
A sage arises from diligent study.
It has never been the case
that one who does not study diligently can become a prominent scholar or a famous person.
Diligent study lies in respecting one's teacher;
when the teacher is respected, their words are trusted,
and the Way is discussed.
Therefore, those who go to teach are not transformed,
those who summon teachers are not transformed,
those who humble themselves are not listened to,
and those who disrespect teachers are not listened to.
If a teacher employs methods that do not transform or listen
and uses them to strongly instruct,
wishing for the Way to prevail and his person to be honored,
is this not far-fetched?
If a scholar places himself in a position where he is not transformed or listened to,
and proceeds independently,
wishing for his name to be prominent and his person to be secure,
this is like embracing something rotten and wishing for it to be fragrant,
or entering water and disliking being wet.
Generally, to persuade means to delight,
not to just talk.
Today's persuaders
often cannot delight,
but instead just talk.
Indeed, not being able to delight but merely talking
is like rescuing someone from drowning and weighing them down with a stone,
or saving the sick and making them drink poison,
causing the world to become even more chaotic;
unworthy rulers who are deeply deluded
arise from this.
Therefore, the duty of a teacher
lies in prevailing by reason
and acting righteously.
If reason prevails and righteousness is established, then one's position is honored;
kings, dukes, and great personages dare not be arrogant,
and even the Son of Heaven
will pay respects without shame.
Any meeting or combination
cannot be guaranteed.
To abandon principles and forsake righteousness in order to seek what cannot be guaranteed,
and yet wish for people to respect oneself,
is this not difficult?
Therefore, a teacher must prevail by reason and act righteously before being respected.
Zēng Zǐ said:
“A gentleman walking on the road,
one can tell if he has a father,
one can tell if he has a teacher.
As for one who has neither father nor teacher,
what more can I say about him!”
This means serving a teacher is like serving a father.
Zēng Diǎn sent Zēng Shēn,
who was overdue and had not arrived.
Everyone saw Zēng Diǎn and said:
“Are you not perhaps worried?”
Zēng Diǎn said:
“Although he may be worried,
since I am alive,
how would he dare to be worried?”
Kǒng Zǐ was in fear in Kuāng,
Yán Yuān arrived late. Kǒng Zǐ said:
“I thought you had died.”
Yán Yuān said:
“Since you are here,
how would Huí dare to die?”
Yán Huí's relationship with Kǒng Zǐ
was like Zēng Shēn's service to his father.
How excellent
were the worthy men of old!
Their respect for teachers was like this,
therefore teachers gave their utmost wisdom and exhausted the Way to teach.
4.3 《Zūn Shī》
Third, Shén Nóng took Xī Zhū as his teacher,
Huáng Dì took Dà Náo as his teacher,
Dì Zhuān Xù took Bó Yí Fù as his teacher,
Dì Kù took Bó Zhāo as his teacher,
Dì Yáo took Zǐ Zhōu Zhī Fù as his teacher,
Dì Shùn took Xǔ Yóu as his teacher,
Yǔ took Dà Chéng Zhì as his teacher,
Tāng took Xiǎo Chén as his teacher,
Wén Wáng and Wǔ Wáng took Lǚ Wàng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn as their teachers,
Qí Huán Gōng took Guǎn Yí Wú as his teacher,
Jìn Wén Gōng took Jiù Fàn and Suí Huì as his teachers,
Qín Mù Gōng took Bǎi Lǐ Xī and Gōng Sūn Zhī as his teachers,
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng took Sūn Shú Áo and Shěn Yǐn Shì as his teachers,
Wú Wáng Hé Lǘ took Wǔ Zǐ Xū and Wén Zhī Yí as his teachers,
Yuè Wáng Gōu Jiàn took Fàn Lǐ and Dà Fū Zhǒng as his teachers.
These ten sages and six worthies
all respected their teachers.
Today, one's esteemed position does not reach that of an emperor,
and one's wisdom does not reach that of a sage,
yet one wishes to be without a respected teacher—
how can this be achieved?
This is why the Five Emperors' lineage ceased,
and why the Three Dynasties perished.
Moreover, when Heaven gives birth to people,
it enables their ears to hear;
but without learning, their hearing is no better than deafness.
It enables their eyes to see;
but without learning, their sight is no better than blindness.
It enables their mouths to speak;
but without learning, their speech is no better than madness.
It enables their minds to know;
but without learning, their knowledge is no better than delusion.
Therefore, all learning
does not necessarily add to one's nature,
but develops one's innate nature.
To be able to preserve what Heaven has given birth to and not corrupt it
is called good learning.
Zǐ Zhāng,
a commoner from Lǔ;
Yán Zhuō Jù,
a great bandit from Liáng Fù;
both studied under Kǒng Zǐ.
Duàn Gān Mù,
a great merchant from Jìn;
studied under Zǐ Xià.
Gāo Hé and Xiàn Zǐ Shí,
violent men from Qí
who were criticized by their villages;
studied under Zǐ Mò Zǐ.
Suǒ Lú Cān,
a notorious trickster from the East;
studied under Qín Huá Lí.
These six people
were destined for punishment, execution, death, and disgrace.
Now, not only have they escaped punishment, execution, death, and disgrace,
but they have also become renowned scholars and distinguished individuals throughout the land,
living out their full lifespans.
Kings, dukes, and great personages follow and treat them with courtesy.
This they gained through learning.
In all learning,
one must strive to advance in one's studies,
with a mind free from distractions.
Be quick in reciting and chanting,
attentive in listening,
observant of joyful expressions,
inquiring about the meaning of texts,
following what pleases the ears and eyes,
not opposing one's aspirations,
retiring to reflect,
seeking what is intended,
debating and explaining promptly
to discuss the Way,
not arguing carelessly,
but always adhering to the principles.
Do not boast when you succeed,
nor be ashamed when you fail;
always revert to the fundamentals.
When alive, attend to nurturing carefully.
The way of careful nurturing
values nurturing the mind above all.
When dead, offer sacrifices respectfully.
The art of respectful sacrifice
prioritizes timeliness.
This is how a teacher is honored.
Cultivate gardens and orchards,
diligently irrigate and soak,
and make it a priority to plant trees.
Weave straw sandals,
tie hunting nets,
and bundle cattails and reeds.
Go to the fields and plains,
laboriously cultivate the land,
and attend to the five grains.
Go to the mountains and forests,
enter rivers and marshes,
catch fish and turtles,
and seek birds and beasts.
This is how a teacher is honored.
Attend to carriages and horses,
be careful in driving.
Prepare clothing,
ensuring it is light and warm.
Approach food and drink,
ensuring it is pure and clean.
Be skilled in seasoning,
ensuring it is sweet and rich.
Always be reverent.
Maintain a gentle demeanor,
and speak thoughtfully.
Be quick in moving,
and always be solemn.
This is how a teacher is honored.
When a Jūnzǐ learns,
when expounding on righteousness, he must invoke his teacher to discuss the Way;
when listening and following, he must exert his utmost to bring glory.
If one listens and follows without exerting one's utmost,
this is called "turning one's back."
If one expounds on righteousness without invoking one's teacher,
this is called "rebellion."
Those who turn their back and rebel
will not be admitted to the court by a worthy ruler,
nor will a Jūnzǐ associate with them as friends.
Therefore, teaching
is the greatest of righteousness;
learning
is the pinnacle of knowledge.
Of the greatest righteousness,
none is greater than benefiting others;
of benefiting others, none is greater than teaching.
Of the pinnacle of knowledge,
none is greater than perfecting oneself;
of perfecting oneself, none is greater than learning.
When one has perfected oneself, as a son one will be filial without being told;
as a minister one will be loyal without being commanded;
as a ruler one will be just without being compelled;
and one will possess great power to be the standard for the world.
Therefore, Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
“How will later generations refer to you, Master?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“How am I worthy of being referred to?
If I must be,
then perhaps it is for loving learning without satiety,
and loving teaching without weariness.
Is it not this?”
When the Son of Heaven enters the Grand School
to sacrifice to the Former Sages,
he defers to age; those who have served as teachers are not treated as subjects.
This shows respect for learning and honor for teachers.
4.4 On False Disciples
Fourthly, the teaching of an accomplished teacher
enables disciples to find peace, joy, rest, recreation, reverence, and solemnity.
If these six qualities are gained through learning,
then the paths of evil and perversity will be blocked,
and the methods of reason and righteousness will prevail.
If these six qualities are not gained through learning,
then a ruler cannot command his minister,
a father cannot command his son,
and a teacher cannot command his disciple.
It is human nature
not to find joy in what brings no peace,
and not to succeed in what brings no joy.
If one does something and finds joy in it,
why wait for the worthy?
Even the unworthy will be encouraged.
If one does something and finds suffering in it,
why wait for the unworthy?
Even the worthy cannot endure it long.
Reflecting on human nature
thus reveals the way to encourage learning.
Zǐhuá Zǐ said:
“Those who rule find joy in that by which they rule,
and those who perish also find joy in that by which they perish.
Thus, cooking an animal is not enough to exhaust
its essence; savoring its dried meat is close.”
If so, then rulers find joy in reason and righteousness,
and those who perish also find joy in tyranny and arrogance.
Their joys differ,
and thus their fortunes and misfortunes also differ.
Those who cannot teach:
their aspirations and disposition are not harmonious,
their choices and rejections frequently change,
and they fundamentally lack constancy,
like the shifting overcast and clear skies, or capricious joy and anger without fixed abode.
Their words and discussions change daily,
acting according to their own whims.
They attribute faults to themselves
but are unwilling to acknowledge their own wrongs,
stubbornly adhering to their errors and acting self-importantly,
and cannot be corrected or changed.
When they see those in power, those with influence and authority, or those with wealth and abundance,
they do not consider their talent,
nor examine their conduct,
but eagerly teach them,
and flatter and fawn upon them,
as if afraid of being too late.
If a disciple's living quarters are neat and clean,
his physical appearance outstanding,
his knowledge and insight broad and clear,
his pursuit of learning keen and swift,
and his main studies nearly complete,
then they will suppress him,
hinder him and keep him in suspense,
and envy and dislike him.
When a disciple leaves, he hopes to finish;
when he stays, he is uneasy;
when he returns home, he is ashamed before his parents and brothers;
when he goes out, he is embarrassed before his friends and fellow villagers.
This is the sorrow of a learner,
and this is why teachers and disciples have different hearts.
It is human nature
to dislike those who differ from oneself.
This is how teachers and disciples create resentment and blame among themselves.
It is human nature
not to be intimate with those one resents,
and not to praise those one dislikes.
The failure of learning and studies,
and the decline of the Way and its methods,
arise from this.
Those who teach well are not like this.
They regard disciples as themselves.
By reflecting on oneself to teach,
one grasps the true nature of teaching.
What one imposes on others
must be what one can practice oneself.
If this is the case, then teacher and disciple are one body.
It is human nature
to love those who are like oneself,
to praise those who are like oneself,
and to help those who are like oneself.
The clarity and prominence of learning and studies,
and the great flourishing of the Way and its methods,
arise from this.
Those who cannot learn:
they find it difficult to follow a teacher yet desire the achievement of learning;
they follow a teacher superficially yet desire profound learning.
One should not scold or insult even plants, trees, chickens, dogs, cattle, or horses.
If one scolds and insults them,
they will in turn scold and insult people.
How much more so when dealing with an accomplished teacher and the words of the Way and its methods?
Thus, those who cannot learn:
when they meet a teacher, they are not suitable;
when they apply their minds, they are not focused;
when they like something, it is not deep;
when they take up a task, they are not quick;
when they debate, they are not thorough;
when they teach others, they are not precise;
they resent their teacher,
are concerned with customs,
and restrain their spirit by the world.
They are proud of their influence and fond of finding fault,
thus they are immersed in cleverness,
confused by small gains,
and misled by desires.
When asked about matters, their answers contradict each other;
when presented with a clear explanation, they have a different intention;
when given a simple statement, they have a contrary view.
When separated, they cannot combine;
when combined, they cannot separate;
when an event occurs, they cannot accept it.
These are the troubles of those who cannot learn.
4.5 《Yòng Zhòng》
Fifthly:
A good learner is like King Qí's
eating of chicken; he must eat several thousand chicken feet before he is satisfied.
Even if not satisfied,
it is as if he has chicken feet.
Indeed, there is nothing that does not have its strengths,
and nothing that does not have its weaknesses.
Humans are also like this.
Therefore, a good learner
borrows others' strengths to compensate for their own weaknesses.
Thus, those who borrow from others can command the world.
