Do not be ashamed of being incapable;
do not dislike being ignorant.
To be ashamed of being incapable,
or to dislike being ignorant,
is a defect;
not to be ashamed of being incapable,
and not to dislike being ignorant,
is esteemed.
Even Jié
and Zhòu still had aspects that were formidable and commendable,
how much more so for the virtuous?
Therefore, scholars say:
"Debate and discussion must be engaged in."
If a debate and discussion can truly be engaged in,
this is teaching.
It is a great teaching.
If a debate and discussion cannot be engaged in,
it is like going out in plain clothes
and returning in brocade.
A Róng person is born among the Róng,
grows up among the Róng, and speaks the Róng language,
without knowing how they acquired it.
A Chǔ person is born among the Chǔ,
grows up among the Chǔ, and speaks the Chǔ language,
without knowing how they acquired it.
Now, if a Chǔ person were to grow up among the Róng,
and a Róng person among the Chǔ,
then the Chǔ person would speak the Róng language,
and the Róng person would speak the Chǔ language.
From this perspective,
I do not know whether the ruler of a fallen state cannot be considered a worthy ruler;
it is merely that their upbringing was not conducive.
Therefore, one's upbringing must be carefully examined.
There is no fox that is purely white in the world,
yet there are purely white fur coats,
which are made by taking many white furs.
Indeed, drawing from the multitude –
this is how the Sān Huáng
and Wǔ Dì greatly established their merits and reputations.
All rulers establish themselves
by relying on the multitude.
To abandon the multitude after one's position is established
is to gain the trivial and lose the fundamental.
One who gains the trivial and loses the fundamental
is never heard to reside in peace.
Thus, by using the courage of the multitude, one need not fear Mèng Bèn;
by using the strength of the multitude, one need not fear Wū Huò;
by using the sight of the multitude, one need not fear Lí Lóu;
by using the wisdom of the multitude, one need not fear Yáo
and Shùn.
Indeed, relying on the multitude
is the great treasure of a ruler.
Tián Pián said to King Qí:
"Mèng Bèn is likely troubled by strategies,
but the borders are not troubled;
the kings of Chǔ and Wèi
do not use persuasive words,
yet their territories are already well-prepared,
and their soldiers are already well-trained;
this is because they rely on the multitude."
5.1 《Zhòng Xià Jì》
First: In the month of midsummer:
the sun is in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well),
Kàng (Neck) culminates at dusk,
Wēi (Rooftop) culminates at dawn.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yán Dì.
Its spirit is Zhùróng.
Its creatures are feathered ones.
Its musical note is Zhǐ.
The pitch pipe is Ruíbīn.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter.
Its odor is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the Stove.
Offer first the lungs.
Xiǎo Shǔ (Minor Heat) arrives.
Mantises are born.
Shrikes begin to sing.
Mockingbirds fall silent.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Míngtáng Grand Temple,
rides a vermilion carriage,
harnessed with red steeds,
carrying a red banner,
wearing vermilion clothes,
adorned with red jade,
eating soybeans and chicken.
Its vessels are tall and coarse.
He nourishes the strong and cunning.
In this month,
he commands the music masters
to repair the táodrums and bí-drums,
tune the qín, sè, guǎn, and xiāo,
grasp the gān, qī, gē, and feathers,
tune the yú, shēng, xūn, and chí,
and arrange the zhōng, qìng, zhù, and yǔ.
He commands the officials
to pray and offer sacrifices for the people to the mountains, rivers, and all plains,
to perform the great rain dance to the sovereign,
using grand music.
Then he commands all counties
to perform rain-praying sacrifices to all feudal lords, ministers, and officials who benefit the people,
to pray for grain harvest.
The farmers then bring in millet.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven tastes the millet with the first chicks,
offers early cherries,
first presenting them in the ancestral temple.
He orders the people not to cut indigo for dyeing,
not to burn charcoal,
and not to expose cloth to the sun.
Gates and village entrances are not to be closed,
customs barriers and markets are not to search.
He releases serious prisoners,
and increases their food.
He separates wandering mares from their herds,
then ties up spirited colts,
and regulates the horses.
In this month,
the summer solstice occurs.
Yīn and Yáng contend,
life and death separate.
The gentleman fasts and purifies himself,
he must conceal himself when residing,
desiring quietude and no agitation,
stopping sounds and colors,
allowing none to enter,
reducing rich flavors,
not seeking perfect harmony,
retreating from desires,
settling his mind and vital energy.
All officials are quiet,
affairs have no shortcuts,
to settle what is achieved in the serene Yīn.
Deer shed their antlers.
Cicadas begin to sing.
Bànxià (pinellia) grows,
Mùjǐn (hibiscus) blooms.
In this month,
one should not use fire in the south.
One can reside in high, bright places,
one can gaze afar,
one can ascend mountains,
one can dwell in pavilions.
If in midsummer one implements the commands of winter,
then hail and sleet will damage the crops,
roads will be impassable,
and fierce soldiers will arrive.
If one implements the commands of spring,
then the five grains will ripen late,
many pests will arise in due season,
and that state will suffer famine.
If one implements the commands of autumn,
then plants and trees will shed their leaves,
fruits will ripen early,
and the people will suffer from plague.
5.2 The Great Music
Second, the origin of music is ancient;
it arises from measure and quantity,
and is rooted in Tài yī.
Tài yī brings forth the Two Modes (liǎng yí),
and the Two Modes bring forth Yīn and Yáng.
Yīn and Yáng transform,
one ascending, one descending,
combining to form patterns.
In a state of渾渾沌沌 (húnhún dùndùn, chaos),
when separated, they recombine;
when combined, they separate again;
this is called the constant of Heaven.
Heaven and Earth are like a chariot wheel,
when they reach their end, they begin again;
when they reach their extreme, they revert;
all things fit perfectly.
The sun, moon, and stars,
some fast, some slow,
the sun and moon not alike,
complete their courses.
The four seasons arise in succession,
some hot, some cold,
some short, some long.
Some soft, some hard.
All things that come into being,
are created by Tài yī,
and transformed by Yīn and Yáng.
Sprouts begin to stir,
coagulating to take shape.
Wherever there is a physical form,
there is sound.
Sound emerges from harmony,
and harmony emerges from appropriateness.
From harmony and appropriateness, the Former Kings established music,
and it was born from this.
When the world is at peace,
and all things are tranquil,
all transforming under their ruler,
then music can be perfected.
To perfect music, there are requirements;
one must regulate desires and appetites.
If desires and appetites are not avoided,
music can be pursued.
To pursue music, there is an art;
it must arise from fairness.
Fairness arises from impartiality,
and impartiality arises from the Dào.
Therefore, only those who have attained the Dào,
can truly discuss music!
A ruined state and slaughtered people,
are not without music,
but their music is not joyful.
Drowning people are not without laughter,
criminals are not without song,
madmen are not without dance,
the music of a chaotic age,
is similar to this.
When ruler and ministers lose their proper places,
father and son lose their proper positions,
husband and wife lose their proper harmony,
and the people groan,
what they consider music,
how can it be so?
In general, music
is the harmony of Heaven and Earth,
the regulation of Yīn and Yáng.
It is Heaven that first creates humans;
humans have no agency in this.
Heaven causes humans to have desires;
humans cannot but seek them.
Heaven causes humans to have dislikes;
humans cannot but avoid them.
Desires and dislikes are received from Heaven;
humans have no part in them,
they cannot be changed,
they cannot be altered.
Among the scholars of this age,
there are those who oppose music;
from where does this arise?
Great music
is that which delights and pleases rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, elders and youngers.
Delight arises from fairness,
and fairness arises from the Dào.
As for the Dào,
when looked at, it is not seen;
when listened to, it is not heard;
it cannot be described.
One who knows the unseen sight,
the unheard sound, the formless form,
is close to knowing it.
As for the Dào,
it is the utmost essence,
it cannot be given a form,
it cannot be given a name;
if forced to give it a name, it is called Tài yī.
Therefore, the One commands,
and the Two obey.
The Former Sages chose the Two to unify the One,
thereby knowing the nature of all things.
Therefore, one who can govern by the One
brings joy to rulers and ministers,
harmonizes near and far,
pleases the common people,
and unites clans and relatives.
One who can cultivate their body by the One
is free from calamity,
completes their lifespan,
and preserves their natural state.
One who can govern their state by the One
eliminates wickedness,
attracts worthy individuals,
and achieves great transformation.
One who can govern the world by the One
ensures appropriate cold and heat,
and timely winds and rains,
and becomes a sage.
Therefore, to know the One is to be clear-sighted;
to be clear-sighted about the Two is to be deluded.
5.3 Extravagant Music
Third, no one fails to live by their life,
yet they do not know what gives them life.
No one fails to know by their knowledge,
yet they do not know what enables their knowing.
To know what enables one's knowing is called knowing the Dào;
not to know what enables one's knowing is called discarding a treasure.
One who discards a treasure will surely suffer its calamity.
The rulers of the world
often regard pearls, jade, spears, and swords as treasures;
the more treasures they have, the more the people resent them,
the more the state becomes endangered,
and the more perilous and burdened their own lives become;
thus, they miss the true nature of treasure.
The music of a chaotic age is similar to this.
The sounds of drums and leather are like thunder,
the sounds of metal and stone are like lightning,
the sounds of strings, flutes, singing, and dancing are like clamor.
To use these to startle the mind and spirit,
to move the ears and eyes,
and to stir up life
may be acceptable,
but to consider this music is not to find joy.
Therefore, the more extravagant the music,
the more the people are oppressed,
the more chaotic the state,
and the more humble the ruler;
thus, they also miss the true nature of music.
What the ancient sage kings valued in music
was its true joy.
Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu created extravagant music,
the sounds of large drums, bells, qìng, pipes, and flutes,
taking enormous size as beauty,
and multitude as spectacle,
bizarre, extraordinary, and rare,
things the ear had never heard,
the eye had never seen,
striving to outdo each other,
without regard for measure.
When the state of Sòng declined,
they made a thousand bells.
When the state of Qí declined,
they made the Dà lǚ.
When the state of Chǔ declined,
they made shamanistic music.
Extravagant it was,
but from the perspective of one who possesses the Dào,
it missed the true nature of music.
When the true nature of music is missed,
its music is not joyful.
When music is not joyful,
its people will surely complain,
and their lives will surely be harmed.
The relationship between their lives and such music
is like ice to scorching sun or charcoal;
instead, they inflict harm upon themselves.
This arises from not knowing the true nature of music,
and instead making extravagance one's pursuit.
Music possesses emotions,
comparable to the skin and physical body having sensibilities.
If there are sensibilities, there must be appropriate sustenance for them.
Cold, warmth, toil, ease, hunger, and satiety—
these six are not fitting.
All sustenance
involves discerning what is unfitting and making it fitting.
If one can maintain a state of fittingness for a long time,
then growth will occur.
Growth,
in its essence, is when the body is still,
yet sometimes one becomes aware,
or one is made to act.
If one continues without turning back,
controlled by desires,
then an endless control by desires will inevitably lead to losing one's innate nature.
Moreover, if desires are endless,
then there will inevitably arise minds of greed, vulgarity, rebellion, and chaos,
and deeds of debauchery, licentiousness, treachery, and deceit.
Thus, the strong oppressing the weak,
the many brutalizing the few,
the brave dominating the timid,
the robust despising the young—
these arise from this.
5.4 *Shìyīn*
Fourthly, the ears naturally desire sounds,
but if the heart is not pleased,
the five tones are before them, yet they will not listen.
The eyes naturally desire colors,
but if the heart is not pleased,
the five colors are before them, yet they will not look.
The nose naturally desires fragrant scents,
but if the heart is not pleased,
fragrant scents are before it, yet it will not smell.
The mouth naturally desires flavors,
but if the heart is not pleased,
the five flavors are before it, yet it will not eat.
Those that desire are
the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth;
that which is pleased or displeased
is the heart.
The heart must be harmonious and peaceful before it is pleased;
the heart must be pleased before the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth have reason to desire.
Therefore, the essential task of music lies in harmonizing the heart,
and harmonizing the heart lies in acting appropriately.
Music has its appropriateness,
and the heart also has its appropriateness.
It is human nature
to desire longevity and dislike premature death,
to desire peace and dislike danger,
to desire honor and dislike disgrace,
to desire ease and dislike toil.
If these four desires are attained,
and the four dislikes are removed,
then the heart will be at ease.
The attainment of these four desires
lies in triumphing over principle (*lǐ*).
If one triumphs over principle to govern the body, life will be preserved entirely;
if life is preserved entirely, longevity will be attained.
If one triumphs over principle to govern the state, laws will be established;
if laws are established, the world will submit.
Therefore, the essential task of comforting the heart lies in triumphing over principle.
Music also has its appropriateness.
If it is too grand, the will is scattered;
listening to what is grand with a scattered will, the ears cannot contain it;
if they cannot contain it, it becomes blocked;
if it is blocked, it causes vibration.
If it is too small, the will is petty;
listening to what is small with a petty will, the ears are not satisfied;
if they are not satisfied, they do not encompass;
if they do not encompass, it is narrow.
If it is too clear, the will is unstable;
listening to what is clear with an unstable will, the ears are extremely sensitive;
if extremely sensitive, they cannot discern;
if they cannot discern, they are exhausted.
If it is too turbid, the will is base;
listening to what is turbid with a base will, the ears do not gather;
if they do not gather, they do not coalesce;
if they do not coalesce, it becomes enraged.
Therefore, being too grand, too small, too clear, or too turbid are all inappropriate.
What is appropriateness?
It is the moderation (*zhōng*) and appropriateness (*shì*) of sound.
What is moderation?
It means not exceeding *jūn* in magnitude,
not exceeding *shí* in weight—
the moderation of magnitude and weight.
The *gōng* note of Huángzhōng
is the root of sound,
the moderation of clarity and turbidity.
Moderation is appropriateness;
listening to the appropriate with appropriateness results in harmony.
Music has no excess;
what is peaceful and harmonious is this.
Therefore, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
because its governance is equitable;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
because its governance is perverse;
the music of a doomed state is sorrowful and lamenting,
because its governance is perilous.
All music is connected to governance,
and it transforms customs;
when customs are established, music transforms them.
Therefore, in an age with the Dào,
one can know its customs by observing its music, and know its governance by observing its customs,
and know its ruler by observing its governance.
Thus, the Former Kings necessarily relied on music to convey their teachings.
The *sè* of Qīngmiào,
with red strings and sparse frets,
one sings and three sigh,
has something beyond mere sound.
The ritual of the Great Sacrifice,
where the dark goblet is placed above and raw fish on the sacrificial stand,
and the great soup is unseasoned,
has something beyond mere taste.
Therefore, the Former Kings' institution of rites and music
was not merely to delight the ears and eyes or satisfy the desires of the mouth and stomach,
but rather to teach the people to equalize their likes and dislikes,
and to practice principle (*lǐ*) and righteousness (*yì*).
5.5 *Gǔyuè*
Fifthly, the origins of music are ancient,
and it must not be abolished.
There are restraints and excesses,
there is rectitude and licentiousness.
The worthy thrive by it,
the unworthy perish by it.
In ancient times, when Zhūxiāngshì ruled the world,
there was much wind and the *yáng* energy accumulated,
all things dispersed and disintegrated,
fruits did not ripen.
Therefore, Shìdá created the five-string *sè*
to invite *yīn* energy,
and thereby stabilize all living beings.
In ancient times, the music of Gětiānshì involved
three people holding ox tails, stamping their feet and singing eight verses:
The first was called *Zàimín*,
the second *Xuánshēn*,
the third *Suìcǎomù*,
the fourth *Fènwǔgǔ*,
the fifth *Jìngtiāncháng*,
the sixth *Dádìgōng*,
the seventh *Yīdìdé*,
the eighth *Zǒngwànwùzhījí*.
In the early days of Táotángshì,
the *yīn* energy was too stagnant, hidden, and deeply accumulated,
the *yáng* channel was blocked,
not following its proper order.
The people's vital energy was suppressed and obstructed,
their muscles and bones were stiff and unextended.
Therefore, dances were created to circulate and guide it.
In ancient times, Huángdì ordered Línglún to create the pitch standards (*lǜ*).
Línglún went west from Dàxià,
then to the northern side of Ruǎnyú,
took bamboo from the valley of Xièxī,
selected those with naturally hollow cavities and uniform thickness,
cut them between two nodes to a length of three *cùn* and nine *fēn*, and blew them,
making the *gōng* note of Huángzhōng,
and called the sound "Shèshǎo".
Next, he made twelve tubes.
He went to the base of Ruǎnyú
and listened to the calls of the male and female phoenixes,
to differentiate the twelve pitch-pipes (*lǜ*).
The male calls were six,
the female calls were also six,
which corresponded perfectly with the *gōng* note of Huángzhōng.
The *gōng* note of Huángzhōng
could generate all of them,
hence it is called the *gōng* note of Huángzhōng,
the root of the *lǜ* and *lǚ* pitch-pipes.
Huángdì also commanded Línglún and Róngjiāng to cast twelve bells
to harmonize the five tones,
and to perform *Yīngsháo*.
In the month of mid-spring,
on the *Yǐmǎo* day,
when the sun was in the Kui constellation,
it was first performed,
and named *Xiánchí*.
Dì Zhuānxù was born from Ruòshuǐ,
resided in Kōngsāng,
and then ascended to become emperor.
It was by the harmony of Heaven
that righteous winds circulated.
His music was like *xīxī*, *qīqī*, *qiāngqiāng*.
Di Zhuānxù (Emperor Zhuānxù) loved its sound,
so he ordered Fēilóng (Flying Dragon) to compose music imitating the sounds of the eight winds,
naming it 《Chéngyún》 (Adopting the Clouds),
to sacrifice to Shàngdì (the Lord on High).
He then ordered Shàn (eel) to lead the music.
Shàn lay down,
beating its belly with its tail,
and its sound was "yīng yīng" (bright and clear).
Di Kù (Emperor Kù) ordered Xián Hēi (Harmonious Black) to make sounds and sing
《Jiǔzhāo》 (Nine Summons), 《Liùliè》 (Six Rows), and 《Liùyīng》 (Six Glories).
Yǒu Chuí (Chuí) made drums, bells, chimes, flutes, ocarinas, and hand-drums.
Di Kù then ordered people to clap, some to beat drums,
strike bells and chimes,
and blow flutes and ocarinas.
He then ordered Fèngniǎo (Phoenixes) and Tiāndí (Celestial Pheasants) to dance to it.
Di Kù was greatly pleased,
and thus brought peace to his imperial virtue.
When Di Yáo (Emperor Yáo) ascended the throne,
he ordered Zhì (Substance) to compose music.
Zhì then imitated the sounds of mountains, forests, streams, and valleys to compose songs.
He covered a clay jar with elk hide and beat it,
and clapped and struck stones,
to imitate the sound of Shàngdì's (the Lord on High's) jade chimes,
thus attracting all beasts to dance.
Gǔsǒu (Old Blind Man) then tuned a five-stringed sè (zither),
and made it into a fifteen-stringed sè.
It was named Dàzhāng (Great Manifestation),
to sacrifice to Shàngdì (the Lord on High).
When Shùn (Shùn) ascended the throne,
he ordered Yán (Prolong) to tune the sè made by Gǔsǒu,
adding eight strings to it,
making it a twenty-three-stringed sè.
Di Shùn (Emperor Shùn) then ordered Zhì to revise 《Jiǔzhāo》 (Nine Summons), 《Liùliè》 (Six Rows), and 《Liùyīng》 (Six Glories),
to make the imperial virtue manifest.
When Yǔ (Yǔ) ascended the throne,
he toiled diligently for the world,
day and night without slackening,
opening up great rivers,
clearing blockages,
carving out Lóngmén (Dragon Gate),
and bringing down and connecting Liáoshuǐ (Liáo Water) to guide the Hé (Yellow River),
dredging the Sānjiāng (Three Rivers) and Wǔhú (Five Lakes),
channeling them into the Dōnghǎi (East Sea),
to benefit the common people.
Thereupon, he ordered Gāotáo (Gāotáo) to compose 《Xiàyuè》 (Summer Music) in nine movements,
to display his achievements.
When Yīn Tāng (Tāng of Yīn) ascended the throne,
Xià (Xià Dynasty) had become lawless,
tyrannizing the myriad people,
encroaching upon and exploiting the feudal lords,
and not adhering to norms and standards.
The world suffered from this.
Tāng thereupon led six states to punish Jié's (Jié's) crimes,
achieving great success and fame,
and the common people enjoyed peace.
Tāng then ordered Yī Yǐn (Yī Yǐn) to compose 《Dàhù》 (Great Protector),
singing 《Chénlù》 (Morning Dew),
and revising 《Jiǔzhāo》 (Nine Summons) and 《Liùliè》 (Six Rows),
to show his goodness.
When Zhōu Wénwáng (King Wén of Zhōu) resided in Qí (Qí),
the feudal lords deserted Yīn's (Yīn's) three licentiousnesses and supported Wénwáng (King Wén).
Sǎn Yíshēng (Sǎn Yíshēng) said:
"Yīn can be attacked."
Wénwáng (King Wén) did not agree.
Zhōugōng Dàn (Duke Dàn of Zhōu) then composed a poem saying:
"Wénwáng (King Wén) is above,
shining brightly in Heaven;
though Zhōu (Zhōu) is an old state,
its mandate is new,"
to regulate Wénwáng's (King Wén's) virtue.
When Wǔwáng (King Wǔ) ascended the throne,
he led six armies to attack Yīn (Yīn).
Before the six armies arrived,
he defeated it with elite troops at Mùyě (Mùyě).
Upon returning,
he presented the captives and severed heads at the Jīng Tàishì (Grand Temple of the Capital),
and ordered Zhōugōng (Duke of Zhōu) to compose 《Dàwǔ》 (Grand Martial) for him.
When Chéngwáng (King Chéng) ascended the throne,
the Yīn (Yīn) people rebelled.
The King ordered Zhōugōng (Duke of Zhōu) to go and punish them.
The Shang (Shang) people used elephants
to commit atrocities against the Dōngyí (Eastern Yi).
Zhōugōng (Duke of Zhōu) then pursued them with his army,
as far as Jiāngnán (south of the Yangtze),
and then composed 《Sānxìang》 (Three Images),
to commend their virtue.
Therefore, the origins of music are ancient,
not merely created by one generation.
6.1 《Jìxiàjì》 (Records of Midsummer)
One account says: In the month of Jìxià (Midsummer):
The sun is in Liǔ (Willow),
the heart constellation is in the west at dusk,
and the Kui constellation is in the east at dawn.
Its days are Bǐng (third heavenly stem) and Dīng (fourth heavenly stem).
Its Emperor is Yándì (Flame Emperor).
Its God is Zhùróng (Zhùróng).
Its creatures are feathered animals.
Its musical note is Zhǐ (G).
The pitch pipe corresponds to Línzhōng (forest bell).
Its number is seven.
Its taste is bitter.
Its smell is burnt.
Its sacrifice is to the Stove God.
Sacrifice first the lungs.
Cool winds begin to arrive.
Crickets reside in houses.
Eagles begin to learn to hunt.
Rotten grass transforms into fireflies and gnats.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Míngtáng (Bright Hall),
rides a vermilion carriage,
drives a red piebald horse,
carries a red banner,
wears vermilion clothes,
adorns red jade,
and eats soybeans and chicken.
Its vessels are tall and coarse.
In this month,
the fishing master is ordered to hunt jiāo (water dragons)
and take tuó (alligators), to raise guī (turtles) and take yuán (soft-shelled turtles).
The foresters are ordered to enter the mountains to gather timber and reeds.
In this month,
the four supervisory grandees are ordered to collect fodder from all counties, to feed sacrificial animals.
The people are ordered to exert all their strength,
to supply Huángtiān Shàngdì (August Heaven and the Lord on High),
the spirits of famous mountains and great rivers, and the gods of the four directions, to worship the spirits of ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
to pray for blessings for the people.
In this month,
the female officials are ordered to dye fabrics,
and to embroider ritual patterns.
They must follow established methods,
without any deviation or error.
Black, yellow, azure, and crimson
must all be of good quality,
not daring to be false or deceptive,
to provide clothing for sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and to serve as flags and emblems, to distinguish ranks of nobility and commonality.
In this month,
trees are flourishing,
and the yin qi (feminine principle) is about to begin its influence. The foresters are ordered to enter the mountains to inspect trees, without any cutting or felling.
No earthworks can be undertaken,
no feudal lords can be assembled,
no armies can be raised or people mobilized.
No major undertakings should be launched,
to support the yang qi (masculine principle).
No decrees should be issued that contradict the season,
to interfere with the affairs of Shénnóng (Divine Farmer).
When floods are abundant and prosperous,
Shénnóng (Divine Farmer) is ordered
to inspect the achievements.
If major undertakings are launched, there will be heavenly calamities.
In this month,
the earth is moist and the heat is humid,
heavy rains fall frequently.
Burning and weeding are carried out along waterways,
beneficial for killing weeds,
as if with hot water.
It can fertilize fields,
and improve the soil quality.
If this order is implemented,
in this month, sweet rain will fall three times,
for thirty-two days.
If in Jìxià (Midsummer) spring orders are implemented,
then grain will fall off and rot,
the state will suffer much from wind and cough,
and the people will migrate.
If autumn orders are implemented,
then hills and lowlands will be flooded,
grain will not ripen,
and there will be many calamities for women.
If winter orders are implemented,
then cold qi will be unseasonable,
eagles and falcons will hunt early,
and the four borders will seek refuge in strongholds.
Central earth:
Its days are Wù (fifth heavenly stem) and Jǐ (sixth heavenly stem).
Its Emperor is Huángdì (Yellow Emperor).
Its God is Hòutǔ (Earth God).
Its creatures are hairless animals.
Its musical note is Gōng (C).
The pitch pipe corresponds to the Gōng (C) note of Huángzhōng (yellow bell).
Its number is five.
Its flavor is sweet.
Its smell is fragrant.
Its sacrifice is to Zhōngliù.
The heart is offered first.
The Son of Heaven dwells in the Tàimiào and Tàishì,
rides in a dàlù,
drives yellow liú horses,
carries a yellow banner,
wears yellow clothes,
adorns himself with yellow jade,
and eats millet and beef.
Its vessels are round and covered.
6.2 Yīnlǜ
Second, it says:
Huángzhōng gives birth to Línzhōng,
Línzhōng gives birth to Tàicù,
Tàicù gives birth to Nánlǚ,
Nánlǚ gives birth to Gūxǐ,
Gūxǐ gives birth to Yìngzhōng,
Yìngzhōng gives birth to Ruíbīn,
Ruíbīn gives birth to Dàlǚ,
Dàlǚ gives birth to Yízé,
Yízé gives birth to Jiázhōng,
Jiázhōng gives birth to Wúshè,
Wúshè gives birth to Zhònglǚ.
A note produced by dividing the length of the previous one into three parts
and adding one part above it is a *shàngshēng* note;
a note produced by dividing the length of the previous one into three parts
and subtracting one part from it is a *xiàshēng* note.
Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, Jiázhōng, Gūxǐ, Zhònglǚ, and Ruíbīn are *shàngshēng*; Línzhōng, Yízé, Nánlǚ, Wúshè, and Yìngzhōng are *xiàshēng*.
In the age of a great sage's perfect rule,
the qi of heaven and earth
combine to produce wind.
When the sun reaches its solstice, the moon strikes its wind,
thereby producing the twelve lǜ.
When the winter solstice occurs in mid-winter,
Huángzhōng is produced.
In late winter, Dàlǚ is produced.
In early spring, Tàicù is produced.
In mid-spring, Jiázhōng is produced.
In late spring, Gūxǐ is produced.
In early summer, Zhònglǚ is produced.
When the summer solstice occurs in mid-summer,
Ruíbīn is produced.
In late summer, Línzhōng is produced.
In early autumn, Yízé is produced.
In mid-autumn, Nánlǚ is produced.
In late autumn, Wúshè is produced.
In early winter, Yìngzhōng is produced.
When the wind-qi of heaven and earth are correct,
then the twelve lǜ are set.
In the month of Huángzhōng,
no earthworks are to be done.
Be careful not to open covers,
in order to secure heaven and close earth.
If one opens covers to storage,
and mobilizes the populace,
the yang qi will leak,
which is called opening the chambers of heaven and earth.
In the month of Dàlǚ,
the count is nearing its end,
the year is about to begin anew,
and one should focus on agriculture. The people
should not be put to any other use.
In the month of Tàicù,
the qi of heaven descends, and yang qi begins to be born.
Heaven and earth are in harmony, and plants and trees flourish.
Order farmers to turn the soil,
without losing the proper time.
In the month of Jiázhōng,
be generous and peaceful,
practice virtue and desist from punishments.
Do not undertake any affairs
that harm living beings.
In the month of Gūxǐ,
clear paths and open roads,
repair and clear canals and ditches.
Implement this order,
and auspicious qi will arrive quickly.
In the month of Zhònglǚ,
do not gather large crowds.
Tour and encourage agricultural work.
Plants and trees are just beginning to grow.
Do not dishearten the people.
In the month of Ruíbīn,
yang qi is ascendant.
Settle the strong and nourish the excellent.
If the imperial court is not peaceful,
plants and trees will wither early.
In the month of Línzhōng,
plants and trees are lush and full.
Yin is about to begin to be punitive.
Do not undertake major affairs
to assist the yang qi.
In the month of Yízé,
amend laws and enforce punishments,
select soldiers and sharpen weapons.
Interrogate and punish the unrighteous,
to attract distant regions.
In the month of Nánlǚ,
hibernating insects all lie low in their holes,
and seal their entrances. Urge farmers to harvest and gather,
not daring to be lazy,
making abundance the main task.
In the month of Wúshè,
swiftly judge the guilty,
applying the law without mercy.
Do not delay legal cases,
making speed the priority.
In the month of Yìngzhōng,
yin and yang do not communicate,
they close to become winter.
Revise and differentiate mourning rites,
distinguish clothing, and discern the end of people's lives.
6.3 Yīnchū
Third, it says:
Xiàhòu Kǒngjiǎ was hunting in Dōngyáng Fùshān.
There was a great wind and blinding darkness.
Kǒngjiǎ became lost
and entered a commoner's house.
The mistress was then giving birth.
Some said,
"The sovereign's arrival is an auspicious day,
this child will surely be greatly fortunate."
Others said,
"It is unpropitious,
this child will surely suffer calamity."
The sovereign then took the child and returned,
saying,
"I will make him my son.
Who dares bring calamity upon him?"
When the child grew to adulthood,
he moved a curtain and broke a rafter.
An axe struck and cut off his foot,
so he became a doorkeeper.
Kǒngjiǎ said,
"Alas!
There is sickness,
it is fate!"
Thereupon he composed the song "Pòfǔ",
which was truly the beginning of the composition of eastern music.
Yǔ was carrying out his great work
when he met the maiden of Túshān.
Yǔ had not yet met her when he toured the southern lands.
The maiden of Túshān then ordered her maidservant to go wait for Yǔ on the sunny side of Túshān.
The maiden then composed a song.
The song said, "Hòurén xī yī,"
which was truly the beginning of the composition of southern music.
The Duke of Zhōu and the Duke of Shào took inspiration from it,
making it the Zhōunán and Shàonán.
King Zhāo of Zhōu personally led an expedition against Jīng.
Xīn Yúmí was tall and strong,
and served as the king's right-hand man.
Returning, they crossed the Hàn River.
The bridge collapsed,
and the king and Duke Cài fell into the middle of the Hàn.
Xīn Yúmí pulled the king to the north bank,
then went back and pulled Duke Cài.
The Duke of Zhōu then enfeoffed him in Xīdí,
and he truly became Chánggōng.
Yīn Zhěngjiǎ moved his residence to Xīhé,
still thinking of his old home.
This was truly the beginning of the composition of western music.
Chánggōng continued this music and resided in Xīshān.
Duke Mù of Qín took inspiration from it,
which was truly the beginning of the composition of Qín music.
The Yǒusōng clan had two beautiful maidens.
A nine-story tower was built for them,
and they always ate and drank to the sound of drums.
The Di ordered a swallow to go observe them.
It chirped as if in pain.
The two maidens loved it and competed to catch it.
They covered it with a jade basket.
After a short while,
they opened it and looked,
and the swallow left two eggs.
It flew north,
and never returned.
The two maidens composed a song. One stanza
said,
"Swallow, swallow, fly away!"
This was truly the beginning of the composition of northern music.
All music
originates in the human heart.
When touched by the heart, it spills forth as sound;
music is formed externally and transforms internally.
Therefore, by hearing its sound, one knows its style;
by examining its style, one knows its intent;
by observing its intent, one knows its virtue.
Prosperity and decline, worthiness and unworthiness, noble persons and petty persons, all are manifested in music,
and cannot be hidden.
Hence it is said that the observation of music is profound.
If the soil is poor, trees and plants will not grow tall.
If the water is turbulent, fish and turtles will not grow large.
If the age is corrupt, rituals will be burdensome and music will be depraved.
The sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
the music of Sāngjiān,
these are what ruinous states delight in,
and what degenerate virtues find pleasing.
When licentious, deviant, provocative, excessive, and unrestrained music emerges,
then dissolute spirits and perverse, arrogant hearts are stirred; once stirred, a hundred wicked deeds and numerous perversions arise from this.
Therefore, a noble person turns to the Way to cultivate virtue,
rectifies virtue to produce music,
and harmonizes music to achieve order.
When music is harmonious, the people will turn towards rectitude.
Fourth, it is said:
To observe the most excellent music,
one must look to the most excellent governance.
Where governance is profound, its music will be profoundly governed;
where governance is superficial, its music will be superficially governed;
in times of chaos, music will be arrogant.
Now, with doors and windows closed,
it can move heaven and earth,
even a single room.
Thus, in the time of Chéng Tāng,
there was a millet stalk that grew in the courtyard,
growing from dusk,
until it was as large as an arm’s span by dawn.
His historian requested to divine its cause.
Tāng dismissed the diviner, saying:
"I have heard that auspicious signs are precursors of blessings;
if one sees an auspicious sign and acts badly, blessings will not arrive.
Ominous signs are precursors of misfortune;
if one sees an ominous sign and acts well, misfortune will not arrive."
Thereupon, he held court early and retired late,
inquired about the sick and offered condolences to the bereaved,
and diligently pacified the common people.
After three days, the millet stalk disappeared by itself.
Therefore, misfortune is what blessing relies upon;
blessing is what misfortune conceals.
Only sages can perceive their ultimate truth;
how can ordinary people know their full extent?
When Zhōu Wénwáng established his state for eight years,
in the sixth month,
Wénwáng had been ill for five days when an earthquake occurred,
in the east, west, south, and north,
but not beyond the state's outskirts.
All the officials requested, saying:
"We have heard that an earthquake
is for the ruler.
Now the King has been ill for five days and an earthquake has occurred, in all four directions but not beyond Zhōu's outskirts.
All the ministers are afraid and ask to move it."
Wénwáng said:
"How can it be moved?"
They replied:
"By undertaking great projects and mobilizing the populace
to expand the capital city,
perhaps it can be moved."
Wénwáng said:
"No.
For Heaven sends omens
to punish the guilty.
I must be guilty,
which is why Heaven punishes me with this.
Now, if I deliberately undertake great projects and mobilize the populace to expand the capital city,
this would be to compound my guilt.
It is not acceptable." Wénwáng said:
"For its prosperity.
I request to change my conduct and accumulate good deeds to move it;
can I then be spared?"
Thereupon, he carefully regulated his rituals, ranks, and leather gifts
for interaction with the feudal lords;
he rectified his decrees
and silk offerings
to treat eminent scholars with respect;
he distributed爵列 (juéliè), ranks, and fields
to reward those with merit, and then with his officials.
After performing these actions for not long,
his illness ceased.
Wénwáng had been on the throne for eight years when the earthquake occurred.
Forty-three years after the earthquake,
Wénwáng reigned for a total of fifty-one years before he died.
This is how Wénwáng stopped calamity and averted omens.
In the time of Sòng Jǐnggōng,
the planet Huǒxīng (Mars) was in the Xīn constellation.
The Duke was afraid
and summoned Zǐwéi to ask him,
saying:
"Huǒxīng is in the Xīn constellation,
what does this mean?"
Zǐwéi replied:
"Huǒxīng
is a Heavenly punishment;
Xīn
is the celestial domain of Sòng;
disaster will fall upon Your Grace.
Nevertheless,
it can be shifted to the prime minister."
The Duke said:
"The prime minister is one with whom I govern the state;
to shift death upon him would be
inauspicious."
Zǐwéi said:
"It can be shifted to the people."
The Duke said:
"If the people die,
for whom shall I be ruler?
I would rather die alone."
Zǐwéi said:
"It can be shifted to the harvest."
The Duke said:
"If the harvest is harmed, the people will starve;
if the people starve, they will surely die.
For a ruler to wish to kill his people to save himself,
who would consider me their ruler?
My fate is indeed exhausted,
you need not speak further."
Zǐwéi hurried back,
knelt facing north and bowed twice, saying:
"I dare to congratulate Your Grace.
Heaven is high but hears the humble.
Your Grace has spoken three words of ultimate virtue,
Heaven will surely reward Your Grace thrice.
This evening, Huǒxīng will shift three mansions,
and Your Grace will extend your life by twenty-one years."
The Duke said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"Three good words
must be met with three rewards.
Huǒxīng shifting three mansions,
each mansion spans seven stars,
each star's shift accounts for one year;
three times seven is twenty-one,
therefore I say Your Grace's life will be extended by twenty-one years.
I request to wait beneath your steps to observe it.
If Huǒxīng does not shift,
I request to die."
The Duke said:
"Very well."
That evening, Huǒxīng indeed shifted three mansions.
Fifth, it is said:
The Five Emperors and Three Kings perfected music.
Rulers of chaotic states
have never known music;
these are ordinary rulers.
Though granted the Heavenly reward of being a ruler,
yet never achieving the reality of a ruler,
this is called a great tragedy.
It is like sitting upright in the evening chamber,
yet what is called upright
is in fact not upright.
Indeed, birth is not due to the transformation of a single qi;
growth is not due to the responsibility of a single thing;
accomplishment is not due to the effort of a single form.
Therefore, where many righteous acts accumulate,
there is no blessing that will not arrive;
where many evil acts accumulate,
there is no misfortune that will not befall.
If the wind and rain are not suitable,
if the sweet rain does not fall,
if the frost and snow are not timely,
if the cold and heat are not appropriate,
if yin and yang are out of order,
if the four seasons change their progression,
people will be depraved, wasted, and unstable,
birds and beasts will miscarry and not reproduce,
grasses and trees will be stunted and not flourish,
the five grains will perish and not ripen.
How can one make music
under such circumstances?
Therefore, in the transformation towards ultimate chaos,
ruler and ministers harm each other,
elders and youngsters kill each other,
fathers and sons endure each other,
elder and younger brothers deceive each other,
close friends betray each other,
husbands and wives insult each other,
day by day they endanger each other,
losing human morality,
their hearts like those of beasts,
indulging in evil and seeking petty gain,
ignorant of righteousness and reason.
The shapes of its clouds:
some are like dogs, like horses, like white swans, like many chariots;
some have a shape like a person,
with a dark garment and a red head,
motionless,
its name is Tiānchōng;
some have a shape like a suspended cauldron and are red,
its name is Yúnjīng;
some have a shape like many horses fighting,
its name is Huámǎ;
some have a shape like many flowers planted and growing tall,
yellow above and white below,
its name is Chīyóu zhī Qí.
Regarding the sun,
there are fighting eclipses (dòu shí),
there are doubled halos (bèi kuì),
there are halos with ears (yùn ěr),
there is lack of light,
there is failure to cast a shadow (bù jí yǐng),
there are many suns appearing together,
there is daytime blindness (zhòu máng),
there is nighttime visibility (xiāo jiàn).
Regarding the moon,
there are close eclipses (bó shí),
there are halos with ears (huī ěr),
there is partial blindness (piān máng),
there are four moons appearing together,
there are two moons appearing together,
there is a small moon supporting a large moon,
there is a large moon supporting a small moon,
there is the moon eclipsing stars,
there is its appearance without light.
Regarding the stars,
there are Yínghuò,
there are comets (huì xīng),
there is Tiānbàng,
there is Tiānchán,
there is Tiānzhú,
there is Tiānyīng,
there is Tiāngān,
there are bandit stars (zéi xīng),
there are fighting stars (dòu xīng),
there are guest stars (bīn xīng).
Regarding the khí,
some are not attached to the sky above,
nor to the earth below,
some are abundant above and sparse below,
some are like the waves of water,
some are like the planks of a mountain,
yellow in spring,
black in summer,
azure in autumn,
and red in winter.
Regarding omens and calamities,
some are born like belts,
there are ghosts throwing things onto battlements,
there are hares giving birth to pheasants,
pheasants also giving birth to quails,
there are locusts swarming in the state,
their sound is "xiōng xiōng,"
there are wandering snakes in the state, east and west,
horses and oxen speak,
dogs and pigs copulate (lián),
there are wolves entering the state,
there are people descending from the sky,
there are dancing owls in the market,
there are flying creatures walking in the state,
horses have horns,
roosters have five feet,
there are pigs born deformed (mí),
many chicken eggs are addled (duàn),
altars to the earth god (shè) move their locations,
there are pigs giving birth to dogs.
If a state has these things,
and its ruler does not know to be alarmed, terrified, and quickly reform,
Shàngdì will send down misfortune,
and dire calamities will surely follow swiftly.
Its devastation, demise, death, and loss,
utter extinction without any remaining kind,
and scattered wandering, following famine, will not be far off.
All these are produced by a disordered state,
they cannot be fully counted;
even if all the bamboo of Jīng and Yuè
were used, they still could not be written down.
Therefore, Zǐhuàzǐ said:
"Indeed, among the people of a disordered age,
the tall and short are dishevelled, there are a hundred diseases,
the people suffer from many illnesses and epidemics,
the roads are filled with infants in cradles,
the blind, bald, hunchbacked, and crippled,
and ten thousand strange things all emerge."
Therefore, how can the ruler of a disordered age hear of ultimate joy?
How can the ruler of a disordered age hear of ultimate joy?
If they do not hear of ultimate joy,
their joy is not joy.
7.1 Yuè lìng (Monthly Ordinances): Mèngqiū Jì
One record states:
In the month of Mèngqiū:
The summer solstice is 46 days past.
The sun is in Yì,
at dusk Dòu is in the middle,
at dawn Bì is in the middle.
Then it is Lìqiū. Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its Emperor is Shàohào.
Its God is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are those with fur (máo).
Its sound is shāng.
The pitch pipe corresponds to Yízé.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent (xīn).
Its odor is rancid (xīng).
Its sacrifice is to the gate.
When sacrificing, the liver is offered first.
Cool winds arrive.
White dew descends.
Cold cicadas chirp.
Hawks then sacrifice birds.
Executions begin to be carried out.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of Zǒngzhāng,
rides in a military carriage, drives white horses,
carries a white banner,
wears white clothes,
adorns himself with white jade,
eats hemp and dog meat.
His vessels are sharp-edged (lián) and deep.
In this month,
Lìqiū is established.
Three days before Lìqiū,
the Grand Historian informs the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"On a certain day Lìqiū will arrive,
and the flourishing virtue resides in Metal."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of Lìqiū,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Sāngōng, Jiǔqīng,诸侯 (zhūhóu), and Dàfū to welcome autumn in the western suburb.
Upon returning,
he then rewards military commanders and warriors in court.
The Son of Heaven then commands generals and commanders,
selects soldiers and sharpens weapons,
and inspects and trains the brave and outstanding;
he exclusively entrusts meritorious individuals
to conquer the unjust;
he interrogates and punishes the violent and arrogant,
to make clear what is liked and disliked;
he tours those distant regions.
In this month,
officials are commanded
to repair laws and regulations,
to renovate prisons,
to prepare shackles and fetters,
to prohibit evil,
to be cautious with crimes and wickedness,
and to diligently apprehend and seize.
Judicial officers (lǐ) are commanded
to observe injuries and examine wounds,
to inspect fractures and scrutinize severances;
when deciding legal cases,
they must be just and fair;
they must execute the guilty,
and strictly impose punishments.
Heaven and Earth begin to be severe,
and one cannot be indulgent.
In this month,
farmers then harvest grain.
The Son of Heaven tastes the new harvest,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
All officials are commanded
to begin collecting and gathering.
Dikes and embankments are repaired,
and dams and blockages are carefully maintained,
to guard against floods.
Palaces are repaired,
walls and ramparts are reinforced,
and city walls are mended.
In this month,
one should not enfeoff marquises, appoint high officials, divide land,
exchange heavy tribute, or send out grand envoys.
If this ordinance is carried out,
then cool winds will arrive for three decades (thirty days).
If winter ordinances are carried out in Mèngqiū,
then yin energy will greatly triumph,
armored insects will damage grains,
and enemy soldiers will come.
If spring ordinances are carried out,
then the state will suffer drought,
yang energy will return,
and the five grains will not bear fruit.
If summer ordinances are carried out,
then there will be many fire disasters,
cold and heat will be unregulated,
and the people will suffer many malarial diseases.
7.2 “Dàngbīng”
Chapter two states:
The ancient sage kings had righteous armies but no cessation of arms.
The origin of warfare is ancient,
coexisting with the very beginning of the people.
All warfare,
is might;
and might,
is power.
It is the nature of people to possess might and power.
This nature is received from Heaven,
not something that humans can create,
nor can the martial adept change it,
nor can the skilled craftsman alter it.
The origin of warfare is ancient.
Huáng Dì and Yán Dì already used water and fire in conflict,
Gònggōng Shì already stirred up trouble,
and the Five Emperors already contended with one another.
They rose and fell in succession,
and the victors held sway.
It is also said that “Chīyóu created weapons,”
but Chīyóu did not create weapons;
he merely improved their instruments.
Before Chīyóu existed,
the people already stripped forests for battle, and the victors became leaders.
Being a leader was still insufficient to govern,
so rulers were established.
Rulers were still insufficient to govern,
so the Son of Heaven was established.
The establishment of the Son of Heaven came from rulers,
the establishment of rulers came from leaders,
and the establishment of leaders came from conflict.
The origin of contention and strife is ancient,
it cannot be prohibited,
it cannot be stopped.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies but no cessation of arms.
If a family has no angry beatings,
then the faults of boys and infants will be immediately apparent;
if a state has no punishments,
then the people's mutual encroachments will be immediately apparent;
if the world has no punitive expeditions,
then the mutual violence of the feudal lords will be immediately apparent.
Therefore, angry beatings cannot be ceased in the family,
punishments cannot be ceased in the state,
and punitive expeditions cannot be ceased in the world;
there are merely skillful and unskillful ways of doing them.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies but no cessation of arms.
If someone chokes to death on food,
to want to prohibit all food in the world
is absurd;
if someone dies by boat,
to want to prohibit all boats in the world
is absurd;
if someone loses their state by using weapons,
to want to cease all weapons in the world
is absurd.
The impossibility of ceasing weapons
is like that of water and fire:
used well, they are a blessing;
used poorly, they are a disaster.
It is the same with those skilled in medicine:
they save people with good medicine,
but kill people with bad medicine.
The righteousness of a righteous army
as a good medicine for the world is also great.
Furthermore, the origin of warfare is distant,
it has never for a moment been unused.
Noble and humble, old and young, wise and foolish are all alike
in this regard; there are merely large and small instances.
Examining the subtle aspects of warfare:
it is warfare when in the heart but not yet expressed;
a hostile gaze is warfare;
a change of countenance is warfare;
arrogant words are warfare;
a push or shove is warfare;
repeated defiance is warfare;
excessive fighting is warfare;
an attack by three armies is warfare.
These eight are all warfare,
a contention of the subtle and the great.
Those of this generation who advocate for the cessation of arms
use warfare their whole lives without knowing it—how absurd!
Therefore, even if their arguments are strong,
their debates eloquent,
and their learning extensive,
they are still not heeded.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies
but no cessation of arms.
If an army is truly righteous,
used to punish tyrannical rulers and relieve the suffering people,
the people will be pleased with it,
like a filial child seeing a loving parent,
or a hungry person seeing delicious food.
The people will cry out and rush to it,
like a powerful crossbow shot into a deep valley,
or like a great accumulation of water breaking its dam.
Even a mediocre ruler would be unable to retain their people in such circumstances,
let alone a tyrannical ruler?
7.3 “Zhènluan”
Chapter three states:
In the current age,
the turbidity is extreme,
and the suffering of the common people
cannot be increased.
The Son of Heaven is cut off,
the worthy are suppressed and hidden,
and the worldly rulers act unrestrainedly,
estranging themselves from the people.
The common people have nowhere to turn for complaint.
If there are worthy rulers and outstanding scholars in the world,
they should examine this discourse,
for then their armies will be righteous.
The people of the world,
who were about to die will live,
who were about to be disgraced will be honored,
and who were suffering will be at ease.
If worldly rulers act unrestrainedly,
then even mediocre people will flee their rulers and abandon their kin,
how much more so the unworthy?
Therefore, when a righteous army arrives,
the worldly rulers will be unable to retain their people,
and even parents will be unable to restrain their children.
For all who lead the people of the world,
there is no greater consideration than to foster the Way and suppress the Unrighteous,
to reward the righteous and punish the unrighteous.
In the present age,
many scholars disapprove of offensive warfare.
To disapprove of offensive warfare but advocate for defensive warfare,
means that the aforementioned methods of fostering the Way and suppressing the Unrighteous, rewarding the righteous and punishing the unrighteous, cannot be put into practice.
The welfare of the world's leaders
depends on examining this discourse.
Offensive warfare and defensive warfare are essentially the same reality,
yet people's choices differ.
If one seeks to remove them through辩说 (biànshuō),
there will ultimately be no settled conclusion.
To truly not know is
absurd;
to know but deceive one's heart is
deceptive.
Deceptive and absurd scholars,
however eloquent, are useless.
They reject what they should accept and accept what they reject,
they benefit it but in turn harm it,
they make it safe but in turn endanger it.
Such discourse is the deepest cause of lasting trouble for the world and greatest harm to the common people.
Those whose heart is to benefit the people of the world
must thoroughly examine this discourse.
Indeed, offensive warfare
has never failed to attack the unrighteous and punish the unjust.
To attack the unrighteous and punish the unjust
brings no greater blessing,
and no greater benefit to the common people.
To prohibit it
is to suppress the Way and attack the righteous,
it is to thwart the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ and further the errors of Jié and Zhòu.
The reason people hate to be unrighteous and unjust
is because of its punishment;
the reason people strive to follow the Way and act righteously
is because of its reward.
Now, if the unrighteous and unjust persist,
their persistence rewards them;
while the Way and righteous actions are thwarted,
their thwarting punishes them.
To reward the bad and punish the good,
and expect the people to be well-governed,
is it not difficult?
Therefore, this discourse is the greatest cause of chaos in the world and harm to the common people.
7.4 “Jìnsāi”
Chapter four states:
Indeed, the intention of defensive warfare
has never failed to defend the unrighteous and save the unjust.
To defend the unrighteous and save the unjust
brings no greater calamity,
and no deeper harm to the people of the world.
Generally, those who engage in defensive warfare,
first use persuasion,
secondly use military force.
Using persuasion, they gather many followers,
thinking of it day and night,
devoting their minds and energy,
reciting it when awake,
dreaming of it when asleep,
causing themselves to have chapped lips and dry lungs,
exhausting their spirit and harming their soul.
They invoke the achievements of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to please their listeners,
and cite the strategies of the Five Hegemons and famous scholars to lend credibility to their cause.
They rise early and retire late,
to inform those who command armies,
Actions speak to the multitudes, thereby clarifying their principles.
If principles are merely spoken of, but not acted upon,
then there will certainly be a reversion to warfare.
When there is a reversion to warfare,
then there will certainly be conflict and struggle. The nature
of conflict and struggle
is that it will certainly kill people.
This is killing innocent people to support the unprincipled and the unjust.
When the unprincipled and the unjust exist,
this prolongs harm to the world and stops benefit to the world.
Even if one desires to be lucky and win,
calamity has only just begun to grow.
The laws of the former kings say:
"Those who do good are rewarded,
those who do not do good are punished."
This is the ancient principle,
and it cannot be changed.
Now, without distinguishing between what is principled and what is unprincipled,
and eagerly undertaking defensive actions,
there is no greater injustice than this;
there is no greater harm to the people of the world than this.
Therefore, those who undertake offensive warfare cannot be
condemned,
offensive warfare cannot be
undertaken,
defensive actions cannot be
condemned,
defensive actions cannot be
undertaken;
only a righteous army is permissible.
If the army is truly righteous,
offensive warfare is also permissible,
and defensive actions are also permissible.
If the army is unrighteous,
offensive warfare is impermissible,
and defensive actions are impermissible.
That Jié of Xià and Zhòu of Yīn were unprincipled to such an extent,
it was by chance;
that Fūchā of Wú and Bó Yáo of Zhì invaded and seized to such an extent,
it was by chance;
that Lì of Jìn, Líng of Chén, and Kāng of Sòng were unvirtuous to such an extent,
it was by chance.
If Jié and Zhòu had known that their states would certainly perish and their bodies die,
and their lineage be utterly destroyed,
I do not know if they would have been so tyrannical and unprincipled as to reach this point;
if King Fūchā of Wú and Bó Yáo of Zhì had known that their states would become ruins,
and their bodies be executed,
I do not know if they would have been so unvirtuous, unprincipled, invasive, and seizing as to reach this point;
if Lì of Jìn had known that he would certainly die by the hand of the Jiànglì clan,
if Líng of Chén had known that he would certainly die by the hand of Xià Zhēngshū,
if Kāng of Sòng had known that he would certainly die at Wēn, I do not know if they would have been so unvirtuous as to reach this point.
These seven rulers,
great and unprincipled, unjust:
the number of innocent people they slaughtered
cannot be counted in tens of thousands;
the dead, whether strong, young, old, or aborted,
truly filled the plains;
they widely filled in deep ravines and great valleys,
plunged into great waters,
piled up ashes,
filled in ditches, trenches, and dangerous obstacles,
dared to face flying arrows,
trampled on white blades,
and furthermore suffered the calamities of freezing, starving, hunger, and cold.
Coming to the present age,
this has become even more severe.
Therefore, the exposed bones are countless,
forming mounds and hills like mountains.
If there were rulers who rose to power and benevolent scholars in the world
who deeply pondered this,
it would truly be heartbreaking,
and it would truly be sorrowful.
Examine the source of this:
it arises from the abandonment of those who embody principle
and the unrestrained actions of those who are unprincipled.
The unrestrained actions of the unprincipled
are a matter of chance.
Therefore, the troubles of the world
do not lie in defensive actions,
but in the good fortune of the unworthy.
When the doctrine of defensive actions is put forth,
the unworthy become even more fortunate,
and the worthy become more doubtful.
Therefore, what greatly disorders the world lies in not discussing its righteousness and eagerly undertaking defensive actions.
7.5 "Huái Chǒng"
Fifthly, it says:
The discourse of the noble person,
is not merely about eloquence;
the deliberation of the scholar,
is not merely about speaking.
It must conform to reason before speaking,
and must align with principle before deliberating.
Therefore, when principle is expounded, kings, dukes, and great men increasingly love reason, and scholars, common people, and the black-haired masses increasingly practice principle.
When the way of principle and reason is manifest,
then the methods of tyranny, deceit, treachery, invasion, and seizure cease.
Tyranny, deceit, and treachery are contrary to principle and reason;
their inherent nature dictates that they cannot both prevail,
they cannot coexist.
Therefore, when an army enters the enemy's territory,
the people know they will be protected,
the black-haired masses know they will not die.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the state or city,
do not harm the five grains,
do not dig up graves,
do not cut down trees,
do not burn stored provisions,
do not burn houses,
do not seize livestock.
When people are captured, support them and return them with a mark,
to make clear what is favored and what is disliked;
keep faith with the people in promises,
to seize the enemy's resources. If, after all this, there are still those who hold grudges, dare to offend, act recklessly, or disobey, then even resorting to military force is permissible.
First, a proclamation and an announcement are made, saying:
"The army has come
to rescue the people from death.
Your superiors are unprincipled,
arrogant, negligent, and indolent;
greedy, cruel, and abusive to the multitudes;
self-willed and reckless;
they disregard the sagely regulations,
scorn and revile the former kings,
reject and disparage old statutes;
upwards, they do not comply with Heaven;
downwards, they do not benefit the people.
Their levies and taxes have no fixed time;
their demands are insatiable;
they punish and kill the innocent;
their rewards and commendations are inappropriate.
Those who are like this
are condemned by Heaven,
and are the enemies of men;
they are unfit to be rulers.
Now, the army has come
to punish those who are unfit to be rulers,
to remove the enemies of the people and align with the Way of Heaven.
If there are people who oppose the Way of Heaven and protect the enemies of the people,
their bodies shall die and their families be executed without pardon.
Those who can lead their families to obey
shall be rewarded with their families;
those who lead their neighborhoods to obey
shall be rewarded with their neighborhoods;
those who lead their townships to obey
shall be rewarded with their townships;
those who lead their cities to obey
shall be rewarded with their cities;
those who lead their states to obey
shall be rewarded with their states."
Thus, conquer the state but do not harm its people,
punishing only those who ought to be punished.
Elevate its outstanding scholars and enfeoff them as marquises;
select its virtuous and good people and honor and exalt them;
seek out its orphans and widows and relieve them;
meet its elders and treat them with respect.
Increase all their stipends,
and elevate their ranks.
Investigate its criminals and rescue and release them;
distribute the gold from the treasuries,
scatter the grain from the granaries,
to pacify and reassure its multitudes,
not privatizing its wealth;
inquire about its popular community shrines and great altars,
those the people do not wish to abandon, and restore them,
specifically augmenting their sacrificial rites.
In this way, the worthy glorify its name,
and the elders are pleased by its rites,
the people cherish its virtue.
Now, if there were someone here
who could grant life or death to one person,
the world would certainly vie to serve him.
A righteous army gives life to many people,
who would not be pleased?
Therefore, when a righteous army arrives,
the people of neighboring states flock to it like flowing water,
the people of the state being punished look to it as to parents.
As it travels further across the land,
it gains more and more people,
and the army does not even have to engage in battle for the people to submit as if transformed.
8.1 "Zhòngqiū Jì"
First, it says:
The month of mid-autumn:
the sun is in Jiǎo,
at dusk Qiānniú is at the meridian,
at dawn Zīkuí is at the meridian.
Its days are gēng and xīn.
Its帝 is Shǎohào.
Its神 is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are those with fur.
Its sound is shāng.
The lǜ corresponds to Nánlǚ.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the gate.
Sacrifice first the liver.
Cool winds arise.
Wild geese arrive.
Swallows return.
All birds store up provisions.
The Son of Heaven dwells in the Zǒngzhāng Tàimiào,
rides the rónglù,
drives white camels,
carries white banners,
wears white clothes,
adorns himself with white jade,
eats sesame and dog meat.
Its vessels are angular and deep.
In this month,
old and infirm people are cared for,
stools and staffs are bestowed,
and gruel is served.
Then the Sīfú is ordered
to prepare and arrange clothing:
embroidered patterns must be regular,
sizes must be appropriate,
lengths must be suitable,
clothing quantities must be measured,
and old customs must be followed.
Caps and sashes must be regular.
Officials are ordered
to strictly enforce all punishments,
and executions must be just.
No one may be wronged or twisted.
If one is wronged or twisted unjustly,
one will in turn suffer calamity.
In this month,
the Zǎizhù are ordered
to inspect the sacrificial animals:
to check for completeness;
to examine their fodder;
to observe their fatness and leanness;
to inspect their colors,
ensuring they match their categories;
to measure their sizes;
to check their lengths,
ensuring all meet the standards.
If all five aspects are properly met,
the Shàngdì will certainly ◇◇ accept the offerings.
The Son of Heaven then performs the Nuó ceremony,
to ward off evil and illness,
and to usher in the autumn qi.
Dog meat is tasted with sesame,
and sacrifices are first made to the sleeping chambers and ancestral temples.
In this month,
city walls can be built,
capitals and towns can be established,
underground passages and cellars can be dug,
and granaries can be repaired.
Then officials are ordered
to urge the people to harvest and gather,
to diligently store vegetables,
and to accumulate many provisions.
Then the planting of wheat is encouraged,
and no one should miss the proper time.
If anyone misses the time, punishment will be imposed without doubt.
In this month,
day and night are equal.
Thunder then begins to cease its sound.
Hibernating insects all burrow into their holes, and all seal their entrances.
The killing qi gradually intensifies,
and the yang qi daily wanes.
Water begins to dry up.
When day and night are equal,
then measurements are standardized,
scales are calibrated,
weights (jūn and shí) are rectified,
and measures (dòu and yǒng) are unified.
In this month,
customs barriers and markets are opened,
merchants and travelers are welcomed,
and goods and valuables are brought in,
to facilitate the people's affairs.
When people from all four directions arrive with diverse goods,
and those from distant lands all come,
then resources will not be scarce,
the ruler will have no lack of provisions,
and all affairs will prosper.
In all undertakings, one must not go against the cosmic numbers,
but must follow the proper time,
and adapt to its kind.
If this order is executed,
white dew will fall for three decades.
If the spring orders are carried out in mid-autumn,
then autumn rains will not fall,
plants and trees will flourish,
and the state will face great fear.
If the summer orders are carried out,
then the state will suffer drought,
hibernating insects will not hide,
and the five grains will sprout again.
If the winter orders are carried out,
then wind disasters will frequently arise,
thunder will cease early,
and plants and trees will die prematurely.
8.2 《Lùn Wēi》
Second, it says:
Righteousness,
is the principle of all affairs,
the origin of intimacy and distance between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
and the locus of order and chaos, safety and danger, victory and defeat.
As for victory over defeat,
do not seek it elsewhere,
but surely return to oneself.
Human nature desires life and abhors death,
desires glory and abhors disgrace.
If the way of life and death, glory and disgrace is unified,
then the soldiers of the three armies can be made to be of one mind.
For any army, one desires its multitude;
one desires its mind to be unified.
If the three armies are of one mind, then their commands can be made invincible.
If commands can be invincible,
then their army will also be invincible in the world.
The supreme army of antiquity
was one where the people held commands in high regard.
They regarded them more highly than all under heaven,
and valued them more than the Son of Heaven.
Their commands were hidden in the hearts of the people,
swift as the skin,
deeply painful and firmly held,
unwavering,
nothing could move them.
If it is like this, then why would an enemy be difficult to defeat?
Therefore it is said: where commands are strong, the enemy is weak;
where commands are trustworthy, the enemy yields.
If victory is achieved here first,
then victory will surely be achieved there.
In general, weapons
are the inauspicious tools of the world;
courage
is the inauspicious virtue of the world.
Wielding inauspicious tools
and employing inauspicious virtues
is only done as a last resort.
Wielding inauspicious tools inevitably kills;
killing
is for the purpose of giving life.
Employing inauspicious virtues inevitably creates awe;
awe
is for the purpose of intimidating.
When enemies are intimidated and the people live,
this is why a righteous army prospers.
Therefore, for the supreme army of antiquity,
even before talented people had gathered,
its awe was already known,
and the enemy had already submitted.
Why would it necessarily need drums and gongs, spears and shields?
Therefore, one who is good at making awe known,
before it is unleashed,
before it is communicated,
is obscure and hidden,
no one knows its true nature.
This is called the sincerity of ultimate awe.
For any army, speed, swiftness, and initiative are desired.
The way to achieve speed, swiftness, and initiative
lies in knowing the distinction between slowness, delay, and falling behind, and speed, swiftness, and initiative.
Speed, swiftness, and initiative,
this is how the victory of a righteous army is determined.
But it cannot remain in one place for long.
To know that it cannot remain in one place for long
is to know where to bolt like a rabbit and rise like a duck, facing death and destruction.
Though there be the dangers of rivers, one crosses them;
though there be the obstructions of great mountains, one breaches them.
Concentrating qi and focusing essence,
with no thoughts in the mind,
no sights in the eyes,
no sounds in the ears,
one is wholly dedicated to warfare.
Rǎn Shū vowed to die for Tián Hóu,
and the entire state of Qí was afraid;
Yù Ràng vowed to die for Xiāngzǐ,
and the entire Zhào clan was terrified;
Chéng Jīng brought death upon the Lord of Hán,
and the people of Zhōu were all in awe.
How much more so for a state of ten thousand chariots,
if it has something it is sincerely resolute about,
then what enemy could it have?
Before blades meet, victory is already secured.
The enemy, grieving, fearing, hesitant, and terrified,
their spirits completely scattered and exhausted,
are all like mad souls,
their bodies and minds separated.
They walk not knowing where they are going,
they run not knowing where they are heading.
Though there are dangerous obstacles and strategic passes,
sharp weapons and keen tools,
their hearts dare not hold them,
their minds dare not dwell on them.
This is why Xià Jié died at Náncháo.
Now, if wood strikes wood, it splinters;
if water is poured into water, it disperses;
if ice is thrown into ice, it sinks;
if mud is thrown into mud, it becomes trapped.
This is the dynamic of speed, slowness, priority, and sequence.
Indeed, in warfare there are great essentials:
to know what the enemy plans but does not carry out, or does not forbid, then you have gained it.
Zhuān Zhū is an example of this.
With a single hand, he raised his sword and reached his goal.
Wú Wáng [Hélǘ] was successful.
How much more so with a righteous army?
The large ones number tens of thousands,
the small ones number thousands.
If their paths are kept secret,
and the enemy's paths are left open,
how can a soldier merely deliberate with Zhuān Zhū?
8.3 《Jiǎnxuǎn》
Thirdly,
the world has a saying:
"Driving market people to battle
can defeat those who are taught by high-salaried instructors;
the old, weak, and weary people
can defeat the enemy's elite soldiers and trained talents;
the scattered and bound captives
can defeat the enemy's orderly formations;
hoes, spades, and white cudgels
can defeat the enemy's long spears and sharp weapons."
This is the argument of those who do not understand warfare.
Suppose there is a sharp sword here,
but when used to stab, it misses,
and when used to strike, it fails to reach.
It is no different from a bad sword.
Therefore, to use a bad sword in battle is unacceptable.
If the chosen elite are good,
and the weapons are sharp,
but they are dispatched at the wrong time,
or unleashed inappropriately,
they are no different from bad soldiers.
Therefore, to use bad soldiers in battle is unacceptable.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì and Chén Nián still desired the sharpness of a sword.
If the chosen elite are good,
and the weapons are sharp,
and an able general commands them,
in ancient times, there were those who became kings and those who became hegemons.
Tāng, Wǔ, Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, and Wú Hélǘ are examples.
Yīn Tāng had seventy good chariots
and six thousand men resolved to die.
He fought at Chéng on the day wùzǐ,
then captured Tuīyí and Dàxī,
ascended from Míngtiáo,
and then entered Cháomén,
thus possessing Xià.
After Jié fled,
he then displayed great benevolence and compassion,
to relieve the common people;
he reversed Jié's policies,
furthered the worthy and good,
and accorded with what the people liked.
Near and far submitted to him,
thus he became King of All Under Heaven.
Wǔ Wáng had three thousand tiger-warriors
and three hundred selected chariots.
He engaged in the jiǎzǐ affair at Mùyě and Zhòu was captured.
He elevated the positions of the worthy,
advanced the remaining elders of Yīn,
and asked what the people desired.
He extended rewards even to birds and beasts,
and imposed punishments without sparing the Son of Heaven.
He treated Yīn as familiarly as Zhōu,
and viewed others as himself.
All under Heaven praised his virtue,
and the myriad people rejoiced in his righteousness.
Thus, he was established as the Son of Heaven.
Qí Huán Gōng had three hundred good chariots
and ten thousand trained soldiers,
making them the vanguard.
He marched across the land within the seas,
and no one under Heaven could stop him.
South to Shíliáng,
west to Fēnghào,
north to Língzhī.
Zhōngshān destroyed Xíng,
and the Dí people exterminated Wèi.
Huán Gōng re-established Xíng at Yíyí,
and re-established Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Jìn Wén Gōng created five companies of five men each,
and one thousand elite soldiers,
first using them to engage the enemy.
No feudal lord could withstand him.
He returned the walls of Zhèng,
protected the fields of Wèi in the east,
and honored the Son of Heaven at Héngyōng.
Wú Hélǘ selected five hundred strong men
and three thousand agile men
to form the vanguard.
He fought with Jīng,
winning all five battles,
and thus occupied Yǐng.
He campaigned eastward as far as Bìlú,
attacked westward as far as Bā and Shǔ,
forced Qí and Jìn northward,
and his commands were carried out in the Central States.
Therefore, all military positions and strategic obstacles
should be convenient;
armor, weapons, and implements
should be sharp;
selected and trained elite soldiers
should be skilled;
and the command of soldiers and people
should be well-taught.
These four
are aids to a righteous army.
They are responses to changing times,
not to be made absolute or solely relied upon.
This is one strategy for victory.
8.4 《Juéshèng》
Fourthly,
indeed, warfare has its fundamental principles:
it must be righteous,
it must be wise,
it must be brave.
If it is righteous, the enemy will be isolated.
If the enemy is isolated, then their superiors and inferiors will be hollow,
and the people will scatter.
If isolated, then fathers and brothers will resent,
the worthy will criticize,
and internal disorder will arise.
If wise, one will know the changes of the times.
If one knows the changes of the times, one will know the transformations of emptiness, fullness, flourishing, and decline,
and the calculations of priority, sequence, distance, proximity, letting go, and seizing.
If brave, one will be able to make decisive judgments.
If one can make decisive judgments, one will be like thunder and lightning, whirlwind and storm,
like collapsing mountains and bursting floods, distinctly separating and falling.
Like the strike of a raptor,
when it grapples and seizes, it kills;
when it hits a tree, it shatters.
This is achieved through wisdom.
Indeed, people are not always brave,
nor are they always timid.
If they have spirit, they are full;
if full, they are brave.
If they have no spirit, they are empty;
if empty, they are timid.
Timidity, bravery, emptiness, and fullness,
their origin is very subtle,
and one must not be unaware of it.
If brave, they fight;
if timid, they flee.
Those who fight and win,
they fight with their bravery.
Those who fight and flee,
they fight with their timidity.
Bravery and timidity are not constant;
they come and go swiftly,
and no one knows their direction,
only the sage alone sees their origin.
Thus, Shāng and Zhōu arose,
and Jié and Zhòu perished.
The reason for the difference between skill and clumsiness
is whether one can increase or diminish the people's spirit,
and whether one can lead the multitude to fight or not.
Although the army is large,
and the soldiers are many,
it is of no use for victory.
If the army is large and the soldiers are many, but they cannot fight,
then the multitude is not as good as the few.
Indeed, the multitude can be a great blessing,
but it can also be a great calamity.
It is like fishing in a deep abyss:
the fish caught can be great,
but the danger can also be great.
A good general,
within all the borders,
everyone fights alongside him.
Even humble porters and common laborers,
for hundreds of miles around,
all come to join the battle.
The situation compels them to do so.
Happiness,
then, is discerning the opportune moment for battle and having a way to restrain and entice them.
In all matters of warfare,
it is crucial to rely on circumstances.
To rely on circumstances
means to use the enemy's strong points as one's own defenses,
and to use the enemy's schemes for one's own purposes.
If one can carefully discern circumstances and act accordingly, victory will be inexhaustible.
An inexhaustible victory is called divine;
divine means unbeatable.
Indeed, in warfare,
being unbeatable is paramount.
Being unbeatable lies with oneself;
the possibility of being beaten lies with the enemy.
The sage always secures what lies with oneself,
and does not depend on what lies with the enemy.
Therefore, one employs the art of being unbeatable to confront a beatable enemy,
