and if this is done, there will be no failure in warfare.
All victories in warfare
are the enemy's failures.
In warfare, victory and failure
must be hidden, must be subtle,
must be accumulated, must be concentrated.
If hidden, victory will be clear;
if subtle, victory will be obvious;
if accumulated, victory will overcome dispersion;
if concentrated, victory will overcome disunion.
All beasts that claw, seize, attack, and bite,
when they use their teeth, horns, claws, and fangs,
must rely on humility, subtlety, and concealment.
This is how they achieve victory.
8.5 《Ài Shì》
Fifth chapter says:
One clothes people
because they are cold;
one feeds people
because they are hungry.
Hunger and cold
are great harms to humans.
To relieve them
is a great righteousness.
People's distress and poverty
are as severe as hunger and cold;
therefore, a wise ruler must pity people's distress
and must grieve for people's poverty.
If this is done, his fame and reputation will be manifest,
and the nation's worthy men will be gained.
In the past, Qín Mù Gōng was riding in a chariot when it broke down.
His right lead horse got loose, and a countryman took it.
Mù Gōng himself went to search for it
and saw the countryman about to eat it on the southern slope of Qí Shān.
Mù Gōng sighed and said,
"Eating the meat of a fine horse without drinking wine
will harm a person; I fear it will harm you!"
Thereupon, he offered them all wine and departed.
After a year,
during the Battle of Hán Yuán,
the Jìn people had already surrounded Mù Gōng's chariot,
Jìn's Liáng Yóu Mǐ had already grabbed the left trace horse of Mù Gōng's chariot,
and Jìn Huì Gōng's right charioteer, Shí Fèn, struck Mù Gōng's armor with a long spear,
hitting it six times through the layers.
More than three hundred countrymen who had once eaten the horse meat on the southern slope of Qí Shān fought with all their might for Mù Gōng beneath the chariot,
and consequently, Qín greatly defeated Jìn
and captured Huì Gōng to bring him back. This is what the Odes refer to when they say:
"A ruler who treats gentlemen correctly
thereby practices his virtue;
a ruler who treats commoners generously
thereby fully utilizes their strength."
How can a ruler not strive to practice virtue and love his people?
If he practices virtue and loves his people, the people will be close to their superiors;
if the people are close to their superiors, they will all gladly die for their ruler.
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ had two white mules and loved them very much.
Yáng Chéng Xū Qú, an officer of the Guangmén gate,
knocked on the gate at night and requested,
"Your servant Xū Qú is ill,
and the doctor instructed him:
'If you obtain the liver of a white mule, the illness will stop;
if not, you will die.'"
The gatekeeper went in to report.
Dǒng Ān Yú, who was attending nearby,
angrily said,
"Hmph!
Xū Qú
is demanding your mules,
please execute him immediately."
Jiǎn Zǐ said,
"Killing a man to save an animal,
is that not inhumane?
Killing an animal to save a man,
is that not humane?"
Thereupon, he summoned the cook to kill the white mule
and took its liver to give to Yáng Chéng Xū Qú.
Not long after,
Zhào raised an army and attacked the Dí.
The officers of the Guangmén gate,
seven hundred on the left,
seven hundred on the right,
all were the first to ascend and capture armored heads.
How can a ruler not love worthy men?
When the enemy comes,
it is to seek profit.
Now, if they come and face death,
they gain no profit by advancing, and instead take flight as their profit.
If all enemies take flight as their profit,
then there will be no blades to meet.
Therefore, if the enemy gains life from us,
then we will gain death from the enemy.
If the enemy gains death from us,
then we will gain life from the enemy.
Whether to gain life from the enemy
or the enemy gains life from us,
how can one not discern this?
This is the essence of warfare.
Survival and destruction, life and death,
are determined by understanding this and nothing more.
9.1 《Jì Qiū Jì》
First chapter says:
In the month of late autumn:
The sun is in Fáng;
at dusk, Xū is at its zenith;
at dawn, Liǔ is at its zenith.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its Emperor is Shǎo Hào.
Its deity is Rù Shōu.
Its creatures are those with fur.
Its note is Shāng.
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Wú Shè.
Its number is nine.
Its taste is pungent.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the gate.
In sacrifices, the liver is offered first.
Wild geese arrive.
Sparrows enter the great waters and become clams.
Chrysanthemums have yellow blossoms.
Jackals sacrifice beasts and slaughter fowl.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right apartment of Zǒng Zhāng,
rides in a military chariot,
drives white pied horses,
carries white banners,
wears white clothes,
adorns white jade,
eats hemp and dog meat.
His vessels are sharp-edged and deep.
In this month,
commands and decrees are strictly enforced.
All officials, noble and humble, are ordered
to diligently gather in
to assemble the hidden stores of heaven and earth,
allowing nothing to be scattered.
The Grand Steward is ordered
to complete the harvest of agricultural produce,
to collect the essentials of the five grains,
and to store the harvest from the imperial fields in the sacred granary, with utmost reverence and caution.
In this month,
when frost begins to fall,
all laborers cease work.
Then the officials in charge are commanded:
"The cold air has fully arrived,
and the people's strength cannot endure it;
they should all enter their homes."
On the first Dīng day,
the Director of Music is ordered to begin learning to play wind instruments.
In this month,
a great sacrifice is offered to the Lord on High,
sacrificial animals are tasted,
and completion is reported to the Son of Heaven.
The feudal lords are assembled.
The hundred prefectures are regulated.
The first day of the new year for the coming year is determined, along with the laws for the feudal lords on the lightness or heaviness of taxes on the people.
The number of tribute duties,
based on the suitability of the land according to distance,
is to supply the needs of the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
without any private appropriation.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven then teaches hunting,
to practice the five military skills.
He inspects the horses.
He orders the charioteers and seven grooms to all harness, carry banners and pennants,
receive chariots by rank,
and array them outside the screen.
The Minister of Education holds a whip,
faces north, and makes an oath.
The Son of Heaven then puts on solemn attire and accoutrements,
holds his bow and grasps his arrows to shoot.
He orders the chief priest
to offer sacrifices of game in the four directions.
In this month,
grasses and trees turn yellow and fall.
One then cuts firewood to make charcoal.
Hibernating insects all burrow into their holes
and seal their entrances.
One then hastens judicial punishments,
leaving no guilty person unpunished.
One recalls those whose emoluments are undue and those whose common maintenance is inappropriate.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven then offers rice to dogs,
and first presents it to the ancestral temple.
If the commands of summer are practiced in late autumn,
then the state will suffer great floods,
weapons will be stored away and disasters will occur,
and the people will suffer much from nasal congestion.
If the commands of winter are practiced,
then the state will have many bandits and thieves,
the borders will be restless,
and the land will be divided.
If the commands of spring are practiced,
then warm winds will arrive,
the people's spirits will become lax,
and military expeditions will surely arise.
9.2 “Shùnmín” (Obeying the People)
The second says:
The former kings first obeyed the hearts of the people,
thus their achievements and fame were established.
Indeed, there were many in ancient times who gained the people's hearts through virtue to establish great achievements and fame.
But those who lost the people's hearts and yet established achievements and fame have never existed.
To gain the people, there must be a way.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
or a city of a hundred households,
there are no people who are not pleased.
Take what the people are pleased with, and the people will be gained.
What the people are pleased with, how can it be manifold?
This is the essence of gaining the people.
In ancient times, when Tāng conquered Xià and brought order to the world,
there was a great drought.
For five years, there was no harvest.
Tāng then prayed in person at Sānglín,
saying:
“If I, the One Man, have sinned,
let it not extend to the multitude.
If the multitude has sinned,
it is on me, the One Man.
Let not the lack of diligence of one man
cause the Heavenly Lord and the spirits to harm the lives of the people.”
Thereupon, he cut his hair,
bound his hands,
offered himself as a sacrifice,
to pray for blessings from the Heavenly Lord.
The people were then greatly pleased,
and heavy rain arrived.
Thus, Tāng understood the transformations of spirits
and the transmission of human affairs.
Wénwáng, residing in Qí and serving Zhòu,
endured grievances and insults with humility and deference.
He appeared at court punctually morning and evening,
his tributes were always appropriate,
and his sacrifices were always reverent.
Zhòu was pleased,
and ordered Wénwáng to be called Xībó,
granting him a thousand *lǐ* of land.
Wénwáng bowed twice, prostrated himself, and declined, saying:
“I wish to petition on behalf of the people for the abolition of the 'Páogé' punishment.”
Wénwáng did not dislike the thousand *lǐ* of land;
he sought to gain the hearts of the people by petitioning for the abolition of the Páogé punishment.
Gaining the people's hearts was more valuable than a thousand *lǐ* of land,
hence it is said that Wénwáng was wise.
Yuèwáng endured the shame of Kuàijī
and desired deeply to gain the people's hearts
so as to inevitably fight to the death against Wú.
He did not rest comfortably on a mattress,
his mouth did not enjoy rich delicacies,
his eyes did not look at beautiful women,
his ears did not listen to bells and drums.
For three years, he toiled his body and exerted his strength,
parching his lips and drying his lungs.
Internally, he drew close to his ministers;
externally, he nurtured the common people,
to win their hearts.
If there were sweet and crisp foods insufficient to share,
he dared not eat them.
If there was wine, he poured it into the river,
sharing it with the people.
He personally tilled the land for food,
and his wife personally wove for clothing.
He forbade rare delicacies,
forbade fine clothing,
and forbade secondary colors.
From time to time, he traveled on the roads,
carrying food in his carriage,
to visit the orphaned, widowed, elderly, weak, sick, poor, troubled, distressed, and those who lacked sustenance.
He would personally feed them.
Then he gathered his high officials and told them,
saying:
“I wish to once contend with Wú for the hearts of the world.
Now, the states of Wú and Yuè
are both mutually devastated.
If our *shì dàfū* step on liver and lungs,
and die on the same day,
I will embrace the Wúwáng's neck, interlock arms, and fall with him—this is my great wish.
If this cannot be achieved,
and internally I assess my state as insufficient to harm Wú,
and externally, I cannot use the feudal lords to harm him,
then I will abandon the state,
release my ministers,
bear a sword and carry a blade,
change my appearance,
change my name,
hold a broom and serve him as a vassal,
to contend with the Wúwáng for a single day's death.
Though I know my neck and torso will not be connected,
my head and feet will be in different places,
my four limbs will be torn apart,
and I will be mocked by the world,
my ambition will surely be fulfilled.”
Thereupon, on another day, he indeed fought Wú at Wǔhú.
The Wú army was greatly defeated,
and he then heavily besieged the royal palace.
The city gates were unguarded,
he captured Fūchāi,
executed the Wú chancellor,
devastated Wú for two years, and then became hegemon.
This was by first obeying the people's hearts.
Qí Zhuāngzi requested to attack Yuè
and asked Hézi.
Hézi said:
“Our former lord left a command saying:
'Do not attack Yuè;
Yuè is a fierce tiger.'”
Zhuāngzi said:
“Though it is a fierce tiger,
it is now dead.”
Hézi told Xiāozi.
Xiāozi said:
“Though it is dead, consider it alive.”
Therefore, whenever undertaking an endeavor,
one must first ascertain the people's hearts before it can be undertaken.
9.3 “Zhīshì” (Knowing 士)
The third says:
Now, suppose there is a thousand-*lǐ* horse here.
Without obtaining a skilled horse trainer,
it is as if it is not taken.
A skilled horse trainer and a horse,
they complement each other, and only then is the horse perfected.
This is like a drumstick and a drum.
Indeed, a *shì* also has a thousand-*lǐ* capacity:
high principles and dying for righteousness—
this is the thousand-*lǐ* capacity of a *shì*.
Only a wise person can make a *shì* achieve their thousand-*lǐ* capacity.
Jìngguō Jūn was good at assessing Ji Mào Biàn.
Ji Mào Biàn was a person who was often criticized,
and Jìngguō Jūn's retainers were displeased.
Shì Wèi used this to remonstrate Jìngguō Jūn,
but Jìngguō Jūn did not listen.
Shì Wèi resigned and left.
Méngcháng Jūn secretly advised Jìngguō Jūn,
Jìngguō Jūn became greatly angry and said:
“Cut off your kind!
Examine my household:
if there is anyone who can serve Ji Mào Biàn,
I will not refuse to do so myself.”
Thereupon, he lodged him in the highest guesthouse,
ordered his eldest son to drive his carriage,
and presented food morning and evening.
Several years later,
Wēiwáng passed away,
and Xuānwáng ascended the throne.
Jìngguō Jūn’s relationship
was very bad with Xuānwáng.
He resigned and went to Xuē,
together with Ji Mào Biàn.
He had not stayed long when
Ji Mào Biàn resigned and departed,
requesting an audience with Xuānwáng.
Jìngguō Jūn said:
“The king’s displeasure with me (Yīng) is very great;
if you go,
you will surely die there.”
Ji Mào Biàn said:
“Indeed, I am not seeking to live.”
He insisted on going,
and Jìngguō Jūn could not stop him.
Ji Mào Biàn departed
and arrived in Qí.
Xuānwáng heard of it
and waited for him, concealing his anger.
Jì Mào Biàn had an audience with King Xuān.
The King said,
"Are you someone Jìngguō Jūn listens to and loves?"
Jì Mào Biàn replied,
"There is love,
but no listening.
When Your Majesty was still the Crown Prince,
Biàn said to Jìngguō Jūn,
'The Crown Prince's physiognomy shows he is not benevolent;
with an overhanging chin and pig-like gaze,
such a person will surely betray and rebel.
It would be better to replace the Crown Prince
and instead establish the child of Wèi Jī, Xiào Shī.'
Jìngguō Jūn wept and said,
'That is impossible,
I cannot bear to do it.'
If Jìngguō Jūn had listened to Biàn and acted accordingly,
there would certainly be no troubles today.
This is one instance.
As for Xuē,
Zhāo Yáng requested to exchange a territory several times its size for Xuē.
Biàn again said,
'You must accept it.'
Jìngguō Jūn said,
'I received Xuē from the former king.
Even if it is disliked by the later king,
what can I say to the former king?
Moreover, the temple of the former king is in Xuē.
How can I give the temple of the former king to Chǔ?'
Again, he would not listen to Biàn.
This is the second instance."
King Xuān sighed deeply,
his expression showing emotion,
and said,
"Was Jìngguō Jūn like this towards me to such an extent!
I was young
and truly did not know this.
Would you, sir, be willing to invite Jìngguō Jūn for me
for a moment?"
Jì Mào Biàn replied,
"Yes, I respectfully obey."
Jìngguō Jūn came,
wearing the robes of King Wēi,
donning his crown,
and carrying his sword.
King Xuān himself went to the outskirts to welcome Jìngguō Jūn,
and wept upon seeing him.
When Jìngguō Jūn arrived,
the King immediately requested him to be prime minister.
Jìngguō Jūn declined,
but accepted out of necessity.
After ten days,
he pleaded illness,
insisted on resigning,
and after three days, his resignation was accepted.
At that time,
Jìngguō Jūn could be said to know himself well.
Knowing himself well,
he therefore did not block criticism.
This is why Jì Mào Biàn pursued pleasure externally and rushed into difficulties.
9.4 "Examining Oneself"
Fourthly:
All things being as they are
must have a cause.
To know that something is so but not know why it is so,
though seemingly correct, is the same as not knowing,
and will ultimately lead to difficulty.
The reason the former kings, renowned scholars, and enlightened masters surpassed the common people was because of their knowledge.
Water flows from the mountains to the sea;
water does not dislike the mountains and desire the sea,
but the height difference makes it so.
Grain grows in the fields and is stored in granaries;
grain has no desires,
but people all make use of it.
Therefore, Zǐlù covered a pheasant and then released it.
Zǐ Lièzǐ learned archery and hit the target.
He reported this to Guān Yǐnzǐ.
Guān Yǐnzǐ said,
"Do you know why you hit the target?"
He replied,
"I do not know."
Guān Yǐnzǐ said,
"Not yet."
He withdrew and practiced for three years,
then reported again.
Guān Yǐnzǐ said,
"Do you know why you hit the target?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ said,
"I know."
Guān Yǐnzǐ said,
"Good,
maintain it and do not lose it."
It is not only archery;
the preservation of a state,
the destruction of a state,
the worthiness of an individual,
the unworthiness of an individual,
all have their reasons.
Therefore, the sages do not examine preservation or destruction, worthiness or unworthiness,
but examine their underlying reasons.
Qí attacked Lǔ
and demanded the Cén tripod.
The ruler of Lǔ sent another tripod.
The Marquis of Qí did not believe it and returned it,
deeming it false,
and sent someone to tell the Marquis of Lǔ,
"Liǔxià Jì considers this to be correct.
Please let us accept it through him."
The ruler of Lǔ requested Liǔxià Jì's help.
Liǔxià Jì replied,
"Your gift
is meant to satisfy the demand for the Cén tripod,
and to save your state from danger.
I also have a state here.
To destroy my state to save yours
is what I find difficult."
Thereupon, the ruler of Lǔ sent the true Cén tripod.
Indeed, Liǔxià Jì can be said to have been able to persuade.
He not only preserved his own state,
but also preserved the state of the ruler of Lǔ.
King Mǐn of Qí fled and resided in Wèi.
One day, walking around,
he said to Gōngyù Dān,
"I have perished,
yet I do not know the reason why.
What, after all, was the reason
for my downfall?
I should have died."
Gōngyù Dān replied,
"Your servant thought Your Majesty already knew,
does Your Majesty still not know?
The reason Your Majesty perished
was because of your worthiness.
All the kings under heaven were unworthy,
and they detested Your Majesty's worthiness,
so they united their armies to attack Your Majesty.
This is why Your Majesty perished."
King Mǐn sighed regretfully and said,
"Is worthiness truly so bitter?"
This is also not knowing the reason why.
This is Gōngyù Dān's fault.
King Shòu of Yuè had four sons.
King Yuè's younger brother, Yù,
wanted to kill them all
and succeed to the throne himself.
He hated three of them and killed them.
The people of the state were displeased
and greatly opposed the ruler.
He then hated the remaining one and wanted to kill him,
but King Yuè did not listen.
The son, fearing certain death,
united with the people of the state who wanted to drive out Yù,
and besieged the royal palace.
King Yuè sighed,
"I did not listen to Yù's words,
and thus encountered this disaster."
He also did not know the reason for his downfall.
9.5 "Profound Understanding"
Fifthly:
Some people say dodder has no roots.
Dodder is not without roots;
its roots are not attached,
like Púlíng.
A lodestone attracts iron;
something draws it.
Trees close together bend towards each other;
something pushes them.
When a sage stands facing south,
taking the welfare and benefit of the people as his purpose,
before commands are even issued, the whole world cranes its neck and stands on tiptoe, then his essence has profoundly connected with the people.
As for harming people, the same is true.
Now, when an attacker
sharpens his five weapons,
wears splendid clothes and eats fine food,
and the day of attack is set,
the target of the attack is unhappy.
It's not that they heard about it;
a spiritual force informs them beforehand.
If one's body is in Qín,
but one's beloved is in Qí,
and after death one's spirit is restless,
it is because the essence travels back and forth.
Virtue
is the steward of the myriad people.
The moon
is the root of all yin.
When the moon is full, clams are plump,
and all yin thrives;
when the moon is dim, clams are lean,
and all yin wanes.
The moon takes form in the heavens,
and all yin transforms in the deep;
the sage embodies virtue within himself,
and the four wild regions are disciplined by benevolence.
When Yǎng Yóujī shot at a rhinoceros,
his arrow struck a rock,
and its feathers were completely embedded,
because of his sincerity towards the rhinoceros.
Bó Lè learned to discern horses;
what he saw was nothing but horses,
because of his sincerity towards horses.
Páo Dīng of Sòng loved to butcher oxen;
what he saw was nothing but dead oxen;
for three years he did not see a living ox.
He used his knife for nineteen years,
and its blade was as if newly sharpened,
following the natural grain,
because of his sincerity towards the ox.
Zhōng Zǐqī heard a lithophone player at night and was saddened. He sent someone to summon the player and asked him:
"Why is your lithophone playing so sorrowful?"
He replied:
"My father unfortunately killed someone
and was not allowed to live.
My mother was allowed to live
and makes wine for the government.
I was allowed to live
and play the lithophone for the government.
I have not seen my mother for three years.
Previously, when I saw my mother at the residence of the Shè family,
I estimated the amount needed to redeem her, but I had no money,
and my body already belonged to the government.
This is why I am sorrowful."
Zhōng Zǐqī sighed and exclaimed:
"How sorrowful!
How sorrowful!
The heart is not an arm,
nor is the arm a mallet or a stone.
Sorrow exists in the heart, yet wood and stone respond to it.
Therefore, the noble person is sincere in one thing and judges another,
is moved in himself and affects others.
Why must it be forcibly explained?"
In Zhōu, there was a man named Shēn Xǐ,
who lost his mother.
He heard a beggar singing outside his gate and was saddened by it,
his countenance showing emotion.
He told his gatekeeper to bring in the singing beggar,
and he himself went to inquire,
saying:
"Why do you beg?"
He spoke with her,
and it turned out to be his mother.
Thus, parents to their children,
and children to their parents,
are one body split into two,
sharing the same qi but breathing differently.
They are like the flowers and fruits of grass,
like the roots and core of trees.
Though in different places, they are interconnected;
hidden intentions reach each other,
pain and illness are mutually relieved,
worries and thoughts are mutually felt.
When alive, they rejoice together;
when dead, they mourn together.
This is called the kinship of flesh and blood.
The spirit arises from sincerity
and responds to the heart.
When two essences connect,
why wait for words?
10.1 《Mèngdōng Jì》
One record says:
In the month of early winter:
the sun is in Wěi,
Wēi culminates at dusk,
and Qī Xīng culminates at dawn.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its emperor is Zhuānxù.
Its deity is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are the shelled.
Its musical note is Yǔ.
Its pitch-pipe is Yìngzhōng.
Its number is six.
Its taste is salty.
Its odor is rotten.
Its sacrifice is Xíng.
The first organ sacrificed to is the kidney.
Water begins to freeze,
the ground begins to congeal.
Pheasants enter the great waters and become mythical clams.
Rainbows hide and are not seen.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the xuántáng,
rides a dark carriage,
is drawn by black horses,
carries dark banners,
wears black clothing,
adorns himself with dark jade,
and eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and covered.
In this month,
winter is established.
Three days before the beginning of winter,
the Grand Historian announces to the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"On such a day, winter begins,
and the predominant virtue is Water."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the beginning of winter,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and Grand Masters to welcome winter at the northern suburb.
Upon returning, he bestows awards upon those who died in service
and shows compassion to orphans and widows.
In this month,
the Grand Diviner is ordered
to pray and sacrifice, using turtle plastrons and milfoil stalks for divination,
to discern the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the hexagrams.
At this time, those who violate laws are to be investigated and punished, with no concealment.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins to wear furs.
He instructs the officials, saying:
"The qi of heaven rises,
the qi of earth descends.
Heaven and earth do not communicate,
and this closure forms winter."
He orders all officials
to diligently store and conceal.
He orders the Minister of Education
to inspect the stored provisions,
ensuring nothing is left uncollected; to fortify city walls,
guard gates and entrances,
repair locks and bolts,
secure passes and keys,
seal up documents,
prepare border defenses,
complete strategic passes,
guard bridges and ferries,
block minor paths,
regulate funeral rites,
distinguish clothing,
inspect the thickness of inner and outer coffins, and plan the size, height, lowness, thinness, and thickness of burial mounds, as well as the ranks of the noble and humble.
In this month,
the master craftsmen are ordered to demonstrate their work.
Sacrificial vessels are displayed,
measured according to standards.
No one should create extravagant or ingenious trifles
to corrupt the superior's mind;
skillful execution is paramount.
The craftsman's name is engraved on the object
to verify its authenticity;
if a craftsman's work is substandard,
he must be punished
to uncover the full extent of the matter.
In this month,
a great steamed feast is held,
and the Son of Heaven prays to the celestial ancestors for the coming year.
Large animal sacrifices are made,
offered to the public altars of soil and grain and to the gate gods and ancestral Five Sacrifices,
and farmers are given rest.
The Son of Heaven then orders generals to practice military skills, training in archery, charioteering, and wrestling.
In this month,
the water wardens and fishing masters are ordered to collect taxes from springs, ponds, and marshes. No one is allowed to encroach upon or exploit the common people and myriad inhabitants,
lest they incur resentment from the populace against the Son of Heaven.
If there be such a person,
they shall be punished without pardon.
If the decrees of spring are enforced in early winter,
then freezing and closing will not be complete,
the qi of the earth will be released,
and many people will flee.
If the decrees of summer are enforced,
then the state will have many violent storms,
winter will not be cold,
and hibernating insects will reappear.
If the decrees of autumn are enforced,
then snow and frost will be untimely,
minor conflicts will frequently arise,
and territory will be encroached upon.
10.2 "Frugal Funerals"
Second:
To carefully understand life
is the essential principle of a sage;
to carefully understand death
is the ultimate achievement of a sage.
He who understands life
does not harm life with external things;
this is called nourishing life.
He who understands death
does not harm death with external things;
this is called bringing peace to the dead.
These two
are what a sage uniquely decides.
All who are born between Heaven and Earth
must surely die.
This is unavoidable.
That a filial son values his parents,
and a loving parent cherishes his child,
and feels pain to the very bones,
is natural.
To abandon what is valued and cherished
to a ditch or gully after death
is something human nature cannot bear to do.
Thus, there is the principle of burying the dead.
Burial (zàng)
is concealment (cáng);
it is what loving parents and filial children take seriously.
Those who take it seriously
consider it from the perspective of the living.
When considering the dead from the perspective of the living,
there is nothing better than inactivity,
nothing better than no display.
No display and no activity;
nothing better than having nothing that can be profited from.
Having nothing that can be profited from, this is called heavy sealing.
In ancient times, there were those who were buried in wide plains and deep mountains and found peace.
This does not refer to pearls, jade, or national treasures.
A burial must be concealed.
If a burial is shallow, foxes and wildcats will dig it up;
if deep, it will reach underground springs.
Therefore, all burials must be on high mounds,
to avoid the trouble of foxes and wildcats and the dampness of underground springs.
This is good,
but it forgets the difficulties posed by treacherous people, thieves, robbers, and rebels.
Is this not a delusion?
It is like a blind musician avoiding a pillar, only to crash into a stake.
The troubles of foxes, underground springs, treacherous people, thieves, robbers, and rebels
are the greater stakes.
Those loving parents and filial children who avoid them
have grasped the true meaning of burial.
Good coffins and outer coffins
are for avoiding ants, snakes, and insects.
Today, the rulers of this greatly chaotic age,
the more they lavish their burials,
their hearts are not truly concerned for the dead,
but rather the living showing off to each other.
Those who are extravagant and wasteful consider it glorious;
those who are frugal and restrained consider it base.
It is not done for the convenience of the dead,
but merely for the praise or blame of the living.
This is not the heart of a loving parent or a filial child.
Even if a father dies,
a filial child's reverence for him does not slacken;
even if a child dies,
a loving parent's affection for him does not cease.
But when burying the cherished and valued,
and using what the living intensely desire
to bring them peace,
how can this be?
As for people and profit,
they will brave flying arrows,
tread on naked blades,
and wade through blood and gore to obtain it.
Ignorant commoners
will abandon relatives, siblings, and close friends to seek profit.
Now, without such dangers,
without such disgrace,
the profit is extremely great:
riding in carriages, eating meat,
and benefiting descendants.
Even a sage cannot prohibit it,
much less in a time of chaos?
The larger the state,
the richer the family,
the more extravagant the burial.
Pearls in the mouth, scales arranged, pearls, jade, trinkets, goods, and treasures,
bells, tripods, vessels, and ewers,
carriages, horses, clothes, blankets, spears, and swords,
their number is countless.
All tools for nourishing life
are followed.
A *tícòu* chamber,
multiple layers of coffins and outer coffins,
piles of stones and piles of charcoal
encircling the outside.
Treacherous people hear of it
and spread the word to each other.
Even if the superiors forbid it with severe power and heavy punishments,
it still cannot be stopped.
Moreover, the longer the dead have been gone,
the more distant the living become;
the more distant the living become,
the more negligent the guardians become;
the more negligent the guardians become while the burial goods remain as before, the situation is certainly not secure.
The common practice of funerals today
is to transport the coffin in a large hearse,
with feathered banners and flags, like clouds, and ornate fans to direct it, pearls and jade to furnish it,
and embroidered robes and patterns to adorn it.
Tens of thousands of people on both sides pulling the ropes to move it,
it can only proceed if organized like an army.
Looking at the world this way,
it is beautiful and extravagant;
but to do this for the dead
is unacceptable.
If it were truly convenient for the dead,
then even if it impoverishes the state and exhausts the people,
those who are loving parents and filial children would not shrink from doing it.
10.3 "Bringing Peace to the Dead"
Third:
The mounds and tombs made in the world
are as high and large as mountains,
the trees planted on them are like forests,
the gate-towers and courtyards are set up, palaces and chambers built, and host-guest areas created like a capital city.
If viewed as a display of wealth to the world, it is acceptable; but to do this for the dead is unacceptable.
As for the dead,
to them ten thousand years are but a blink.
Human lifespan,
at its longest, does not exceed a hundred years;
a moderate lifespan does not exceed sixty years.
To consider a hundred or sixty years from the perspective of infinite time, their feelings will certainly not correspond.
To consider the dead from the perspective of infinity, then
one grasps it.
Suppose there is a person here
who places a stone inscription on top of a mound,
saying:
"The contents within
include many pearls, jade, trinkets, wealth, and precious vessels,
which must be dug up.
Digging them up will surely make one immensely rich,
riding in carriages and eating meat for generations."
People would surely laugh at him,
considering him greatly deluded.
The extravagant burials of the world are similar to this.
From ancient times to the present,
there has been no state that has not perished;
and if there is no state that has not perished,
then there is no tomb that has not been dug up.
From what we hear and see,
Qí, Jīng, and Yān have all perished;
Sòng and Zhōngshān have already perished;
Zhào, Wèi, and Hán have all perished;
they are all former states.
Above these, the number of perished states is countless.
Therefore, ancient great tombs have all been dug up.
And yet the world still competes to make them.
Is this not tragic?
Rulers who do not govern their people,
fathers who are not filial to their parents,
elder brothers who are not fraternal to their younger brothers,
all those whom the villagers shun and drive away,
who dread the toil of farming and gathering firewood,
who are unwilling to engage in official affairs,
but pray for the pleasure of beautiful clothes and extravagant food,
when their cleverness and schemes are exhausted
and they have no means to achieve this,
then they gather large groups of followers
in deep mountains, vast swamps, and dense thickets,
to attack and seize.
They also observe famous mounds and great tombs with rich burials,
seek out convenient dwellings,
and subtly dig them up,
day and night without cease,
until they certainly obtain what they can profit from,
and share it among themselves.

To have what is loved and valued, yet allow treacherous people, thieves, robbers, and rebels to ultimately desecrate it—this is a great matter for filial children, loyal ministers, loving fathers, and friends.
Yáo was buried in Gǔlín,
with trees planted throughout;
Shùn was buried in Jìshì,
and the shops did not change their locations;
Yǔ was buried in Kuàijī,
without troubling laborers.
Therefore, the former kings buried the dead with frugality and restraint,
not because they begrudged the expense,
nor because they disliked the labor,
but because they considered the dead.
What the former kings abhorred
was the disgrace of the dead.
If burials are extravagant, they will surely be disgraced;
if they are frugal, they will not be disgraced.
Therefore, the burials of the former kings
were necessarily frugal, integrated, and uniform.
What is meant by integrated?
What is meant by uniform?
To be buried in mountains and forests means to be integrated with mountains and forests;
to be buried on slopes and in lowlands means to be uniform with slopes and lowlands.
This is what is meant by loving the dead.
Many love the dead,
but few know how to love the living.
Thus, before Sòng fell, its eastern tombs were excavated;
before Qí fell, Lord Zhuāng's (Zhuāng Gōng) tomb was excavated.
If a state is peaceful and still suffers like this,
how much more so a hundred generations later, when the state has already perished?
Therefore, filial sons, loyal ministers, loving fathers, and friends must not fail to observe this.
To love them and instead harm them, to bring them peace and instead endanger them—
is this not what is meant?
The *Shī* says:
"Dare not bare a tiger,
dare not cross a river on foot.
People know one thing,
but do not know the other."
This speaks of not knowing similar categories.
Therefore, they alternately denounce each other,
and alternately affirm each other.
What they denounce is precisely what they affirm,
and what they affirm is precisely what they denounce.
Right and wrong are not yet settled,
yet joy and anger, strife and contention,
are used in reverse.
I do not denounce strife, nor do I denounce contention,
but I denounce the reasons for strife, and the reasons for contention.
Therefore, all strife and contention
are the application of what has already been settled as right and wrong.
But today, many do not first settle right and wrong, but instead rush into strife and contention.
This is the greatest confusion.
When Lǔ Jìsūn had a funeral,
Kǒngzǐ went to offer condolences.
He entered the gate and turned left,
taking the guest's seat.
The host prepared a shroud of *yúfán* jade.
Kǒngzǐ hurried across the courtyard,
ascended the steps,
and said:
"To use precious jade as a shroud
is like exposing a corpse in the open field."
To cross the courtyard and ascend the steps
was against ritual;
nevertheless, it was to correct a mistake.
10.4 *Yì Bǎo* (Different Treasures)
Fourth:
The ancients were not without treasures,
but what they treasured was different.
Sūnshū Āo was ill,
and about to die.
He admonished his son, saying:
"The King has repeatedly offered me fiefs,
but I have not accepted them.
After I die,
the King will surely grant you a fief.
You must not accept profitable land.
Between Chǔ and Yuè, there is a hill called Yǒuqǐn (有寢之丘).
Its land is unprofitable,
and its name is very inauspicious.
The Jīng people fear ghosts,
and the Yuè people believe in portents.
The only place that can be held for a long time
is this one."
When Sūnshū Āo died,
the King indeed granted his son a fief of beautiful land,
but the son declined,
requesting Yǒuqǐn (有寢之丘).
Therefore, it has not been lost to this day.
Sūnshū Āo's wisdom
lay in knowing how to make the unprofitable profitable,
in knowing how to make what others disliked his own joy.
This is why those who possess the Way differ from the common folk.
When Wǔ Yuán fled,
Jīng urgently sought him. He ascended Mount Tàiháng and looked towards Zhèng, saying:
"This state,
though its terrain is dangerous and its people are wise,
its ruler is a conventional ruler,
unworthy of undertaking great deeds with."
He left Zhèng and went to Xǔ.
He saw Lord Xǔ (Xǔ Gōng) and asked where he should go.
Lord Xǔ did not answer,
but spat towards the southeast.
Wǔ Yuán bowed twice and accepted the gift, saying:
"I know where to go now."
Thereupon, he went to Wú.
Passing through Jīng,
he reached the riverbank.
Wanting to cross,
he saw an old man
rowing a small boat,
about to fish.
He followed and made a request.
The old man ferried him across the river.
When asked his name and family,
Wǔ Yuán refused to tell.
He took off his sword and gave it to the old man,
saying:
"This is a thousand-gold sword;
I wish to present it to you, venerable sir."
The old man refused to accept, saying:
"According to the laws of Jīng,
he who captures Wǔ Yuán
will be ennobled as a duke (holding a *guī* scepter),
receive ten thousand *yán* of grain as salary,
and a thousand *yì* of gold.
Long ago, Zǐxú passed by,
and I still did not take him.
Why would I want your thousand-gold sword now?"
After Wǔ Yuán arrived in Wú,
he sent men to search for him on the riverbank, but could not find him. Every time he ate, he would offer a sacrifice to him,
praying:
"O venerable sir of the riverbank!
Heaven and Earth are truly vast,
and truly numerous.
Why would you not do something?
Yet you have nothing to do.
You do something, yet have nothing to do it for.
Your name cannot be heard,
your person cannot be seen.
Perhaps it is only the venerable sir of the riverbank!"
A countryman from Sòng,
while plowing, found a jade.
He presented it to Sīchéng Zǐhǎn,
but Zǐhǎn would not accept it.
The countryman pleaded:
"This is a treasure of us countrymen;
I beg you, Prime Minister, to grant me the favor of accepting it."
Zǐhǎn said:
"You consider jade a treasure;
I consider not accepting it a treasure."
Therefore, the elders of Sòng said:
"Zǐhǎn is not without treasures;
what he treasures is different."
If one shows a hundred *jīn* of gold and a handful of cooked rice to a child,
the child will surely take the cooked rice.
If one shows the *Héshì* (Héshì) jade and a hundred *jīn* of gold to a commoner,
the commoner will surely take the hundred *jīn*.
If one shows the *Héshì* (Héshì) jade and the ultimate words of the *Dàodéjīng* to a worthy person,
the worthy person will surely take the ultimate words.
The more refined one's knowledge,
the more refined what one takes;
the coarser one's knowledge,
the coarser what one takes.
10.5 *Yì Yòng* (Different Applications)
Fifth:
All things are different,
and their application by humans varies.
This is the origin of order and chaos, survival and destruction, life and death.
Therefore, a state that is vast and great,
with strong armies and wealth,
is not necessarily secure;
being honored, noble, and exalted
does not necessarily mean prominence.
It lies in how they are used.
Jié and Zhòu (Jié, Zhòu) used their talents to bring about their downfall;
Tāng and Wǔ (Tāng, Wǔ) used their talents to establish their kingship.
Tāng saw a fowler who had set nets
on all four sides.
His prayer went:
"Those who fall from heaven,
those who emerge from the earth,
those who come from the four directions,
may they all enter my net!"
Tāng said:
"Alas!
He catches them all!
Who but Jié would do this?"
Tāng removed three sides of the net,
leaving only one,
and changed the prayer, instructing:
"In the past, spiders wove nets.
Now, people learn to untie them.
Those who wish to go left, go left;
those who wish to go right, go right;
those who wish to go high, go high;
those who wish to go low, go low.
I only take those who defy their fate."
The states south of the Hàn river heard this and said:
"Tāng's virtue extends even to birds and beasts!"
Forty states submitted to him.
A person who sets nets on all four sides
does not necessarily catch birds;
Tāng removed three sides,
leaving one,
and with it netted forty states—
not just birds.
Zhōu Wénwáng (周文王) sent men to dig a pond,
and they found the bones of a dead person.
The officials reported this to Wénwáng (文王).
Wénwáng (文王) said:
"Rebury them."
The officials said:
"This person has no owner."
Wénwáng (文王) said:
"He who possesses the world
is the master of the world;
he who possesses a state
is the master of that state.
Am I not his master now?"
So he ordered the officials to rebury the bones with clothes and a coffin.
When the world heard of this, they said:
"Wénwáng (文王) is virtuous!
His benevolence extends even to decaying bones,
how much more so to living people?"
Some obtain treasures and endanger their states;
Wénwáng (文王) obtained decaying bones and used them to convey his intention.
Therefore, for the sage, there is nothing that cannot be utilized.
When a disciple of Kǒngzǐ (孔子) came from afar,
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) leaned on his staff and asked:
"Is your father not ailing?"
He grasped his staff and bowed,
asking:
"Are your parents not ailing?"
He put down his staff and asked:
"Are your brothers not ailing?"
He moved forward by a small step and backed away from him,
asking:
"Are your wife and children not ailing?"
Thus, Kǒngzǐ (孔子) used a six-foot staff
to illustrate the distinctions of noble and humble,
and to discern the meaning of distant and close relations.
How much more so would he do this with an esteemed position and generous emoluments?
In ancient times, people valued skill in archery
for honoring the aged and supporting the elderly.
Now, people value skill in archery
for attacking, fighting, invading, and plundering.
Those of lesser character use it to oppress the weak and brutalize the few,
making interception and plunder their business.
When a benevolent person obtains candy,
it is to nourish the sick and support the aged.
When Zhí (跖) and Jiǎo (蹻) obtain candy,
it is to open locks and take out bolts.
11.1 《Zhòngdōng Jì (仲冬紀)》
Another account states:
In the middle month of winter:
The sun is in Dǒu (斗).
At dusk, Dōngbì (東壁) is at its meridian;
at dawn, Zhěn (軫) is at its meridian.
Its days are Rén (壬) and Guǐ (癸).
Its emperor is Zhuānxū (顓頊).
Its spirit is Xuánmíng (玄冥).
Its creatures are shelled animals.
Its note is Yǔ (羽).
The pitch-pipe matches Huángzhōng (黃鐘).
Its number is six.
Its taste is salty.
Its smell is rotten.
Its sacrifice is Xíng (行).
Sacrifice first the kidneys.
Ice grows stronger.
The earth begins to crack.
The hé'è (鶡鴠) bird does not sing.
Tigers begin to mate.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Xuántáng (玄堂) and Tàimiào (太廟),
rides in a black carriage,
drives iron-black horses,
carries a black banner,
wears black clothes,
wears black jade,
and eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and covered.
He orders the officials, saying:
"Undertake no earthworks,
open no hidden stores,
mobilize no large crowds,
in order to solidify heaven and close the earth."
If hidden stores are opened
or large crowds are mobilized,
the earth's vital energy will leak out.
This is called opening the chambers of heaven and earth.
All hibernating creatures will die,
the people will suffer many diseases and epidemics,
and be followed by mourning.
It is called Chàngyuè (暢月, the month of fluidity).
In this month,
the director of eunuchs is ordered
to reiterate the palace regulations,
inspect the gates and entrances,
and strictly guard the chambers,
ensuring they are tightly closed.
Inspect women's affairs,
and allow no licentiousness.
Even noble relatives and close attendants
are not to be exempt.
Then the Grand Brewer is ordered
to ensure that glutinous rice and rice are pure,
麴 (qū) and 糱 (niè) are timely,
steeped grain and cooked rice are clean,
spring water is fragrant,
pottery is good,
and the fire's temperature is right.
All six elements must be used,
and the Grand Brewer supervises them,
allowing no error or deviation.
The Son of Heaven then orders officials
to offer sacrifices and prayers to the Four Seas, great rivers, famous springs, deep pools, and wells.
In this month,
if farmers have not gathered and stored their harvest,
or if cattle, horses, and livestock have wandered off,
they may be taken without question.
In mountains, forests, swamps, and marshes,
those who can forage, hunt, and capture birds and beasts
are guided by the Wild Game Warden.
Those who encroach upon and plunder others
are punished without pardon.
In this month,
the winter solstice occurs.
Yin and Yang contend,
and all living things stir.
The gentleman fasts and purifies himself,
must keep himself secluded,
desires tranquility for his body,
avoids sounds and sights,
restrains desires,
calms his form and nature,
desires stillness in his affairs,
in order to await the establishment of Yin and Yang.
The rue herb begins to grow.
The lǐtǐng (荔挺) grass sprouts.
Earthworms coil up.
Deer shed their antlers.
Spring water moves.
At the winter solstice,
forest trees are felled,
and bamboo arrows are gathered.
In this month,
idle officials may be dismissed,
and useless implements discarded.
Plaster the palace courtyards, gates, and entrances,
and build prisons.
This is how to assist heaven and earth in their closing and storing.
If in mid-winter the summer regulations are followed,
then the state will suffer drought,
the air will be dark and misty,
and thunder will roar.
If the autumn regulations are followed,
then the heavens will send untimely rain,
gourds will not ripen,
and the state will face a great war.
If the spring regulations are followed,
then insect pests will cause damage,
springs will diminish and dry up,
and the people will suffer many diseases and epidemics.
11.2 《Zhìzhōng (至忠)》
Another account states:
Utterly loyal words are offensive to the ear and unsettling to the heart.
Without a virtuous ruler, who could listen to them?
Therefore, what a virtuous ruler delights in
is what an unworthy ruler punishes.
No ruler dislikes those who are violent and plunder,
yet they cause it to happen daily.
What good is disliking it then?
Suppose there is a tree here,
and one desires its beauty,
but people water it occasionally,
yet they dislike it,
and cut its roots themselves;
then there will surely be no living tree.
Indeed, disliking to hear loyal words
is precisely cutting one's own essence.
Jīng Zhuāng'āi Wáng (荊莊哀王) was hunting in Yúnmèng (雲夢)
and shot a suísì (隨兕) rhinoceros,
hitting it.
Shēn Gōngzǐ Péi (申公子培) coerced the king and seized it.
The king said:
"How violent and disrespectful he is!"
He was about to order an official to punish him.
All the high officials on his left and right advanced to remonstrate, saying:
"Zǐ Péi (子培)
is a worthy man,
and moreover a minister who has served the king a hundredfold.
There must be a reason for this;
we wish the king would investigate it first."
Less than three months later,
Zǐ Péi (子培) fell ill and died.
Jīng 荊 mobilized its army
and battled Jìn 晉 at Liǎngtáng 兩棠,
achieving a great victory over Jìn 晉.
Upon returning, it rewarded those who had rendered meritorious service.
Shēn Gōngzǐ Péi 申公子培’s younger brother Jìn 進 requested a reward from the official, saying: “Other people’s merits were gained on the battlefield;
my brother’s merits were gained from under the chariot.”
The King asked:
“What do you mean by that?”
He replied:
“My brother incurred the name of being violent and disrespectful,
and risked the crime of death right by Your Majesty’s side.
His foolish heart intended to be loyal to Your Majesty personally
and preserve Your Majesty’s thousand-year longevity.
My brother once read an old record which said:
‘He who kills Suí Sī 隨兕
will surely die
within three months.’ It was for this reason that my brother was alarmed and terrified and contended against it,
so he submitted to his crime and died.”
The King ordered someone to open the archives and look,
and indeed, it was found in the old records.
Thereupon, he richly rewarded him.
Shēn Gōngzǐ Péi 申公子培,
his loyalty may be called Mùxíng 穆行.
The meaning of Mùxíng 穆行
is that people knowing it does not make one more zealous,
and people not knowing it does not make one disheartened;
conduct is none higher than this.
Qí Wáng 齊王 suffered from chronic illness,
and sent someone to Sòng 宋 to welcome Wén Zhì 文摯.
When Wén Zhì 文摯 arrived,
he examined the King’s illness
and told the Crown Prince:
“The King’s illness can certainly be cured.
However,
if the King’s illness is cured,
then I, Zhì 摯, will surely be killed.”
The Crown Prince asked:
“Why?”
Wén Zhì 文摯 replied:
“Unless the King is angered, his illness cannot be cured;
if the King is angered, then I, Zhì 摯, will surely die.”
The Crown Prince bowed his head and strongly pleaded, saying:
“If only the King’s illness can be cured,
I and my mother will contend with our lives before the King for you.
The King will surely favor me and my mother.
Please, sir, do not worry.”
Wén Zhì 文摯 said:
“Very well.
I ask to die for the King.”
He set a date with the Crown Prince,
but then failed to appear three times.
Qí Wáng 齊王 was already furious.
When Wén Zhì 文摯 arrived,
he did not untie his shoes before stepping onto the bed,
and trod on the King’s robe.
He asked about the King’s illness.
The King was angry and did not speak to him.
Wén Zhì 文摯 then spoke words to further infuriate the King.
The King shouted and rose,
and his illness was then cured.
The King was greatly enraged and displeased,
and intended to boil Wén Zhì 文摯 alive.
The Crown Prince and the Queen urgently pleaded against it but could not succeed.
Indeed, Wén Zhì 文摯 was boiled alive in a cauldron.
He was cooked for three days and three nights,
but his countenance did not change.
Wén Zhì 文摯 said:
“If you truly wish to kill me,
then why not cover the cauldron
to cut off the qi of yin and yang?”
The King had it covered,
and only then did Wén Zhì 文摯 die.
It is easy to be loyal in a well-governed age,
but difficult to be loyal in a corrupt age.
Wén Zhì 文摯 was not unaware that curing the King’s illness would lead to his own death;
he acted for the Crown Prince, accomplishing his righteousness through difficulty.
11.3 《Zhōng Lián 忠廉》
The third says:
That which the scholar deems inviolable is what he values greatly;
if he values it greatly, it is more esteemed than wealth and high position,
and profit is insufficient to sway his intent.
Though nominally a feudal lord,
actually possessing ten thousand chariots,
it is insufficient to bend his will.
If truly humiliated, he finds no joy in living.
Such a person,
if he has power, will certainly not be selfish;
if he holds office, will certainly not be corrupt;
if he leads troops, will certainly not retreat.
Loyal ministers are also like this.
If it benefits the lord and is advantageous to the state, they will not dare to refuse, sacrificing their lives and abandoning their families to pursue it. If a state has such scholars,
then it can be said to have men of worth.
Such men are indeed hard to find,
and the trouble is that even if one gets them, one might not be wise enough to utilize them.
Wú Wáng 吳王 wanted to kill Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌, but no one could kill him.
Wú Wáng 吳王 was troubled by this.
Yāo Lí 要離 said:
“I can do it.”
Wú Wáng 吳王 said:
“How can you?
I once pursued him with six horses along the river,
but could not catch him;
I shot arrows at him,
having my hands full on both sides,
but could not hit him.
Now, when you draw a sword, you cannot lift your arm;
when you get into a chariot, you cannot climb onto the crossbar.
How can you?”
Yāo Lí 要離 said:
“A scholar’ worries about not being courageous,
why worry about not being able?
If Your Majesty can truly assist,
I request to surely be able.”
Wú Wáng 吳王 said:
“Very well.”
The next morning, Wú Wáng 吳王 accused Yāo Lí 要離 of a crime,
seized his wife and children,
burned them, and scattered their ashes.
Yāo Lí 要離 fled
and went to see Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 in Wèi 衛.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 was pleased and said:
“Wú Wáng 吳王’s wickedness
is what you have seen
and what the feudal lords know.
Now that you have escaped and left, that is also good.”
Yāo Lí 要離 stayed with Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 for a while.
He then said to Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌:
“The wickedness of Wú 吳 is becoming even more severe.
I ask to go with the Prince to seize the state.”
Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 said:
“Good.”
Thereupon, he and Yāo Lí 要離 crossed the river together.
In the middle of the river,
Yāo Lí 要離 drew his sword and stabbed Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 grabbed him
and threw him into the river.
When he floated up, he took him again and threw him in.
This happened three times.
Finally, he said:
“You are the finest warrior in the world.
I grant you this to complete your name.”
Yāo Lí 要離 was spared from death
and returned to Wú 吳.
Wú Wáng 吳王 was greatly pleased
and asked to share the state with him.
Yāo Lí 要離 said:
“No.
I request to surely die.”
Wú Wáng 吳王 stopped him.
Yāo Lí 要離 said:
“Killing my wife and children, burning them and scattering their ashes
to facilitate this matter,
I consider to be inhumane.
To kill a new lord for an old lord,
I consider to be unrighteous.
To be grabbed and float in the river,
thrown in and come out three times,
was merely a favor from Wángzǐ Qìngjì 王子慶忌 who did not kill me.
I am already humiliated.
To be inhumane and unrighteous,
and moreover already humiliated,
I cannot live.”
Wú Wáng 吳王 could not stop him,
and he indeed fell on his sword and died.
Yāo Lí 要離 can be said not to have been moved by rewards.
Therefore, to not abandon one’s righteousness in the face of great profit
can be called incorruptible.
Because of his incorruptibility, he did not forget his humiliation due to wealth and high position.
Wèi Yìgōng 衛懿公 had a minister named Hóng Yǎn 弘演,
who was away on an envoy mission.
The Dí 翟 people attacked Wèi 衛.
Its people said:
“Those whom our lord grants positions and salaries
are cranes;
those whom he values and enriches
are palace women.
If the lord sends palace women and cranes to fight,
how can we fight?”
Thereupon, they dispersed and left.
When the Dí 翟 people arrived,
they reached Yìgōng 懿公 at Róngzé 榮澤,
killed him,
and ate all his flesh,
leaving only his liver.
When Hóng Yǎn 弘演 arrived,
he reported his mission to the liver.
After finishing,
he cried out to heaven and wept.
After expressing his utmost grief, he stopped
and said:
“I request to be your shroud.”
Thereupon, he committed suicide, first pulling out his own internal organs,
and then placing Yìgōng 懿公’s liver inside.
Huán Gōng heard of this and said,
“The state of Wèi perished
because it was without the Dào.
Now there is a minister like this;
it cannot but be preserved.”
Thereupon, Wèi was re-established in Chǔqiū.
Hóng Yǎn can be called loyal,
sacrificing his life and escaping death to serve his lord.
Not only did he serve his lord,
but he also enabled the ancestral temple of Wèi to be re-established,
and the sacrifices to continue without interruption.
He can be called meritorious.
11.4 *Dāngwù*
Fourth, it says:
If eloquence is not relevant to the discussion,
if trustworthiness is not in accordance with reason,
if courage is not in accordance with righteousness,
if law is not appropriate for the task,
then it is like being confused and riding a swift steed,
or being mad and wielding a Wú Gānjiàng sword.
Those who cause great chaos in the world
are surely these four.
What is valued in eloquence
is its relevance to the discussion;
what is valued in trustworthiness
is its adherence to reason;
what is valued in courage
is its practice of righteousness;
what is valued in law
is its appropriateness for the task.
One of Zhí’s followers asked Zhí,
“Does a thief also have the Dào?”
Zhí said,
“How could he not have the Dào?
To guess what is within the house,
and find it in the hidden compartment, that is sagacity;
to enter first, that is courage;
to exit last, that is righteousness;
to know the opportune moment, that is wisdom;
to distribute evenly, that is benevolence.
Without understanding these five,
one cannot become a great thief;
there is no such person in the world.”
He spoke comprehensively, criticizing the Six Kings and Five Hegemons,
claiming that Yáo had a reputation for unkindness,
Shùn had unfilial conduct,
Yǔ had intentions of excessive drinking,
Tāng and Wǔ had acts of banishment and killing,
and the Five Hegemons had schemes of tyranny and chaos.
The world praises them all,
and people all avoid speaking ill of them,
which is confusion.
Therefore, he was buried holding a golden hammer,
saying,
“When I meet the Six Kings and Five Hegemons below,
I will strike (毃) their heads.”
Such discernment is worse than having no discernment.
In Chǔ, there was a man named Zhígōng.
His father stole a sheep, and Zhígōng reported it to the authorities.
The authorities seized the father and were about to execute him.
Zhígōng requested to take his place.
When he was about to be executed,
he told the officer,
“My father stole a sheep, and I reported it.
Is this not trustworthy?
My father is to be executed, and I requested to take his place.
Is this not filial?
If someone who is trustworthy and filial is executed,
will there be anyone in the state who is not executed?”
Kīng Wáng heard of this
and spared him from execution.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said,
“How strange is Zhígōng’s trustworthiness!
He used his father to gain a reputation.”
Thus, Zhígōng’s trustworthiness
is worse than having no trustworthiness.
In Qí, there were two men who loved bravery.
One lived in the eastern quarter,
the other in the western quarter.
Suddenly, they met on the road and said,
“Shall we have a drink?”
After several rounds of wine,
they said,
“Shall we seek some meat?”
One said,
“Is it your meat?
Or my meat?
Why should we look for other meat?
Let’s just prepare (each other) for dipping.”
Thereupon, they drew their knives and ate each other,
stopping only when dead.
Such courage is worse than having no courage.
Zhòu had three brothers by the same mother.
The eldest was named Wēizǐ Qǐ,
the second was Zhōngyǎn,
and the youngest was Shòudé.
Shòudé was none other than Zhòu,
who was very young.
When Zhòu’s mother gave birth to Wēizǐ Qǐ and Zhōngyǎn, she was still a concubine.
Later, she became the principal wife and gave birth to Zhòu.
Zhòu’s father and mother wanted to enthrone Wēizǐ Qǐ as the crown prince.
The Grand Historian argued based on the law, saying,
“A son by the principal wife
cannot be set aside for a son by a concubine.”
Thus, Zhòu became the heir.
Such an application of law
is worse than having no law.
11.5 *Chángjiàn*
Fifth, it says:
The reason why wisdom differs
is due to long-term vision versus short-term vision.
The present in relation to the past
is like the past in relation to future generations.
The present in relation to future generations
is also like the present in relation to the past.
Therefore, by clearly understanding the present, one can know the past;
by knowing the past, one can know the future.
Past, present, and future are one.
Thus, the sage understands a thousand years of the past
and a thousand years of the future.
Jīng Wén Wáng said,
“Guǎn Ráo has repeatedly offended me with righteousness and
contravened me with ritual.
Living with him makes me uneasy.
But if I abandon him, I will gain nothing.
If I do not honor him with office myself,
then when there are sages in later generations,
they will criticize me.”
Thereupon, he appointed him as a Grandee of the Fifth Rank.
“Shēn Hóu Bó is good at maintaining my will.
Whatever I desire, he does it for me first.
Living with him makes me feel at ease.
If I abandon him, I will suffer no loss.
If I do not distance him myself,
then when there are sages in later generations,
they will criticize me.”
Thereupon, he sent him away.
Shēn Hóu Bó went to Zhèng,
flattered the heart of the lord of Zhèng,
and did what he desired first.
After three years, he understood the government of the state of Zhèng.
Five months later, the people of Zhèng killed him.
Thus, the sages of later generations
made Wén Wáng act well in the ancient world.
Jìn Píng Gōng had a large bell cast.
When the bell was finished, he had the craftsmen listen to it.
They all thought it was in tune,
but then he showed it to Shī Kuàng. Shī Kuàng said,
“It is out of tune.
Please recast it.”
Píng Gōng said,
“The craftsmen all think it is in tune,
but you think it is out of tune.
Why?”
Shī Kuàng said,
“If there are no connoisseurs of music in later generations, then so be it. But if there are connoisseurs of music,
they will know that the bell is out of tune.
I secretly feel ashamed for you, my lord.”
When it reached Shī Juān,
he indeed knew that the bell was out of tune.
This shows that Shī Kuàng wanted the bell to be perfectly in tune,
for the sake of future connoisseurs of music.
Lǚ Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was enfeoffed in Lǔ.
These two lords were very friendly with each other.
They said to each other, “How should one govern a state?”
Tàigōng Wàng said,
“Honor the worthy and reward merit.”
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said,
“Cherish relatives and prioritize kindness.”
Tàigōng Wàng said,
“Lǔ will be weakened from this.”
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said,
“Even if Lǔ is weakened,
those who possess Qí will certainly not be of the Lǚ clan.”
Thereafter, Qí grew larger day by day,
until it became a hegemon.
Twenty-four generations later, Tián Chéngzǐ possessed the state of Qí.
Lǔ was weakened day by day,
until it barely maintained its existence as a vassal.
Thirty-four generations later, it perished.
Wú Qǐ (吳起) governed the territory west of the Hé (河).
Wáng Cuò (王錯) slandered him to Wèi Wǔhóu (魏武侯).
Wǔhóu (武侯) sent someone to summon him.
When Wú Qǐ (吳起) arrived at Ānmén (岸門),
he stopped his chariot to rest, and gazing towards Xīhé (西河),
tears streamed down his face.
His servant said to Wú Qǐ (吳起):
“I have secretly observed your intentions;
you regard letting go of the world as easily as letting go of a slipper.
Now you are leaving Xīhé (西河) and weeping,
why is this?”
Wú Qǐ (吳起) wiped his tears and replied:
“You do not understand.

If the lord trusts me and allows me to exert my full ability, Qín (秦) can certainly be vanquished, and Xīhé (西河) can become a royal domain. Now, the lord listens to the words of slanderers and does not understand me.
It will not be long before Xīhé (西河) is taken by Qín (秦),
and the state of Wèi (魏) will be diminished from this point on.”
Wú Qǐ (吳起) indeed left Wèi (魏) and entered Chǔ (楚).
After some time,
Xīhé (西河) was entirely taken by Qín (秦),
Wèi (魏) daily grew weaker, and Qín (秦) daily grew stronger.
This is why Wú Qǐ (吳起) foresaw it and wept.
Wèi Gōngshū Cuò (魏公叔痤) fell ill.
Huì Wáng (惠王) went to inquire about his health,
saying:
“Gōngshū’s (公叔) illness is indeed
very severe!
What shall we do about the altars of the land and grain?”
Gōngshū (公叔) replied:
“I have a chamberlain, Gōngsūn Yāng (公孫鞅);
I wish Your Majesty would heed him in governing the state.
If you cannot heed him,
do not allow him to leave the country.”
The King did not respond,
and upon exiting, he said to his attendants:
“Is it not grievous?
With Gōngshū’s (公叔) wisdom,
he now tells寡人 (guǎrén) that I must heed Gōngsūn Yāng (公孫鞅) in governing the state.
How perverse!”
When Gōngshū (公叔) died,
Gōngsūn Yāng (公孫鞅) traveled west to Qín (秦).
Qín Xiàogōng (秦孝公) heeded him,
and Qín (秦) indeed grew strong,
while Wèi (魏) indeed grew weak.
It was not Gōngshū Cuò (公叔痤) who was perverse,
but the King of Wèi (魏) who was perverse.
Indeed, the trouble with the perverse
is that they always consider the non-perverse to be perverse.
12.1 The Annals of Jìdōng (季冬紀)
The first part says:
In the month of Jìdōng (季冬):
The sun is in Wùnǚ (婺女).
At dusk, Lóuzhōng (婁中) culminates.
At dawn, Dǐzhōng (氐中) culminates.
Its days are Rén (壬) and Guǐ (癸).
Its emperor is Zhuānxū (顓頊).
Its spirit is Xuánmíng (玄冥).
Its creatures are those with shells.
Its sound is Yǔ (羽).
Its lǜ (律) is Dàlǚ (大呂).
Its number is six.
Its taste is salty.
Its odor is decaying.
Its sacrifice is Xíng (行).
One first sacrifices to the kidneys.
Wild geese face north.
Magpies begin to nest.
Young pheasants crow.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Xuántáng (玄堂),
rides in a black chariot,
drives black horses,
carries black banners,
wears black clothes,
adorns himself with black jade,
and eats millet and pork.
Its vessels are large and covered.
The appropriate official is commanded to perform the great nuó (儺) ceremony,
to perform the pángzhé (旁磔) sacrifice,
to bring out the earth oxen,
to send away the cold qi (氣).
Migratory birds become fierce and swift.
All the sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
and to the emperor’s ministers and the gods of Heaven and Earth are performed.
In this month,
the fishing master is commanded to begin fishing,
and the Son of Heaven personally attends.
Fish are tasted,
and first offered in the ancestral temple.
As ice is abundant,
and the waters are again firm,
ice is commanded to be gathered.
When the ice has been brought in,
the people are instructed
to bring out the five kinds of grain.
The Sīnóng (司農) is commanded
to calculate the plowing work,
to repair plows and hoes,
and to prepare farming implements.
The music master is commanded
to convene a grand wind instrument ensemble and then dismiss it.
The four superintendents
are then commanded to collect firewood and brushwood,
to supply the ancestral temple and the firewood for all a hundred sacrifices.
In this month,
the sun exhausts its position,
the moon exhausts its cycle,
the stars revolve in the heavens,
the reckoning is nearing its end,
the year is about to begin anew,
and the focus is exclusively on agriculture; the people
are not to be otherwise employed.
The Son of Heaven then, with his qīng dàfū (卿大夫), rectifies the national statutes,
discusses the seasonal ordinances,
to prepare for the appropriateness of the coming year.
The Tàishǐ (太史) is commanded
to arrange the ranks of the feudal lords,
and to allot them sacrificial animals,
to supply the offerings for Huángtiān Shàngdì (皇天上帝) and the altars of the land and grain.
The states of the same surname are commanded
to supply fodder and livestock for the ancestral temple.
The zǎi (宰) are ordered to list the numbers of land and fields from the qīng dàfū (卿大夫) down to the common people, and to assign them sacrificial animals,
to supply the sacrifices for famous mountains, forests, and rivers.

All the people in the nine provinces under Heaven must contribute their efforts to supply the sacrifices for Huángtiān Shàngdì (皇天上帝), the altars of the land and grain, and the ancestral temple, mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
When this command is carried out,
it is called “one cycle completed,”
which is thirty-two days.
If in Jìdōng (季冬) the autumn ordinances are implemented,
then white dew will fall early,
shelled creatures will become monstrous,
and neighboring states will seek protection.
If the spring ordinances are implemented,
then many embryos will be damaged,
the state will have many persistent diseases;
this is called "rebellion."
If the summer ordinances are implemented,
then floods will ruin the state,
seasonal snow will not fall,
and ice and frost will melt away.
12.2 The Virtue of Scholars (士節)
The second part says:
A scholar’s conduct
is to not avoid difficulty when righteousness is involved,
to forget profit when facing adversity,
to sacrifice life for the sake of justice,
and to view death as returning home.
One who is like this
cannot be befriended by a ruler,
nor can he be made a minister by the Son of Heaven.
The great ones establish order throughout the world,
the lesser ones establish order in a single state;
this must be achieved through such people.
Therefore, for a lord who desires to achieve great accomplishments and fame,
it is imperative to diligently seek out such people.
A wise ruler labors in seeking out people,
and rests in governing affairs.
In Qí (齊), there was a man named Běiguō Sāo (北郭騷).
He wove fishing nets,
bound cattails and reeds,
and wove straw sandals
to support his mother, but it was still not enough.
He went to the door and met Yàn Zǐ (晏子), saying:
“I wish to beg for something to support my mother.”
Yàn Zǐ’s (晏子) servant said to Yàn Zǐ (晏子):
“This is a worthy man of Qí (齊).
His righteousness prevents him from serving the Son of Heaven as a minister,
or befriending feudal lords.
He does not take profit carelessly,
nor does he avoid harm carelessly.
Now, he begs for something to support his mother;
this means he approves of your righteousness,
you must give it to him.”
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) sent someone to divide grain from the granary and gold from the treasury and give it to him.
He declined the gold but accepted the grain.
After some time,
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) was suspected by the Lord of Qí (齊)
and fled.
He passed by Běiguō Sāo’s (北郭騷) door and bid farewell.
Běiguō Sāo (北郭騷) bathed and came out to meet Yàn Zǐ (晏子), saying:
“Where are you going, Master?”
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) replied:
“I am suspected by the Lord of Qí (齊),
and am going to flee.”
Běiguō Zǐ (北郭子) said:
“Master, take care!”
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) got into his chariot,
sighed deeply and exclaimed:
“Is it not fitting that I, Yīng (嬰), should flee?
I truly do not know men well enough!”
Yàn Zǐ (晏子) departed.
Běiguō Zǐ summoned his friend and told him:
“I admire Yàn Zǐ’s righteousness,
and once I begged him for means to support my mother.
I have heard it said:
‘For those who support their parents,
they themselves must bear the difficulty.’
Now Yàn Zǐ is suspected,
and I will die to clear his name.”
He donned his clothes and cap,
ordered his friend to hold a sword and carry a casket, and follow him.
They arrived at the sovereign’s court,
and he requested to speak, saying:
“Yàn Zǐ
is a worthy man of the world.
If he leaves now, the state of Qí will surely be invaded.
Since the state will surely be invaded,
it is better to die first.
I request to offer my head to clear Yàn Zǐ’s name.”
Then he said to his friend:
“Put my head in the casket,
and offer it as proof.”
He withdrew and slit his own throat.
His friend then presented it as proof.
His friend said to the onlookers:
“Běiguō Zǐ died for the sake of the state,
and I will die for Běiguō Zǐ.”
He also withdrew and slit his own throat.
The sovereign of Qí heard of this,
was greatly alarmed,
and rode a post-horse to personally pursue Yàn Zǐ.
He caught up with him at the outskirts of the capital,
pleaded with him, and brought him back.
Yàn Zǐ had no choice but to return.
When he heard that Běiguō Sāo had died to clear his name,
he said:
“Is it not fitting that I, Yīng, should have departed?
I have indeed failed to understand gentlemen well enough.”
12.3 《Jiè Lì》
Thirdly:
It is easy to gain followers with wealth and nobility,
but difficult to gain followers in poverty and lowliness.
When Jìn Wén Gōng was exiled,
wandering throughout the world,
destitute and lowly,
Jiè Zǐtuī did not leave him.
This was due to something he possessed.
When he returned to his state and had a myriad chariots,
Jiè Zǐtuī left him.
This was due to something he lacked.
He could manage the difficult,
but not the easy.
This is why Wén Gōng did not become a true king.
When Jìn Wén Gōng returned to his state,
Jiè Zǐtuī refused to accept rewards.
He composed a poem for himself, saying:
“There was a dragon flying,
traversing the whole world.
Five serpents followed it,
serving as its assistants.
The dragon returned to its homeland,
and found its place.
Four serpents followed it,
and received its dew and rain.
One serpent was ashamed,
and died upright in the wilderness.
It hung a letter on the sovereign’s gate,
and then hid beneath the mountain.”
Wén Gōng heard this and said:
“Alas!
This must be Jiè Zǐtuī.”
He avoided his dwelling, changed his clothes,
and commanded his officers and common people, saying:
“Whoever can find Jiè Zǐtuī
shall be granted the rank of highest minister
and a million acres of land.”
Someone encountered him in the mountains,
carrying a pot, a lid, and a parasol.
He asked:
“May I ask where Jiè Zǐtuī is?”
He replied:
“If Jiè Zǐtuī truly does not wish to be seen and desires to be hidden,
how could I alone know of him?”
Then he turned his back and walked away,
never to be seen again throughout his life.
How greatly divergent are the hearts of men!
Is it not profound?
Today’s fortune-seekers,
rising early and retiring late,
with parched lips and dry throats,
ponder it day and night,
yet still cannot obtain it.
Now, having obtained it, he earnestly flees from it.
Jiè Zǐtuī is far removed from worldly ways.
In the East, there was a gentleman named Yuán Jīngmù.
He was going somewhere
but starved on the road.
A bandit from Húfù, named Qiū,
saw him and offered a pot of food to feed him.
Yuán Jīngmù ate three mouthfuls before he could see.
He asked:
“Who are you?”
He replied:
“I am Qiū, a man from Húfù.”
Yuán Jīngmù said:
“Alas!
Are you not a bandit?
Why did you feed me?
By my principles, I cannot eat your food.”
He pressed his hands to the ground and tried to vomit it out.
It did not come out,
and with a gasping sound, he collapsed and died.
When the people of Zhèng descended to Xīyán,
when Zhuāng Qiáo rampaged through Yǐng,
when the people of Qín besieged Chángpíng,
Hán, Jīng, and Zhào —
the generals, commanders, and noblemen of these three states were all mostly arrogant,
and their soldiers and common people were all mostly strong.
They violently attacked each other, killing each other.
The weak and fragile bowed and pleaded to avoid death,
and their soldiers in turn ate each other,
not discerning righteousness,
hoping to luckily survive.
If Yuán Jīngmù had eaten and not died,
he would have detested its unrighteousness and still not been willing to avoid death.
Now, these people conspire for themselves;
is this not far-fetched?
12.4 《Chéng Lián》
Fourthly:
Stone can be broken,
but its hardness cannot be taken away;
cinnabar can be ground,
but its redness cannot be taken away.
Hardness and redness
are inherent in their nature.
Nature
is what is received from Heaven;
it is not chosen or acquired.
The self-respecting noble gentleman
cannot be easily tainted and defiled,
just like this.
In ancient times, when Zhōu was about to rise,
there were two gentlemen
residing in Gūzhú,
named Bó Yí and Shú Qí.
The two said to each other:
“We hear that in the West there is an autocratic lord
who seems to possess the Dao.
Why should we remain here now?”
The two journeyed west to Zhōu,
and arrived at Qíyáng,
but Wén Wáng had already passed away.
Wǔ Wáng ascended the throne.
Observing the virtue of Zhōu,
the king sent Shú Dàn to meet Jiāo Gé within the four inner regions of Cì,
and made an oath with him, saying:
“Your wealth shall be increased by three grades,
and your office shall be advanced by one rank.”
He made three identical written oaths,
sealed them with the blood of a sacrifice,
buried one within the four inner regions,
and each took one copy home.
He also sent the Grand Guardian, Zhào Gōng, to meet Wēizǐ Kǎi beneath Gòngtóu,
and made an oath with him, saying:
“You shall forever be a grand marquis,
maintain the constant sacrifices of Yīn,
mutually support Sānglín,
and be entitled to Mèngzhū as your private domain.”
He made three identical written oaths,
sealed them with the blood of a sacrifice,
buried one beneath Gòngtóu,
and each took one copy home.
Bó Yí and Shú Qí heard of this,
looked at each other and laughed, saying:
“Alas,
how strange!
This is not what we call the Dao.
In ancient times, when Shénnóng Shì ruled the world,
he offered timely sacrifices with utmost reverence but did not pray for blessings. Regarding people,
he governed with utmost loyalty and trustworthiness but sought nothing in return.
He delighted in righteousness and shared it,
delighted in good governance and shared it.
He did not use others’ flaws to perfect himself,
nor others’ lowliness to elevate himself.
Now Zhōu, seeing Yīn’s depravity and chaos,
hastily acts as its rectifier and governor,
plotting from above and engaging in bribery,
blocking hills and safeguarding power.
They slaughter sacrificial animals and make oaths as a sign of trustworthiness,
using the four inner regions and Gòngtóu to make their actions clear,
proclaiming dreams to persuade the masses,
and engaging in killing and conquest to seize profit.
By these means they succeed Yīn;
this is exchanging chaos for tyranny.”
I have heard that the gentlemen of antiquity,
when they encountered an age of order,
did not shirk their responsibilities,
and when they encountered an age of chaos,
they would not compromise their existence.
Now the world is dark,
the virtue of Zhōu has declined.
Rather than align myself with Zhōu and defile my person,
it is better to avoid it and keep my conduct pure."
The two men traveled north,
and starved to death beneath Shǒuyáng.
Among human emotions, there is nothing that does not have something held dear,
and nothing that does not have something held lightly.
When one has something held dear, one desires to preserve it;
when one has something held lightly, one uses it to nurture what is held dear.
Bóyí and Shúqí,
these two gentlemen,
both sacrificed their lives and abandoned their existence to uphold their ideals;
their priorities were fixed beforehand.
12.5 《Bù Qīn》
Fifth:
The world is held lighter than the self,
yet a gentleman offers his self for others.
Those who offer their self for others,
