such is their importance,
yet people do not know this.
By what path can they be gained?
A sagacious ruler must know his gentlemen,
and so gentlemen exhaust their strength and wisdom,
speak frankly and contend fiercely,
without shirking hardship.
Yù Ràng and Gōngsūn Hóng exemplify this.
At that time,
Zhì Bó and Méngcháng Jūn understood this.
The rulers of the world today,
rejoice when they acquire a hundred *lǐ* of territory,
and all within their four borders offer congratulations.
But they do not rejoice when they gain a gentleman,
nor do they know to congratulate each other.
They do not understand the relative importance of things.
Tāng and Wǔ
ruled kingdoms of a thousand chariots,
and all gentlemen rallied to them.
Jié and Zhòu
were Sons of Heaven,
yet all gentlemen abandoned them.
Kǒng and Mò
were commoner scholars;
lords of ten thousand chariots
and rulers of a thousand chariots
could not compete with them for gentlemen.
From this perspective,
dignity, wealth, and power are not enough to attract gentlemen;
one must truly know them, and only then is it possible.
Yù Ràng's friend said to Yù Ràng:
"Why is your conduct so misguided?
You once served the Fàn clan and the Zhōngháng clan;
the feudal lords completely destroyed them,
yet you did not avenge them.
But when it came to the Zhì clan,
you insisted on avenging them.
Why?"
Yù Ràng said:
"I shall tell you the reason.
As for the Fàn clan and the Zhōngháng clan,
when I was cold, they did not clothe me;
when I was hungry, they did not feed me.
They made me share my sustenance with a thousand others.
This was treating me as a commoner.
If others treat me as a commoner,
then I will serve them as a commoner.
But with the Zhì clan, it was different.
When going out, he transported me in his carriage;
when staying in, he provided me amply with sustenance.
Among the numerous officials in the court,
he invariably showed me special courtesy.
This was treating me as a national hero.
If others treat me as a national hero,
then I will serve them as a national hero."
Yù Ràng,
a national hero,
still considered how others treated him.
How much more so for an average person?
Méngcháng Jūn was forming an alliance.
Gōngsūn Hóng said to Méngcháng Jūn:
"You had better send someone west to observe the King of Qín.
Perhaps the King of Qín is a sagely ruler;
you might fear you cannot even become his minister,
how then can you have time to form an alliance to challenge him?
Perhaps the King of Qín is an unworthy ruler;
it would not be too late for you to form an alliance to challenge him then."
Méngcháng Jūn said:
"Excellent.
I wish to ask you to go."
Gōngsūn Hóng respectfully assented,
and went to Qín with ten chariots.
King Zhāo of Qín heard of it,
and wished to humiliate him with words
to observe Gōngsūn Hóng.
When Gōngsūn Hóng saw King Zhāo,
King Zhāo said:
"How large is the territory of Xuē?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"A hundred *lǐ*."
King Zhāo smiled and said:
"My state,
with territory thousands of *lǐ* in extent,
still dares not to initiate a challenge.
Now Méngcháng Jūn's territory is a mere hundred *lǐ*,
and yet he wishes to challenge me. Is that permissible?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"Méngcháng Jūn loves gentlemen,
but Your Majesty does not."
King Zhāo said:
"How does Méngcháng Jūn love gentlemen?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"Those who righteously refuse to serve the Son of Heaven,
and refuse to befriend feudal lords,
who, when successful, are not ashamed to be a ruler,
and when unsuccessful, are unwilling to be a minister –
of such men there are three.
Those who can govern and serve as teachers to Guǎn [Zhòng] and Shāng [Yāng],
whose righteous counsel is heeded and followed,
and who can make their lords become hegemons or true kings –
of such men there are five.
Those who, should a stern ruler of ten thousand chariots
insult their envoy,
would retreat and commit suicide,
and would stain their clothes with their own blood –
of such men there are seven, like your servant."
King Zhāo smiled and apologized, saying:
"Why does the guest speak like this?
I appreciate Méngcháng Jūn, and wish the guest to carefully convey my intentions."
Gōngsūn Hóng said: "Respectfully assented."
Gōngsūn Hóng can be said to be 'unassailable'.
King Zhāo
was a powerful king.
Méngcháng Jūn
was a lord of a thousand chariots.
To establish the righteousness of a thousand-chariot state and be unassailable
can truly be called a gentleman's achievement.
12.6 《Xù Yì》
In the eighth year of Qín,
the year being Guīntān,
in autumn,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day, the first day of the month,
on that first day of the month,
a worthy person inquired about the "Twelve Annals."
Wénxìn Hóu said:
"I once learned the teachings of Huángdì to Zhuānxù.
He said: 'There is a great circle above,
and a great square below.
If you can emulate them,
you will be the father and mother of the people.'
It is said that in the pure ages of antiquity,
this was the way to emulate Heaven and Earth.
The 'Twelve Annals'
are for recording order and chaos, survival and destruction,
and for understanding longevity and early death, good and bad fortune.
Look up to Heaven,
examine the Earth below,
and discern humans in between.
If one does this, right and wrong, permissible and impermissible, will have nowhere to hide.
Heaven says 'follow,'
and following leads to life;
Earth says 'solidify,'
and solidifying leads to peace;
Humans say 'trust,'
and trust leads to obedience.
When all three are appropriate,
action occurs effortlessly.
'Action' here
means acting according to principle.
Follow the numbers,
adhere to the principles,
and equalize one's personal biases.
Indeed, private viewing makes the eyes blind,
private hearing makes the ears deaf,
and private deliberation makes the mind mad.
If all three are privately focused, wisdom has no way to be public.
If wisdom is not public,
then blessings daily diminish,
and calamities daily grow.
One can know this by observing the setting sun in the west."
Zhào Xiāngzǐ was strolling in his park,
and came to a bridge.
His horse shied and refused to advance.
Qīngpíng was attending as charioteer.
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Go forward and look beneath the bridge;
it seems there is someone there."
Qīngpíng (青荓) advanced and looked beneath the beam.
Yùràng (豫讓) lay back down,
feigning death.
He yelled at Qīngpíng (青荓),
“Go!
I, your elder, am about to undertake an important matter.”
Qīngpíng (青荓) said,
“We have been friends since youth.
You are about to undertake a great deed,
and if I speak of it,
that would be to lose the way of friendship.
You are about to assassinate my lord,
and if I do not speak of it,
that would be to lose the way of a minister.
For one such as me, only death is fitting.”
Thereupon, he withdrew and killed himself.
Qīngpíng (青荓) did not rejoice in death;
he valued the integrity of a minister
and detested abandoning the way of friendship.
Qīngpíng (青荓) and Yùràng (豫讓) can be called friends.
13.1 *Yǒu Shǐ* (有始)
First, it says: Heaven and Earth have a beginning.
Heaven forms through subtlety,
Earth takes shape through solidity.
The union and harmony of Heaven and Earth
is the great principle of generation.
One discerns this through cold and heat, sun and moon, day and night;
one explains it through diverse forms, diverse capabilities, and different suitabilities.
For things, union leads to formation, separation to generation.
To understand union and formation,
to understand separation and generation,
then Heaven and Earth are balanced.
Being balanced means
that one must examine their nature and attend to their forms.
Heaven has nine fields (jiǔyě 九野),
Earth has nine regions (jiǔzhōu 九州),
the land has nine mountains (jiǔshān 九山),
mountains have nine passes (jiǔsài 九塞),
marshes have nine swamps (jiǔsǒu 九藪),
winds have eight types (bāděng 八等),
waters have six rivers (liùchuān 六川).
What are the nine fields?
The center is called Jūntiān (鈞天);
its stars are Jiǎo (角), Kàng (亢), Dī (氐).
The east is called Cāngtiān (蒼天);
its stars are Fáng (房), Xīn (心), Wěi (尾).
The northeast is called Biàntiān (變天);
its stars are Jī (箕), Dǒu (斗), Qiānniú (牽牛).
The north is called Xuántiān (玄天);
its stars are Wùnǚ (婺女), Xū (虛), Wēi (危), Yíngshì (營室).
The northwest is called Yōutiān (幽天);
its stars are Dōngbì (東壁), Kuí (奎), Lóu (婁).
The west is called Hàotiān (顥天);
its stars are Wèi (胃), Mǎo (昴), Bì (畢).
The southwest is called Zhūtiān (朱天);
its stars are Zīsuī (觜嶲), Cān (參), Dōngjǐng (東井).
The south is called Yántiān (炎天);
its stars are Yúguǐ (輿鬼), Liǔ (柳), Qīxīng (七星).
The southeast is called Yángtiān (陽天);
its stars are Zhāng (張), Yì (翼), Zhěn (軫).
What are the nine regions?
Between the Hé (河) and the Hàn (漢) is Yùzhōu (豫州),
namely Zhōu (周).
Between the two Hé (河) rivers is Jìzhōu (冀州),
namely Jìn (晉).
Between the Hé (河) and the Jì (濟) is Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
namely Wèi (衛).
The east is Qīngzhōu (青州),
namely Qí (齊).
Above the Sì (泗) is Xúzhōu (徐州),
namely Lǔ (魯).
The southeast is Yángzhōu (楊州),
namely Yuè (越).
The south is Jīngzhōu (荊州),
namely Chǔ (楚).
The west is Yōngzhōu (雍州),
namely Qín (秦).
The north is Yōuzhōu (幽州),
namely Yān (燕).
What are the nine mountains?
Kuàijī (會稽),
Tàishān (太山),
Wángwū (王屋),
Shǒushān (首山),
Tàihuá (太華),
Qíshān (岐山),
Tàiháng (太行),
Yángcháng (羊腸),
Mèngmén (孟門).
What are the nine passes?
Dàfén (大汾),
Míng'è (冥阨),
Jīngruǎn (荊阮),
Fāngchéng (方城),
Yáo (殽),
Jǐngxíng (井陘),
Cīchùlìngcī (疵處令疵),
Gōuzhù (句注),
Jūyōng (居庸).
What are the nine swamps?
Jùqū (具區) in Wú (吳),
Yúnmèng (雲夢) in Chǔ (楚),
Yánghuá (陽華) in Qín (秦),
Dàlù (大陸) in Jìn (晉),
Pǔtián (圃田) in Liáng (梁) and Zhèng (鄭),
Mèngzhū (孟諸) in Sòng (宋),
Hǎiyú (海隅) in Qí (齊),
Jùlù (鉅鹿) in Zhào (趙),
Dàzhāozhāoyú (大昭昭余) in Yān (燕).
What are the eight winds?
The northeast is called Yánfēng (炎風),
the east is called Tāofēng (滔風),
the southeast is called Xūnfēng (熏風),
the south is called Jùfēng (巨風),
the southwest is called Qīfēng (淒風),
the west is called Liáofēng (飂風),
the northwest is called Lìfēng (厲風),
the north is called Hánfēng (寒風).
What are the six rivers?
The Héshuǐ (河水),
Chìshuǐ (赤水),
Liáoshuǐ (遼水),
Hēishuǐ (黑水),
Jiāngshuǐ (江水),
Huáishuǐ (淮水).
Within the Four Seas,
it is 28,000 *lǐ* (里) from east to west,
and 26,000 *lǐ* (里) from north to south.
Waterways extend 8,000 *lǐ* (里),
and those that receive water also extend 8,000 *lǐ* (里).
There are six main valleys,
six hundred famous rivers,
three thousand land-feeding streams,
and ten thousand small streams.
Within the four cardinal points,
it is 509,700 *lǐ* (里) from east to west,
and also 509,700 *lǐ* (里) from north to south.
All the myriad stars revolve with Heaven,
but the pivot star (tiānshū jíxīng 天樞極星) does not move.
At the winter solstice, the sun travels the distant path,
circling the four cardinal points;
this is called Xuánmíng (玄明).
At the summer solstice, the sun travels the near path,
and it participates in the above.
Beneath the pivot, there is no day or night.
South of the báimín (白民),
beneath the jiànmù (建木),
at midday there is no shadow,
and if one calls, there is no echo;
this is indeed the center of Heaven and Earth.
Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things
are like one person's body;
this is called Great Unity (dàtóng 大同).
The multitude of ears, eyes, noses, and mouths,
the multitude of five grains, cold, and heat;
this is called Great Diversity (zhòngyì 眾異).
Then the myriad things are complete.
Heaven bestows the myriad things,
and the sages observe them
to discern their categories.
The explanation lies in how Heaven and Earth take shape,
how thunder and lightning are produced,
the essence of yin (yīn 陰) and yang (yáng 陽) materials,
and where people and beasts find peace.
13.2 *Yìng Tóng* (應同)
Second, it says: Whenever a sovereign or king is about to rise,
Heaven must first show auspicious signs to the common people.
During the time of Huángdì (黃帝),
Heaven first showed large earthworms and large ants.
Huángdì (黃帝) said, "The *tǔ* (土) *qì* (氣) prevails."
Because the *tǔ* (土) *qì* (氣) prevailed,
its color was yellow,
and its affairs were those of *tǔ* (土).
When Yǔ was alive,
Heaven first revealed that the grass and trees would not wither in autumn and winter.
Yǔ said, "The wood element is ascendant."
Since the wood element was ascendant,
its color was therefore esteemed as green,
and its affair was wood.
When Tāng was alive,
Heaven first revealed that metal blades grew from water.
Tāng said, "The metal element is ascendant."
Since the metal element was ascendant,
its color was therefore esteemed as white,
and its affair was metal.
When King Wén was alive,
Heaven first revealed a red crow holding a vermilion book in its beak, gathering on the altars of Zhōu.
King Wén said, "The fire element is ascendant."
Since the fire element was ascendant,
its color was therefore esteemed as red,
and its affair was fire.
That which replaces fire will certainly be water.
Heaven will first reveal the water element to be ascendant.
When the water element is ascendant,
its color is therefore esteemed as black,
and its affair is water.
When the water element arrives and one does not know to prepare for it,
it will then shift to earth.
Heaven acts at its proper time,
but does not assist agriculture below.
Things of the same kind naturally call to each other;
when their energies are alike, they combine;
when their sounds are similar, they respond.
Thus, strike the `gōng` note and the `gōng` string resonates;
strike the `jiǎo` note and the `jiǎo` string resonates.
Pour water on level ground,
and the water flows to the damp.
Place fire on even kindling,
and the fire goes to the dry.
Mountain clouds are like grass and tangled vegetation;
water clouds are like fish scales;
drought clouds are like smoke and fire;
rain clouds are like water ripples.
There is nothing that does not resemble its origin to show to people.
Thus, one uses a dragon to bring rain,
and uses a body to chase a shadow.
Where an army is stationed,
thorny bushes will surely grow.
Whence misfortune and fortune come,
the common people consider it fate,
how can they know its source?
If nests are overturned and eggs destroyed,
then the fènghuáng will not arrive;
if beasts are disemboweled and their fetuses eaten,
then the qílín will not come;
if marshes are drained and fish taken,
then turtles and dragons will not remain.
The resemblance of things to each other
cannot be fully recorded.
A son does not conceal for his parents,
nor a minister for his ruler.
When they are the same, they come;
when they are different, they leave.
Therefore, even if a ruler is revered,
if he calls white black,
a minister cannot obey;
even if a father is亲亲 (qīnqīn),
if he calls black white,
a son cannot follow.
The Huángdì said:
"Vast and obscure,
relying on the might of Heaven,
and sharing the same energy with the origin."
Therefore it is said that sharing the same energy is superior to sharing the same righteousness;
sharing the same righteousness is superior to sharing the same strength;
sharing the same strength is superior to sharing the same dwelling;
sharing the same dwelling is superior to sharing the same name.
Emperors share the same energy,
kings share the same righteousness,
hegemons share the same strength.
Those who strive share the same dwelling, which is meager;
those who perish share the same name, which is coarse.
The coarser one's wisdom,
the coarser that which one shares;
the more refined one's wisdom,
the more refined that which one shares.
Therefore, in all intentions, one must be refined.
Indeed, refinement
is what the Wǔdì and Sānwáng used to achieve success.
Achievement, order, similarity, and sameness all have their corresponding connections.
Thus, when Yáo acted with goodness, all good things arrived;
when Jié acted with evil, all evil things came.
The "Shāng Zhēn" says:
"Heaven sends down calamities and distributes auspicious signs,
each has its function,"
meaning that fortune and misfortune are sometimes invited by people.
Therefore, a country's disorder is not merely disorder,
but it will also invite invaders.
Disorder alone may not lead to ruin,
but inviting invaders leaves no means of survival.
In the use of troops,
they are used for profit,
and used for righteousness.
Attacking a disordered state leads to swift submission,
and swift submission profits the attacker.
Attacking a disordered state is righteous,
and righteousness brings honor to the attacker.
When there is both honor and profit,
even an average ruler would do it,
how much more so a wise ruler?
Therefore, ceding territory, offering treasures,
and using humble words to submit
are not enough to stop an attack;
only good governance is sufficient.
If there is good governance, those who seek profit will not attack,
and those who seek fame will not invade.
Whenever people attack and invade,
if not for profit, then it is for the sake of fame.
If neither fame nor substance is gained,
even if a country is strong and great,
why would it attack?
The explanation lies in Shǐ Mò's arrival, which caused the discontinuation of the attack on Wèi;
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ can be said to have understood the movements of affairs.
13.3 "Qù Yōu"
The third says:
Those who listen in the world
often have biases;
when there are many biases, listening will surely be erroneous.
There are many reasons for bias,
but the essential ones are always due to what a person likes
or dislikes.
One looking east cannot see the west wall;
one looking south cannot see the north side;
it is because the mind is focused elsewhere.
There was a man who lost his axe.
He suspected his neighbor's son.
He observed his walk, as if he had stolen the axe;
his expression, as if he had stolen the axe;
his speech, as if he had stolen the axe;
his actions and demeanor, everything seemed like he had stolen the axe.
Later, he dug in his own valley and found his axe.
Another day, he saw his neighbor's son again,
and his actions and demeanor were in no way like those of an axe thief.
His neighbor's son had not changed,
but he himself had changed.
This change was due to nothing else
but having a bias.
According to the old laws of Zhū,
armor skirts were made of silk.
Gōngxī Jì told the ruler of Zhū:
"It would be better to use woven cords.
The reason armor is solid
is that it fills the holes.
Now the holes are filled,
but only half the strength is borne.
Moreover, with woven cords, it is not like that;
when the holes are filled, the full strength is borne."
The ruler of Zhū thought this was correct
and said,
"How can we obtain woven cords?"
Gōngxī Jì replied,
"If the ruler uses them, the people will make them."
The ruler of Zhū said,
"Good."
He issued an order,
commanding officials that armor must be made with woven cords.
Gōngxī Jì, knowing his advice had been adopted,
then ordered his own family to make woven cords.
Someone criticized him, saying:
"The reason Gōngxī Jì wanted to use woven cords
is that his family made many of them."
The ruler of Zhū was displeased,
and thereupon issued another order,
commanding officials that armor must not be made with woven cords.
This was the ruler of Zhū's bias.
If making armor with woven cords was beneficial,
even if Gōngxī Jì made many woven cords,
what harm was there?
If using woven cords was not beneficial,
even if Gōngxī Jì made no woven cords,
what good would it do?
Whether woven cords were made or not
was insufficient to discredit Gōngxī Jì's advice.
The intention behind using woven cords
must be carefully examined.
There was an ugly man in Lǔ.
His father went out and saw Shāng Duō,
then returned and told his neighbor,
"Shāng Duō is not as good as my son."
Yet his son was extremely ugly,
and Shāng Duō was extremely beautiful.
That he considered the most beautiful not as good as the most ugly
was a bias due to love.
Therefore, only by knowing the ugliness of beauty
and the beauty of ugliness
can one then truly understand beauty and ugliness.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"He who stakes with tiles is carefree,
he who stakes with a belt-hook is anxious,
he who stakes with gold is fearful.
Their skill is the same,
yet some are fearful;
this must be because they value something external.
When something external is valued,
the inner spirit leaks and becomes depleted."
The people of Lǔ can be said to have valued something external.
This explanation lies in the desire of the Qí people to obtain gold,
and in the mutual jealousy of the Qín Mohists;
all of them had something they particularly cherished.
Lǎodān, however, attained this understanding.
If one stands alone like a planted tree,
one will certainly not conform to the customs of the world,
so how can one be expanded upon?
13.4 *Tīngyán* (Listening to Words)
Fourth: In listening to words, one must be discerning.
Without discernment, good and bad are not distinguished.
When good and bad are not distinguished,
there is no greater chaos.
The Three Dynasties distinguished good and bad,
thus they reigned.
Now, the world is increasingly in decline,
and the Way of the Sage Kings has fallen into disuse and been cut off.
Most rulers of the age excessively indulge in their pleasures,
enlarge their bells and drums,
and lavishly build their terraces, pavilions, parks, and gardens,
thereby seizing the people's wealth;
they lightly risk the lives of the people,
to vent their anger;
the old and weak freeze and starve,
the young and robust are short-lived or emaciated,
almost all are exhausted and impoverished,
and furthermore, they die as captives.
They attack innocent states to seize territory,
and execute guiltless people to gain profit;
yet they wish for the security of their ancestral temples and the safety of their altars of soil and grain –
is this not difficult?
Today, if people say:
"So-and-so has much wealth,
his house is damp and crumbling,
his guard dog is dead,
his situation is ripe for tunneling into,"
they will surely condemn it.
But if they say:
"Such-and-such a state is starving,
its city walls are dilapidated,
its defenders and equipment are few,
it can be attacked and usurped,"
they do not condemn it;
this shows they do not understand categories.
The *Zhōushū* says:
"What is past cannot be reached,
what is coming cannot be awaited;
one who enlightens his own generation
is called Son of Heaven."
Therefore, in the present age,
if there is someone who can distinguish good from bad,
his reigning will not be difficult.
Good and bad are rooted in righteousness,
not in love;
the Way of love and profit is profound.
One who is adrift at sea,
after traveling for a month or so,
rejoices upon seeing something that resembles a human.
When a full year has passed,
he rejoices upon seeing something he once saw in the Central States.
Indeed, the longer one is separated from people,
the deeper one's longing for people becomes!
The people of a chaotic age
have also been separated from Sage Kings for a long time.
Their desire to see them
is ceaseless day and night.
Therefore, the efforts of worthy kings and outstanding scholars who wish to care for the common people
must not be neglected.
Merit precedes fame,
actions precede merit,
words precede actions.
If one does not understand actions, how can one listen to words?
If one does not understand the situation, how can one properly respond to words?
When conveying words to others,
is there a distinction?
Or is there no distinction?
Zàofù first learned by practicing with Dàdòu,
Fēngmén first learned by practicing with Gānyíng,
driving Dàdòu,
shooting Gānyíng,
without changing what people take as their nature.
Not changing this
is how they achieved distant pursuits and swift catches,
and how they eliminated harm and restrained violence.
All people must also have something with which they cultivate their minds,
only then can they listen and speak.
If they do not cultivate their minds,
they cultivate it through learning and inquiry.
There has never been anyone, ancient or modern,
who could listen and speak without learning.
This explanation lies in Bái Guī's refutation of Huìzǐ,
Gōngsūn Lóng's persuasion of Yān Zhāowáng to cease warfare, and his encounter with Kōng Luò,
Kǒng Chuān's debate with Gōngsūn Lóng,
and Zhái Jiǎn's challenging of Huìzǐ's doctrines.
The arguments of these four gentlemen
were all full of complexities
and must be discussed individually.
13.5 *Jǐntīng* (Careful Listening)
Fifth:
In ancient times, Yǔ, while bathing, thrice grasped his hair,
and while eating, thrice rose from his meal,
to respectfully treat worthy scholars,
making clear his own shortcomings.
By making clear his own shortcomings,
he did not contend with others.
He waited for them with pleasantness, ease, and tranquility,
allowing them to express themselves naturally;
he affirmed what was so,
allowing them to speak for themselves.
The rulers of doomed states do the opposite;
they consider themselves superior and belittle others.
When others are belittled, speakers hold back and do not fully express themselves,
and listeners, considering themselves superior, fail to grasp [the truth].
Even if they possess the whole world, what good is it?
This is to turn darkness into light,
chaos into order,
defeat into success,
danger into security.
Hence, Yīn and Zhōu perished,
Bǐ Gān died;
they were perverse and insufficient to be elevated.
Therefore, the nature of a ruler
is not so much mistaken in what he doubts,
but rather in what he does not doubt;
not so much mistaken in what he does not know,
but rather in what he thinks he knows.
Therefore, even if there is no doubt,
even if something is known,
it must be examined by principles,
measured by standards,
and verified by calculations.
If this is done, right and wrong will not be mistaken,
and actions and measures will not be flawed.
How could Yáo have judged the whole world worthy and then tested Shùn?
How could Shùn have judged the whole world worthy and then tested Yǔ?
They made their decisions based on what they heard.
That the ear can make decisions
is contrary to the true nature of life.
Now, deluded people,
if they do not know to turn away from the true nature of life,
and secondly, if they do not know to observe how the Five Emperors and Three Kings achieved success,
then how can they know that their own age is untenable?
How can they know their own shortcomings?
The highest know it,
the next best know that they do not know.
If one does not know, one asks;
if one cannot, one learns.
The *Zhōu Zhēn* says:
"If one reflects on this,
learning virtue is never too late."
Learning from the worthy and asking questions
is how the Three Dynasties prospered.
To not know and yet consider oneself to know
is the root of a hundred calamities.
Fame is not established in vain,
merit is not achieved by itself,
a state does not exist empty-handedly;
there must be worthy individuals.
The Way of the worthy
is profound and difficult to know,
subtle and difficult to perceive.
Therefore, if one sees the worthy and is not moved, one is not stirred in the heart;
if one is not stirred in the heart, one's understanding is not deep.
Not deeply understanding the words of the worthy
is the greatest misfortune.
If the ruler is worthy and the world is well-governed, then the worthy are in high positions;
if the ruler is unworthy and the world is chaotic, then the worthy are in low positions.
Now, the Zhōu dynasty has perished,
and the Son of Heaven has been cut off.
There is no greater chaos than having no Son of Heaven.
Without a Son of Heaven, the strong defeat the weak,
the many oppress the few,
they slaughter each other with weapons,
unable to rest.
The present age is experiencing this.
Therefore, in the present age,
if one seeks a virtuous scholar (yǒudào zhī shì),
then within the four seas, amidst mountains and valleys, in remote and secluded places,
such a one may fortunately be found.
If he is found, what desire will not be fulfilled?
What undertaking will not be accomplished?
Tàigōng fished at Zīquán,
during the reign of Zhòu.
Therefore, King Wén obtained him and became king.
King Wén,
with a thousand chariots;
Zhòu,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
The Son of Heaven lost him, and the state with a thousand chariots gained him.
This is the difference between knowing and not knowing.
The common people,
can be employed without being known,
and commanded without being treated with ritual.
But as for the virtuous scholar (yǒudào zhī shì),
he must be treated with ritual and known,
only then can his intelligence and ability be fully utilized.
The explanation lies in Shèngshū's (勝書) thuyết on Zhōugōng,
which can be called "able to listen";
Qí Huángōng's (齊桓公) meeting with Xiǎochén Jì (小臣稷),
and Wèi Wénhóu's (魏文侯) meeting with Tián Zifāng (田子方),
all can be called "able to treat scholars with ritual."
13.6 《Wùběn》
Sixth:
If we try to observe the records of antiquity,
the assistants of the Three Kings (Sān Wáng),
there was none whose name was not glorious,
and none whose reality was not secure,
because their achievements were great.
The 《Shī》 (詩) says:
"Dark and chilly it is,
clouds rise densely,
watering our public fields,
and extending to our private ones."
The assistants of the Three Kings,
were all able to extend their public achievements to their private benefit.
The assistants of vulgar rulers,
their desire for fame and reality was the same as that of the Three Kings' assistants,
yet none of their names escaped disgrace,
and none of their realities escaped danger,
because they had no achievements (gōng).
They all worry that their own person is not esteemed in the state,
but do not worry that their lord is not esteemed throughout the world;
they all worry that their family is not rich,
but do not worry that their state is not great.
This is why they seek glory but incur greater disgrace,
and seek security but encounter greater danger.
The root of security and danger, glory and disgrace, lies with the lord;
the root of the lord lies with the ancestral temple (zōngmiào);
the root of the ancestral temple lies with the people;
the governance or disorder of the people lies with the officials (yǒusī).
The 《Yì》 (易) says:
"Returning from the path,
what blame is there?
Auspicious."
This means that if the root is not different, then the actions will eventually have joy.
Now, when holding office, they are chaotic;
when facing wealth, they are greedy for gain;
when close to the ruler, they hold back remonstrance;
when leading the multitude, they are weak and timid.
With such conduct, to expect much from the lord,
is this not difficult?
Now, if there is a person here,
whose self-cultivation and accounting are shameful,
and who, upon encountering wealth, exhausts it for himself,
if such a person is rich,
he has no source but theft.
Therefore, glory and wealth do not come by themselves,
but are based on meritorious achievements.
Now, if meritorious achievements are very slight, but expectations are high,
this is deceit;
to seek glory and wealth without meritorious achievements,
this is fraud;
the ways of fraud and deceit,
the gentleman does not follow.
Most people's discussions say:
"If the ruler employs me, the state will certainly be free from trouble."
Employing oneself is not necessarily correct,
and if one still has troubles while deeming oneself virtuous,
how can employing oneself in the state
prevent troubles?
The self
is what one controls.
To abandon what one controls,
and usurp what one does not control,
is perverse;
one cannot yet govern the state or administer officials.
As for internally serving parents
and externally associating with friends,
these can certainly be achieved.
If one is not yet filial to parents,
and not yet sincere with friends,
these are things not yet achieved.
How can one be good at them?
Therefore, when judging a person, do not use what he has not yet achieved,
but use what he has already achieved;
by this, you can know what he has not yet achieved.
In ancient times, those who served rulers
must first prove their ability before being appointed,
and must clarify the situation before accepting.
Even if the lord gives excessively,
the minister does not simply take it.
The 《Dàyǎ》 (大雅) says:
"The Supreme Lord (Shàngdì) looks upon you;
do not have a divided heart,"
this speaks of the conduct of a loyal minister.
The explanation lies in Zhèngjūn's (鄭君) question about the meaning of Bèizhān (被瞻),
and Bó Yí's (薄疑) response to Wèi Sījūn (衛嗣君) with "no heavy taxes."
These two scholars both approached knowing the root.
13.7 《Yù Dà》
Seventh:
Formerly, Shùn (舜) desired to encompass antiquity and the present but did not succeed,
yet he was sufficient to become an Emperor.
Yǔ (禹) desired to be an Emperor but did not succeed,
yet he was sufficient to rectify diverse customs.
Tāng (湯) desired to follow Yǔ but did not succeed,
yet he was sufficient to subdue the four wild regions.
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) desired to equal Tāng but did not succeed,
yet he was sufficient to make the kingly way (wángdào) widely known.
The Five Hegemons (Wǔ Bó) desired to succeed the Three Kings but did not succeed,
yet they were sufficient to become the leaders of the feudal lords.
Kǒngqiū (孔丘) and Mò Dí (墨翟) desired to practice the great way (dàdào) in the world but did not succeed,
yet they were sufficient to achieve prominent fame.
Thus, though a great principle (dàyì) may not be fully realized,
something has already been achieved.
The 《Xiàshū》 (夏書) says:
"The virtue of the Son of Heaven is widely extended,
he is sage and divine,
he is martial and refined."
Therefore, effort lies in deeds,
and deeds lie in greatness.

When the earth is vast, there are auspicious omens (chángxiáng), non-submissive tribes (bùtíng), strange mothers (qímǔ), various beasts (qúndǐ), celestial pheasants (tiāndí), and lack of circumference (bùzhōu).
When mountains are great, there are tigers, leopards, bears, and monstrous insects (xiīqú).
When waters are vast, there are hornless dragons (jiāolóng), dragons (yuán), turtles (tuó), sturgeons (zhān), and perch (wěi).
The 《Shāngshū》 (商書) says:
"From the temple of five generations,
one can observe wonders;
from a chief of ten thousand men,
one can generate strategies."
There are no pools or marshes in an empty room (kōng zhōng),
no great fish in a well,
no tall trees in a new forest.
For the success of any endeavor,
it must rely on spaciousness, vastness, multitude, and duration,
this is truth.
Jìzǐ (季子) said:
"Swallows and sparrows vie for a good spot under a single roof,
mothers and young feed each other,
and joyfully make merry together,
thinking themselves safe.
If the chimney flue cracks,
and fire burns the beams above,
the swallows and sparrows do not change their expression.
Why is this?
They do not know that calamity is about to reach them.
Are they not foolish?
Among ministers, few escape the intelligence of swallows and sparrows.
Ministers promote their ranks, salaries, wealth, and honor;
fathers, sons, and brothers form cliques in a state,
joyfully making merry together,
and thereby endanger their altars of soil and grain (shèjì).
Their situation is as close as the chimney flue,
yet they never know it.
Their intelligence is no different from that of swallows and sparrows.
Therefore it is said:
'If the world is in great chaos,
there are no safe states;
if a state is utterly chaotic,
there are no safe families;
if a family is entirely chaotic,
there are no safe persons.'
This is what is meant.
Therefore, the stability of the small
must rely on the great,
and the security of the great
must rely on the small.
Small and great, noble and humble,
mutually depend on each other,
only then can all find their joy."
The stabilization of the humble and small lies in the nobility of the great.
The explanation lies in Bó Yí's (薄疑) thuyết to Wèi Sījūn (衛嗣君) with the kingly art (wángshù),
Dù Hè's (杜赫) thuyết to Zhōu Zhāowénjūn (周昭文君) on pacifying the world,
and Kuāng Zhāng's (匡章) refutation of Huìzǐ (惠子) by demonstrating the kingly status of the King of Qí (Qí Wáng).
14.1 《Xiàoxíng》
Chapter One:
In general, governing the world and administering the state
must prioritize the root before the branches.
What is meant by the root
is not farming, cultivating, planting, and harvesting;
it is cultivating the people.
Cultivating the people
is not making the poor rich or
the few numerous;
it is cultivating their foundation.
In cultivating the foundation, nothing is more valuable than filial piety (xiào).
If the ruler is filial,
his name will be illustrious and honored,
his subordinates will obey,
and the world will praise him.
If a minister is filial,
he will be loyal in serving his lord,
incorruptible in holding office,
and willing to die when facing danger.
If scholars and common people are filial,
they will farm diligently,
defend and fight resolutely,
and not abandon or retreat.
Filial piety,
the fundamental task of the Sān Huáng and Wǔ Dì,
is the guiding principle for all affairs.
Indeed, if one holds to a single principle, and a hundred virtues arrive, a hundred evils depart, and the world follows,
it is only filial piety.
Therefore, when judging a person, one must first consider those close to him and then those distant,
first those important and then those less important.
Now, if there is a person here
who acts respectfully towards his close and important relatives,
and is not dismissive or rude towards those less important and distant,
this is truly adhering to the path of filial piety,
the means by which the former kings governed the world.
Therefore, loving one's parents,
one dares not hate others;
respecting one's parents,
one dares not slight others.
When love and respect are fully demonstrated in serving one's parents,
glory and radiance extend to the common people
and reach throughout the four seas;
this is the filial piety of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
Zēng Zǐ said:
"The body
is a legacy from one's parents.
Using the legacy of one's parents,
how dare one not be respectful?
Not being dignified in one's dwelling is
not filial.
Not being loyal in serving one's lord is
not filial.
Not being respectful when holding office is
not filial.
Not being sincere with friends is
not filial.
Not being brave in battle is
not filial.
If the five constant virtues are not followed,
calamity reaches one's parents.
How dare one not be respectful?"
The Shāng Shū says:
"Among the three hundred punishments,
no crime is more serious than unfilial conduct."
Zēng Zǐ said:
"The former kings governed the world with five principles:
valuing virtue,
valuing the noble,
valuing the old,
respecting elders,
and loving the young.
These five principles
were how the former kings brought order to the world.
Valuing virtue
means it is close to sageliness.
Valuing the noble
means it is close to the ruler.
Valuing the old
means it is close to one's parents.
Respecting elders
means it is close to one's elder brothers.
Loving the young
means it is close to one's younger brothers."
Zēng Zǐ said:
"Parents give life;
a son dares not kill it.
Parents place it;
a son dares not abandon it.
Parents make it complete;
a son dares not mutilate it.
Therefore, not taking a boat if one can walk,
not taking a shortcut if there's a main path,
being able to keep one's limbs whole
to guard the ancestral temple,
can be called filial."
There are five ways of providing nourishment:
Repairing palaces and houses,
making the bed and mat comfortable,
and regulating food and drink are
the ways to nourish the body.
Arranging colorful objects,
displaying various hues,
and presenting beautiful patterns are
the ways to nourish the eyes.
Rectifying the six lǜ,
harmonizing the five sounds,
and mixing the eight musical instruments are
the ways to nourish the ears.
Cooking the five grains,
preparing the six domestic animals,
and harmonizing seasonings are
the ways to nourish the mouth.
Harmonizing one's expression,
speaking pleasant words,
and being respectful in actions are
the ways to nourish the will.
These five ways,
used successively and with increasing importance,
can be called good nourishment.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn descended the hall and injured his foot.
After healing, he did not go out for several months,
still looking sorrowful.
His disciples asked him:
"Our master descended the hall and injured his foot.
After healing, he did not go out for several months,
still looking sorrowful.
May we ask the reason?"
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:
"Excellent is your question.
I heard it from Zēng Zǐ,
and Zēng Zǐ heard it from Zhòngní:
Parents give birth to one whole;
a son should return whole.
Not damaging one's body,
not harming one's form,
can be called filial.
A superior man does not walk even a foot without being mindful.
I forgot the path of filial piety,
therefore I am sorrowful."
Therefore it is said:
The body is not one's private possession;
it is a legacy from one's venerable parents.
The fundamental teaching for the people is called filial piety;
its practice is called nourishment.
Nourishment is possible,
but respect is difficult.
Respect is possible,
but peace of mind is difficult.
Peace of mind is possible,
but seeing it through to the end is difficult.
After parents have passed away,
to conduct oneself respectfully
without leaving an ill name for one's parents
can be called being able to finish well.
Ritual (Lǐ) is to follow these;
righteousness (yì) is to be appropriate in these;
trust (xìn) is to be trustworthy in these;
strength (qiáng) is to strengthen these.
Joy (lè) arises from conforming to these,
and punishment (xíng) arises from opposing these.
14.2 Běnwèi
Chapter Two:
Seek it at its root,
and you will surely find it within ten days;
seek it at its branches,
and you will toil without success.
The establishment of merit and fame
comes from the root of affairs,
which is the transformation brought about by obtaining worthy individuals.
Who but worthy individuals can understand the transformation of affairs?
Therefore it is said that the root lies in obtaining worthy individuals.
A woman of the Yǒuxún clan was picking mulberries
and found a baby in a hollow mulberry tree.
She presented him to her lord.
Her lord ordered a chef (fú rén) to raise him.
Investigating the circumstances,
it was said:
"His mother lived by the Yī River.
Pregnant,
she dreamt that a spirit told her:
'The mortar will gush water and flow eastward;
do not look back.'
The next day,
she saw the mortar gushing water,
told her neighbors,
and ran eastward for ten lǐ.
When she looked back, her entire town was submerged by water,
and she herself transformed into a hollow mulberry tree."
Therefore, he was named Yī Yǐn.
This is the reason for Yī Yǐn's [Yī Yǐn] birth from an empty mulberry tree. He grew up to be virtuous.
Tāng [Tāng] heard of Yī Yǐn,
and sent someone to invite him from the Yǒu Shēn [Yǒu Shēn] clan.
The Yǒu Shēn clan refused.
Yī Yǐn also wished to join Tāng.
Tāng then proposed to take a wife from them through marriage.
The Yǒu Shēn clan was pleased,
and sent Yī Yǐn as a concubine with their daughter.
Therefore, when a wise ruler seeks a man of the Way,
there is nothing he will not use to get him; and when a man of the Way seeks a wise ruler,
there is nothing he will not do to serve him;
only when they find each other do they find joy.
They become close without planning,
and trustworthy without making promises.
They exhaust their wisdom and strength for each other,
facing danger and enduring hardship,
and are joyful in their aspirations.
This is how great achievements and fame are attained.
Indeed, it is not only
that a scholar who is isolated and self-reliant,
or a ruler who is ambitious and prefers solitude,
will surely see their reputation fade and extinguish,
and their state be endangered.
Therefore, Huáng Dì [Huáng Dì] established the Four Faces,
and Yáo [Yáo] and Shùn [Shùn] only succeeded after obtaining Bó Yáng [Bó Yáng] and Xù Ěr [Xù Ěr].
This is how the virtues of worthy men are known.
Bó Yá [Bó Yá] played the qín [qín],
and Zhōng Zǐ Qī [Zhōng Zǐ Qī] listened to it.
As Bó Yá played, his thoughts were on Tài Shān [Tài Shān].
Zhōng Zǐ Qī said:
"Excellent indeed is the qín playing!
Lofty and majestic like Tài Shān."
After a short while,
his thoughts were on flowing water.
Zhōng Zǐ Qī again said:
"Excellent indeed is the qín playing!
Vast and surging like flowing water."
When Zhōng Zǐ Qī died,
Bó Yá smashed his qín and broke its strings,
never playing the qín again for the rest of his life,
believing that there was no one in the world worthy for whom to play the qín again.
It is not only the qín that is like this;
worthy men are also the same.
Even if there is a worthy man,
if there is no proper etiquette to receive him,
how can the worthy man fully devote his loyalty?
It is like poor horsemanship;
a jī [jī] horse will not cover a thousand lǐ [lǐ] by itself.
Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn.
He purified him in the ancestral temple,
fumigated him with reeds,
lit torches of rush-lights,
and consecrated him with the blood of a boar sacrifice.
The next day,
he held court and met him.
Yī Yǐn spoke to Tāng about the ultimate flavors.
Tāng asked:
"Can these be prepared in response?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"Your country is small,
insufficient to gather them.
Only when you become the Son of Heaven can they be gathered.
Of the three groups of creatures,
those that live in water are fishy,
those that eat meat are gamy,
and those that eat grass are rank.
Even bad smells can be made beautiful,
each having its method.
Of all the origins of flavor,
water is the foremost beginning.
The five flavors, the three ingredients,
nine boilings, and nine transformations,
fire governs them.
Sometimes fast, sometimes slow,
removing fishiness, eliminating gaminess, and dispelling rankness,
must be done by its victor,
without losing its principle.
In the matter of blending and harmonizing,
it must involve sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, and saltiness,
in order, quantity,
their combination is extremely subtle,
all having their origins.
The transformations within the cauldron
are exquisite, subtle, and delicate;
the mouth cannot express them,
the mind cannot comprehend them.
They are like the subtleties of archery and charioteering,
the transformations of yīn [yīn] and yáng [yáng],
and the cycles of the four seasons.
Thus, it is long-lasting without spoiling,
cooked without being mushy,
sweet without being cloying,
sour without being harsh,
salty without being reduced,
pungent without being fiery,
bland without being thin,
rich without being greasy.
The finest meats are:
the lips of the xīngxīng [xīngxīng] (orangutan),
the roasted badger,
the jade-like meat of the juànxié [juànxié] (sea swallow),
the tenderloin of the shùdàng [shùdàng] (rhinoceros),
the sinews of the máoxiàng [máoxiàng] (yak and elephant).
West of the Liú Shā [Liú Shā],
south of the Dān Shān [Dān Shān],
there is the egg of the phoenix,
eaten by the Wò Mín [Wò Mín] people.
The finest fish are:
the zhuān [zhuān] from Dòngtíng [Dòngtíng],
the ěr [ěr] from the Dōng Hǎi [Dōng Hǎi].
The fish from the Lǐ Shuǐ [Lǐ Shuǐ]
is named Zhū Biē [Zhū Biē],
it has six legs,
and a hundred green pearls.
The fish from the Guàn Shuǐ [Guàn Shuǐ]
is named Yáo [Yáo],
its shape is like a carp but it has wings,
it often flies at night from the Xī Hǎi [Xī Hǎi],
and swims in the Dōng Hǎi.
The finest vegetables are:
the píng [píng] from Kūnlún [Kūnlún],
the flowers of the Shòu Mù [Shòu Mù] tree.
East of Zhǐ Gū [Zhǐ Gū],
in the country of Zhōng Róng [Zhōng Róng],
there are leaves of red wood and black wood.
South of Yú Mào [Yú Mào],
on the cliff of the South Pole,
there is a vegetable,
its name is Jiā Shù [Jiā Shù],
its color is like jade.
The yún [yún] of Yáng Huá [Yáng Huá].
The qín [qín] of Yúnmèng [Yúnmèng].
The jīng [jīng] of Jù Qū [Jù Qū].
The grass of Jìn Yuān [Jìn Yuān],
named Tǔ Yīng [Tǔ Yīng].
The finest seasonings are:
the jiāng [jiāng] of Yáng Pǔ [Yáng Pǔ],
the guì [guì] of Zhāo Yáo [Zhāo Yáo],
the
jùn [jùn] of Yuè Luò [Yuè Luò],
the pickled minced fish of zhānwěi [zhānwěi] (sturgeon and paddlefish),
the salt of Dà Xià [Dà Xià],
the dew of Zǎi Jiē [Zǎi Jiē],
its color is like jade,
the eggs of Cháng Zé [Cháng Zé].
The finest grains are:
the hé [hé] of Xuán Shān [Xuán Shān],
the sù [sù] of Bù Zhōu [Bù Zhōu],
the jì [jì] of Yáng Shān [Yáng Shān],
the jù [jù] of Nán Hǎi [Nán Hǎi].
The finest waters are:
the dew of Sān Wēi [Sān Wēi];
the well of Kūnlún;
the hill of Jǔ Jiāng [Jǔ Jiāng],
named Yáo Shuǐ [Yáo Shuǐ];
the water of Yuē Shān [Yuē Shān];
the mountain of Gāo Quán [Gāo Quán],
on which there is a gushing spring,
the plain of Jì Zhōu [Jì Zhōu].
The finest fruits are:
the fruit of Shā Táng [Shā Táng];
north of Cháng Shān [Cháng Shān],
above Tóu Yuān [Tóu Yuān],
there are a hundred fruits,
eaten by all the emperors;
east of Jī Shān [Jī Shān],
in the place of Qīng Niǎo [Qīng Niǎo],
there is sweet lú [lú] (persimmon);
the orange of Jiāng Pǔ [Jiāng Pǔ];
the pomelo of Yúnmèng.
Stone ear fungus from the Hàn [Hàn] River.
These are the means to achieve them.
The finest horses are:
the pair of Qīng Lóng [Qīng Lóng],
the team of Yí Fēng [Yí Fēng].
Unless one first becomes the Son of Heaven,
these cannot be obtained and gathered.
The Son of Heaven cannot be forced into being,
one must first know the Way.
The Way means stopping at the other and being present in oneself;
when oneself is perfected, the Son of Heaven is perfected.
When the Son of Heaven is perfected, then the ultimate flavors are gathered.
Therefore, examining the near is how one knows the distant,
and perfecting oneself is how one perfects others.
The Way of the sagely king is essential,
how could it be about pursuing many other endeavors!"
14.3 "Shǒu Shí" [Shǒu Shí]
Third:
The sage in their affairs
appears slow but is swift, appears late but is quick, in order to await the opportune moment.
Wáng Jìlì was trapped and died.
Wénwáng grieved over this,
not forgetting the humiliation at Yǒulǐ,
but the time was not yet ripe.
Wǔwáng served him,
toiling day and night without ceasing,
also not forgetting the disgrace at Wángmén.
He waited for twelve years,
and then accomplished the affair of the jiǎzǐ cycle.
Indeed, such a time is not easily obtained.
Tàigōng Wàng,
a scholar from the Eastern Yí,
desired to bring stability to the world but had no ruler to serve.
Hearing of Wénwáng's virtue,
he therefore fished by the Wèi River to observe him.
Wǔ Zǐxū wanted to see the King of Wú but could not.
A guest spoke of him to Prince Guāng,
who saw him but disliked his appearance,
did not listen to his counsel, and dismissed him.
The guest pleaded with Prince Guāng.
Prince Guāng said:
"His appearance is precisely what I most detest."
The guest reported this to Wǔ Zǐxū.
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"This is easily remedied.
I wish that the Prince would sit in the hall,
with heavy curtains, and merely see my clothes or hands,
and I will then explain."
The Prince agreed.
Halfway through Wǔ Zǐxū's explanation,
Prince Guāng lifted the curtains,
clasped his hand, and invited him to sit.
When the explanation was finished,
Prince Guāng was greatly pleased.
Wǔ Zǐxū believed that the one who would possess the state of Wú must be Prince Guāng.
He retired and farmed in the wilderness for seven years.
Prince Guāng replaced Wúwáng Liáo as king,
and appointed Zǐxū.
Zǐxū then reformed laws and institutions,
promoted the virtuous and capable,
selected and trained soldiers,
and practiced warfare.
Six years later,
they then achieved a great victory over Chǔ at Bójǔ,
winning all nine battles,
pursuing the fleeing enemy for a thousand lǐ.
King Zhāo fled to Suí,
and Wú then occupied Yǐng,
personally shooting at the royal palace
and whipping the grave of Jīng Píng three hundred times.
His farming in the past
was not forgetting the revenge for his father;
it was awaiting the opportune moment.
Among the Mohists, there was Tián Jiū, who wished to see Qín Huìwáng.
He stayed in Qín for three years but could not obtain an audience.
A guest spoke of him to the King of Chǔ.
He went to see the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ was pleased with him,
and gave him a general's credentials to go to Qín.
Upon arrival,
he was thus able to see Huìwáng.
He told others:
"The way to reach Qín
is actually through Chǔ?"
Things indeed exist that are near when approached indirectly, and distant when approached directly.
The opportune moment is also like this.
If there is the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ but not the opportune time of Jié and Zhòu,
nothing will be accomplished.
If there is the opportune time of Jié and Zhòu but not the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ, likewise nothing will be accomplished.
The sage's perception of the opportune moment
is like a person's steps and their shadow, inseparable.
Therefore, a scholar of the Way, when they have not encountered their time,
hides and disperses,
diligently awaiting the opportune moment.
When the time arrives,
some rise from commoner status to become the Son of Heaven;
some, from leading a thousand chariots, obtain the empire;
some, from humble origins, assist three kings;
some, from being a mere commoner, avenge a lord of ten thousand chariots.
Therefore, what the sage values
is only the opportune moment.
When water freezes solid,
Hòujì does not sow;
Hòujì's sowing must await spring.
Therefore, even if a person is wise but does not encounter the opportune moment,
they will have no achievements.
When the leaves are flourishing and beautiful,
one can pluck them all day and not notice (the effort);
but once autumn frost has fallen,
all the forests wither.
The difficulty or ease of an undertaking
does not lie in its size,
but in knowing the opportune moment.
During the disaster of Zhèng Zǐyáng,
a rabid dog brought about its collapse.
During the disaster of Qí Gāoguó,
a lost ox brought about its collapse.
The masses then used these incidents to kill Zǐyáng and Gāoguó.
At that time,
even a dog or an ox could serve as a precursor to action for people,
how much more so when people themselves act as precursors?
Hungry horses fill the stables,
silent,
having not yet seen fodder.
Hungry dogs fill the kennels,
silent,
having not yet seen bones.
When they see bones and fodder,
their agitation cannot be contained.
The people in a disordered world,
silent,
have not yet seen a worthy person;
when they see a worthy person, they will move and cannot be stopped.
What moves them is not their physical form,
but their heart, is it not?
Qí, by becoming an Eastern Emperor, was beleaguered by all under Heaven, and Lǔ took Xúzhōu.
Hándān, by bringing its people into distress over Shòulíng, allowed Wèi to take Jiǎnshì.
That Lǔ and Wèi, though small, both achieved their ambitions against large states
was because they met their opportune moment.
Therefore, for worthy rulers and outstanding scholars who wish to care for the black-haired people,
a chaotic age provides the opportunity.
Heaven does not grant a second chance,
the opportune moment does not linger long,
and one cannot be skilled in two things simultaneously;
success lies in seizing the opportune moment.
14.4 *Yì Shǎng*
Fourth:
When spring qi arrives, plants and trees grow.
When autumn qi arrives, plants and trees shed their leaves.
Their growth and shedding are caused by something;
they are not spontaneous.
Therefore, when that which causes them arrives,
there is nothing that cannot be done.
When that which causes them does not arrive,
there is nothing that can be done.
The ancients carefully discerned that which causes things,
thus everything was put to use.
The instruments of reward and punishment
are what superiors use to govern.
If what is applied is righteousness,
then the Way of loyalty, trustworthiness, intimacy, and love will be manifest.
Being manifest for a long time, it will grow increasingly strong,
and the people will embrace it as their very nature.
This is called accomplished instruction.
When instruction is accomplished, even abundant rewards and severe punishments cannot deter them.
Therefore, those skilled in instruction
achieve accomplished instruction without relying on rewards and punishments;
and when instruction is accomplished, rewards and punishments cannot deter them.
The same applies when rewards and punishments are used improperly.
The Way of deceit, treachery, disorder, greed, and perversity will flourish.
Flourishing for a long time without ceasing,
the people will detest it as their very nature.
This is true for the peoples of Róng, Yí, Hú, Mó, Bā, and Yuè.
Even abundant rewards and severe punishments cannot deter them.
The people of Yǐng had their two-plank walls;
Wú Qǐ changed this and was disliked,
yet rewards and punishments were rectified, and the people became content and happy.
The people of Dīqiāng,
when captured,
do not worry about being bound,
but worry about dying and not being cremated.
All these are consequences of accomplished wickedness.
Therefore, one must be careful
where rewards and punishments are applied,
lest they become accomplished and harm the people.
In the past, Jìn Wéngōng was about to battle the Chǔ people at Chéngpú.
He summoned Jiù Fàn and asked:
"Chǔ's forces are numerous, ours are few.
What should be done?"
Jiù Fàn replied:
"Your servant has heard that a ruler of elaborate rituals
is deficient in refinement;
a ruler of many battles
is deficient in deception.
Your Lord should also simply deceive them."
Wéngōng reported Jiù Fàn's words to Yōng Jì.
Yōng Jì said:
"If one drains the pond to catch fish,
will one not obtain them?
But the next year there will be no fish.
If one burns the brush to hunt,
will one not obtain game?
But the next year there will be no beasts.
The way of deceit and falsehood,
though it may be temporarily effective now,
will have no recurrence later;
it is not a long-term strategy."
Wén Gōng used Jìu Fàn's words
and defeated the Chǔ people at Chéngpú.
Upon returning, he distributed rewards,
with Yōng Jì placed first.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"The achievement at Chéngpú
was Jìu Fàn's strategy.
Your Lordship used his words, but rewarded him after others.
Is this perhaps not right?"
Wén Gōng said:
"Yōng Jì's words
are of benefit for a hundred generations.
Jìu Fàn's words
were for a temporary urgency.
How can one prioritize a temporary urgency over a benefit for a hundred generations?"
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"Facing difficulty, using stratagem
is sufficient to repel the enemy.
Upon return, honoring the worthy
is sufficient to repay kindness.
Wén Gōng, though not consistent from beginning to end,
was sufficient to become a hegemon."
If rewards are heavy, the people will turn to them.
If the people turn to them, then things will be accomplished.
If accomplished through stratagem,
its accomplishment will be ruined,
its victory will be defeated.
Many have been victorious in the world,
but only five became hegemons.
Wén Gōng was one of them;
he knew what victory was accomplished for.
To win but not know what victory is accomplished for
is the same as having no victory.
Qín won against the Róng but was defeated at Xiáo.
Chǔ won against the Zhū Xià but was defeated at Bójǔ.
Wǔ Wáng achieved it,
thus with one victory he became king of All Under Heaven.
If deceptions fill the country,
it cannot be secure;
the danger is not only external.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ escaped from the siege
and rewarded five meritorious individuals,
with Gāo Shè at the head.
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"Within Jìnyáng,
Shè had no great merit.
Why was he rewarded first?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"My state was imperiled,
the altars of soil and grain were in danger,
and my person was in distress and confinement.
Shè was the only one who interacted with me without losing the etiquette between ruler and subject.
That is why I placed him first."
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"Xiāngzǐ can be said to be skilled in rewarding.
By rewarding one man, no one in All Under Heaven who served as a subject dared to be disrespectful."
Once the six armies were formed, they could not be easily changed.
He annexed Dài to the north,
and pressed Qí to the east.
He ordered Zhāng Mèngtán to climb over the city wall and secretly meet
Wèi Huán and Hán Kāng to schedule an attack on Zhì Bó,
cutting off his head to make a drinking cup.
Thus, the Three Families were established.
Was this not due to the appropriate use of rewards and punishments?
14.5 《Cháng Gōng》
Fifthly, it is said:
For all order and chaos, survival and destruction,
safety and danger, strength and weakness,
there must be a 'meeting' or 'encounter,'
and only then can things be accomplished;
if each is singular, they cannot be established.
Therefore, although Jié and Zhòu were unworthy,
their downfall was due to encountering Tāng and Wǔ.
Encountering Tāng and Wǔ was Heaven's will,
it was not due to Jié and Zhòu's unworthiness.
Although Tāng and Wǔ were virtuous,
their becoming kings was due to encountering Jié and Zhòu.
Encountering Jié and Zhòu
was Heaven's will,
it was not due to Tāng and Wǔ's virtue.
If Jié and Zhòu had not encountered Tāng and Wǔ,
they might not necessarily have perished.
If Jié and Zhòu had not perished,
although unworthy,
their disgrace would not have reached this extent.
If Tāng and Wǔ had not encountered Jié and Zhòu,
they might not necessarily have become kings.
If Tāng and Wǔ had not become kings,
although virtuous,
their fame would not have reached this extent.
Therefore, a ruler who achieves great merit
is not spoken of as unworthy;
a ruler of a doomed state is not spoken of as virtuous.
It is like a good farmer:
he discerns what soil is suitable,
and carefully attends to plowing and weeding;
but he may not necessarily have a harvest.
However, the one who does harvest
is certainly this person.
The beginning lies in encountering timely rain.
Encountering timely rain
is Heaven's (Earth's) doing,
not something a good farmer can bring about.
The state of Yuè suffered a great famine.
The king was afraid
and summoned Fàn Lí to deliberate.
Fàn Lí said:
"Why is Your Majesty worried?
The current famine
is a blessing for Yuè and a disaster for Wú.
The state of Wú is very rich and has surplus wealth.
Its king is young,
of limited wisdom and shallow talent,
fond of fleeting fame,
and does not consider future troubles.
If Your Majesty were to offer heavy tribute and humble words to request grain from Wú,
then food could be obtained.
Once food is obtained,
Yuè will eventually possess Wú,
so why should Your Majesty worry?"
The King of Yuè
said: "Good."
So he sent someone to request food from Wú.
The King of Wú was about to give it to them.
Wǔ Zǐxū advanced to remonstrate, saying:
"It cannot be given!
Wú and Yuè
share borders and are neighbors,
with easy roads and frequent communication.
They are states of enmity, rivalry, and war.
If Wú does not destroy Yuè,
Yuè will certainly destroy Wú.
Could states like Yān, Qín, Qí, Jìn,
situated in mountains and landlocked,
possibly cross the Five Lakes and Nine Rivers, traverse seventeen passes to possess Wú?
Therefore, it is said: if Wú does not destroy Yuè,
Yuè will certainly destroy Wú.
Now you are about to transport grain
and give them food;
this is to strengthen our enemy and nourish our foe.
When wealth is depleted and the people are afraid,
regret will be too late.
It is better not to give it but to attack them;
this is their destined fate.
This is how our former kings became hegemons."
Furthermore, famine
is a recurring matter,
like a deep abyss or a steep bank –
which state does not have it?
The King of Wú said:
"Not so.
I have heard it said:
'A righteous army does not attack the submissive;
a benevolent person feeds the hungry.'
Now, to attack them when they are submissive is not a righteous army;
to not feed the hungry
is not a benevolent character.
Without benevolence or righteousness,
even if I gained ten Yuè states,
I would not do it."
So he gave them food.
Within three years, Wú also suffered a famine.
He sent someone to request food from Yuè.
The King of Yuè did not give it,
but instead attacked Wú.
Fūchā was captured.
The King of Chǔ wanted to take Xī and Cài.
So he first feigned goodwill towards the Marquis of Cài
and conspired with him, saying:
"I want to acquire Xī,
what should I do?"
The Marquis of Cài said:
"The Lady of Xī
is my wife's sister.
I will arrange a feast for the Marquis of Xī and his wife,
and Your Majesty can come along,
and we can ambush them."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he and the Marquis of Cài entered Xī with the pretext of a feast,
and joining them,
they captured Xī.
Afterwards,
they stopped at Cài
and also captured Cài.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ fell ill
and summoned the Crown Prince, instructing him:
"When I die and have been buried,
don the mourning attire and ascend Mount Xiàwū to look out."
The Crown Prince respectfully assented.
When Jiǎnzi died
and was buried,
Xiāngzǐ wore mourning clothes,
summoned his ministers, and told them,
"I wish to ascend Xiàwū to look out."
The ministers all remonstrated, saying,
"Ascending Xiàwū to look out
is a form of recreation.
To engage in recreation while in mourning clothes
is inappropriate."
Xiāngzǐ said,
"This was the command of the late sovereign,
and I dare not disregard it."
The various ministers respectfully assented.
Xiāngzǐ ascended Xiàwū and looked out over Dài.
The scenery was very beautiful.
Thereupon, Xiāngzǐ said,
"The late sovereign must have taught me this for a reason."
Upon returning,
he considered how to conquer Dài.
He first befriended the Lord of Dài.
The Lord of Dài was fond of women,
so Xiāngzǐ requested to give his elder sister in marriage to him.
The Lord of Dài assented.
After his sister had gone,
his acts of kindness towards Dài became myriad.
Mǎjùn was suitable for horses,
so the Lord of Dài presented fine horses to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ paid a visit to the Lord of Dài and invited him to a banquet.
All the horses from Mǎjùn were brought forth.
Xiāngzǐ first ordered hundreds of dancers to hide weapons in their sleeves.
He also prepared a large bronze dou (a type of vessel).
When the Lord of Dài arrived,
and the drinking was in full swing,
Xiāngzǐ overturned the dou and struck him.
With one blow,
his brains splattered on the ground.
The dancers, grasping their weapons, engaged in combat
and killed all of his attendants.
Thereupon, Xiāngzǐ used the Lord of Dài's carriage to welcome his wife (Xiāngzǐ's sister).
When his wife heard the news from afar,
she sharpened her hairpin and stabbed herself with it.
Thus, the Zhào clan to this day has the evidence of the stabbed hairpin (cìjī) and the name of the overturned dou (fǎndǒu).
These three rulers
derived their success from certain actions.
They did not entirely follow principles,
yet later generations praise them,
because they achieved merit.
If one achieves merit in this way without making mistakes,
even becoming a king is acceptable.
14.6 "Shènrén"
Six says:
Great achievements and fame are of Heaven;
for this reason, one must not be careless in selecting people.
Shùn's meeting with Yáo was
of Heaven;
Shùn tilled at Lìshān,
made pottery by the Hébīn,
fished at Léizé,
and the world rejoiced in him,
and outstanding scholars followed him—
that was of man.
Yǔ's meeting with Shùn was
of Heaven;
Yǔ traveled throughout the world
to seek worthy men,
benefited the common people,
and cleared all the stagnant and obstructed waters of floods, rivers, and swamps that could be opened—
Yǔ did all of that,
which was of man.
Tāng's meeting with Jié and
Wǔ's meeting with Zhòu were
of Heaven;
Tāng and Wǔ cultivated themselves, accumulated good deeds, and acted righteously
to relieve the people's suffering—
that was of man.
When Shùn was farming and fishing,
his virtue was no different from when he was Son of Heaven.
Before he met his opportune time,
with his followers,
he
dug up earth's resources,
utilized water's benefits,
braided cattails and reeds,
tied fishing nets,
and his hands and feet were constantly calloused;
only then was he free from the worries of cold and hunger.
When he met his opportune time,
he ascended to become Son of Heaven,
worthy scholars submitted to him,
and the myriad people praised him.
Men and women,
with joyful and harmonious hearts,
all bore him up and rejoiced in him.
Shùn himself composed a poem saying:
"Beneath the whole Heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
to the very borders of the land,
there is no one who is not the king's subject,"
which showed that he possessed everything.
Possessing everything,
his virtue did not increase;
possessing nothing,
his virtue did not diminish;
the times made it so.
Before Báilǐ Xī met his opportune time,
he caused Guó to perish and was captured by Jìn,
herded cattle in Qín,
and was sold for five sheepskins.
Gōngsūn Zhī obtained and pleased him,
and presented him to Mùgōng.
After three days,
Mùgōng requested to entrust affairs to him.
Mùgōng said,
"To buy him for five sheepskins and then entrust affairs to him,
will not this be laughed at by the world?"
Gōngsūn Zhī replied,
"To trust a worthy man and employ him is
your lord's sagacity;
to defer to a worthy man and humble oneself before him is
your minister's loyalty.
If the lord becomes a sagacious ruler
and the minister a loyal minister,
and that worthy man is trusted,
the realm will submit,
and enemy states will fear.
Who will then have time to laugh?"
Mùgōng thereupon employed him.
His plans were always appropriate,
and his actions always brought success;
his virtue did not increase.
If Báilǐ Xī, though worthy,
had not met Mùgōng,
he certainly would not have achieved this fame.
How do we know there are no Báilǐ Xīs in the world today?
Therefore, a ruler who wishes to seek out scholars
must strive to be broad-minded.
Kǒngzǐ was distressed between Chén and Cài,
for seven days he did not taste food,
and his soup of smartweed had no grain.
Zǎiyú was exhausted,
yet Kǒngzǐ played the zither and sang in his room,
and Yán Huí gathered vegetables outside.
Zǐlù and Zǐgòng spoke to each other, saying,
"Our Master was twice expelled from Lǔ,
had his tracks erased in Wèi,
had his tree cut down in Sòng,
and was distressed in Chén and Cài.
Those who kill our Master are without guilt,
and those who insult our Master are not prohibited.
Yet our Master plays the zither, sings, and dances,
never ceasing his music.
Is this how a gentleman has no sense of shame?"
Yán Huí had no reply,
so he went in and reported this to Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ, startled, pushed his zither away
and sighed deeply, saying,
"Yóu and Cì
are petty men.
Call them here,
and I will speak to them."
Zǐlù and Zǐgòng entered.
Zǐgòng said,
"To be in such a state can be called distress."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"What kind of talk is that?
A gentleman's understanding of the Way is called success;
being confined from the Way is called distress.
Now I, Qiū, uphold the Way of benevolence and righteousness,
and thereby encounter the troubles of a chaotic age.
This is its proper course,
how can it be called distress?
Therefore, I examine myself within and find no fault with the Way,
and face difficulties without losing my virtue.
When the great cold arrives
and frost and snow descend,
it is then that I know the vigor of the pine and cypress.
Formerly, Huángōng succeeded from Jǔ,
Wéngōng succeeded from Cáo,
and King Yuè succeeded from Kuàijī.
The strait of Chén and Cài,
for me, Qiū, is it not perhaps a blessing!"
Kǒngzǐ brightly resumed playing his zither and singing,
and Zǐlù vigorously grasped his shield and danced.
Zǐgòng 曰:
“I do not know how high heaven is,
nor how deep the earth is.”
In ancient times, those who attained the Dào,
were joyful even in poverty,
and joyful even in prominence.
What they rejoiced in was not poverty or prominence,
but that the Dào was attained in themselves.
Then poverty and prominence were one,
like the sequence of cold and heat, wind and rain.
Therefore, Xǔ Yóu dallied in Yǐngyáng,
and Gòng Bó achieved his aspirations in Gòngshǒu.
14.7 《Yùhé》
The seventh section says:
In all encounters and convergences,
if the time is not right,
one must wait until it is right before acting.
Thus, the bǐyì bird dies on the tree,
and the bǐmù fish dies in the sea.
Kǒngzǐ traveled throughout the land,
twice seeking to serve rulers of the world.
From Qí to Wèi,
he met over eighty lords.
Three thousand people offered their allegiance to become his disciples,
and seventy of them were accomplished followers.
Among these seventy people,
if a lord of ten thousand chariots could employ even one, they could serve as a teacher.
It was not that there were no capable people,
yet with all his travels, Kǒngzǐ only reached the position of Sīkòu in Lǔ.
This is why the Son of Heaven's lineage was sometimes broken,
and why the feudal lords fell into great disorder.
When there is disorder, many foolish people are fortunate,
and when they are fortunate, they are certainly not equal to their task.
If they are not equal to their task for long,
then fortune turns into calamity.
The greater their fortune,
the greater their calamity,
and the calamity does not affect them alone.
Therefore, a Jūnzǐ does not rely on luck,
does not act recklessly,
but must thoroughly examine himself before undertaking a task,
and only then acts.
Anyone who can listen and speak well
must be adept at discussion and debate.
Few rulers of the world can discern those who are adept at discussion and debate.
How can their encounters not be reckless?
Anyone who can listen to music
must be skilled in the five notes.
Few people can truly understand the five notes.
How can their preferences not be reckless?
There was a guest who, by playing a wind instrument, met the king of Yuè.
The notes Yǔ, Jiǎo, Gōng, Zhǐ, Shāng were not amiss,
but the king of Yuè did not appreciate them.
He considered them "rustic" sounds and instead favored them.
The Dào of persuasion also has such instances.
There was a woman who became a wife.
Someone told her parents:
"Marriage does not necessarily lead to childbirth.
Valuables and belongings
can be hidden outside the house
in case she does not bear children."
Her parents thought this was sound advice,
so they instructed their daughter to always hide things outside.
Her parents-in-law learned of this
and said:
"For her to be our daughter-in-law and yet have ulterior motives,
she cannot be kept."
So they expelled her.
The wife's parents,
considering that the person who advised them had their interests at heart, believed him to be loyal,
and praised him for life,
without understanding the true reason for the outcome.
The destruction of ancestral temples
and the loss of the empire
also stem from this.
Therefore, it is said that encounters and convergences are not constant.
Persuasion
is merely circumstantial.
Just like people's perception of beauty,
everyone knows how to praise what is beautiful,
but beautiful people are not necessarily met with favor.
Thus, Mó Mǔ served Huángdì,
and Huángdì said:
"Uphold your feminine virtue and never forget it;
maintain your uprightness and never diminish it.
Even if you are ugly, what harm is there?"
As for people's taste in flavors,
everyone praises sweet and crisp,
but sweet and crisp are not necessarily accepted.
Wén Wáng enjoyed iris stew.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it and tried to emulate him.
He wrinkled his nose and ate it,
and only after three years could he tolerate it.
There was a person with a terrible odor.
His relatives, brothers, wife, concubines, and acquaintances could not live with him.
He suffered and lived by the sea.
Among the people by the sea, there was one who found his odor pleasing,
and followed him day and night, unable to leave.
Persuasion can also be like this.
In Chén, there was an ugly person,
named Dūnqià Chóumí,
with a prominent forehead, broad face,
skin like flushed scarlet,
eyes drooping over his nose,
long elbows, and a twisted body.
The Marquis of Chén saw him and was very pleased with him.
He made him manage the state externally
and control his person internally.
When Chǔ assembled the feudal lords,
the Marquis of Chén was ill and could not attend,
so he sent Dūnqià Chóumí to offer his apologies.
The King of Chǔ found his name strange and met him first.
There was a guest who presented a document slandering his name and appearance.
The King of Chǔ was angry,
assembled his grandees and told them:
"If the Marquis of Chén does not know that he is unfit to be employed,
that is ignorance;
if he knows and still employs him,
that is an insult;
to be both insulting and ignorant,
we cannot but attack him."
He raised an army to attack Chén,
and it was lost after three months.
His ugliness was enough to shock people,
his words were enough to destroy a state,
yet his friendship with the Marquis of Chén was supreme,
and even in ruin, their friendship did not wane.
Indeed, those who are not fit to be favored are favored,
while those who are fit to be favored are neglected.
This is why states fall into disorder
and the world declines.
The suffering, sorrow, and toil
of the people under heaven arise from this.
In general, the fundamental way to promote people
is, primarily, by their aspirations;
secondly, by their conduct;
and thirdly, by their achievements.
If none of these three are possible,
the state will surely be ruined and perish,
and great calamities will arise in abundance.
One's person will surely suffer death and disaster;
to reach seventy or ninety years of age would still be considered fortunate.
The descendants of sages and saints,
in turn, become evil people,
thereby harming themselves.
How can they be alone in this?
14.8 《Bìjǐ》
The eighth section says:
External things cannot be relied upon.
Thus, Lóng Páng was executed,
Bǐgān was disemboweled,
Jīzǐ feigned madness,
È Lái died,
and Jié and Zhòu perished.
There is no ruler who does not desire his ministers to be loyal,
yet loyalty is not necessarily trusted.
Thus, Wǔ Yuán was exiled to the Jiāng,
and Cháng Hóng died, his blood stored for three years turned into jade.
There are no parents who do not desire their children to be filial,
yet filial piety is not necessarily loved.
Thus, Xiàojǐ was doubted,
and Zēngzǐ grieved.
Zhuāngzǐ was walking in the mountains
and saw a very beautiful, tall, and large tree,
with abundant branches and leaves.
A woodcutter stopped by it but did not cut it down.
When asked why,
he said:
"It is of no use."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This tree, by being useless, was able to complete its natural lifespan."
He left the mountains
and arrived at a town,
staying at an old friend's house.
His old friend was delighted
and prepared wine and meat,
instructing his servant to kill a goose to entertain him.
The servant asked:
"One goose can cackle,
and one cannot.
Which should I kill?"
The master of the house said:
"Kill the one that cannot cackle."
The next day,
a disciple asked Zhuāngzǐ:
"Yesterday, the tree in the mountains survived its natural lifespan by being useless,
but today, the master's goose died because it was useless.
What will you choose?"
Zhuāngzǐ smiled and said:
"Zhōu will choose to be between usefulness and uselessness.
Being between usefulness and uselessness,
it seems right but is not,
and thus one cannot escape trouble."
But if one rides on the Dào and Dé, it is not so:
no criticism, no blame;
sometimes a dragon, sometimes a snake;
transforming with the times,
never insisting on any one course.
Sometimes up, sometimes down,
taking the harvest as a measure,
and floating among the ancestors of all things;
they treat things as things but are not made into things by things.
How then can they be entangled?
This is what Shénnóng and Huángdì made their law.
But as for the nature of all things and the tradition of human relations, it is not so:
success leads to ruin,
greatness to decline,
integrity to mutilation,
honor to loss,
straightness to bending,
union to separation,
love to destruction,
much wisdom to scheming,
unworthiness to deceit.
How can one be certain of these? "
Niú Quē, a great scholar from Shàngdì,
traveled down to Hándān
and encountered bandits in the middle of Óushā.
The bandits demanded the contents of his satchel,
and he gave them.
They demanded his carriage and horses, and he gave them.
They demanded his clothes and bedding, and he gave them.
Niú Quē walked away.
The bandits said to one another:
"This is a prominent man of the world.
Now we have shamed him like this.
He will surely report us to the lord of ten thousand chariots,
