and the lord of ten thousand chariots will surely execute us with his state's power.
We will surely not live.
It would be better to pursue and kill him
to erase our tracks."
Thereupon they pursued him,
traveled thirty *lǐ*,
caught up with him, and killed him.
This was because of his fame.
Mèng Bèn was crossing a river;
he went ahead of the boatman.
The boatman was angered
and struck him on the head with an oar,
not knowing it was Mèng Bèn.
In the middle of the river,
Mèng Bèn glared at the boatman with wide eyes,
his hair stood on end,
his eyes split,
his temples bristled.
Everyone in the boat was thrown into the river.
Had the boatman known it was Mèng Bèn,
he would not have dared to look him straight in the eye,
nor would he have gone ahead while crossing.
How much less would he have shamed him?
This was because of not knowing.
Both knowing and not knowing
are not to be relied upon.
Only harmony and moderation are close to it.
Yet, it cannot be certain,
for there are those who do not discern harmony and moderation,
so harmony and moderation cannot always be avoided.
Sòng Huán Sīmǎ had a precious pearl.
He committed a crime and fled into exile.
The king sent someone to ask where the pearl was.
He said, "I threw it into the pond."
Thereupon, they drained the pond to search for it,
but found nothing,
and the fish died.
This illustrates how misfortune and fortune follow each other.
Zhòu committed wickedness in Shāng,
and calamity filled heaven and earth.
What good was harmony and moderation then?
Zhāng Yì loved politeness.
At his gate and among his screens, in gatherings, everyone hurried to him.
He respected even his carriage servants, relatives, and young children,
to settle his person,
but he did not live out his natural lifespan;
he died of an internal fever.
Shàn Bào loved ascetic practices.
He departed from society and abandoned the dusty world,
did not eat grains,
did not wear warm furs.
He dwelled in mountains, forests, and caves,
to preserve his life,
but he did not reach his full years;
a tiger ate him.
Kǒngzǐ was traveling and stopped to rest.
His horse bolted
and ate the crops of a countryman.
The countryman seized his horse.
Zǐgòng asked to go explain it,
but after his speech,
the countryman did not listen.
An uncouth person who had just begun serving Kǒngzǐ said,
"Allow me to go explain it."
He then said to the countryman,
"You do not plow in the Eastern Sea,
and I do not plow in the Western Sea.
How could my horse not eat your grain?"
The countryman was greatly pleased
and said to his companions,
"All explanations should be this eloquent,
unlike the person before!"
He untied the horse and returned it.
If an explanation can be so informal and still work,
how can external things be certain?
A *jūnzǐ* acts on his own initiative:
he respects others but is not necessarily respected,
he loves others but is not necessarily loved.
The one who respects and loves others
is himself;
those who are respected and loved
are others.
A *jūnzǐ* must focus on what is within himself,
not what is necessarily in others.
If he focuses on what is within himself, he will always meet with success.
15.1 *Shèn Dà*
Chapter One says:
A wise ruler becomes more fearful the greater he is,
and more anxious the stronger he is.
Generally, to be great
means to diminish neighboring states;
to be strong
means to overcome one's enemies.
Overcoming one's enemies incurs much resentment,
and diminishing neighboring states incurs much trouble.
With much trouble and much resentment,
even if the state is strong and great,
how can one not be fearful?
How can one not be anxious?
Therefore, a wise ruler thinks of danger in security,
of hardship in prosperity,
and of loss in gain.
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
"As if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice,"
to speak of caution in affairs.
Jié was without Dào,
violent, stubborn, and greedy.
The world trembled with fear and suffered because of him.
Those who spoke differed,
all in disagreement and agitated,
their true feelings hard to ascertain.
Gān Xīn exercised tyrannical power,
oppressing the feudal lords
and the common people.
The virtuous were filled with resentment.
He killed Lóng Páng
to subjugate the wicked multitude.
The masses were dejected
and all harbored distant ambitions,
none daring to speak directly;
their lives were like a constant fright.
The great ministers shared the suffering,
and without conspiring, they rebelled.
Jié became increasingly self-righteous,
boasting of his faults and excusing his wrongs.
The path of the ruler was severely blocked,
and the people of the state were in great disarray.
Tāng then became fearful
and worried about the unrest in the world.
He wanted to send Yī Yǐn to observe Kuàng Xià,
but feared he would not be trusted.
Tāng therefore personally shot at Yī Yǐn.
Yī Yǐn fled to Xià for three years
and returned to report at Bó,
saying:
"Jié is infatuated with Mòxī,
fond of Wǎnyǎn,
and does not care for his people.
The people's will cannot endure this;
those above and below hate each other.
The people's hearts are filled with accumulated grievances,
all saying:
'Heaven does not care for us,
the mandate of Xià is ending.'"
Tāng said to Yī Yǐn:
"What you tell me about Kuàng Xià is exactly like the poetry."
Tāng and Yī Yǐn made an oath,
to show their determination to destroy Xià.
Yī Yǐn again went to observe Kuàng Xià,
listening to Mòxī.
Mòxī said:
"Last night the Son of Heaven dreamt that there was a sun in the west,
and a sun in the east.
The two suns fought each other,
the western sun won,
and the eastern sun did not win."
Yī Yǐn reported this to Tāng.
Shāng suffered a drought,
but Tāng still dispatched his army,
to fulfill his oath with Yī Yǐn.
Therefore, he ordered the army to emerge from the east of the capital
and advance westward.
Before weapons clashed, Jié
fled. Chasing him to Dàshā,
his body was dismembered,
and he was slaughtered by all under Heaven.
As he could not be rectified through remonstrance,
even if he later regretted it,
what could be done?
Tāng was established as the Son of Heaven,
and the people of Xià greatly rejoiced,
as if they had found a loving parent.
Courtiers did not change their positions,
farmers did not abandon their fields,
merchants did not alter their shops,
and those near and far were like the people of Xià.
This is called utmost impartiality,
this is called utmost peace,
this is called utmost trust.
Tāng fully implemented Yī Yǐn’s covenant,
not avoiding the drought calamity,
and Yī Yǐn’s descendants enjoyed sacrifices from Shang for generations.
King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
and upon entering Yīn,
before alighting from his carriage,
he commanded that the descendants of Huángdì be enfeoffed in Zhù,
the descendants of Dì Yáo in Lí,
and the descendants of Dì Shùn in Chén;
after alighting from his carriage,
he commanded that the descendants of the Former Lord of Xià be enfeoffed in Qǐ,
and the descendants of Chéng Tāng be established in Sòng to maintain the Sānglín sacrifices.
King Wǔ then, in fear,
sighed deeply and shed tears.
He ordered Zhōu Gōng Dàn to bring in the surviving elders of Yīn,
and asked about the reasons for Yīn’s downfall,
and also asked what the populace approved of and what the people desired.
The surviving elders of Yīn replied:
“We wish to restore the policies of Pán Gēng.”
King Wǔ thereupon restored the policies of Pán Gēng;
he distributed the grain from Jùqiáo
and disbursed the money from Lùtái,
to show the people his impartiality;
he released those imprisoned and saved the condemned,
distributed wealth and forgave debts,
to relieve the poor and distressed;
he sealed Bǐgān’s tomb,
pacified Jīzǐ’s palace,
and marked Shāng Róng’s village gate.
Scholars passing by would quicken their steps,
and carriages passing by would lower their occupants;
within three days,
those who had plotted with him were enfeoffed as feudal lords,
the grandees were rewarded with land and altars,
and commoners had their taxes abolished.
Then he crossed the Yellow River
and returned west to report at the ancestral temple;
he pastured his horses on Huàshān
and his oxen in Táolín;
horses would not be ridden again,
and oxen would not be harnessed again;
he smeared the drums, flags, armor, and weapons with sacrificial blood,
stored them in the armories,
and never used them again in his lifetime.
This was the virtue of King Wǔ.
Therefore, the outer gates of the Míngtáng in Zhōu were not closed,
to show all under Heaven that nothing was concealed.
Only by not concealing can one guard the greatest treasures.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he captured two prisoners and questioned them,
saying:
“Does your state have any omens?”
One prisoner replied:
“Our state has omens.
Stars appearing in daytime and blood raining from the sky?
These are the omens of our state.”
The other prisoner replied:
“These are indeed omens.
However,
they are not the greatest ones.
The greatest omens of our state,
the greatest of them,
are when sons do not listen to fathers,
younger brothers do not listen to elder brothers,
and the ruler’s commands are not carried out.
These are the greatest omens.”
King Wǔ moved from his mat and bowed twice to him.
This was not honoring the captive,
but honoring his words.
Therefore, the Yì says:
“Hesitantly treading on a tiger’s tail,
ultimately auspicious.”
Zhào Xiāngzǐ attacked Dì,
conquering Zuǒrén and Zhōngrén.
He sent an envoy to report the victory to him,
but Xiāngzǐ was eating a meal of rice balls
and looked worried.
His attendants said:
“In one morning, two cities have fallen;
this is cause for joy,
why does Your Lord now look worried?”
Xiāngzǐ said:
“The great rivers, Jiāng and Hé,
do not last more than three days in flood;
a swirling wind and violent rain do not last a whole morning,
and midday does not last for an instant.
Now, the virtue and conduct of the Zhào clan
have not accumulated much,
yet in one morning two cities have fallen.
Will ruin befall me?”
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
“The Zhào clan will surely prosper!”
Indeed, worry leads to prosperity,
and joy leads to ruin;
victory is not the difficult part,
maintaining it is the difficult part.
Wise rulers maintain victory with this understanding,
hence their blessings extend to later generations.
Qí, Jīng, Wú, and Yuè all experienced victory,
but ultimately met ruin,
because they did not understand how to maintain victory.
Only a ruler who possesses the Way can maintain victory.
Kǒngzǐ’s strength
could lift the latch of a city gate,
but he would not be known for his strength;
Mòzǐ was skilled in defense and attack,
subduing Gōngshū Bān,
but he would not be known for military prowess.
Those who are good at maintaining victory
use strategy to strengthen the weak.
15.2 《Quánxūn》
Secondly, it says:
Profit cannot be twofold,
and loyalty cannot be both ways.
If one does not abandon small gains, one cannot achieve great gains;
if one does not abandon small loyalty, great loyalty will not be attained.
Therefore, small gains
are the ruiners of great gains;
small loyalty
is the betrayer of great loyalty.
Sages abandon the small and choose the great.
In the past, Jīng Gōngwáng fought Jìn Lìgōng at Yānlíng.
The Jīng army was defeated,
and Gōngwáng was wounded.
Before the battle, Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn was thirsty and sought a drink.
The attendant Yáng Gǔ carried rice wine and offered it to him.
Zǐfǎn angrily shouted:
“Hmph!
Withdraw!
It’s wine.”
The attendant Yáng Gǔ replied:
“It’s not wine.”
Zǐfǎn said:
“Quickly withdraw!
It’s wine.”
The attendant Yáng Gǔ again said:
“It’s not wine.”
Zǐfǎn took it and drank it.
Zǐfǎn was a man who loved wine,
and found it sweet and could not stop drinking,
until he was drunk.
After the battle ended,
Gōngwáng wanted to fight again and deliberated on the matter.
He sent someone to summon Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn.
Zǐfǎn declined, citing a heart ailment.
Gōngwáng rode his chariot to see him.
He entered the tent
and, smelling the odor of wine, returned,
saying:
“In today’s battle,
I was personally wounded;
my reliance was on the Sīmǎ.
Yet the Sīmǎ is like this,
forgetting the altars of the Jīng state and disregarding our people.
I have no one to fight with again.”
Thereupon, he dismissed the army and departed,
and had Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn executed as a punishment.
Therefore, when the attendant Yáng Gǔ offered the wine,
it was not to make Zǐfǎn drunk;
his intention was to show him loyal affection,
but it was precisely enough to kill him.
Hence it is said,
small loyalty
is the betrayer of great loyalty.
In the past, Jìn Xiàngōng sent Xún Xī to request passage through Yú to attack Guó.
Xún Xī said:
“Please let me use the jade disk of Chuíjí and the fine horses from Qūchǎn
to bribe the Duke of Yú,
and request passage;
it will surely be granted.”
Xiàngōng said:
“The jade disk of Chuíjí
is a treasure of my late sovereign;
the fine horses from Qūchǎn
are my lord’s excellent steeds.
If he accepts our gifts but does not grant us passage,
what then?”
Xún Xī 曰:
“Not so.
If they do not lend us the way,
they will certainly not accept us.
If they accept our tribute and lend us the way,
it would be like taking treasures from the inner treasury and storing them in the outer treasury,
and taking horses from the inner stable and placing them in the outer stable.
What is there for Your Lordship to worry about?”
Xiàn Gōng agreed to it.
So he sent Xún Xī with a team of horses from Qū as a front-hall gift,
and added the jade disc of Chuíjí,
to borrow a path from Yú to attack Guó.
The Duke of Yú was tempted by the treasures and horses and wanted to agree.
Gōng zhī Qí remonstrated, saying:
“It cannot be agreed to.
Yú and Guó
are like the wheel and its spoke protector;
the wheel relies on the spoke protector,
and the spoke protector also relies on the wheel.
Such is the situation of Yú and Guó.
Our ancestors had a saying:
‘When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.’
Guó's survival depends on Yú,
and Yú's survival also depends on Guó.
If you lend them the way,
then Guó will perish in the morning, and Yú will follow in the evening.
How can you lend them the way?”
The Duke of Yú did not listen,
and lent them the way.
Xún Xī attacked Guó,
and conquered it.
Returning, he then attacked Yú,
and also conquered it.
Xún Xī took the jade disc and led the horses to report back.
Xiàn Gōng joyfully said:
“The jade disc is still the same,
but
the horses' teeth have grown a little longer.”
Hence it is said that small gains destroy great gains.
In the state of Zhōngshān there was a man named Yóu.
Zhì Bó wanted to attack him but had no route,
so he cast a large bell,
wide enough for two carriage tracks, and sent it to him.
The ruler of Yóu was about to cut down cliffs and fill in ravines to welcome the bell.
Chìzhāng Mànzhī remonstrated, saying:
“The 'Shī' says:
‘Only by following principles can a state be settled.’
How could we obtain this from Zhì Bó?
Zhì Bó is greedy and untrustworthy.
He must want to attack us but has no route,
hence he made a large bell,
wide enough for two carriage tracks, and sent it to you.
If you then cut down cliffs and fill in ravines to welcome the bell,
his army will surely follow.”
He did not listen.
After a while,
he remonstrated again,
and the ruler said:
“A great state is showing favor,
and you are opposing it,
which is inauspicious.
Let it go.”
Chìzhāng Mànzhī said:
“For a minister to be disloyal and not upright is a crime;
if loyalty and uprightness are not heeded,
then it is permissible to distance oneself.”
He broke the axle and left,
arriving in Wèi seven days before Yóu fell.
The desire for the bell prevailed,
and when the desire for the bell prevailed, the counsel for Yóu's safety was blocked.
Whenever listening to advice,
one must carefully examine what prevails,
therefore the highest [wisdom] is to first overcome [one's desires].
Chāngguó Jūn led the armies of five states to attack Qí.
Qí sent Chù Zǐ as general,
to meet the armies of all states at Jì Shàng.
The King of Qí wanted to fight,
and sent a messenger to Chù Zǐ,
shaming and denouncing him, saying:
“If you do not fight,
I will surely wipe out your clan
and dig up your ancestral graves.”
Chù Zǐ was distressed by this,
and wished for the Qí army to be defeated.
So he fought with the armies of all states,
and when the battle began,
he struck the gong to retreat,
and the army was utterly routed.
The armies of all states pressed on them,
and Chù Zǐ then departed with a single carriage,
no one knowing his whereabouts,
nor hearing his voice.
Dá Zǐ then led the remaining troops
and encamped at Qín Zhōu.
Having no means to reward them,
he sent someone to request gold from the King of Qí.
The King of Qí angrily said:
“You have destroyed the likes of those young men,
how can I give you gold?”
He fought with the Yān people,
suffered a great defeat,
Dá Zǐ died,
and the King of Qí fled to Jǔ.
The Yān people pursued the defeated army into the capital,
and greatly contended for gold in Měitáng.
This is an example of those who are greedy for small gains and lose great gains.
15.3 《Xià Xián》
Thirdly:
A man of principle naturally prides himself before a ruler,
and an unworthy ruler also prides himself before a man of principle.
Day by day they pride themselves against each other,
when will they ever get along?
It is like the debates of the Rú and Mò schools and the customs of Qí and Jīng.
A wise ruler is not like this;
even if a scholar prides himself before him,
he treats him with even greater courtesy.
How can the scholar not return to him?
Where scholars gather,
the world follows.
An Dì is
the one to whom the world comes;
a Wáng is
the one to whom the world goes.
A person who has attained the Way,
though honored as Son of Heaven, is not arrogant,
though possessing the whole world, does not boast,
though humble as a commoner, is not disheartened or constrained,
though poor and without food or clothing, is not worried or intimidated.
Steadfastly sincere in what he inherently possesses,
clearly without doubt in what he relies upon,
resolute that he will certainly not change or shift,
harmonious in his transformation with yin and yang,
firm and solid in his heart,
empty and without artifice,
far-reaching in his aspirations,
profound and unfathomable,
resolute in his integrity,
humble and unwilling to assert his own righteousness,
lofty in his disdain for clever thought,
genuinely indifferent to
worldly slander or praise. He takes Heaven as his standard,
virtue as his conduct,
and the Way as his root.
He transforms with all things without end or limit,
his essence fills Heaven and Earth without exhaustion,
his spirit covers the universe without equal.
No one knows his beginning,
no one knows his end,
no one knows his gate,
no one knows his origin,
no one knows his source.
Its greatness has no outside,
its smallness has no inside.
This is called ultimate nobility.
If there is such a scholar,
the Five Dì could not make him their friend,
the Three Wáng could not make him their teacher.
If one casts off the appearance of an Dì or Wáng,
then one can nearly obtain him.
Yáo did not, as an Dì, meet Shàn Quǎn,
but faced north to ask him.
Yáo was the Son of Heaven,
Shàn Quǎn was a commoner.
Why was he treated with such extreme courtesy?
Shàn Quǎn was a scholar who had attained the Way;
a person who has attained the Way
cannot be treated with arrogance.
Yáo considered his virtue, conduct, understanding, and wisdom and found himself inferior,
thus he faced north to ask him.
This is called ultimate impartiality.
Who but one of ultimate impartiality could treat worthy men with courtesy?
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was the son of Wén Wáng,
the younger brother of Wǔ Wáng,
and the paternal uncle of Chéng Wáng.
He held court with seventy men from humble alleys and windowed shacks.
Wén Wáng initiated it but did not complete it,
Wǔ Wáng continued it but did not achieve it.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn held the young lord and brought it to completion,
hence he is called Chéng Wáng.
Was it not solely by humbling himself before scholars?
Qí Huán Gōng sought to see the minor minister Jì,
going three times in one day but failing to be granted an audience.
His attendant said:
“A ruler of ten thousand chariots,
seeking to see a commoner,
going three times in one day and failing to be granted an audience,
you can stop now.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Not so.
Scholars who disdain high official positions and emoluments
naturally slight their lord;
but when their lord disdains a hegemon,
he also slights his scholars.
Even if you, Master, disdain high official positions and emoluments,
how dare I disdain a hegemon?”
Then he went to see him,
unable to be stopped.
The world often cites Huán Gōng’s private conduct.
Though his private conduct was not refined,
he could still be a hegemon.
If he had truly followed this principle and cultivated his private conduct,
being a king would still be too little.
Zǐchǎn was the Chancellor of Zhèng.
He went to see Húqiū Zǐlín,
and when sitting with his disciples, he always sat according to age,
thus relying on his position as Chancellor at the gate.
To be the Chancellor of a state of ten thousand chariots and yet be able to disregard it,
and in planning aspirations and discussing conduct,
to search for people with one's heart,
could that be anyone but Zǐchǎn?
Therefore, as Chancellor of Zhèng for eighteen years,
he inflicted punishments on three people,
and killed two people.
No one picked up the peaches and plums that fell from the trees onto the path,
and no one picked up the awls and knives left on the road.
Wèi Wénhóu saw Duàngān Mù,
stood until he was weary and dared not rest.
Upon returning, he saw Zhái Huáng,
seated himself in the hall and spoke with him.
Zhái Huáng was displeased.
Wénhóu said:
“If I were to give Duàngān Mù an office, he would not accept it;
if I were to give him emoluments, he would not receive them.
Now you desire an office, the position of Chancellor;
you desire emoluments, the rank of High Minister.
Having already accepted my substance,
you yet demand my courtesy.
Is this not difficult?”
Therefore, when a virtuous ruler employs people,
those who are unwilling to accept substance are accorded great courtesy.
There is no higher courtesy to a scholar than restraining one's desires;
if desires are restrained, then commands will be followed.
Wénhóu can be said to have been good at showing courtesy to scholars.
Because he was good at showing courtesy to scholars, he defeated Jīng in the south at Liándī;
he defeated Qí in the east at Chángchéng,
captured the Marquis of Qí,
presented him to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven rewarded Wénhóu with the rank of High Minister.
15.4 《Bàogēng》
Fourthly: Although a state may be small,
if its food is sufficient to feed the worthy people of the world,
its chariots are sufficient to transport the worthy people of the world,
and its wealth is sufficient to treat the worthy people of the world with courtesy,
and it associates with the worthy people of the world as companions,
this is how Wén Wáng became king.
Even if one cannot become king now,
to achieve peace and security through this,
is it not easy?
This is how Zhào Xuānmèng was spared,
how Zhōu Zhāowén Jūn became prominent,
and how Méngcháng Jūn repelled the Jīng army.
The way of the ancients who established great achievements and fame, and secured their states and saved themselves,
was no other;
they must have followed this path.
Capable scholars cannot be subdued by arrogance or indulgence.
Formerly, when Zhào Xuānmèng was about to go up to Jiàng,
he saw beneath a bent mulberry tree
a starving person lying down, unable to rise.
Xuānmèng stopped his chariot,
got down to feed him,
purified the food and offered it to him.
The starving person swallowed twice before he could see.
Xuānmèng asked him:
“Why are you so hungry?”
He replied:
“Your servant was an official in Jiàng,
and on my return, my provisions ran out.
I was ashamed to beg and disliked taking without permission,
hence I came to this state.”
Xuānmèng gave him two slices of dried meat,
he bowed to receive them but dared not eat.
When asked why,
he replied:
“Your servant has an old mother,
I intend to give these to her.”
Xuānmèng said:
“Eat these,
and I will give you more.”
Then he again gave him two bundles of dried meat and one hundred coins,
and then departed.
Two years later,
Jìn Línggōng wished to kill Xuānmèng,
and hid armed men in a room to await him,
then invited Xuānmèng to drink wine.
Xuānmèng knew of the plot,
and left in the middle of the drinking.
Línggōng ordered the men in the room to pursue and kill him quickly.
One man pursued swiftly,
and reached Xuānmèng first.
Seeing Xuānmèng’s face, he said:
“Alas,
my lord!
I beg to die in your stead.”
Xuānmèng said:
“What is your name?”
He turned and ran while replying:
“What does a name matter!
Your servant is the starving person from beneath the bent mulberry tree.”
He turned back, fought, and died.
Xuānmèng thus survived.
This is what the 《Shū》 refers to as
“virtue is hardly small.”
Xuānmèng’s virtue towards one scholar still saved his life,
how much more so for virtue towards ten thousand people?
Therefore, the 《Shī》 says:
“Valiant warriors,
pillars of dukes and marquises,”
“Numerous are the excellent scholars,
through whom Wén Wáng found peace.”
How can a ruler not strive to show kindness to scholars?
Scholars are difficult to know,
only extensive association is effective,
for then there is nowhere to hide.
Zhāng Yí,
a collateral descendant of the Wèi clan,
was about to travel west to Qín,
passing through Dōng Zhōu.
A guest spoke of him to Zhōu Zhāowén Jūn, saying:
“Zhāng Yí, a man from the Wèi clan,
is a talented scholar
who is about to travel west to Qín.
May Your Lord treat him with courtesy and respect.”
Zhāowén Jūn met him and said:
“I hear you are traveling to Qín.
My state is small,
not enough to retain you.
However,
will your travels necessarily be successful?
If by chance you do not succeed,
please return to me.
Although my state is small,
I invite you to share it with me.”
Zhāng Yí turned around and ran,
bowing twice to the north.
When Zhāng Yí departed,
Zhāowén Jūn saw him off and provided him with resources.
When he arrived in Qín,
he stayed for a time,
and Huì Wáng was pleased with him and made him Chancellor.
Of all those Zhāng Yí was indebted to in the world,
none was like Zhōu Zhāowén Jūn.
Zhōu,
a state of a thousand chariots,
its importance outweighed a state of ten thousand chariots.
It caused Qín Huì Wáng to treat it as a mentor.
At the Fēngzé assembly,
the King of Wèi once acted as charioteer,
and the King of Hán as the right-hand attendant.
Their names and titles are not forgotten even today,
this was the power of Zhāng Yí.
Méngcháng Jūn was formerly in Xuē,
when the Jīng people attacked it.
Chúnyú Kūn was sent by Qí as an envoy to Jīng,
and on his return,
he passed through Xuē.
Méngcháng Jūn ordered someone to treat him with courtesy and personally escorted him to the outskirts,
saying to Chúnyú Kūn:
“The Jīng people are attacking Xuē.
If you, Master, are not concerned about this,
then Wén has no way to serve you again.”
Chúnyú Kūn said:
“I respectfully heed your command.”
When he arrived in Qí,
he made his report.
The King said:
“What did you see in Jīng?”
He replied:
“Jīng is very strong,
and Xuē also does not measure its strength.”
The King said:
“What do you mean?”
He replied:
“Xuē does not measure its strength,
and has established a pure temple for the former kings.
Jīng is strong and attacking Xuē,
so Xuē’s pure temple will surely be in danger.
Therefore, I say Xuē does not measure its strength,
and Jīng is also very strong.”
The King of Qí knew it from their expressions,
saying:
"Alas!
The temple of my late lord is there."
He swiftly raised troops to rescue it,
and thus Xuē was completely preserved.
The pleas of kneeling and tripping,
the audiences of bowing while seated,
though meager, were indeed meager.
Therefore, a good persuader
lays out the situation,
speaks of the method,
and sees another's urgency
as if he himself were in peril.
How could one use brute force?
Brute force is contemptible.
If persuasion is not heeded,
the responsibility does not solely lie with the one being persuaded,
but also with the persuader.
15.5 On Accordant Persuasion
Fifthly:
A good persuader is like a skillful artisan,
who relies on the strength of others to make it his own strength;
he comes along with their coming,
and goes along with their going;
he sets no fixed form,
but grows and develops with them;
his words echo theirs;
he rises and falls with them,
following where they go.
Though one's own strength be great,
and one's talent robust,
it is used to control their destiny.
Calling against the wind
does not make one's voice louder;
looking from a height
does not make one's eyes clearer;
it is the reliance on convenience that matters.
Huì Àng met Sòng Kāng Wáng,
and Kāng Wáng stamped his foot, cleared his throat, and spoke rapidly, saying:
"What I like are the brave and strong;
I do not like those who practice benevolence and righteousness.
What will the guest teach me?"
Huì Àng replied:
"I have a method here
that makes a person, though brave, unable to be stabbed;
though strong, unable to be hit.
Does Your Majesty have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Good!
This is what I wish to hear."
Huì Àng said:
"To be unable to be stabbed and
unable to be hit,
this is still an insult.
I have a method here
that makes a person, though brave, not dare to stab;
though strong, not dare to hit.
Does Your Majesty have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Good!
This is what I wish to know."
Huì Àng said:
"Not daring to stab
and not daring to hit,
this is not because they lack the intent.
I have a method here
that makes people originally have no such intent.
Does Your Majesty have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Good!
This is what I desire."
Huì Àng said:
"To have no such intent
does not yet mean having a heart of love and benefit.
I have a method here
that makes all men and women under Heaven joyfully desire to love and benefit him.
This is superior to being brave and strong,
and stands above the four burdens.
Does Your Majesty have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"This is what I wish to obtain."
Huì Àng replied:
"Kǒng, Mò are examples of this.
Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí,
though without territory they were lords,
though without office they were chiefs;
all men and women under Heaven stretched their necks and stood on tiptoe, wishing to bring peace and benefit to them.
Now Your Majesty, the lord of ten thousand chariots,
if you truly have this aspiration,
then all within your four borders will obtain its benefits.
This is far superior to Kǒng and Mò."
Sòng Wáng had nothing to respond.
Huì Àng hurried out.
Sòng Wáng said to his attendants:
"He is eloquent!
The guest has convinced me with his persuasion."
Sòng Wáng was a common lord,
yet his heart could still be swayed.
This is due to accord.
With accord, the poor and humble can overcome the rich and noble,
the small and weak can control the strong and great.
Tián Zàn, wearing patched clothes, met Jīng Wáng.
Jīng Wáng said:
"Sir, why are your clothes so shabby?"
Tián Zàn replied:
"There are clothes worse than these."
Jīng Wáng said:
"May I hear of them?"
He replied:
"Armor is worse than these."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"In winter it is cold,
in summer it is hot;
no clothes are worse than armor.
Zàn is poor,
hence his clothes are shabby.
Now Your Majesty, the lord of ten thousand chariots,
rich and noble beyond compare,
yet you like to clothe your people in armor;
your servant cannot understand this.
Is it perhaps for its righteousness?
The business of armor is the business of war:
cutting off people's heads,
gouging out people's bellies,
demolishing people's city walls,
punishing people's fathers and sons.
Its name is also extremely inglorious.
Is it perhaps for its practicality?
If one intends to harm others,
others will certainly intend to harm him;
if one intends to endanger others,
others will certainly intend to endanger him.
Its practicality is also extremely unsettling.
Of these two,
your servant sees nothing for Your Majesty to gain."
Jīng Wáng had nothing to respond.
Although his persuasion did not gain wide acceptance,
Tián Zàn can be said to have established his method.
As for the meaning of ceasing hostilities,
he did not yet understand it.
Guǎn Zǐ was captured in Lǔ.
Lǔ bound him and put him in a cage,
and had laborers carry him to Qí.
They sang and pulled him along.
Guǎn Zǐ feared that Lǔ would stop and kill him,
and wished to reach Qí quickly.
So he said to the laborers:
"I will sing for you,
and you will harmonize with me."
His songs were suitable for marching quickly,
the laborers did not get tired,
and they traveled very fast.
Guǎn Zǐ can be said to have been able to accord.
The laborers got what they wanted,
and he also got what he wanted.
With this technique,
using it in a state of ten thousand chariots,
his hegemony would still be small;
Huán Gōng would be difficult to deal with in this way.
15.6 On Not Expanding
Sixthly:
The wise in undertaking affairs must rely on opportune timing.
When the timing is not certain to succeed,
their human affairs are not expanded;
success is acceptable, and failure is also acceptable.
They entrust what they cannot do to what they can,
like a boat and a cart.
In the north there is a beast
named Jué,
with the front of a rat and the rear of a rabbit.
When it scurries, it stumbles;
when it runs, it falls.
It constantly gathers sweet grass for Qióngqióng Jùxū and gives it to them.
When Jué is in trouble or danger,
Qióngqióng Jùxū will surely carry it away and run.
This is entrusting what one cannot do to what one can.
Bào Shú, Guǎn Zhòng, and Zhào Hū
were three good friends.
They wished to establish the state of Qí together,
believing Prince Jiū would surely be enthroned.
Zhào Hū said:
"The three of us in the state of Qí
are like the legs of a tripod;
remove one, and it cannot stand.
Moreover, Prince Xiǎo Bái will surely not be enthroned.
It is better for the three of us to assist Prince Jiū."
Guǎn Zhòng 曰:
“不可。
夫國人惡公子糾之母，
以及公子糾；
公子小白無母，
而國人憐之。
事未可知，
不若令一人事公子小白。
夫有齊國必此二公子也。”
故令 Bào Shū 傅公子小白，
Guǎn zǐ、Zhào Hū 居公子糾所。
公子糾外物則固難必。
雖然，
Guǎn zǐ 之慮近之矣。
若是而猶不全也，
其天邪，
人事則盡之矣。
齊攻廩丘。
趙使 Kǒng Qīng 將死士而救之，
與齊人戰，
大敗之。
齊將死。
得車二千，
得尸三萬以為二京。
Níng Yuè 謂 Kǒng Qīng 曰:
“惜矣，
不如歸尸以內攻之。
越聞之，
古善戰者，
莎隨賁服，
卻舍延尸，
彼得尸而財費乏，
車甲盡於戰，
府庫盡於葬。
此之謂內攻之。”
Kǒng Qīng 曰: (
“ (敵) 齊不尸則如何？”
Níng Yuè 曰:
“戰而不勝，其罪一。
與人出而不與人入，
其罪二。
與之尸而弗取，
其罪三。
民以此三者怨上，
上無以使下，
下無以事上。
是之謂重攻之。”
Níng Yuè 可謂知用文武矣。
用武則以力勝，
用文則以德勝。
文武盡勝，
何敵之不服？
Jìn Wén Gōng 欲合諸侯。
Jiù Fàn 曰:
“不可。
天下未知君之義也。”
公曰:
“何若？”
Jiù Fàn 曰:
“天子避叔帶之難，
出居于鄭。
君奚不納之，
以定大義？
且以樹譽。”
Wén Gōng 曰:
“吾其能乎？”
Jiù Fàn 曰:
“事若能成，
繼文之業，
定武之功，
闢土安疆，
於此乎在矣。
事若不成，
補周室之闕，
勤天子之難，
成教垂名，
於此乎在矣。
君其勿疑。”
Wén Gōng 聽之，
遂與草中之戎、驪土之翟，
定天子于成周。
於是天子賜之南陽之地，
遂霸諸侯。
舉事義且利，
以立大功。
Wén Gōng 可謂智矣。
此 Jiù Fàn 之謀也。
出亡十七年，
反國四年而霸，
其聽皆如 Jiù Fàn 者耶！
Guǎn zǐ、Bào Shū 佐齊桓公舉事，
齊之東鄙人有常致苦者。
Guǎn zǐ 死，
Shù Diāo、Yì Yá 用，
國之人常致不苦，
不知致苦，
卒為齊國良工，
澤及子孫。
知大禮，
知大禮雖不知國可也。
七曰:
三代所寶莫如因，
因則無敵。
Yǔ 通三江、五湖，
決伊闕，
迵溝陸，
注之東海，
因水之力也。
Shùn 一徙成邑，
再徙成都，
三徙成國，
而 Yáo 授之禪位，
因人之心也。
Tāng、Wǔ 以千乘制夏、商，
因民之欲也。
如秦者立而至，
有車也；
適越者坐而至，
有舟也。
秦、越，遠塗也，
竫立安坐而至者，
因其械也。
Wǔ Wáng 使人候殷，
反報 Qí Zhōu 曰:
“殷其亂矣。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“其亂焉至？”
對曰:
“讒慝勝忠良。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“尚未也。”
又往，
反報曰:
“其亂加矣。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“焉至？”
對曰:
“賢者出走矣。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“尚未也。”
又往，
反報曰:
“其亂甚矣。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“焉至？”
對曰:
“百姓不敢誹怨矣。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
遽告 Tài Gōng。
Tài Gōng 對曰:
“讒慝勝忠良，
命曰戮；
賢者出走，
命曰崩；
百姓不敢誹怨，
命曰刑勝。
其亂至矣，
不可以駕矣。”
故選車三百，
虎賁三千，
朝要甲子之期，
而 Zhòu 為禽，
則 Wǔ Wáng 固知其無與為敵也。
因其所用，
何敵之有矣？
Wǔ Wáng 至鮪水。
殷使 Jiāo Gé 候周師，
Wǔ Wáng 見之。
Jiāo Gé 曰:
“西伯將何之？
無欺我也。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“不子欺，
將之殷也。”
Jiāo Gé 曰:
“朅至？”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“將以甲子至殷郊，
子以是報矣。”
Jiāo Gé 行。
天雨，
日夜不休，
Wǔ Wáng 疾行不輟。
軍師皆諫曰:
“卒病，
請休之。”
Wǔ Wáng 曰:
“吾已令 Jiāo Gé 以甲子之期報其主矣。
今甲子不至，
是令 Jiāo Gé 不信也。
Jiāo Gé 不信也，
其主必殺之。
吾疾行以救 Jiāo Gé 之死也。”
King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] indeed reached the outskirts of Yīn [Yīn] on the *jiǎzǐ* day.
Yīn [Yīn] had already arrayed its forces in advance.
Upon reaching Yīn [Yīn],
he engaged in battle
and won a great victory.
This was the righteousness of King Wǔ [Wǔwáng].
If one does what others desire,
and oneself does what others dislike,
what advantage is there in arraying forces in advance?
It merely allowed King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] to reap without sowing.
When King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] entered Yīn [Yīn],
he heard that there was an elder in Yīn [Yīn].
King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] went to see him
and asked why Yīn [Yīn] had perished.
The Yīn [Yīn] elder replied:
"If Your Majesty wishes to know,
then please make noon the appointed time."
King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] and Duke Dàn of Zhōu [Zhōugōng Dàn] agreed to meet early the next day,
but could not find him.
King Wǔ [Wǔwáng] was puzzled by this.
Duke Zhōu [Zhōugōng] said:
"I already understand.
This is a gentleman;
he would not take advantage of his lord's misfortune
to reveal his evils to Your Majesty.
He could not bear to do so.
As for setting a time and not appearing,
speaking and not being trustworthy—
this is why Yīn [Yīn] perished,
and he has already used this to inform Your Majesty."
Indeed, those who observe Heaven
examine the constellations to know the four seasons,
because of [the correlations].
Those who calculate the calendar
observe the moon's movements to know the new and full moons,
because of [the correlations].
When Yǔ [Yǔ] went to the Naked Country,
he entered naked and exited clothed,
because of [the customs].
When Mòzǐ [Mòzǐ] met King Jīng [Jīngwáng],
he wore embroidered robes and played the *shēng*,
because of [the circumstances].
When Kǒngzǐ [Kǒngzǐ] led Mǐzǐxiá [Mǐzǐxiá] to see Lady Lí [Lífūrén],
because of [the context].
Tāng [Tāng] and Wǔ [Wǔ] encountered chaotic times
and faced suffering people.
They championed their righteousness
and achieved their merits,
because of [the prevailing conditions].
Therefore, adapting leads to success;
being rigid leads to failure.
Those who adapt have no rivals.
Even if a state is large,
and its people are numerous,
what good is it [if it does not adapt]?
15.8 "Chájīn" [Chájīn]
Eighth says:
Why do superiors not follow the laws of the former kings?
It is not that they are not virtuous,
but because those laws cannot be followed.
The laws of the former kings
have come down through the ages from antiquity.
Some people have added to them,
and some people have subtracted from them.
How can they be followed?
Even if people had not added or subtracted from them,
they still could not be followed.
The decrees of the East and the Xia [Dōng、Xià],
and the laws of antiquity and the present,
differ in language and vary in their principles.
Therefore, many ancient decrees do not accord with present-day speech,
and many present-day laws do not conform to ancient laws.
People of different customs
are similar to this.
What they desire to do may be the same,
but what they desire to do may be different. Unclear pronouncements are not pleasing,
just like the differences in boats, carriages, clothing, caps, flavors, sounds, and sights.
People consider themselves right
and instead criticize each other.
The scholars of the world are mostly argumentative;
they speak of profit and twist words,
not seeking the truth of things,
but striving to undermine each other,
making winning their sole objective.
How then can the laws of the former kings
be followed?
Even if they could be obtained,
they still could not be followed.
For all laws of the former kings
had a specific relevance to their time,
and the time does not arrive with the law.
Even if a law from the past were to arrive today,
it still could not be followed.
Therefore, one should select the established laws of the former kings,
but follow the principles by which they became laws.
What are the principles by which the former kings made laws?
The principles by which the former kings made laws were human nature.
And one is also human.
Therefore, by examining oneself, one can understand others;
by examining the present, one can understand the past.
The past and present are one,
and others are the same as oneself.
A man of understanding
values knowing the distant from the near,
the past from the present,
and the unseen from what is seen.
Therefore, by observing the shadow beneath the hall,
one knows the movements of the sun and moon and the changes of yin and yang.
By seeing the water in a bottle freeze,
one knows the coldness of the world and the hiding of fish and turtles.
By tasting one sliver of meat,
one knows the flavor of the entire pot and the seasoning of the whole cauldron.
The people of Jīng [Jīng] wanted to attack Sòng [Sòng].
They sent men to mark the Yōngshuǐ [Yōngshuǐ] River in advance.
The Yōngshuǐ [Yōngshuǐ] suddenly rose.
The Jīng [Jīng] people did not know this;
they followed the markers and crossed at night.
More than a thousand men drowned,
and the army was startled and abandoned its camps.
At the time they first placed the markers, it could have served as a guide,
but now the water had changed and risen significantly.
The Jīng [Jīng] people still followed the markers to guide themselves;
this is why they failed.
The rulers of today,
who follow the laws of the former kings,
are similar to this.
Their times have already diverged from the laws of the former kings,
yet they say,
"These are the laws of the former kings,"
and follow them,
using them to govern.
Is this not tragic?
Therefore, a state without laws will fall into chaos,
but holding onto laws without changing them leads to perversity.
Perversity and chaos cannot maintain a state.
When the world changes and times shift,
it is proper to reform the laws.
This is comparable to a good physician:
diseases change in myriad ways,
and medicines also change in myriad ways.
If the disease changes but the medicine does not,
those who were once long-lived people
will now become child-ghosts.
Therefore, in all undertakings, one must act according to the law,
but those who change laws adapt according to the times.
If one follows this principle, there will be no errors in action.
Those who dare not debate laws
are the common people;
those who defend them to the death
are the officials;
those who change laws according to the times
are wise rulers.
Thus, among the seventy-two sages who ruled the world,
their laws were all different.
They did not intentionally contradict each other,
but the circumstances of their times were different.
Therefore, it is said that a good sword is valued for its sharpness,
not for being Mòyé [Mòyé];
a good horse is valued for traveling a thousand *lǐ*,
not for being Jì'áo [Jì'áo].
Achieving success and fame—
this is the "thousand *lǐ*" of the former kings.
There was a man from Chǔ [Chǔ] who was crossing a river.
His sword fell from the boat into the water.
He immediately carved a mark on his boat, saying,
"This is where my sword fell."
When the boat stopped,
he entered the water at the spot he had marked to search for it.
The boat had already moved,
but the sword had not.
To search for a sword like this,
is it not foolish?
To govern one's state with a fixed law is like this.
The times have already moved on,
but the law does not move.
To use this to govern,
is it not difficult?
There was a person crossing a river
who saw someone pulling an infant, about to throw it into the river.
The infant cried.
The person asked the reason,
and the man said,
"His father is a good swimmer."
Even if his father is a good swimmer,
how could his son immediately be a good swimmer?
To employ things based on this reasoning would certainly be perverse.
The governance of the state of Jīng [Jīngguó]
is similar to this.
16.1 "Xiānshí" [Xiānshí]
Chapter One:
Generally, whenever a state perishes,
those who possess the Way invariably depart first.
This has been true from ancient times to the present.
Territory follows the city,
the city follows the people,
and the people follow the worthy.
Therefore, a worthy ruler gains the worthy, and thereby gains the people;
when the people are gained, the city is gained;
when the city is gained, the territory is gained.
Indeed, for territory to be gained, must one necessarily traverse its land and persuade its people?
It is merely a matter of grasping its essence.
Zhōng Gǔ (終古), the Grand Astrologer of Xià (夏),
brought forth his maps and laws, held them, and wept.
Jié (桀) of Xià (夏) was deluded,
and his tyrannical chaos intensified.
So Grand Astrologer Zhōng Gǔ (終古) fled to Shāng (商). [19) Tāng (湯) rejoiced and announced to the feudal lords, saying:
"The King of Xià (夏) is without the Way,
tyrannizing the populace,
impoverishing his kinsmen,
humiliating his meritorious ministers,
disregarding his worthy and good,
abandoning righteousness and listening to slander.
The common people all resent him,
and ministers who uphold the law
have defected to Shāng (商)."
Xiàng Zhì (向摯), the Inner Scribe of Yīn (殷), seeing Zhòu (紂)'s increasing tyranny, chaos, and delusion,
then took his maps and laws
and fled to Zhōu (周).
King Wǔ (武) was greatly pleased,
and announced to the feudal lords, saying:
"The King of Shāng (商) is in great disorder,
immersed in the vice of wine,
keeping Jī Zǐ (箕子) far away,
and drawing close to Gū (姑) and Xī (息). [38) Dájǐ (妲己) wields political power,
rewards and punishments are arbitrary,
laws and regulations are not followed,
three innocent people have been killed,
the people are greatly disobedient,
and ministers who uphold the law
have fled to the state of Zhōu (周)."
Tú Shǔ (屠黍), the Grand Astrologer of Jìn (晉), seeing the disorder in Jìn (晉),
and seeing the Duke of Jìn (晉公) as arrogant and lacking virtue and righteousness,
returned to Zhōu (周) with his maps and laws.
Duke Wēi (威公) of Zhōu (周) saw him and asked,
saying:
"Among the states of the world, which will perish first?"
He replied:
"Jìn (晉) will perish first."
Duke Wēi (威公) asked for the reason.
He replied:
"When I was in Jìn (晉),
I dared not speak directly.
I showed the Duke of Jìn (晉公) the celestial omens—
that the movements of the sun, moon, and stars were often amiss—
and he said:
'What can this do?'
Then I showed him that human affairs were largely unrighteous,
and the common people were all resentful and grieving,
and he said:
'What harm can this cause?'
Then I showed him that neighboring states were disobedient,
and worthy and good people were not promoted,
and he said:
'What harm can this cause?'
Like this,
he did not know why he would perish.
Therefore, I said Jìn (晉) would perish first."
Three years later,
Jìn (晉) indeed perished.
Duke Wēi (威公) again saw Tú Shǔ (屠黍) and asked,
saying:
"Which is next?"
He replied:
"Zhōngshān (中山) is next."
Duke Wēi (威公) asked for the reason.
He replied:
"Heaven created people and ordained distinctions.
Having distinctions
is the righteousness of humanity,
which differentiates them from birds, beasts, and deer,
and is why the relationship between ruler and minister, and high and low, is established.
The customs of Zhōngshān (中山)
are to treat day as night,
and night as day,
with men and women intimately entwined,
without rest.
They indulged in licentious and wanton pleasures,
and their songs and ballads favored sadness.
Their ruler did not know to despise this.
This is the custom of a perishing state.
Therefore, I said Zhōngshān (中山) is next."
Two years later,
Zhōngshān (中山) indeed perished.
Duke Wēi (威公) again saw Tú Shǔ (屠黍) and asked,
saying:
"Which is next?"
Tú Shǔ (屠黍) did not reply.
Duke Wēi (威公) pressed him with the question.
He replied:
"You are next."
Duke Wēi (威公) was then afraid.
He sought out the elders of the state,
found Yì Shì (義蒔) and Tián Yì (田邑) and treated them with reverence,
found Shǐ Lín (史驎) and Zhào Pián (趙駢) and made them admonishing ministers.
He abolished thirty-nine harsh decrees,
and reported this to Tú Shǔ (屠黍).
He replied:
"Perhaps you may yet complete your life!"
He said:
"I have heard that:
when a state prospers,
Heaven sends it worthy men and outspoken critics;
when a state perishes,
Heaven sends it corrupt people and flattering sycophants."
Duke Wēi (威公) died,
and his coffin,
after nine months, could not be buried.
Zhōu (周) then split into two.
Therefore, the words of those who possess the Way
must not be taken lightly.
The Zhōu (周) tripod depicted the Tāotiè (饕餮),
which has a head but no body.
It eats people but cannot swallow them,
and harm returns to its own body.
This illustrates the retribution of karma.
Doing evil is likewise.
When Bái Guī (白圭) was in Zhōngshān (中山),
the King of Zhōngshān (中山) wanted to keep him,
but Bái Guī (白圭) firmly declined and
left in his carriage.
He then went to Qí (齊),
and the King of Qí (齊) also wanted to keep him in office,
but he again declined and left.
People asked him why.
He said:
"Both these states are about to perish.
What I have learned is that a state has five 'ends.'
What are these five 'ends'?
He said:
If there is no one to trust, then trust is ended.
If there is no one to praise, then reputation is ended.
If there is no one to love, then affection is ended.
If travelers have no provisions and residents have no food, then wealth is ended.
If one cannot employ others, nor employ oneself, then achievements are ended.
If a state has these five,
it will certainly perish without a trace.
Zhōngshān (中山) and Qí (齊) both suffer from these."
If the King of Zhōngshān (中山) and the King of Qí (齊)
had heard of the five 'ends' and changed their ways,
they would certainly not have perished.
The trouble lay in not hearing,
or even if they heard, not believing.
Thus, the ruler's essential task
lies solely in being good at listening.
For instance, to cede five territories to Zhào (趙),
and then mobilize all forces to resist the army at Jìshàng (濟上),
is of no benefit.
This is to abandon that by which one survives,
and to create that by which one perishes.
16.2 "Viewing the World" (Guān Shì 觀世)
Chapter Two:
Although there are men of the Way in the world,
they are indeed few.
One worthy man in a thousand *lǐ* (里)
is like shoulders brushing;
one sage in successive generations
is like heels following.
The coming of worthy men and sages
is difficult like this,
yet governance necessarily depends on them.
How then can good governance be achieved?
Even if by chance they exist,
they may not be recognized;
if unrecognized, it is the same as having no worthy men.
This is why periods of good governance are short,
and periods of chaos are long.
Therefore, kingship does not last beyond four generations,
and hegemony does not last beyond six generations;
perishing states follow one after another,
and imprisoned rulers succeed each other.
If worthy men are obtained, there are no such troubles.
This is why the more than four hundred states enfeoffed by Zhōu (周),
and the more than eight hundred subservient states,
none exist today;
even those that exist have all once perished.
A worthy ruler, knowing this to be the case,
therefore becomes more cautious day by day,
to complete his life.
This is like one climbing a mountain:
though already high up,
looking left and right,
there are still towering mountains above.
The company that a xìanzhě keeps
is similar to this.
When one is already a xìanzhě,
and one’s conduct is already noble,
one looks around
and still finds everyone more xìanzhě than oneself.
Therefore, Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"If I keep company with those who are not as good as me,
I will not associate with them,
for they will hinder me.
If I keep company with those who are equal to me,
I will not associate with them,
for they will not benefit me."
Only a xìanzhě will associate with those who are more xìanzhě than themselves.
For a xìanzhě to be able to associate with someone,
one must treat them with courtesy.
If the ruler is xìanzhě and the era is well-governed,
then the xìanzhě will be in high positions.
If the ruler is unworthy and the era is chaotic,
then the xìanzhě will be in low positions, and sycophants will advance. Now the Zhōu dynasty has perished,
and the world is in ruins.
There is no greater chaos than having no Tiānzǐ;
without a Tiānzǐ, the strong overcome the weak,
the many oppress the few,
they mutually annihilate with weapons,
and cannot rest.
Sycophants advance,
and the present age is exactly like this.
Therefore, in this current age, if one wishes to seek a scholar of the Dào,
then it must be on the banks of rivers and seas,
in the depths of mountains and valleys,
in remote, secluded, and quiet places.
Only then might one be fortunate enough to find them.
Tài Gōng fished at Zīquán
during the reign of Zhòu.
Therefore, Wén Wáng found him
and became king.
Wén Wáng was a ruler of a thousand chariots,
Zhòu was a Tiānzǐ.
The Tiānzǐ lost him,
and the ruler of a thousand chariots gained him.
This is the difference between knowing and not knowing.
The common people
can be employed without being known,
and commanded without courtesy.
But as for scholars of the Dào,
they must be treated with courtesy and known,
only then can their intelligence and ability be fully utilized.
Yàn Zǐ traveled to Jìn.
He saw a man wearing a fur coat inside-out, carrying firewood, resting by the road,
and thought him a jūnzǐ.
He sent someone to ask him,
saying,
"Why are you here?"
The man replied,
"A man from Qí has burdened me,
my name is Yuè Shífù."
Yàn Zǐ exclaimed,
"Hī!"
He immediately unharnessed his left horse to ransom him,
and carried him home in his carriage.
Upon arriving at his residence,
Yuè Shífù entered without a word of thanks.
Yuè Shífù became angry
and requested to sever ties.
Yàn Zǐ had someone respond, saying,
"Yīng has never before had your acquaintance,
but now I have freed you from misfortune.
Am I still unworthy in your eyes?"
Yuè Shífù said,
"I have heard that a jūnzǐ bows to those who do not know him,
but stands tall before those who know him.
That is why I request to sever ties."
Yàn Zǐ then came out to see him and said,
"Previously, I only saw the guest's appearance.
Now I see the guest's aspirations.
Yīng has heard that those who examine reality do not dwell on reputation,
and those who observe conduct do not criticize words.
Can Yīng be dismissed without being abandoned?"
Yuè Shífù replied,
"If you treat me with such courtesy,
how dare I not respectfully comply."
Yàn Zǐ then treated him as his principal guest.
Common people take credit for their achievements,
and once credited, they become arrogant.
Now Yàn Zǐ had the merit of freeing a man from distress,
yet he humbled himself to him.
He is indeed far removed from common ways.
This is the way to complete one's achievements.
Zǐ Lièzǐ was impoverished,
and his face showed signs of hunger.
A guest spoke of this to Zhèng Zǐyáng,
saying,
"Zǐ Liè Yǔkòu
is surely a scholar of the Dào,
yet he lives in your state and is impoverished.
Are you not perhaps displeased with scholars?"
Zhèng Zǐyáng ordered an official to give him several tens of measures of grain.
Zǐ Lièzǐ went out to meet the envoy,
bowed twice, and declined.
After the envoy left,
Zǐ Lièzǐ entered his home.
His wife looked at him and beat her chest,
saying,
"I have heard that the wives and children of those who follow the Dào
all live in comfort and happiness.
Now your wife and children show signs of hunger,
and the ruler, having made a mistake, sent food to you,
yet you refused it.
Is this not fate?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ smiled and said to her,
"The ruler does not know me personally,
but sends me grain based on others' words.
Later, if he blames me,
he will also do so based on others' words.
This is why I did not accept it."
In the end, the common people indeed rebelled
and killed Zǐyáng.
To accept someone's sustenance
and not die in their calamity is unrighteous;
to die in their calamity is to die for a ruler without the Dào.
To die for a ruler without the Dào
is contrary to the Dào.
Zǐ Lièzǐ avoided unrighteousness and averted acting contrary to the Dào.
How far-sighted he was!
Moreover, even when facing the distress of hunger and cold,
he still did not take what was unrighteously offered,
foreseeing the outcome.
To foresee the outcome and then act,
is far beyond ordinary human nature.
16.3 《Zhī Jiē》
Thirdly:
The human eye sees by illumination.
If it is blind, it is the same as not seeing.
The means by which it illuminates
and the means by which it is blind are different.
A blind person has never seen by illumination,
therefore they have never seen.
A blind person's eyes have no means to connect.
To speak of seeing when there is no means to connect is foolish.
Knowledge is also like this.
The means by which one connects with knowledge and the means by which one connects with ignorance are the same.
What one can connect with and what one cannot connect with are different.
A wise person can connect with things far away,
while a foolish person can connect with things nearby.
If one can only connect with things nearby, and you tell them about distant transformations,
how can they comprehend?
If there is no means to comprehend,
however skillful the speaker,
they cannot make it understood.
A Róng tribesman saw someone drying coarse cloth and asked,
"Why is it so rough and tangled?"
Someone pointed to hemp and showed it to him.
He angrily said,
"How can something so fine and tangled
be made into something rough and tangled?"
Therefore, a ruined state is not without wise scholars,
nor is it without xìanzhě.
It is because its ruler has no means to connect with them.
The problem of having no means to connect,
is to consider oneself wise,
where wisdom necessarily fails to connect.
Now, to fail to connect and still consider oneself wise,
is perverse.
If this is the case, the state cannot survive,
and the ruler cannot be secure.
If wisdom has no means to connect,
but one knows oneself not to be wise,
then one will not hear of a ruined state,
nor hear of a imperiled ruler.
Guǎn Zhòng was ill.
Huán Gōng went to visit him and asked,
"Zhòngfù is seriously ill.
What advice will you give to this lonely one?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied,
"Among the common folk of Qí, there is a saying:
'One who stays does not load,
one who travels does not bury.'
Now, your servant is about to embark on a long journey.
How can I be asked for advice?"
Huán Gōng said,
"I wish, Zhòngfù, that you would not decline."
Guǎn Zhòng replied,
"I wish for Your Highness to keep Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, Cháng Zhīwū, and Wèi Gōngzǐ Qǐfāng at a distance."
The Duke said,
"Yì Yá cooked his own son to please me.
Can he still be doubted?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied,
"It is human nature
not to dislike one's child.
If one can be so cruel to one's own child,
what regard will one have for Your Highness?"
Gōng [Duke] again said:
“Shù Diāo castrated himself to be close to Us;
can he still be doubted?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“It is human nature
not to dislike one’s own body.
If he can be so cruel to his own body,
what would he not do to Your Lordship?”
Gōng [Duke] again said:
“Cháng zhī Wū is perceptive regarding life and death,
and can cure grievous illnesses;
can he still be doubted?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Life and death are destiny;
grievous illness is misfortune.
If Your Lordship does not rely on destiny
and uphold your roots,
but instead trusts Cháng zhī Wū,
he will use this to do anything he wants.”
Gōng [Duke] again said:
“Wèi Gōngzǐ Qǐfāng has served Us for fifteen years.
When his father died, he did not dare to return to mourn him;
can he still be doubted?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“It is human nature
not to dislike one’s own father.
If he can be so cruel to his father,
what would he not do to Your Lordship?”
Gōng [Duke] said:
“Agreed.”
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
he [Duke Huán] expelled all of them.
Food was not sweet,
the palace was not managed,
grievous illnesses arose,
the court was not solemn.
After three years,
Gōng [Duke] said:
“Was Zhòngfù not too extreme?
Who said Zhòngfù was exhaustive?”
Thereupon, he recalled and reinstated all of them.
The next year,
Gōng [Duke] fell ill.
Cháng zhī Wū came out from inside and said:
“Your Lordship will pass away on a certain day.”
Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Cháng zhī Wū conspired to rebel,
blocked the palace gates,
built high walls,
and allowed no one access,
falsely claiming it was the Duke’s order.
A woman climbed over the wall and entered,
reaching the Duke’s quarters.
Gōng [Duke] said:
“I wish to drink.”
The woman said:
“I have nothing available.”
Gōng [Duke] again said:
“I wish to drink.”
The woman said:
“I have nothing available.”
Gōng [Duke] said:
“Why?”
She replied:
“Cháng zhī Wū came out from inside and said:
‘Your Lordship will pass away on a certain day.’
Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Cháng zhī Wū conspired to rebel,
blocked the palace gates,
built high walls,
and allowed no one access,
thus there is nothing available.
Wèi Gōngzǐ Qǐfāng has taken forty households and lands and gone down to Wèi.”
Gōng [Duke] sighed deeply,
and with tears flowing, said:
“Alas!
How far-sighted
the sage’s insights are!
If the dead have knowledge,
what face will I have to see Zhòngfù?”
He covered his face with his sleeve and died in the Shòugōng [Palace of Longevity].
Insects flowed out of the door,
and the entrance was covered with the gate-panels of Yángmén.
He was not buried for three months.
This was because he did not fully heed Guǎn Zhòng’s words.
Duchess Huán did not slight the difficulty and dislike Guǎn Zǐ,
but she had no way to meet him.
Without a way to meet,
she naturally rejected his loyal advice, and cherished those whom she honored and valued.
16.4 “Huǐguò” [Regret]
Fourthly:
If a hole is a xún [eight-foot unit] deep, a person’s arm certainly cannot reach the bottom.
Why is this?
Because it does not reach.
Wisdom also has its limits.
Where it does not reach,
even if the speaker is eloquent,
and the doctrine profound,
it cannot be perceived.
Thus Jīzǐ was distressed in Shāng,
and Fàn Lǐ wandered to the Jiāng [River].
In the past, Qín Mùgōng [Duke Mù of Qín] raised an army to raid Zhèng.
Jiǎn Shū remonstrated, saying:
“This cannot be done.
I have heard:
To raid a state’s city,
with chariots, one should not travel more than a hundred lǐ;
with men, not more than thirty lǐ.
This is all based on the agility of their spirit and the fullness of their strength,
so that upon arrival,
they can overcome the enemy and destroy them,
and leave quickly.
Now, to travel several thousand lǐ and repeatedly cross the territories of other feudal lords to raid a state,
Your Minister does not know how this can be done.
May Your Lordship reconsider it seriously.”
Mùgōng [Duke Mù] did not listen.
Jiǎn Shū saw the army off outside the gate,
wearing mourning clothes, and wept,
saying:
“O army!
I see you go out, but I will not see you return!”
Jiǎn Shū had sons named Shēn and Shì,
who went with the army.
Jiǎn Shū said to his sons:
“If Jìn intercepts the army, it will certainly be at Xiáo.
You will die not on the southern bank,
but certainly on the northern bank,
to make it easy for me to collect your corpses.”
Mùgōng [Duke Mù] heard this
and sent someone to rebuke Jiǎn Shū, saying:
“We have raised an army;
we do not know how it will fare.
Now you weep while seeing them off;
this is weeping over Our army.”
Jiǎn Shū replied:
“Your Minister does not dare to weep over the army.
Your Minister is old;
I have two sons,
both of whom are going with the army.
By the time they return,
either they will be dead, or Your Minister will certainly be dead.
That is why I weep.”
The army then proceeded,
passing through Zhōu.
Wángsūn Mǎn blocked the gate and peered at them,
saying:
“Alas!
This army must have a flaw.
If it has no flaw,
I will never speak of the Dao again.
Qín is none other than
a state established by the Zhōu court.
Passing through the Son of Heaven’s city,
they should sheath their armor and bind their weapons,
with everyone on both sides dismounting,
as a courtesy to the Son of Heaven.
Now, they wear military uniforms and proudly carry their banners,
the left does not bow over the crossbar,
and five hundred chariots have their right-hand men leaping over the side.
Their strength is indeed great,
but they lack courtesy.
How can they be without a flaw?”
The army passed through Zhōu and went east.
The Zhèng merchants Xián Gāo and Xī Shī were going west to trade in Zhōu.
On the way, they encountered the Qín army
and said:
“Aha!
This army has come a long way.
They must be attacking Zhèng.”
Immediately, they sent Xī Shī back to report,
and then falsely claimed the order of Zhèng Bó [Count of Zhèng] to welcome them,
saying:
“Our humble lord has long heard that your great state was coming.
As the great state did not arrive,
Our humble lord and his soldiers secretly worried for the great state,
having nothing to do with it daily,
only fearing that the soldiers would be exhausted and the provisions scarce.
How long it has been!
He sent his minister to offer a jade disc as a gift,
and twelve oxen as a feast.”
The three Qín commanders replied:
“Our humble lord sent no such message;
he sent his three ministers Bǐng,
Shù, and Shì to await Jìn’s way on the eastern border.
We passed by and thus mistakenly entered the land of the great state.”
They dared not refuse outright,
and bowed twice, touching their heads to the ground, to receive it.
The three commanders then became fearful and deliberated, saying:
“We traveled several thousand lǐ, repeatedly crossing the lands of other feudal lords to raid someone.
We haven’t even arrived, and the people already know of it.
Their preparations must already be complete.”
They turned the army around and departed.
At this time,
Jìn Wéngōng [Duke Wén of Jìn] had just died,
and was not yet buried.
Xiān Zhěn spoke to Xiānggōng [Duke Xiāng],
saying:
“The Qín army must be attacked.
Your minister requests to attack them.”
Xiāng Gōng 曰：
「先君薨，
屍在堂，
見 Qín shī lì ér yīn jī zhī，
無乃非為人子之道歟？ 」
Xiān Zhěn 曰：
「不弔吾喪，
不憂吾哀而不假道，
是死吾君而弱其孤也。
若是而擊，
可大強。
臣請擊之。 」
Xiāng Gōng 不得已而許之。
Xiān Zhěn 遏 Qín shī 於 Xiáo 而擊之，
大敗之，
獲其三帥以歸。
Mù Gōng 聞之，
素服廟臨，
以說於眾曰：
「天不為 Qín guó，
使寡人不用 Jiǎn Shū zhī jiàn，
以至於此患。 」
此 Mù Gōng 非欲敗於 Xiáo yě，
智不至也。
智不至則不信。
而言不可不信，
師之不反也從此生，
故不至之為害大矣。
16.5 《Lè Chéng》
五曰：
大智不形，
大器晚成，
大音希聲。
Yǔ zhī jué jiāng shuǐ yě，
民聚瓦礫。
事已成，
功已立，
為萬世利。
Yǔ zhī suǒ jiàn zhě yuǎn yě，
而民莫之知，
故民不可與慮化舉始，
而可以樂成功。
Kǒngzǐ 始用於 Lǔ。
Lǔ rén yī sòng zhī yuē：
「麛裘而鞞，
投之無戾；
鞞而麛裘，
投之無郵。 」
用三年，
男子行乎塗右，
女子行乎塗左，
財物之遺者，
民莫之舉。
大智之用，
固難踰也。
Zǐchǎn 始治 Zhèng，
使田有封洫，
都鄙有服。
民相與誦之曰：
「我有田疇，
而 Zǐchǎn fù zhī。
我有衣冠，
而 Zǐchǎn zhù zhī。
孰殺 Zǐchǎn，
吾其與之。 」
後三年，
民又誦之曰：
「我有田疇，
而 Zǐchǎn zhí zhī。
我有子弟，
而 Zǐchǎn huì zhī。
Zǐchǎn ruò sǐ，
其使誰嗣之？ 」
使 Zhèng Jiǎn Gōng、Lǔ Āi Gōng dāng mín zhī fěi zǐ yě ér yīn fú suì yòng，
則國必無功矣，
Zǐchǎn、Kǒngzǐ bì wú néng yǐ。
非徒不能也，
雖罪施於民可也。
今世皆稱 Jiǎn Gōng、Āi Gōng wéi xián，
稱 Zǐchǎn、Kǒngzǐ wéi néng，
此二君者，
達乎任人也。
舟車之始見也，
三世然後安之。
夫開善豈易哉？
故聽無事治。
事治之立也，
人主賢也。
Wèi gōng Zhōngshān，
Lè Yáng jiàng，
已得 Zhōngshān，
還反報 Wén Hóu，
有貴功之色。
Wén Hóu zhī zhī，
命主書曰：
「群臣賓客所獻書者，
操以進之。 」
主書舉兩篋以進。
令將軍視之，
書盡難攻 Zhōngshān zhī shì yě。
將軍還走，
北面再拜曰：
「Zhōngshān zhī jǔ，
非臣之力，
君之功也。 」
當此時也，
論士殆之日幾矣，
Zhōngshān zhī bù qǔ yě，
奚宜二篋哉？
一寸而亡矣。
Wén Hóu xián zhǔ yě，
而猶若此，
又況於中主耶？
中主之患，
不能勿為，
而不可與莫為。
凡舉無易之事，
氣志視聽動作無非是者，
人臣且孰敢以非是邪疑為哉？
皆壹於為，
則無敗事矣。
此 Tāng、Wǔ zhī suǒyǐ dà lì gōng yú Xià、Shāng，
而 Gōujiàn zhī suǒyǐ néng bào qí chóu yě。
以小弱皆壹於為而猶若此，
又況於以強大乎？
Wèi Xiāng Wáng yǔ qún chén yìn，
酒酣，
Wáng wèi qún chén zhù yuē：
「令群臣皆得志。 」
Shǐ Qǐ xìng ér duì yuē：
「群臣或賢或不肖，
賢者得志則可，
不肖者得志則不可。 」
Wáng yuē：
「皆如 Xīmén Bào zhī wéi rén chén yě。 」
Shǐ Qǐ duì yuē：
「Wèi shì zhī xíng tián yě yǐ bǎi mǔ，
Yè dú èr bǎi mǔ，
是田惡也。
Zhāng shuǐ zài qí páng ér Xīmén Bào fú zhī yòng，
是其愚也；
知而弗 yán，
是不忠也。
愚與不忠，
不可效也。 」
Wèi Wáng wú yǐ yìng zhī。
明日，
zhào Shǐ Qǐ ér wèn yān，
曰：
「Zhāng shuǐ yóu kěyǐ guàn Yè tián hū？ 」
Shǐ Qǐ duì yuē：
Wáng yuē：
「Zǐ hé bù wèi guǎ rén wèi zhī？ 」
Shǐ Qǐ yuē：
「Chén kǒng Wáng zhī bù néng wéi yě。 」
Wáng yuē：
「Zǐ chéng néng wèi guǎ rén wèi zhī，
guǎ rén jìn tīng zǐ yǐ。 」
Shǐ Qǐ jìng nuò，
yán zhī yú Wáng yuē：
「Chén wèi zhī，
mín bì dà yuàn chén。
Dà zhě sǐ，
qícì nǎi jiè chén。
Chén suī sǐ jiè，
yuàn Wáng zhī shǐ tā rén suì zhī yě。 」
Wáng yuē：
「Nuò。 」
Shǐ zhī wéi Yè lìng。
Shǐ Qǐ yīn wǎng wèi zhī。
Yè mín dà yuàn，
yù jiè Shǐ Qǐ。
Shǐ Qǐ bù gǎn chū ér bì zhī。
Wáng nǎi shǐ tā rén suì wéi zhī。
Shuǐ yǐ xíng，
mín dà dé qí lì，
xiāng yǔ gē zhī yuē：
「Yè yǒu shèng lìng，
shí wèi Shǐ Gōng，
jué Zhāng shuǐ，
guàn Yè páng，
zhōng gǔ chì lǔ，
shēng zhī dào liáng。 」
Shǐ mín zhī kě yǔ bù kě，
則無所用矣。
Xián zhǔ zhōng chén，
bù néng dǎo yú jiāo lòu，
則 míng bù guàn hòu、shí bù jí shì yǐ。
Shǐ Qǐ fēi bù zhī huà yě，
yǐ zhōng yú zhǔ yě。
Wèi Xiāng Wáng kěwèi néng jué shàn yǐ。
Chéng néng jué shàn，
zhòng suī xuānhuá ér fú wèi biàn。
That establishing merit is difficult,
must it necessarily come from chaos?
That a state is ruined and destroyed,
is also like this.
Therefore, amidst chaos,
one cannot fail to understand its taste.
An ordinary ruler uses it (chaos) to stop at what is good,
while a worthy ruler uses it to establish merit.
16.6 "Cháwēi"
Six says:
If order and chaos, survival and destruction were like high mountains and deep ravines,
like white chalk and black lacquer,
then there would be no need for wisdom;
even the foolish could manage.
However, order and chaos, survival and destruction are not like that;
they are like what can and cannot be known,
like what can and cannot be seen.
Therefore, wise scholars and worthy men collectively ponder and worry to seek them out,
yet there are still the affairs of Guǎnshū and Càishū, and the plot of the eight Eastern Yí states not submitting.
Thus, order and chaos, survival and destruction,
their beginnings are like an autumn down.
If one discerns the autumn down,
then no great matter will be overlooked.
According to the laws of Lǔguó,
if a person from Lǔ became a servant or concubine in a feudal state,
and someone was able to redeem them,
they could take the money from the treasury.
Zǐgòng redeemed a person from Lǔ in a feudal state,
and upon returning, he declined to take the money.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Cì has made a mistake.
From now on,
people from Lǔ will not redeem others.
Taking the money would not diminish one's conduct;
not taking the money will lead to no one redeeming people again."
Zǐlù rescued a drowning person,
and that person bowed to him with an ox.
Zǐlù accepted it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"People from Lǔ will surely rescue drowning persons."
Kǒngzǐ saw things in detail,
observing their far-reaching transformative influence.
A border town of Chǔ was called Bēiliáng.
Its maiden and a maiden from a border town of Wú were gathering mulberries on the border.
They played and injured the maiden from Bēiliáng.
The people of Bēiliáng took their injured child and denounced the people of Wú.
The people of Wú responded disrespectfully,
so they angrily killed one and left.
The people of Wú went to retaliate,
slaughtering their entire family.
Duke Bēiliáng was enraged,
saying:
"How dare the people of Wú attack our town?"
He raised an army and counterattacked them,
killing all the old and weak.
King Yímèi of Wú heard of this and was furious.
He sent men to raise an army and invade the border town of Chǔ,
conquering Yí before leaving.
Wú and Chǔ consequently became greatly hostile.
Prince Guāng of Wú then led his army to battle the Chǔ people at Jīfù,
greatly defeating the Chǔ people,
capturing their commanders Pānzǐchén, Xiǎowéizǐ, and Chénxiànì.
He also counterattacked Yǐng,
and returned with the consort of King Jīngpíng,
this being the battle of Jīfù.
For all who govern a state,
the best know the beginning,
the next best know the end,
the next best know the middle.
If they cannot do these three,
the state will surely be endangered,
and their person will surely be impoverished.
The "Xiàojīng" says:
"High without danger,
is how one long maintains nobility;
full without overflowing,
is how one long maintains wealth.
When wealth and nobility do not leave one's person,
then one can protect one's altars of soil and grain,
and bring harmony to one's people."
Chǔ was unable to do this.
Prince Guīshēng of Zhèng led an army to attack Sòng.
Huá Yuán of Sòng led an army to meet him at Dàjí,
with Yáng Zhēn as charioteer.
The next day, intending to battle,
Huá Yuán killed a sheep to feast his soldiers,
but Yáng Zhēn was not included.
The next day, during the battle,
Yáng Zhēn angrily said to Huá Yuán:
"Yesterday's affair,
you controlled it;
today's affair,
I control it."
He then drove the chariot into the Zhèng army.
The Sòng army was defeated,
and Huá Yuán was captured.
A crossbow mechanism, if it differs by even a grain of rice, will not fire.
Battle
is a great mechanism.
To feast the soldiers and forget one's charioteer,
to be defeated and captured because of this,
is it not proper?
Therefore, in all battles, one must fully and thoroughly prepare,
know oneself and know the enemy,
only then can one succeed.
The Jìshì of Lǔ and the Hòushì fought chickens.
The Hòushì armored their chicken,
and the Jìshì made metal spurs for theirs.
The Jìshì's chicken did not win.
Jì Píngzǐ was enraged,
and consequently invaded the palace of the Hòushì and expanded his own residence.
Hòu Zhāobó was enraged,
and slandered him to Duke Zhāo,
saying:
"During the dì sacrifice in Duke Xiāng's temple,
there were only two dancers;
the rest all danced at Jìshì's place.
The Jìshì's lawlessness and disrespect for superiors have gone on for a long time;
if they are not punished, the altars of soil and grain will surely be in danger."
The Duke was enraged,
and without proper investigation,
he then ordered Hòu Zhāobó to lead his army to attack the Jìshì,
and they entered his palace.
The Zhòngsūnshì and Shūsūnshì conspired with each other, saying:
"Without the Jìshì,
our clans will surely perish soon."
They then raised their armed men and went,
breaching the northwest corner to enter.
The three families became one,
and Hòu Zhāobó was defeated and died.
Duke Zhāo was afraid,
and consequently fled to Qí,
dying in Gānhóu.
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ listened to the slander but did not discern its righteousness,
fearing that Lǔguó would not overcome the Jìshì,
and unaware of the fear of the Zhòngsūnshì and Shūsūnshì who shared the same trouble with the Jìshì;
this was not understanding human nature.
If one does not understand human nature,
even if one's position is exalted,
what benefit is there for security?
If Lǔguó feared it could not overcome one Jìshì,
how much more so three Jìshì?
Those with common evils naturally help each other.
Evaluating things was so mistaken here.
It was not only the Zhòngsūnshì and Shūsūnshì,
all of Lǔguó was afraid.
If all of Lǔguó was afraid,
then he was an enemy to the entire state;
his ability to reach Gānhóu and die there was still distant (i.e., it was a great escape).
16.7 "Qùyòu"
Seven says:
Xièzǐ, a Mohist from the east, was going west to see King Huì of Qín.
King Huì asked Táng Gūguǒ, a Mohist from Qín, about him.
Táng Gūguǒ feared the king would favor Xièzǐ as more worthy than himself,
and replied:
"Xièzǐ
is a glib debater from the east,
his character is very cunning;
he will try to gain influence through persuasion to capture the young ruler."
The King then concealed his anger and waited for him.
When Xièzǐ arrived,
he tried to persuade the King,
but the King did not listen.
Xièzǐ was displeased,
and so he took his leave and departed.
When listening to words,
one seeks what is good.
If what is said is good,
even if he tries to capture the young ruler,
what harm is there?
If what is said is not good,
even if he does not try to capture the young ruler,
what benefit is there?
Not taking goodness as the standard for honesty,
but merely taking 'capturing the young ruler' as the standard for perversity,
King Huì lost the basis for listening.
If one uses one's will like this,
even if one is tired from seeing guests,
and one's ears and eyes are exhausted,
one still gains nothing.
This is why Shǐ Dìng was able to carry out his wickedness,
this is why Shǐ Dìng was able to impersonate spirits to harm people,
to unjustly kill the innocent,
causing disruption among officials,
and the state was almost in great danger.
When a person grows old,
their physical form increasingly declines,
but their wisdom increasingly flourishes.
Now, as King Huì (惠王) grows old,
do both his physical form and wisdom decline?
King Wēi of Jīng (荊威王) studied writing under Shěn Yǐnhuá (沈尹華).
Zhāolí (昭釐) disliked this.
King Wēi (威王) was fond of making robes.
There was a palace attendant who assisted him in making robes.
Zhāolí (昭釐) said to King Wēi (威王):
“The people of the state all say:
‘The king is a disciple of Shěn Yǐnhuá (沈尹華).’”
The king was displeased
and consequently estranged Shěn Yǐnhuá (沈尹華).
The palace attendant
was a petty person.
With a single remark, he caused King Wēi (威王) not to hear the methods of the former kings,
prevented literary scholars from advancing,
and allowed Zhāolí (昭釐) to act on his private interests.
Therefore, the words of petty persons
must not be left unexamined.
Moreover, repeatedly angering the sovereign
is to clear a path for treacherous individuals.
Once the path for treachery is cleared and evil is obstructed and repelled,
is this not difficult?
Indeed, agitating an arrow makes it fly far;
agitating water makes it dry up;
agitating a ruler makes him perverse.
When he is perverse, there will be no noble men.
Those who cannot be agitated
are solely those who possess principles beforehand.
A neighboring father had a neighbor
who possessed a withered wútóng (梧桐) tree.
The neighboring father spoke ill of the wútóng (梧桐) tree.
The neighbor immediately cut it down.
The neighboring father then asked for it to be made into firewood.
That person was displeased and said:
“If neighbors are so devious,
how can one be a neighbor to them?”
This is a case of being greatly constrained.
Whether one asks for it to be made into firewood or not,
this cannot be used to doubt the goodness or badness of the withered wútóng (梧桐) tree.
There was a man from Qí (齊) who desired gold.
Early one morning,
he donned his robes and cap,
went to the place where gold was sold,
saw someone holding gold,
and immediately seized and took it.
The official apprehended and bound him,
and asked:
“Everyone was present;
why did you seize another's gold?”
He replied to the official:
“I truly saw no one,
only the gold.”
This is truly a case of being greatly constrained.
Indeed, when a person is greatly constrained,
they naturally take day for night,
white for black,
and Yáo (堯) for Jié (桀).
The ruin caused by such constraint is also great.
Are the rulers of fallen states
all greatly constrained?
Therefore, all people must distinguish constraints before they can know;
distinguishing constraints
then allows them to preserve their innate nature.
16.8 *Zhèng Míng* (正名)
The eighth section says:
When names are correct, there is order;
when names are lost, there is chaos.
What causes names to be lost
is perverse rhetoric.
If rhetoric is perverse, then what is acceptable is unacceptable and what is not so is so,
what is right is wrong and what is not wrong is right.
Therefore, the discourse of the noble person
is merely sufficient to speak of the reality of the worthy and the full extent of the unworthy,
merely sufficient to illustrate what obstructs order and what causes chaos,
and merely sufficient to understand the nature of things and the means by which people live.
All disorder
arises from names and punishments not corresponding.
Even if a ruler is unworthy,
he would still employ the worthy,
still listen to the good,
and still do what is proper.
His trouble lies in that those called "worthy"
are merely unworthy,
what is called "good" is merely evil and perverse,
and what is called "proper" is merely contrary.
This is when names and realities are filled differently, and sounds and realities are called differently.
If the worthy are unworthy, the good are evil and perverse, and the proper are contrary,
how can the state not be in chaos and the self not be in danger?
King Mǐn of Qí (齊湣王) thereby knew eloquent scholars,
but did not know what a "scholar" truly was.
Therefore, when Yǐn Wén (尹文) asked him why,
the king had no answer.
This is why Wáng Yùdān (王玉丹) was trusted and Zhuó Chǐ (卓齒) was appointed.
Appointing Zhuó Chǐ (卓齒) and trusting Wáng Yùdān (王玉丹),
was this not bringing enmity upon himself?
Yǐn Wén (尹文) met King Qí (齊王).
King Qí (齊王) said to Yǐn Wén (尹文):
