“I am very fond of scholars, yet there are no scholars in the state of Qí (齊).
Why is this?”
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“May I ask what you mean by ‘scholar’?”
The king had no answer.
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“Now, if there is a person here
who is filial in serving parents,
loyal in serving the ruler,
trustworthy in befriending others,
and fraternal in residing in the community—
can such a person with these four virtues be called a scholar?”
King Qí (齊王) said:
“This is truly what is called a scholar.”
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“If Your Majesty obtained such a person,
would you be willing to take him as a minister?”
The king said:
“That is what I desire but cannot obtain.”
At this time, King Qí (齊王) was fond of valor.
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“If such a person in the imperial court
is deeply insulted but does not fight,
will Your Majesty take him as a minister?”
The king said:
“No.
If a high official is insulted but does not fight,
this is a disgrace.
If he is disgraced, I will not take him as a minister.”
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“Although he is insulted and does not fight,
he has not lost his four virtues.
One who has not lost his four virtues
has not lost his qualification as a scholar.
If he has not lost his qualification as a scholar,
and Your Majesty takes him as a minister;
but if he loses his qualification as a scholar,
and Your Majesty does not take him as a minister;
then was the one you previously called a scholar not a scholar?”
The king had no answer.
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“Now, if there is a ruler here,
who is about to govern his state,
and the people have faults, he condemns them;
and if the people have no faults, he still condemns them.
If the people have committed crimes, he punishes them;
and if the people have no crimes, he still punishes them.
And he resents the people for being difficult to govern—is this acceptable?”
The king said:
“No.”
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“I secretly observe that the governance of Qí (齊) by the lower officials
is precisely like this.”
The king said:
“If I governed the state truly like this,
then even if the people were not governed well,
I would not resent them.
Perhaps it has not reached that point.”
Yǐn Wén (尹文) said:
“I dare not speak without evidence.
Please allow me to present the evidence.
Your Majesty's decree states:
‘One who kills shall die;
one who injures shall be punished.’
There are people who fear Your Majesty's decree,
are deeply insulted but dare not fight.
This is upholding Your Majesty's decree.
Yet Your Majesty says, ‘One who is insulted but dares not fight
is disgraced.’
Indeed, calling him disgraced
is condemning him, though he has no fault, Your Majesty disgraces him.
Therefore, you remove his name from the register and do not take him as a minister.
Not taking him as a minister
is punishing him. This is punishing him when he has committed no crime.”
King Qí (齊王) had no answer.
All these arguments were like this,
hence the state was ruined and his person endangered,
and he fled to Gǔ (穀),
like Wèi (衛).
King Mǐn of Qí (齊湣王) was a hegemon of the Zhōu (周) royal house.
This is why Tàigōng (太公) grew old.
Duke Huán (桓公) once achieved hegemony with this,
due to Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) clear and precise discernment of names and realities.
17.1 *Shěn Fēn* (審分)
The first section says:
All rulers must discern divisions,
only then can governance reach its peak,
the paths of treachery, deceit, and perversity can cease,
and evil influences and harsh maladies will not arise on their own.
Indeed, governing oneself and governing the state
are arts based on the same principle.
Now, when it comes to cultivating many lands,
if the lord works them, it will be slow,
for there will be those who hide their strength;
if the land is divided, it will be fast,
for there will be nowhere to hide (laziness).
The lord also has land.
If the ministers and the lord share the same land,
then the ministers will have a place to conceal their wickedness,
and the lord will have no means to avoid their burdens.
It is difficult to do good,
but easy to employ the good.
How do we know this?
If a man and a swift horse run together,
the man cannot outrun the swift horse;
but if he rides in a chariot and employs the swift horse,
then the swift horse cannot overcome the man.
If a ruler likes to personally manage the affairs of his officials,
he is like running alongside the swift horse,
and will surely fall short in many areas.
Indeed, a ruler also has a chariot;
if he does not abandon his chariot,
then all good people will exert their utmost strength and ability,
and the flattering, fawning, obsequious, wicked, cunning, and glib people will have nowhere to conceal their villainy,
while upright, impoverished, honest, straightforward, loyal, and sincere scholars will all compete to strive and gallop.
The ruler's chariot
is that by which he governs things.
If one comprehends the principle of governing things,
then the four extremities (of the world) can be possessed.
If one does not know how to govern things but relies on oneself,
exerting one's intelligence and ability,
multiplying one's instructions and decrees,
and being fond of acting on one's own judgment;
if this is the case, then the hundred officials will be distressed and chaotic,
the elder and younger will overstep each other,
ten thousand evils will arise in unison,
and authority and power will be divided and transferred.
Such a state cannot endure,
nor can it be taught.
This is the custom of a perishing state.
The reason why Wáng Liáng was able to manage horses
was that he held their reins with judicious restraint,
and no four horses dared not exert their utmost strength.
A ruler who possesses the Way
also has reins by which he manages his ministers.
What are these reins like?
Rectifying names and clarifying divisions –
these are the reins of governance.
Therefore, examine their reality and scrutinize their names
to ascertain their true nature;
listen to their words and observe their categories,
preventing them from becoming extravagant or rebellious.
Indeed, names often do not correspond to their realities, and affairs often do not match their intended use.
Therefore, a ruler cannot but scrutinize names and divisions.
If names and divisions are not scrutinized,
it is like disliking obstruction yet increasing the blockage.
The responsibility for obstruction and blockage
does not lie with the ministers,
but with the ruler.
The ministers of Yáo and Shùn were not uniquely righteous,
nor were the ministers of Tāng and Yǔ uniquely loyal;
they simply followed the proper method.
The ministers of Jié and Zhòu were not uniquely base,
nor were the ministers of Yōu and Lì uniquely perverse;
they simply deviated from the principle.
Now, if there is a person here
who asks for an ox but names it a horse,
or asks for a horse but names it an ox,
what he seeks will surely not be obtained.
And if he then resorts to threats and anger,
the officials will surely complain,
and the oxen and horses will surely become disturbed and chaotic.
The hundred officials are the many officials;
the myriad things are the herd of oxen and horses.
If names are not rectified
and duties are not clearly divided,
and punishments are frequently employed,
there is no greater chaos.
Indeed, words may seem intelligent and insightful,
yet their reality may be confused by errors;
they may be praised as highly virtuous,
yet filled with baseness;
commended for their purity,
yet followed by corrupt deeds;
appointed to positions of public law,
yet act with greed and perversion;
employed for their bravery,
yet suppressed by exhaustion and timidity.
These five instances
are all cases of calling an ox a horse
and a horse an ox,
where names are not rectified.
Therefore, if names are not rectified,
the ruler will be troubled, wearied, and toiling,
and official duties will be chaotic, rebellious, and perverse.
The perishing of a state
and the damage to names
originate from this.
That what is sought turns blacker the more it is whitewashed, and the more it is sought the more it is not obtained,
is this not this very principle?
Therefore, the essential task of ultimate governance
lies in rectifying names.
When names are rectified, the ruler will not be troubled or toiling.
When he is not troubled or toiling, he will not harm the master of his ears and eyes.
He asks but does not instruct,
knows but does not act,
harmonizes but does not boast,
accomplishes but does not claim.
Those who stop do not proceed,
those who proceed do not stop.
He assigns according to form,
is not controlled by things,
and is willing to make no one a servant.
Pure and tranquil in his impartiality,
his spirit penetrates the six directions,
his virtue shines beyond the seas,
his intent observes the infinite,
his renown flows without end.
This is called settling one's nature in the great deep,
and it is named "non-being."
Therefore, to attain the Way and forget people
is truly to greatly attain people,
for it is not lacking in the Way;
to know virtue and forget knowledge
is truly to greatly attain knowledge,
for it is not lacking in virtue;
ultimate knowledge does not anticipate,
tranquility then illuminates anticipation,
for it is not lacking in illumination;
great illumination does not concern itself with small matters,
yet it manages all matters,
for it is not lacking in management;
no person is incapable,
wholeness then perfects ability,
for it is not lacking in wholeness.
Therefore, in wholeness, one abandons ability;
in managing, one abandons affairs;
in knowing, one abandons anticipation;
what is known then becomes subtle.
If this is the case, one can then follow one's heaven-given nature,
and one's spirit and vital energy can wander in the realm of tranquility,
and one's form and nature can rest in their natural place.
He completes all things without dominating them,
his beneficence covers all under heaven, yet no one knows his surname or origin.
Even if he does not fully possess the five qualities,
those who love him are indeed correct.
17.2《Jūn Shǒu》
Secondly, it is said:
One who attains the Way must be tranquil.
A tranquil person is ignorant,
and knowing is then unknowing.
This can be spoken of as the Way of the ruler.
Hence it is said, "Internal desires not going out are called a bolt (shìng),
external desires not coming in are called a closure (bì)."
Both bolted and closed:
the operation of Heaven is secret.
It has a level but does not use it to level,
it has a plumb line but does not use it to rectify;
Heaven's great tranquility,
being both tranquil and peaceful,
can serve as the rectification for all under heaven.
The body contains the mind,
the mind contains wisdom.
Ah, wisdom!
Deeply hidden, its reality cannot be spied upon.
The *Hóng Fàn* says:
"Heaven secretly assists the lower people."
To assist secretly
is how it brings things forth.
Therefore it is said, "Without going out the door, one knows all under heaven;
without peeking through the window, one knows the Way of Heaven."
The further one goes out,
the less one knows.
Therefore, widely learned people and powerfully remembering scholars are deficient,
the tasks of serving the ears and eyes and deep contemplation fail,
the discernment of "hard and white" and the argument of "no thickness" are external.
Not going out
is how one brings forth;
not acting
is how one acts.
This is called summoning yang with yang,
and summoning yin with yin.
At the utmost limit of the Eastern Sea,
the water reaches and then returns;
beneath the heat of summer,
it transforms into cold.
Therefore it is said, Vast Heaven is formless,
yet all things are accomplished thereby;
ultimate essence is inactive,
yet all things are transformed thereby;
the great Sage has no affairs,
yet all thousands of officials perfectly exert their abilities.
This is what is meant by "teaching without teaching,"
and "proclamation without words."
Thus, there are means to know if the lord is wild,
by the aptness of his words;
there are means to know if the lord is confused,
by the correctness of his words.
The lord
takes what is inapt as apt,
and what is incorrect as correct.
Aptness and correctness do not lie with the lord,
but with the ministers.
Therefore, a good ruler has no specific knowledge;
next to that, he has no affairs.
If he has specific knowledge, there will be something incomplete;
if he has affairs, there will be something not far-reaching.
If incomplete and not far-reaching,
this is why officials are doubtful,
and where wickedness originates.
Those who make carriages today
complete them only after many officials.
How could a state be merely like making a carriage?
It is sustained by the collective wisdom and abilities of many;
one thing or one method cannot secure a carriage.
As for one capable of responding to myriad situations without fixed methods, and of managing affairs,
only one who possesses the Dào can do this.
A rustic from Lǔ presented a locked casket to Sòng Yuánwáng.
Yuánwáng issued an order throughout the state
for all skilled individuals to come and unlock it.
No one could unlock it.
Ér Yuè's disciple requested to go and unlock it,
and was able to unlock one,
but could not unlock the other,
and moreover said:
"It's not that it can be unlocked and I cannot unlock it;
it is inherently unlockable."
He then asked the rustic from Lǔ.
The rustic said:
"Indeed,
it is inherently unlockable.
I made it, and I know it is unlockable.
Now, not having made it, you know it is unlockable;
this shows you are more skilled than I."
Thus, a disciple like Ér Yuè's
unlocked it
by "not unlocking."
Zhèng Dàshī Wén played the se all day until he was inspired,
then bowed twice before his se and said:
"I learn from you,
I learn from the inexhaustible."
Thus, a master like Dàshī Wén
lets his animal instincts lead him,
which is how he hits the mark.
Therefore, deliberation injures the self,
clever distinctions lead to self-destruction,
flaunting ability invites calamity,
and having a fixed position leads to madness.
Thus, the most divine wander fleetingly and their form is not seen;
the most sagely change customs and shift traditions, yet no one knows their origin;
they depart from the world and separate from the crowd, yet there is nothing they do not embrace;
they rule the people as if isolated and alone, yet cannot be obstructed or blocked.
This ensures that the true nature of treachery and evil is revealed, and that dangerous, perverse, slanderous, malicious, flattering, and cunning people have no way to enter.
All treacherous, evil, dangerous, and perverse people enter through a cause.
What cause?
The cause is the ruler's actions.
If the ruler likes to act on his own,
then those who guard their posts will abandon their posts and flatter the ruler's actions.
If they flatter the ruler's actions,
when there are faults, the ruler has no one to blame,
and thus the ruler is daily encroached upon, and the ministers daily gain.
This is why those who should act are still,
and those who should be still act;
the noble are debased,
and the debased are honored –
this arises from here.
This is why the state declines and enemies attack it.
Xīzhòng made carriages,
Cāngjié made writing,
Hòujì made agriculture,
Gāotáo made laws,
Kūnwú made pottery,
Xià Gǔn made cities.
The creations of these six people were appropriate,
yet they were not the way of the ruler.
Therefore, it is said that creators cause agitation,
while followers bring peace.
Only the way of the ruler,
which grasps the essence of destiny,
can manage the world without strain;
this is called a complete person.
17.3 《Rènshù》
Thirdly:
All officials
take good governance as their duty
and chaos as their crime.
Now, if there is chaos without accountability,
then chaos will only grow.
If the ruler uses showing violence as a display of ability,
and uses initiating actions as self-exertion,
and ministers use not contending to maintain their positions,
and use obedience to gain favor,
then the ruler takes the place of the officials,
and the ministers gain by following to advance their careers.
If the relationship between ruler and minister is not fixed,
though the ears hear, they cannot listen;
though the eyes see, they cannot see;
though the mind knows, it cannot act;
it is the situation that forces this.
The ears' hearing relies on stillness,
the eyes' seeing relies on clarity,
the mind's knowing relies on reason.
If ruler and minister exchange roles,
then the three aforementioned functions are abolished.
The ruler of a ruined state,
it's not that his ears cannot hear,
it's not that his eyes cannot see,
it's not that his mind cannot know;
but when ruler and minister are in disarray,
and upper and lower ranks are not distinguished,
though he hears, how does he hear?
Though he sees, how does he see?
Though he knows, how does he know?
He gallops on, relying on his ears [alone];
this is something the foolish cannot achieve.
If they cannot achieve it, they do not know it;
if they do not know it, they do not believe it.
One without bones cannot be made to know ice.
A ruler with territory,
if he can discern these words,
then disaster will have no way to arrive.
Moreover, ears, eyes, intelligence, and skill
are inherently unreliable;
only cultivating principles and following reason are effective.
Hán Zhāolíhóu inspected the sacrificial pig for the ancestral temple;
the pig was small.
Zhāolíhóu ordered an official to replace it.
The official brought another pig,
and Zhāolíhóu said:
"Is this not the same pig as before?"
The official had no reply.
He ordered his officer to punish him.
An attendant asked:
"How did Your Majesty know?"
The lord said:
"I knew by its ears."
Shēn Bùhài heard this
and said:
"How do you know deafness?
By the keenness of its ears.
How do you know blindness?
By the brightness of its eyes.
How do you know madness?
By the aptness of its words.
Therefore, it is said: remove hearing, and without a means to hear, there is keenness;
remove seeing, and without a means to see, there is brightness;
remove intelligence, and without a means to know, there is impartiality.
If these three
are not relied upon, there is order;
if these three are relied upon, there is chaos."
This speaks of the unreliability of ears, eyes, and mind's intelligence.
Ears, eyes, and mind's intelligence,
their means of knowing are very deficient,
their means of hearing and seeing are very shallow.
To rely on what is shallow and deficient to widely govern the world, pacify diverse customs, and rule myriad people,
such a theory is certainly unworkable.
Within a distance of ten li, the ear cannot hear;
beyond a curtain or wall, the eye cannot see;
within a palace of three mu, the mind cannot know.
How then can one extend eastward to Kāiwú, southward to Fǔ Duōjí, westward to Fú Shòumí, and northward to Huái Dān'ěr?
How can this be done?
Therefore, a ruler of men
must not fail to discern these words.
The way of order and chaos, security and danger, survival and extinction,
is indeed not two.
Thus, the most intelligent abandon intelligence,
the most benevolent forget benevolence,
the most virtuous are not virtuous.
Without words or thoughts,
calmly awaiting the opportune moment;
when the moment arrives, they respond,
and those with a relaxed mind prevail.
The principle of response is
clarity, purity, impartiality, and simplicity,
and correcting the beginning and end;
this is the principle of governance:
no initiating, only responding;
no leading, only following.
The ancient kings,
what they initiated was little,
what they relied on was much.
Following (the Way)
is the art of the ruler;
acting
is the duty of the minister.
When one acts, there is disturbance;
when one follows, there is tranquility.
Following winter to bring cold,
following summer to bring heat,
what business does the ruler have?
Therefore it is said that the Way of the ruler, without knowledge and without action, is superior to having knowledge and action,
and then it is attained.
An officer in charge of affairs requested instructions from Qí Huán Gōng.
Huán Gōng said:
"Report it to Zhòng Fù."
The officer made another request.
The Duke said, "Report it to Zhòng Fù,"
and this happened three times.
A retainer said:
"First it's Zhòng Fù,
then it's Zhòng Fù.
How easy it is to be a ruler!"
Huán Gōng said:
"Before I obtained Zhòng Fù, it was difficult.
After I obtained Zhòng Fù,
how could it not be easy?"
When Huán Gōng obtained Guǎn Zǐ,
affairs became greatly easy.
How much more so if one obtains the Way and its methods?
Kǒng Zǐ was in distress between Chén and Cài,
eating coarse vegetable soup,
and for seven days tasted no grain.
He slept during the day.
Yán Huí sought rice,
obtained it, and cooked it.
When it was almost done,
Kǒng Zǐ saw Yán Huí grab food from the pot and eat it.
A moment later,
the food was ready,
and he presented it to Kǒng Zǐ.
Kǒng Zǐ pretended not to have seen it.
Kǒng Zǐ rose and said:
"Today I dreamed of my late ancestors.
Food must be clean before being offered."
Yán Huí replied:
"That is not possible.
Earlier, soot fell into the pot.
To discard the food would be inauspicious,
so I grabbed it and ate it."
Kǒng Zǐ sighed and said:
"What is trusted is the eye,
yet the eye cannot always be trusted;
what is relied upon is the heart,
yet the heart is not always reliable.
Disciples, remember this:
it is indeed not easy to know people."
Therefore, knowing is not difficult,
but knowing people, as Kǒng Zǐ found, is difficult.
17.4 *Wù Gōng*
Fourth:
If a person's intention is good,
even if ignorant, they can be made a superior.
Thus Lǐ Zǐ said:
"Without a dog, one cannot get a rabbit.
If a rabbit transforms into a dog,
it is no longer a rabbit."
A ruler who enjoys acting as an official to others
is similar to this.
Their ministers obscure them,
and people constantly forbid them.
If the ruler obscures themselves, no one dares to forbid it.
To act as an official for oneself
is the most profound form of self-obscurement.
A broom is used daily and not kept in a box.
Thus, if used, it wears out;
if moved, it becomes dim;
if it acts, it becomes weary.
Wearing out, dimness, and weariness—these three are not the Way of the ruler.
Dà Náo made the *jiǎzǐ* calendar,
Qián Rú made the slave-head method,
Róng Chéng made the calendar,
Xī Hé made sun-gazing,
Shàng Yí made moon-gazing,
Hòu Yì made year-gazing,
Hú Cáo made clothes,
Yí Yì made bows,
Zhù Róng established markets,
Yí Dí made wine,
Gāo Yuán built houses,
Yú Xǔ made boats,
Bó Yì dug wells,
Chì Jì made mortars,
Chéng Yǎ made chariots,
Hán Āi trained charioteers,
Wáng Hài trained oxen,
Shǐ Huáng made maps,
Wū Péng made medicine,
Wū Xián made divination.
These twenty offices
are how the sagely ruler governed the world.
The sagely king could not perform the duties of the twenty offices,
yet he enabled the twenty officers to fully exert their skills and complete their abilities,
because the sagely king was above.
What the sagely king could not do, he enabled others to do;
what he did not know, he enabled others to know.
Nourishing his spirit and cultivating his virtue, he transformed things.
Why must he toil his body and exhaust his ears and eyes?
Thus, the virtue of the sagely king
is like the moon just rising,
illuminating the six directions to its utmost without obstruction;
it is bright like the light of the sun,
transforming myriad things without hindrance.
His spirit is united with the Great One,
giving rise to life without hindrance,
and his will cannot be obstructed;
his essence penetrates the spirits and gods,
profound, subtle, and mysterious,
yet its form is unseen.
Today, seated facing south,
all evils correct themselves,
and the world reverts to its true nature.
The common people all delight in their aspirations and peacefully nurture their nature, and nothing is left undone.
Therefore, a good ruler
diligently brings forth the true nature of life,
and the hundred officials are already well-governed,
the common people are already close,
and his renown is already manifest.
Guǎn Zǐ reported to Huán Gōng,
saying:
"To reclaim land and expand cities,
open up fields and plant grain,
and fully exploit the benefits of the land,
your minister is not as good as Níng Sù.
I request that he be appointed as Grand Administrator of Fields.
To perform ceremonies with appropriate deference,
advancing and retreating with practiced ease,
your minister is not as good as Xí Péng.
I request that he be appointed as Grand Master of Protocol.
To enter early and leave late,
offend the ruler's countenance,
offer loyal remonstrance,
not shirk death,
nor value wealth and status,
your minister is not as good as Dōng Guō Yá.
I request that he be appointed as Grand Remonstrance Minister.
On flat plains and within broad city walls,
where chariots do not get entangled,
and soldiers do not turn their heels,
and when the drums beat, the soldiers of the three armies view death as returning home,
your minister is not as good as Wáng Zǐ Chéng Fù.
I request that he be appointed as Grand Marshal.
To adjudicate cases impartially,
not killing the innocent,
nor falsely accusing the blameless,
your minister is not as good as Xián Zhāng.
I request that he be appointed as Grand Judge.
If Your Highness wishes to govern the state and strengthen the army,
these five gentlemen are sufficient.
If Your Highness desires to become hegemon or king,
then Yí Wú is here."
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
He ordered the five gentlemen to all fulfill their duties,
receiving their commands from Guǎn Zǐ.
After ten years,
he united the feudal lords nine times,
and rectified the world once.
All this was due to the abilities of Yí Wú and the five gentlemen.
Guǎn Zǐ, being a minister,
did not rely on his own inabilities,
but fully utilized the abilities of the five gentlemen.
How much more should a ruler do so?
If a ruler understands that knowing ability and inability can govern the people,
then deceitful, strange, foolish, and dangerous words will all be suppressed,
and the hundred officials and various officers will exert all their strength and exhaust their wisdom.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings governed the people,
and their subordinates indeed did nothing more than exert all their strength and exhaust their wisdom.
Indeed, a ruler who knows not to rely on their own ability, courage, strength, sincerity, and trustworthiness
is close to the ideal.
All rulers
should remain calm, employ virtuous transformation to listen for the essentials.
If this is so, their physical nature will become more robust,
and their ears and eyes will become keener;
the hundred officials will be diligent in their duties,
and none will dare to be lax;
people will perform their tasks
to fulfill their names.
When name and reality are mutually preserved,
this is called knowing the Way.
17.5 *Zhī Dù*
Chapter Five:
A sagacious ruler
does not personally see myriad things.
He is sagacious in what the lord of men grasps.
A ruler who possesses methods
does not personally perform every task.
He understands the essentials of all officials.
When he understands the essentials of all officials,
his affairs are simplified and the state is well-governed.
When he is sagacious in what the lord of men grasps,
his authority is concentrated and corruption ceases.
When corruption ceases, flatterers do not come,
and true intentions are clear;
when intentions are not disguised,
the truth of affairs is revealed.
This is called ultimate governance.
In an age of ultimate governance,
the people do not delight in empty words and hollow rhetoric,
nor do they delight in heterodox learning and widespread theories.
The worthy and the unworthy each return to their true nature.
Their conduct is genuine,
not adorned with artificiality;
they are simple, honest, and pure,
to serve their superiors.
If this is the case, then the skilled and the clumsy, the foolish and the wise, the brave and the timid can all be known.
Thus, officials can be easily exchanged,
and when officials are easily exchanged, each fulfills their duties appropriately.
Therefore, those with positions are secure in their roles,
and their proposals are not heard;
those without positions are held accountable for their actual achievements,
to verify their words.
If these two points are clear,
then useless words will not enter the court.
When the ruler conforms to the true nature of life,
and discards feelings of love and hate,
using emptiness and non-action as his foundation,
listening to useful words is called a court.
Generally, a court
is where people collectively seek principles and righteousness,
and collectively establish laws and regulations.
When the superior conforms to the true nature of life,
then men of principle and righteousness arrive,
the application of laws and regulations is established,
perverse and crooked individuals withdraw,
and greedy, deceitful people are kept far away.
Therefore, the key to governing the world
lies in eliminating corruption;
the key to eliminating corruption
lies in governing officials;
the key to governing officials
lies in governing the Way;
the key to governing the Way
lies in understanding the true nature of life.
Thus, Zǐhuázi said:
"Be profound but not expansive;
reverently guard a single matter;
rectifying one's nature is what pleases.
Do not be all-encompassing among the multitudes,
but strive to perfect one ability.
When ability is fully perfected,
the four barbarians will then be pacified.
Only that which accords with Heaven's decree,
is not all-encompassing yet all-encompassing.
This is why Shénnóng endured,
and Yáo and Shùn were illustrious."
If the ruler considers himself wise and others foolish,
himself skillful and others clumsy,
then the foolish and clumsy will petition,
and the skillful and wise will issue directives.
The more directives, the more petitions there will be,
and the more petitions there are,
there will be nothing that is not petitioned.
Even if the ruler is skillful and wise,
there is nothing he does not know.
By knowing nothing,
he responds to every petition;
his path will certainly become exhausted.
How can one be a ruler of men
if one is frequently exhausted by one's subordinates?
If one is exhausted and does not know one's exhaustion,
the trouble will then turn into self-aggrandizement,
this is called a ruler of double blockage,
and no state can be preserved.
Therefore, a ruler who possesses the Way
acts by reliance, not by doing;
holds accountable, not by directing;
abandons thoughts and intentions,
and waits in quiet emptiness;
does not usurp the words
or seize the tasks;
supervises names and scrutinizes realities;
allows officials to manage themselves,
taking not-knowing as the Way,
and taking "what is to be done?" as a treasure.
Yáo said:
"What should be done to extend rule to where the sun and moon shine?"
Shùn said:
"What should be done to subdue those beyond the four wildernesses?"
Yǔ said:
"What should be done to govern Qīngqíu,
the transformed wonders of the nine Yang regions, and the limits of the arms' reach?"
In the time of Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
he appointed Rèn Dēng as the magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
When submitting his report,
Rèn Dēng said to Xiāngzǐ:
"There is a scholar in Zhōngmóu named Dǎn Xūjǐ,
I request an audience for him."
Xiāngzǐ met him and appointed him as Zhōng Dàfū.
The prime minister said:
"Could it be that Your Lordship heard of him but did not see him?
To be appointed Zhōng Dàfū so easily,
is not the ancient custom of the Jìn state."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"When I appointed Dēng,
I had already heard of him and seen him.
As for the one Dēng recommended,
I have heard of him and seen him.
This 'hearing and seeing people' would never end."
So he did not question it further,
and appointed him Zhōng Dàfū.
Why did Xiāngzǐ trust people?
Because the worthy exerted their full strength.
The trouble for a ruler of men
is invariably in appointing people but being unable to use them,
or using them but consulting with those who do not understand.
One who crosses a river relies on a boat,
one who travels far relies on a steed,
and one who seeks hegemony relies on the worthy.
Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Guǎn Yíwú, Bǎilǐ Xī,
these were the boats and steeds of hegemonic rulers.
To dismiss kinsmen and retainers,
is not to alienate them;
to appoint cooks, fishermen, butchers, or even enemies and slaves,
is not to flatter them;
It is the Way to uphold the altars of earth and grain and establish glorious achievements,
it cannot be otherwise.
It is like a master craftsman building a palace:
he measures size and knows the timber required,
he estimates the work and knows the number of people needed.
Therefore, when Xiǎochén and Lǚ Shàng were heeded, the world knew of the kingship of Yīn and Zhōu;
when Guǎn Yíwú and Bǎilǐ Xī were heeded,
the world knew of the hegemony of Qí and Qín;
how can it be merely a distant steed?
Indeed, those who achieve kingship or hegemony rely on people,
and those who lose their states also rely on people.
Jié used Yáng Xīn,
Zhòu used È Lái,
Sòng used Táng Yāng,
Qí used Sū Qín,
and the world knew of their downfall.
To desire achievement by employing the wrong people
is like desiring a long night on the summer solstice,
or shooting a fish by pointing at the sky and expecting to hit it.
Even Yáo and Shùn would be in difficulty,
how much more so a common ruler?
17.6 "Guarding Against Influence"
Chapter Six:
If one loses by calculation,
and seeks by trust,
it is doubtful.
If one loses by influence,
and seeks by state,
it is perilous.
A fish that can swallow a boat,
if placed on land, cannot overcome an ant.
If authority is equal, they cannot command each other;
if influence is equal, they cannot annex each other;
if order and chaos are equal, they cannot rectify each other.
Therefore, the distinction between large and small, heavy and light, few and many, order and chaos must not be overlooked;
this is the gate of fortune and misfortune.
All states with cap-and-girdle attire,
where boats and chariots pass,
without the use of translators for barbarians,
cover an area of three thousand *lǐ* square.
Ancient kings
chose the center of the world to establish their state,
the center of the state to establish their palace,
and the center of the palace to establish their ancestral temple.
The Son of Heaven's territory,
one thousand *lǐ* square, was considered a state,
intended to maximize governance.
It was not that they could not make it larger,
but its greatness was not as good as smallness,
its multitude not as good as fewness.
The numerous enfeoffments
were not to favor the worthy privately,
but to facilitate influence and preserve prestige,
and to broaden righteousness.
When righteousness is broad and beneficial, there is no enemy.
One without enemies is secure.
Therefore, observing ancient times,
those who had numerous enfeoffments
had enduring fortune
and renowned names.
Shénnóng ruled the world for seventeen generations,
sharing it with the whole world.
When a king establishes enfeoffments,
the nearer they are, the larger they are;
the further they are, the smaller they are.
On the seacoast, there are feudal lords with territories of ten *lǐ*.
To use the great to command the small,
to use the heavy to command the light,
to use the many to command the few—
this is how a king secures his household and completes his dominion.
Therefore, it is said:
To rely on Téng and Fèi is laborious;
to rely on Zōu and Lǔ is leisurely;
to rely on Sòng and Zhèng is like galloping twice the distance in a day;
to rely on Qí and Chǔ is simply to lift and add them to the net.
The greater the resources used,
the easier the desired outcome.
If Tāng had not had É,
if Wǔ had not had Qí,
even if their virtue were perfect,
they could not have succeeded.
Even with the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ,
they still relied on understanding *shì* (strategic advantage);
how much more so for those inferior to Tāng and Wǔ?
Therefore, to use the great to support the small brings good fortune;
to use the small to support the great brings ruin.
To use the heavy to command the light brings obedience;
to use the light to command the heavy brings ill fortune.
From this perspective,
he who desires to bring order to an age,
to secure the lives of the common people,
whose achievements and fame are inscribed on plates and bowls,
whose seals are engraved on jars and mirrors—
his *shì* (strategic advantage) cannot be too honored,
his substance cannot be too abundant.
With abundant substance and honored *shì*,
and wise gentlemen to manage it,
even encountering an era of chaos,
the king would still be considered inadequate.
The people of the world
are impoverished and suffering.
The more severe the people's poverty and suffering,
the easier it is for the king.
Anyone who is a king
is the savior of the impoverished and suffering.
Boats are used on water,
carriages on land,
sleds on muddy roads,
sand-carts on sand,
and clogs on mountains—
this is making use of the inherent *shì* (condition).
Then commands will be carried out.
When one's position is honored, one's teachings are accepted;
when one's authority is established, villainy ceases.
This is the way to govern people.
Therefore, for a state of ten thousand chariots to command a state of a thousand chariots is easy;
for a state of a thousand chariots to command a single household is easy;
for a single household to command an individual is easy.
If one fails to recognize this,
even Yáo and Shùn could not succeed.
If feudal lords do not wish to be subordinates,
yet have no choice,
and their *shì* (condition) is not convenient,
then how can subservience be easy?
Weighing the heavy and the light,
assessing the large and the small,
establishing many enfeoffments—this is to make their *shì* (condition) convenient.
A king
is *shì*;
a king
is *shì* without rivals.
If *shì* has rivals, then the king's rule will be overthrown.
He who knows that the small is better than the great, and the few are more virtuous than the many,
then he knows he has no rival.
If one knows one has no rival, then the paths of resemblance, suspicion, and doubt are far removed.
Therefore, the laws of the former kings
established the Son of Heaven so that the feudal lords would not doubt him;
established the feudal lords so that the grandees would not doubt them;
established the legitimate heir so that illegitimate offspring would not doubt him.
Doubt gives rise to contention;
contention gives rise to chaos.
It is for this reason that if the feudal lords lose their positions, the world falls into chaos;
if grandees have no ranks, the court falls into chaos;
if wives and concubines are not distinguished, the household falls into chaos;
if legitimate and illegitimate offspring are not separated, the clan falls into chaos.
Shènzǐ said:
"Now, if one rabbit runs,
a hundred people chase it.
It is not that one rabbit is enough for a hundred people to share,
but because the division is not yet settled.
If the division is not settled,
even Yáo would exert himself in vain,
how much more so ordinary people?
If rabbits pile up in the marketplace,
passersby do not even glance at them.
It is not that they do not desire rabbits,
but the division is already settled.
If the division is settled,
even a rude person will not contend.
Therefore, governing the world and the state
lies simply in settling the divisions."
King Zhuāng besieged Sòng for nine months;
King Kāng besieged Sòng for five months;
King Shēng besieged Sòng for ten months.
Chǔ besieged Sòng three times and could not destroy it.
It was not that it could not be destroyed,
but if Sòng were attacked by Chǔ,
when would it ever stop?
The establishment of achievements
differs with the worthy and unworthy, the strong and the weak, the well-governed and the chaotic.
Qí Jiǎn Gōng had a minister named Zhū Yù Yāng,
who admonished Jiǎn Gōng, saying:
"Chén Chéngcháng and Zǎi Yǔ,
these two ministers deeply resent each other,
and I fear they will attack each other.
If they attack each other persistently, it will endanger the superior.
I wish, my lord, that you would remove one of them."
Jiǎn Gōng said:
"This is not something you, a petty person, can understand."
Not long after,
Chén Chéngcháng indeed attacked Zǎi Yǔ in the court,
and then attacked Jiǎn Gōng in the ancestral temple.
Jiǎn Gōng sighed deeply and said:
"I failed to use Yāng's words,
which led to this calamity."
Losing the proper method,
without the proper *shì*,
even regretting not listening to Yāng is the same as having no regret,
which means not knowing to rely on what is reliable and relying on what is not reliable.
The Zhōu tripods depicted images
because their principles were universally understood.
When principles are understood,
it is the way of the ruler.
17.7 "No Duplicity"
Seventh saying:
To govern the state by listening to the deliberations of the masses
will lead to the state's peril in no time.
How do we know this to be so?
Lǎo Dān valued softness;
Kǒngzǐ valued benevolence;
Mò Dí valued integrity;
Guān Yǐn valued purity;
Zǐ Lièzǐ valued emptiness;
Chén Pián valued impartiality;
Yáng Shēng valued self-interest;
Sūn Bìn valued *shì*;
Wáng Liáo valued precedence;
Ér Liáng valued precedence.
There are drums and gongs to unify the ears;
uniform laws and decrees to unify the hearts;
the wise are not allowed to be clever,
the foolish are not allowed to be clumsy,
so as to unify the multitude;
the brave are not allowed to go first,
the timid are not allowed to fall behind,
so as to unify strength.
Therefore, unity brings order,
diversity brings chaos;
unity brings security,
diversity brings danger.
Indeed, he who can unify the ten thousand differences,
making the foolish and the wise, the skilled and the clumsy, all exert their utmost effort and ability,
as if emerging from a single opening,
is he not a sage!
Wisdom without method,
ability without instruction,
and relying on strength, speed, penetration, and habit,
are insufficient for accomplishment.
17.8 "Holding to Unity"
Eighth saying:
Heaven and Earth, Yin and Yang do not change,
yet produce ten thousand different things.
The eyes do not lose their clarity,
yet distinguish between white and black;
the ears do not lose their acuity,
yet hear sounds clear and濁.
The king holds to unity,
and thereby sets all things right.
An army must have a general,
to unify it;
a state must have a ruler,
to unify it;
the world must have a Son of Heaven,
to unify it;
the Son of Heaven must hold to unity,
to consolidate it.
Unity brings order;
duality brings chaos.
Now, if one were to drive a team of black horses,
and four people were employed,
each holding a whip,
they would not be able to get out of the gate—
because there is no unity.
The King of Chǔ asked Zhān Zǐ about governing a state.
Zhān Zǐ replied:
"I have heard of cultivating oneself,
but not of governing a state."
Did Zhān Zǐ mean that a state could be left ungoverned?
He believed that the root of governing a state lies in cultivating oneself.
When one is cultivated, the family is in order;
when the family is in order, the state is governed;
when the state is governed, the world is at peace.
Therefore, it is said that one cultivates oneself to bring order to the family,
orders the family to govern the state,
and governs the state to bring peace to the world.
These four
differ in position but are the same in root.
Thus, the affairs of the sage,
when broadly expounded, encompass the universe and exhaust the sun and moon;
when concisely stated, they do not go beyond oneself.
A benevolent parent cannot transmit [virtue] to a child,
nor can a loyal minister instill [it] in a ruler.
Only those who possess the talent are close to it.
Tián Pián used Daoist principles to persuade the King of Qí.
The King of Qí responded:
"What寡人 possesses is the state of Qí.
I wish to hear about the governance of Qí."
Tián Pián replied:
"My words,
without explicit governance, can achieve governance.
It is like a forest,
without explicit timber, it can yield timber.
I wish Your Majesty to take the governance of Qí for yourself.
Pián speaks superficially;
to speak broadly,
how can it be only about the governance of Qí?
Changes and responses all have their patterns,
acting according to nature and entrusting things, none are inappropriate.
Péng Zǔ achieved longevity,
the Three Dynasties flourished,
the Five Emperors shone brightly,
and Shén Nóng achieved greatness."
Wú Qǐ said to Shāng Wén:
"It is truly fated to serve a ruler!"
Shāng Wén asked:
"What do you mean?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"Governing within the four borders,
establishing disciplined teaching,
changing customs,
making rulers and ministers righteous,
and fathers and sons orderly—
who is more capable, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not as good as you."
Wú Qǐ said:
"Today, if one is appointed as a minister,
their lord feels secure and important;
today, if one resigns their seal and office,
their lord feels insecure and insignificant—
who is more capable, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not as good as you."
Wú Qǐ said:
"When soldiers and horses are arrayed in formation,
horses are as numerous as men;
men are in front of horses.
Seizing a drumstick and striking a single drum,
making the soldiers of the three armies
delight in death as if it were life—
who is more capable, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not as good as you."
Wú Qǐ said:
"In these three aspects,
you are all not as good as I,
yet your position is above mine.
It is truly fate to serve a ruler!"
Shāng Wén said:
"Excellent.
You asked me,
and I shall also ask you.
When the world changes, the ruler is young,
ministers suspect each other,
and the common people are unsettled—
does this fall to you,
or to me?"
Wú Qǐ remained silent, not answering.
After a short while, he said:
"To you."
Shāng Wén said:
"This is why I am superior to you."
Wú Qǐ saw his strengths,
but did not see his weaknesses;
he knew why he was capable,
but did not know why he was unworthy.
Thus, he was victorious at Xīhé,
but was trapped by Wáng Cuò,
leading to great disaster and downfall,
and could not die a natural death.
Indeed, Wú was victorious over Qí,
but not over Yuè;
Qí was victorious over Sòng,
but not over Yān.
Therefore, only those who understand the transformations of strengths and weaknesses,
or gains and losses, can preserve their state and protect their person.
18.1 *Shěn Yìng* (Careful Responses)
Chapter One:
When a ruler speaks and responds,
one must be careful.
Whenever a ruler has discernment,
he does not wish to speak first.
When others initiate, I respond;
when others lead, I follow.
Using their initiatives as my entries,
using their words as their declarations,
and holding them accountable for their declared names based on the reality,
then speakers will not dare to speak recklessly,
and the ruler will hold the key.
Kǒng Sī requested to leave.
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"The rulers under Heaven are all like寡人;
where will you go?"
Kǒng Sī replied:
"I have heard that a gentleman is like a bird;
when alarmed, it flies away."
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"If all rulers are unworthy and act thus,
avoiding the unworthy,
and encountering the unworthy,
do you consider yourself capable of judging all rulers under Heaven?"
When a bird flies,
it leaves what alarms it and follows what does not alarm it.
Leaving what alarms and following what does not alarm—
this cannot be known.
If it leaves what alarms and follows what alarms,
why would the bird fly away at all?
Kǒng Sī's reply to the Lord of Lǔ was also mistaken.
King Huì of Wèi sent someone to tell Marquis Zhāo of Hán:
"Zhèng was destroyed by the Hán clan.
I wish Your Majesty to enfeoff their descendants.
This is called the righteousness of preserving the fallen and continuing the severed.
If Your Majesty enfeoffs them, it will be a great name."
Marquis Zhāo was troubled by this.
Gōngzǐ Shí Wǒ said:
"I request to go and respond to him."
Gōngzǐ Shí Wǒ arrived in Wèi,
met the King of Wèi, and said:
"Your great state commands our humble state to enfeoff the descendants of Zhèng.
Our humble state dares not accept this.
Our humble state is troubled by your great state.
In the past, the descendant of Chū Gōng, Shēng Shì, became Duke of Jìn.
He was imprisoned at Tóngdī,
and your great state did not pity him.
Yet you bid our humble state to preserve the fallen and continue the severed.
Our humble state dares not accept this."
The King of Wèi was ashamed and said:
"Indeed, it was not寡人's intention.
Please, my guest, do not speak of it again."
This was to use an unrighteous act to carry out an unrighteous act.
Although the King of Wèi had no answer,
Hán's unrighteousness became even greater.
Gōngzǐ Shí Wǒ's argument
was merely sufficient to conceal wrong and perpetuate error.
King Zhāo of Wèi asked Tián Qū:
"When寡人 was Crown Prince,
I heard your opinion, Sir, saying:
'Being a sage is easy.'
Is that so?"
Tián Qū replied:
"That is what I stated."
King Zhāo said:
"Then are you a sage, Sir?"
Tián Qū replied:
"To know one is a sage without having achieved any merits
is like Yáo knowing Shùn;
to wait for their merits before knowing they are Shùn the sage
is like common folk knowing Shùn the sage.
Now Qū has not achieved any merits,
yet Your Majesty asks Qū, 'Are you a sage?'
May I ask if Your Majesty is also a Yáo?"
King Zhāo had no reply.
Tián Qū's reply was
that King Zhāo surely did not say,
"I know [you are] a sage";
he asked, "Are you a sage, Sir?"
Tián Qū then used "knowing a sage" to reply to King Zhāo.
King Zhāo had what he did not possess,
but Tián Qū did not perceive it.
Zhào Huìwáng said to Gōngsūn Lóng:
"I have been striving for more than ten years to cease military actions, but I have not succeeded.
Can military actions not be ceased?"
Gōngsūn Lóng replied:
"The intention to cease military actions
is the heart of universal love for all under Heaven.
Universal love for all under Heaven
cannot be merely an empty name;
it must have substance.
Currently, Lìn and Líshí have been ceded to Qín,
and Your Majesty wears plain white mourning clothes;
while you attacked Qí in the east and gained territory,
and Your Majesty adds to his meals and sets out wine.
Qín gains territory and Your Majesty wears mourning clothes,
Qí loses territory and Your Majesty adds to his meals—
this is not the heart of universal love.
This is why ceasing military actions has not succeeded."
Now, if there is a person here
who is rude, disrespectful, and lax, yet seeks respect;
who is partisan and unjust, yet seeks order;
who is troublesome, noisy, and constantly changing, yet seeks tranquility;
who is violent, cruel, and greedy, yet seeks stability—
even Huángdì would be troubled by such a person.
Wèi Sìjūn wished to levy heavy taxes to accumulate grain,
but the people were not at ease.
He told Bó Yí:
"The people are truly foolish.
Accumulating grain
is for the sake of the people.
What difference does it make whether it is stored by themselves or kept by the ruler?"
Bó Yí replied:
"That is not so.
If it is with the people and the ruler does not know it,
it is not as good as being with the ruler;
if it is with the ruler and the people do not know it,
it is not as good as being with the people."
Whenever you listen, you must reflect upon yourself;
if you are discerning, then there will be nothing you command that is not obeyed.
A state that endures long becomes firm;
if firm, it is difficult to destroy.
Now, Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu no longer exist—
they all failed to reflect upon themselves.
Gōngzǐ Dá served as prime minister of Zhōu.
Shēn Xiàng spoke to him and then went to battle.
Gōngzǐ Dá criticized him, saying:
"Master Shēn spoke to me and then went to battle.
Is he acting as my prime minister?"
Shēn Xiàng said:
"I, Xiàng, am unworthy.
However,
Your Lordship became prime minister at twenty years old,
and when you see an elder, you send him to battle.
May I ask who is at fault?"
Gōngzǐ Dá had no reply.
To fight
is not customary;
to send someone else to fight
is to be severe and reckless.
It means that even if one is respectful and temperate, people still fight,
and the responsibility does not lie with the esteemed.
Therefore, although people may sometimes make mistakes,
there is still nothing to replace being respectful and temperate.
Self-error is not enough to make things difficult;
but if one is severe and reckless, it can.
18.2 《Chóngyán》
Second:
The words of a ruler
must not be taken lightly.
Gāozōng, being the Son of Heaven,
upon ascending the throne, entered a period of mourning and silence,
not speaking for three years.
The high ministers and grandees were afraid
and worried about it.
Gāozōng then spoke, saying:
"With I, the one man, to rectify the four quarters,
I only feared that my words might be inappropriate,
which is why I did not speak."
The ancient Sons of Heaven
regarded their words with such gravity,
hence their words left no room for error.
Chéngwáng and Táng Shūyú were at ease together,
and Chéngwáng picked up a parasol tree leaf to make a gui-tablet,
and gave it to Táng Shūyú, saying:
"With this, I enfeoff you."
Shūyú was pleased
and told Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng then inquired, saying:
"Is the Son of Heaven going to enfeoff Yú?"
Chéngwáng replied:
"I, the one man, was merely playing with Yú."
Zhōu Gōng responded:
"Your subject has heard that
the Son of Heaven has no jesting words.
When the Son of Heaven speaks,
the historian records it,
the musicians chant it,
and the scholars praise it."
Thereupon, Shūyú was enfeoffed in Jìn.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn can be said to have spoken well;
with a single statement, he made Chéngwáng even more careful with his words,
clarified the principle of brotherly love,
and solidified the support for the royal house.
Jīng Zhuāngwáng governed for three years,
did not attend court, and delighted in riddles.
Chéng Gōngjiǎ entered to remonstrate.
The King said:
"I forbid remonstrance;
now you remonstrate,
what is the reason?"
He replied:
"Your subject does not dare to remonstrate;
I wish to propose a riddle to Your Majesty."
The King said:
"Why not propose it to me?"
He replied:
"There is a bird that alights on a mound in the south;
for three years it neither moves, flies, nor sings.
What kind of bird is this?"
The King shot it and said:
"There is a bird that alights on a mound in the south.
Its not moving for three years
is to settle its will and resolve;
its not flying
is to develop its wings;
its not singing
is to observe the people's rules.
Though this bird has not flown,
when it flies, it will soar to the sky;
though it has not sung,
when it sings, it will startle people.
Jiǎ, withdraw!
I understand now."
The next day at court,
five people were promoted,
and ten people were demoted.
The officials were greatly pleased,
and the people of Jīng congratulated each other.
Therefore, the 《Shī》 says:
"Why has it been so long?
There must be a reason.
Why does it stay in place?
There must be a cause."
Was this not referring to Zhuāngwáng?
Chéng Gōngjiǎ's riddle
was superior to the advice of Tàizǎi Pǐ.
Tàizǎi Pǐ's advice,
though listened to by Fūchā,
led the state of Wú to become ruins;
Chéng Gōngjiǎ's riddle,
understood by Jīngwáng,
made the state of Jīng a hegemon.
Qí Huánggōng and Guǎn Zhòng discussed attacking Jǔ.
Before the plan was launched, it was heard throughout the state.
Huánggōng was surprised and said:
"I discussed attacking Jǔ with Zhòngfù,
but before the plan was launched, it was heard throughout the state.
What is the reason for this?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There must be a sage in the state."
Huánggōng said:
"Aha!
Among those who worked today,
there was one who carried a foot-measure and looked upwards.
Could it be he?"
He then ordered the workers to return,
without allowing substitutes.
A short while later,
Dōngguō Yá arrived.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This must be him."
He then ordered the attendants to invite him up
and stand on the steps according to rank.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
so why did you speak of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Your subject has heard that a gentleman excels at planning,
while a common person excels at guessing.
Your subject merely guessed it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
how did you infer it?"
He replied:
"I have heard that a noble person has three countenances:
one who is clearly joyful and happy
has the countenance of bells and drums;
one who is sorrowful and pure
has the countenance of mourning clothes;
one who is flushed and full of vigor,
with hands and feet twitching,
has the countenance of war.
The other day, when I observed your Lordship on the platform,
flushed and full of vigor,
with hands and feet twitching,
this was the countenance of war.
Your Lordship opened his mouth and did not close it, what
was spoken of was Jǔ;
your Lordship raised his arm and pointed,
what was indicated was Jǔ.
I privately considered that among the feudal lords who are disobedient,
perhaps only Jǔ remains.
Therefore, I spoke of it."
Generally, the ear hears by sound;
now, not hearing his sound,
but by his expression and arm,
this means Dōngguō Yá did not listen with his ears but heard.
Huán Gōng and Guǎn Zhòng, though they were
good at concealing, could not hide it.
Therefore, the sagely person listens to the soundless,
and sees the formless.
Zhān Hé, Tián Zifāng, and Lǎo Dān are examples of this.
18.3 "Jīngyù"
Third, it says:
Sagely persons understand each other without waiting for words;
there are those who speak before words.
There was a man by the sea who loved seagulls.
Every morning he would live by the sea
and play with the seagulls.
The seagulls that came
numbered in the hundreds without ceasing;
they were all around him,
and he played with them all day without leaving.
His father told him:
"I hear that all the seagulls come to you.
Catch some and bring them,
I want to play with them."
The next day, when he went to the sea,
no seagulls came.
Shèng Shū said to Zhōu Gōng Dàn:
"The court is small, and the people are many.
If I speak slowly, it will not be heard;
if I speak quickly, people will know it.
Should I speak slowly,
or quickly?"
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Speak slowly."
Shèng Shū said:
"There is an affair here,
if I speak subtly, it will not be clear;
if I do not speak, it will not be accomplished.
Should I speak subtly,
or not speak?"
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Do not speak."
Thus, Shèng Shū was able to persuade by not speaking,
and Zhōu Gōng Dàn was able to listen by not speaking.
This is called listening without words.
A plan without words,
an affair not heard of,
even if Yīn hated Zhōu,
they could not find fault.
Mouths sealed, not speaking,
communicating subtly to each other,
even if Zhòu had many suspicions,
he could not know it.
Eyes seeing the formless,
ears hearing the soundless,
even if Shāng had many spies,
they could not glimpse it.
Sharing dislikes and sharing likes,
with all desires held,
even if one is the Son of Heaven,
one cannot separate them.
Kǒngzǐ saw Wēn Bó Xuězǐ,
and left without speaking.
Zǐgòng said:
"Our Master has long desired to see Wēn Bó Xuězǐ;
now he has seen him but did not speak.
What is the reason for this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"For a person such as he,
upon seeing him, the Way is already present;
there is no room for sound."
Therefore, to know one's will without having seen the person,
and to have one's heart and will both seen upon seeing the person—
this is due to a natural accord.
How could sagely persons' mutual understanding
depend on words?
Bái Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Can one speak subtly with others?"
Kǒngzǐ did not answer.
Bái Gōng said:
"What if one throws a stone into water?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No one can retrieve it."
Bái Gōng said:
"What if one throws water into water?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Zī and Mǐn rivers merge,
Yì Yá tasted and knew it."
Bái Gōng said:
"Then, can one truly not speak subtly with others?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Why not?
Only one who 'knows what words mean' can."
Bái Gōng did not understand.
One who 'knows what words mean' does not speak with words.
Words belong to the category of 'what is meant'.
One who seeks fish gets wet;
one who hunts beasts runs;
they do not enjoy it.
Therefore, ultimate words transcend words;
ultimate action is non-action.
What the shallow-minded contend over is ultimately trivial.
Bái Gōng did not understand.
This is why Bái Gōng died in the ancestral temple.
Qí Huán Gōng assembled the feudal lords,
and the people of Wèi arrived late.
The Duke held court and plotted with Guǎn Zhòng to attack Wèi.
After court, he entered.
Wèi Jī saw the Duke coming,
descended the hall, bowed twice,
and begged for the transgression of the Lord of Wèi.
The Duke said:
"I have no reason regarding Wèi,
why do you plead?"
She replied:
"When I saw your Lordship entering,
your steps were high and your spirit strong,
you had the intention of attacking a state.
Seeing me, your expression changed;
you intend to attack Wèi."
The next day, the Duke held court,
bowed to Guǎn Zhòng and advanced towards him.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Has your Lordship spared Wèi?"
The Duke said:
"How does Zhòngfù know this?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Your Lordship's bow at court was respectful,
and your speech was slow.
Seeing me, you showed a look of shame.
This is how I knew it."
The Duke said:
"Excellent.
Zhòngfù manages external affairs,
the Lady manages internal affairs.
I know I shall never be laughed at by the feudal lords."
What Huán Gōng concealed was unspoken,
yet now Guǎn Zǐ perceived it through his countenance and voice,
and the Lady perceived it through his gait and spirit.
Although Huán Gōng did not speak,
it was like a torch illuminating the dark night.
Jìn Xiāng Gōng sent an envoy to Zhōu, saying:
"Our humble state's humble ruler is gravely ill.
The tortoise shells for divination said:
'Sāntú is the cause of the affliction.'
Our humble state's humble ruler has sent his humble servant, desiring to borrow the road to pray for blessings."
The Son of Heaven permitted it.
At court,
after the ceremony for the envoy was complete,
the guest left.
Cháng Hóng said to Liú Kāng Gōng:
"Praying for blessings at Sāntú
and receiving ceremony from the Son of Heaven,
this is an affair of gentleness and auspiciousness.
Yet the guest's countenance was martial.
There is probably another matter.
I wish for your Lordship to be prepared."
Liú Kāng Gōng then alerted his war chariots and soldiers to await them.
Jìn indeed sent sacrificial officiants first,
and then ordered Yáng Zǐ to lead 120,000 soldiers to follow them.
They crossed at Jítjīn,
attacked Liáo Ruǎn, Liáng, and Mán Shì by surprise,
and annihilated three states.
This is a case where the outward form and the name do not match,
which sagely persons scrutinize.
Cháng Hóng was indeed discerning.
Therefore, words are insufficient to decide minor matters.
Only one who 'knows what words mean' is capable.
18.4 "Líwèi"
Fourth,
speech
is for conveying meaning.
When speech and meaning are detached from each other,
it is inauspicious.
Among the customs of a disordered state,
there are many rumors,
and people do not care about the truth of the matter.
They strive to discredit each other,
and strive to praise each other.
Discrediting and praising form factions,
and the multitude's clamor reaches the heavens.
The worthy and unworthy are indistinguishable.
If one governs a state with this,
even a worthy ruler will be deluded by it,
how much more so an unworthy one?
The affliction of the deluded
is not to regard themselves as deluded.
Therefore, within profound delusion there is enlightenment,
and within deep darkness there is illumination.
The rulers of doomed states
do not regard themselves as deluded,
hence they are all like Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
However, there has never been a state that perished
for a different reason.
In the state of Zhèng, many people hung up written appeals.
When Zǐchǎn ordered that no appeals be hung up,
Dèng Xī submitted them.
When Zǐchǎn ordered that no appeals be submitted,
Dèng Xī leaned them against things.
If the orders were endless,
then Dèng Xī's responses would also be endless.
Thus, the distinction between what is permissible and what is not permissible would be lost.
If the distinction between what is permissible and what is not permissible is lost,
and punishments and rewards are applied,
the more severe the punishments,
the more severe the disorder.
This is a prohibition for governing a state.
Therefore, argument that does not accord with reason is deceitful;
knowledge that does not accord with reason is fraudulent.
Fraudulent and deceitful people
were those whom the Former Kings punished.
Reason
is the ultimate standard of right and wrong.
The Wěi River was very high,
and a rich man from Zhèng drowned.
Someone found his body.
The rich man's family offered to ransom it,
but the finder demanded a large sum of gold.
They informed Dèng Xī.
Dèng Xī said:
"Rest easy.
No one else will sell it."
The finder of the body became worried,
and informed Dèng Xī.
Dèng Xī again replied:
"Rest easy.
He will certainly have nowhere else to buy it."
Indeed, harming loyal ministers
is similar to this.
If one has no accomplishments and fails to win the people,
then one is harmed by one's lack of accomplishments and failure to win the people;
if one has accomplishments and wins the people,
then one is harmed by one's accomplishments and success in winning the people.
A ruler who lacks proper standards
cannot comprehend this.
Is this not tragic?
Bǐgān and Cháng Hóng died because of this;
Jī Zǐ and Shāng Róng suffered hardship because of this;
Zhōu Gōng and Shào Gōng were doubted because of this;
Fàn Lǐ and Zǐ Xū were exiled because of this.
Life and death, survival and destruction, safety and danger,
all stem from this.
When Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
Dèng Xī made it his business to challenge him.
He made an agreement with those among the people who had lawsuits:
for a major lawsuit, one set of outer garments;
for a minor lawsuit, one undershirt and trousers. Those among the people who offered garments and undershirt-trousers to learn litigation
were innumerable.
They made wrong into right,
and right into wrong.
Right and wrong had no fixed standard,
and what was permissible and what was not changed daily.
Whoever wished to win, won;
whoever wished to be condemned, was condemned.
Zhèng state fell into great disorder,
and the people's mouths clamored.
Zǐchǎn was troubled by this,
so he killed Dèng Xī and executed him publicly.
Then the people's hearts were appeased,
right and wrong were established,
and laws were enforced.
People of the present age
often wish to govern their states,
but none execute people like Dèng Xī.
This is why they desire to govern but only create more disorder.
There was a man in Qí who served someone.
When his master faced difficulty, he did not die for him.
He met an old acquaintance on the road.
The acquaintance said:
"Surely you did not die for him?"
He replied:
"Indeed.
One serves another for profit.
Death is not profitable,
so I did not die."
The acquaintance said:
"Can you still face other people?"
He replied:
"Do you think that dying makes one able to face other people?"
This anecdote was transmitted many times.
Not dying for one's lord or superior
is a great injustice,
yet his words are still not to be dismissed.
It is clear that words alone are insufficient to decide matters.
Indeed, words
are merely the outward manifestation of meaning.
To examine the manifestation and discard the meaning is perverse.
Therefore, the ancients,
when they grasped the meaning, would disregard the words.
Those who listen to words observe the meaning through the words.
If one listens to words and the meaning cannot be known,
it is no different from deceitful speech.
There was a man from Qí named Chúnyú Kūn,
who tried to persuade King Wèi with "following" arguments.
King Wèi found his arguments compelling,
prepared ten carriages,
and was about to send him to Jīng.
As he was about to leave,
someone presented "transverse" arguments to King Wèi,
and King Wèi then stopped his departure.
He lost the "following" intention,
and also lost the "transverse" accomplishment.
Indeed, having many abilities is not as good as having few,
and having eloquence is not as good as having none.
The cauldron of Zhōu depicted Chuí biting his own finger;
the Former Kings thereby showed that excessive cleverness is not to be indulged.
18.5 "Licentious Speech"
Fifth,
without words, there is no way to communicate with each other,
but following words leads to disorder.
Within disordered words, there is still meaning,
which is called the heart-mind.
If words do not deceive the heart-mind,
then it is close to the truth.
All words
are for conveying the heart-mind.
If words and the heart-mind are separated,
and superiors have no way to verify them,
then inferiors will often speak one thing and do another,
or do one thing and say another.
When words and actions contradict each other,
no inauspiciousness is greater.
In the matter of Kōng Xióng,
Qín and Zhào made a treaty with each other,
which stated:
"From now on,
whatever Qín wishes to do,
Zhào shall assist;
whatever Zhào wishes to do,
Qín shall assist."
Not long after,
Qín raised an army to attack Wèi,
and Zhào wished to assist Wèi.
King Qín was displeased,
and sent an envoy to rebuke King Zhào, saying:
"The treaty states:
'Whatever Qín wishes to do,
Zhào shall assist;
whatever Zhào wishes to do,
Qín shall assist.'
Now Qín wishes to attack Wèi,
but Zhào instead wishes to save Wèi.
This is not according to the treaty."
King Zhào told Píngyuán Jūn.
Píngyuán Jūn told Gōngsūn Lóng.
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
"You can also send an envoy to rebuke King Qín, saying:
'Zhào wishes to save Wèi,
but now King Qín alone does not assist Zhào.
This is not according to the treaty.'"
Kǒng Chuān and Gōngsūn Lóng debated at Píngyuán Jūn's residence,
engaging in deep and eloquent arguments,
even to the point of "concealing three (tusks) ears."
Gōngsūn Lóng's argument for "concealing three (tusks) ears" was very eloquent,
but Kǒng Chuān did not respond.
After a short while,
Kǒng Chuān excused himself and left.
The next day,
Kǒng Chuān attended court.
Píngyuán-jūn said to Kǒng Chuān:
“In the past, Gōngsūn Lóng’s words were very eloquent.”
Kǒng Chuān said:
“Indeed.
He almost managed to make it sound like one has three (teeth) ears.
Although that is difficult in reality.
I wish to ask you something,
to say that having three (teeth) ears is very difficult and actually incorrect,
and to say that having two (teeth) ears is very easy and actually correct,
I wonder if you will follow that which is easy and correct?
Or that which is difficult and incorrect?”
Píngyuán-jūn did not reply.
The next day,
he said to Gōngsūn Lóng:
“You must not debate with Kǒng Chuān again.”
Jīng Zhùguó Zhuāng Bó ordered his father to look at the sun;
the sun,
he said, “is in the sky”;
“How does it look?”
He said, “perfectly round”;
“Look at the time,”
he said,
“it is now.”
He ordered the usher to “harness the chariot”;
he replied, “there are no horses.”
He ordered the attendant to “fetch his hat”;
he replied, “it has been offered to the ruler.”
He asked about “the age of the horse”;
the stableman replied, “twelve years old and thirty teeth.”
There was a person who appointed a minister who did not flee;
when the minister fled,
Zhuāng Bó executed him,
but the appointer was not punished.
In Sòng, there was a man named Chéng Zǐ,
who lost a black gown.
He searched for it on the road,
and saw a woman wearing a black gown.
He grabbed her and would not let go,
wanting to take her gown,
saying:
“Just now, I lost a black gown.”
The woman said:
“Although you lost a black gown,
this is truly one I made myself.”
Chéng Zǐ said:
“You had better quickly give me the gown.
The one I lost before
was a black gown made of raw silk.
Your gown now
is a black gown made of thin silk.
By using a thin silk black gown to compensate for a raw silk black gown,
how could you not benefit?”
The King of Sòng said to his prime minister, Táng Yāng:
“I have executed and killed many people,
yet my officials fear me less and less.
Why is this?”
Táng Yāng replied:
“Those whom Your Majesty punishes
are all evil people.
By punishing the evil,
the good naturally do not fear.
If Your Majesty wishes your officials to fear you,
it would be better to make no distinction between good and evil, and punish them occasionally.
If you do this, then your officials will fear.”
Not long after,
the Lord of Sòng killed Táng Yāng.
Táng Yāng’s reply
would have been better left unsaid.
Huì Zǐ created laws for King Huì of Wèi.
When the laws were finished,
he showed them to the people,
and the people all praised them.
He presented them to King Huì,
King Huì praised them,
and showed them to Zhái Jiǎn.
Zhái Jiǎn said:
“They are good.”
King Huì said:
“If they are good, can they be implemented?”
Zhái Jiǎn said:
“No.”
King Huì said:
“Good, yet cannot be implemented,
why?”
Zhái Jiǎn replied:
“Now, when lifting a large log,
the front calls out ‘Yú xǔ!’,
and the rear also responds to it.
This is good for those lifting the large log.
Are there no songs of Zhèng or Wèi?
Yet, they are not as suitable as this.
Indeed, the state is also like a large log.”
18.6 《Bù Qū》
Chapter Six says:
The insightful scholar believes he has attained the Way, but he has not.
Nevertheless,
in his responses to things,
his words are hard to exhaust.
Although his words are exhaustive,
whether they bring calamity or fortune is yet unknown.
If insight is used to understand principles and clarify meanings,
then insight brings fortune;
if insight is used to adorn wrongs and delude fools,
then insight brings calamity.
The ancients valued good governance
to pursue tyranny and prohibit evil.
King Huì of Wèi said to Huì Zǐ:
“In ancient times, those who possessed a state
were necessarily worthy individuals.
Now, I am truly not as capable as you, Master,
and I wish to pass on the state.”
Huì Zǐ declined.
The King again earnestly requested, saying:
“There is no one here who possesses a state,
and if I pass it to a worthy person,
the people’s hearts of greed and contention will cease.
I wish for you, Master, to agree to this for me.”
Huì Zǐ said:
“If that is what Your Majesty says,
then I, Shī, cannot agree.
Your Majesty is indeed the lord of a myriad chariots,
and giving the state to someone else is still permissible.
Now I, Shī,
am a commoner.
If I could have a state of a myriad chariots and declined it,
this would curb the hearts of greed and contention even more greatly.”
King Huì said to Huì Zǐ:
“In ancient times, those who possessed a state
were necessarily worthy individuals.”
A grandee who received and was worthy was Shùn,
so this meant he wanted Huì Zǐ to be Shùn;
one who declined and was worthy was Xǔ Yóu,
so this meant Huì Zǐ wanted to be Xǔ Yóu;
one who passed it on and was worthy was Yáo,
so this meant King Huì wanted to be Yáo.
The actions of Yáo, Shùn, and Xǔ Yóu
were not solely about passing to Shùn or Yóu declining,
other actions also fit this.
Now, without other actions,
but desiring to be Yáo, Shùn, and Xǔ Yóu,
therefore King Huì wore a commoner’s cap and was held captive in Juǎn,
King Wēi of Qí almost did not receive him,
Huì Zǐ changed his clothes and cap,
rode in a chariot and fled,
almost not making it out of the Wèi border.
All actions must not rely on luck,
but must be genuine.
Kuāng Zhāng said to Huì Zǐ in front of King Wèi:
“Locusts, leafhoppers, and armyworms,
farmers catch and kill them,
why?
Because they harm the crops.
Now, when you travel,
the many have several hundred chariots, and several hundred people on foot;
the few have several dozen chariots,
and several dozen people on foot.
These are all people who do not plow but eat,
and their harm to the crops is also great.”
King Huì said:
“Huì Zǐ, Shī,
it is difficult for him to respond to you in words.
Nevertheless,
allow me to express his intent.
Huì Zǐ said:
‘Those who are now building a city,
some wield large rammers on the city wall,
some carry baskets and rush below the city,
some wield measuring rods and indicators to observe carefully.
Someone like me, Shī,
is one who wields the measuring rod and indicators.
If you make a weaving woman transform into silk,
she cannot weave silk;
if you make a master carpenter transform into wood,
he cannot work wood;
if you make a sage transform into a farmer,
he cannot govern farmers.
I, Shī, am one who governs farmers.’
Why do you compare me, Shī, to leafhoppers and armyworms?”
Huì Zǐ’s governance of Wèi was fundamental,
yet his governance did not govern.
During King Huì’s time,
there were fifty battles and twenty defeats,
the number of those killed was countless,
and even great generals and beloved sons were captured.
The great state was foolish,
and became a laughingstock for all under Heaven.
They had to choose to speak of his taboo,
and then asked the Grand Scribe of Zhōu to change his name.
Hándān was besieged for three years, but they could not take it.
The soldiers and people were exhausted,
the state was empty,
and the armies of all under Heaven arrived from all directions.
The common people slandered,
and the feudal lords did not praise.
After apologizing to Zhái Jiǎn and listening to his counsel again,
the altars of soil and grain were preserved.
Precious items were scattered,
territory was ceded on all four sides,
and the state of Wèi thus declined from this point on.
A仲fù is a great name;
ceding territory is a great deed.
When advised, they did not listen, did not believe.
To listen and end up like this
cannot be called skillful.
To be unskillful and yet govern,
there is no greater harm to all under Heaven
— it was fortunate that only Wèi listened.
To take harming all under Heaven as a deed,
and to take governing it as a name –
is not Kuāng Zhāng's error
also acceptable?
Bái Guī had just met with Huì Zǐ.
Huì Zǐ lectured him on 'strength' (彊),
and Bái Guī had nothing to respond with.
Huì Zǐ left.
Bái Guī told others, saying:
"There was a man who had just taken a wife.
When the wife arrived,
she should have behaved with composure, demureness, and charming steps.
But the young man held a burning torch, huge in size.
The new wife said:
'The torch is huge.'
Upon entering the gate,
there was a depression in the gate.
The new wife said:
'Fill it in;
it will injure people's feet.'
This is not to say that she was an unhelpful family member,
but there was something much too excessive.
Now, Huì Zǐ's encounter with me is still new,
and his lecture to me has something much too excessive."
Huì Zǐ heard this and said:
"Not so.
The 《Shī》 says:
'Harmonious and amiable gentlemen
are the parents of the people.'
愷 means great,
悌 means senior.
If a gentleman's virtue
is both senior and great,
then he is a parent of the people.
When parents teach their children,
do they really wait a long time?
Why compare me to a new wife?
Does the 《Shī》 say,
'Harmonious and amiable new wife'?"
To criticize impurity based on impurity,
to criticize perversion based on perversion,
is for the criticizer and the criticized to be the same.
Bái Guī said:
"Huì Zǐ's encounter with me is still new,
and his lecture to me has something much too excessive."
Huì Zǐ heard this and criticized him,
thereupon thinking of himself as the parent to him.
His own error was also much more excessive than Bái Guī's.
18.7 《Yìng Yán》
Seventh:
Bái Guī said to King Wèi:
"If you use the cauldron from Shìqiū to cook a chicken,
if you add too much seasoning, it will be bland and inedible;
if you add too little, it will be burnt and uncooked.
Yet, when you look at it, it is elegantly beautiful, but utterly useless.
Huì Zǐ's words
are similar to this."
Huì Zǐ heard this and said:
"Not so.
If the three armies were starving and gathered around the cauldron,
and it was just the right size for a steamer,
then no other cauldron would be more suitable than this one."
Bái Guī heard this and said:
"The useless thing –
could it be that it merely adds its steamer?"
Bái Guī's argument contradicts itself,
and he diminishes King Wèi excessively.
To call Huì Zǐ's words elegantly beautiful but utterly useless
is to say that King Wèi considers someone whose words are useless to be a Zhòngfù,
