and thus considers useless words to be beautiful.
Gōngsūn Lóng advised King Zhāo of Yān on ceasing military action.
King Zhāo said:
"Excellent!
I wish to discuss this with you, sir."
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
"I secretly believe Your Majesty will not do it."
The King said: "Why?"
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
"Previously, Your Majesty wished to defeat Qí.
All the scholars under Heaven
who wished to defeat Qí,
Your Majesty fully supported them.
Those who understood Qí's dangers, obstacles, key passes, and the relations between its lord and ministers,
Your Majesty fully supported them.
Even those who understood but did not wish to defeat Qí,
Your Majesty still did not support them.
In the end, Qí was indeed defeated, and that was considered a功.
Now Your Majesty says, 'I greatly favor ceasing military action.'
All the scholars of the feudal lords
who are present in Your Majesty's court
are all skilled in the use of arms.
Therefore, I know Your Majesty will not do it."
The King had nothing to respond with.
Sīmǎ Xǐ challenged the Mohist Master before King Zhōngshān on the principle of 'non-aggression' (fēi gōng),
saying:
"Does the doctrine you, Master, teach advocate non-aggression?"
The Mohist Master said:
"Yes."
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
"Now, if the King raises an army to attack Yān,
will you, Master, disapprove of the King?"
The Mohist Master replied:
"Then will the Prime Minister approve of the attack?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
"Yes."
The Mohist Master said:
"Now, if Zhào raises an army to attack Zhōngshān,
will the Prime Minister approve of it?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ had nothing to respond with.
Lù Yuè said to Zhōu Pō:
"If you do not cherish Zhào,
all under Heaven will surely follow."
Zhōu Pō said:
"I indeed desire all under Heaven to follow.
If all under Heaven follows, then Qín benefits."
Lù Yuè responded:
"Then do you desire Qín to benefit?"
Zhōu Pō said:
"I do."
Lù Yuè said:
"If you desire it,
then why do you not follow?"
The Wèi commissioner Mèng Áng ceded the territories of Jiàng, Jì, and Ānyì to King Qín.
The King was pleased
and ordered Qǐ Jiǎ to request the position of Sītú for Mèng Áng from King Wèi.
King Wèi was displeased
and replied to Qǐ Jiǎ:
"Áng is my minister.
I would rather appoint Zāng as Sītú
than use Áng.
I wish Your Majesty would instruct me with another person instead."
Qǐ Jiǎ left
and met Mèng Áng in the court,
saying:
"How went your business, sir?"
Qǐ Jiǎ said:
"You are greatly scorned by your lord.
Your lord said:
'I would rather appoint Zāng as Sītú
than use you.'"
Mèng Áng entered to see the King
and said to King Wèi:
"What did the Qín envoy say?"
The King said:
"He requested you to be Sītú."
Mèng Áng said:
"How did Your Majesty respond?"
The King said:
"I would rather use Zāng
than use Áng."
Mèng Áng sighed deeply and said:
"It is fitting that Your Majesty is controlled by Qín.
Why does Your Majesty doubt Qín's good minister?
If Jiàng, Jì, and Ānyì were given to Qín by an ox carrying a letter,
even that ox would be considered good.
Although I am unworthy,
am I not even as good as an ox?
Moreover, Your Majesty ordered the three generals to first tell me, 'Treat Áng as yourself,'
which shows respect for your minister.
You ordered two minor ministers,
and ordered your minister to be responsible;
even if Áng were worthy, could he truly accomplish it?"
Three days later,
King Wèi finally listened to Qǐ Jiǎ.
Whenever a lord confers a high office upon his great official,
it is for the sake of benefit.
Now, the country's territories have been ceded by an inch and a pound,
and consequently a high office is obtained.
Furthermore, what land is there to provide it with?
High office is what human subjects desire.
Mèng Yǎng let Qín get what it wanted,
and Qín in turn let Mèng Yǎng get what it wanted.
If the debt has been repaid,
what more debt is there?
Even if Wèi were strong, it could not demand the undemanded,
much less when it is weak?
For the King of Wèi to appoint Mèng Yǎng as Sìtú
in order to abandon his debt would be foolish.
When the King of Qín was establishing the emperor,
Xǔ Wǎn, the magistrate of Yíyáng, deceived the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi was about to enter Qín.
Wèi Jìng said to the King:
"Which is more important, Hénèi or Liáng?"
The King said:
"Liáng is more important."
Then he asked:
"Which is more important, Liáng or your own person?"
The King said:
"My person is more important."
Then he asked:
"If Qín seeks Hénèi,
will Your Majesty grant it?"
The King said:
"I will not grant it."
Wèi Jìng said:
"Hénèi is among the lesser three considerations,
your person is among the greater three considerations.
Qín seeks the lesser, and Your Majesty does not listen;
it seeks the greater, and Your Majesty listens to it.
I secretly find this unacceptable for Your Majesty."
The King said:
"That is very true."
Thereupon, he halted his journey.
Although Qín had a great victory at Chángpíng,
it took three years to resolve,
the soldiers and people were weary,
and provisions were scarce.
At this time,
the two Zhōus were intact,
and their northern parts survived.
Wèi took Táo and encroached upon Wèi,
gaining six hundred *lǐ* of territory.
With this power,
yet to enter too early,
why wait for Wèi Jìng's persuasion?
If one enters when it is not yet possible to enter,
the trouble is that there will be a time when it *is* possible to enter, and one does;
the trouble is that there will be a time when it *is* possible to enter, and one does not.
The timing of entering and not entering
must be thoroughly considered.
18.8 《Jùbèi》
Eighth says:
Suppose there are Yì and Féngméng, and the bow Fánruò here,
but without a string,
then it certainly cannot hit the target.
Hitting is not solely due to the string,
but the string is the means for the bow to hit.
Indeed, establishing merit and fame also requires means;
if one does not obtain the means,
even if one's virtue surpasses Tāng and Wǔ,
one will toil without achievement.
Tāng was once restricted at Yìbó,
King Wǔ was once in distress at Bìchéng,
Yī Yǐn was once confined to the kitchen,
Tàigōng once lived in seclusion by fishing.
Their virtue was not diminished,
their wisdom was not foolish,
they simply lacked the means.
Therefore, in all cases of establishing merit and fame,
even the virtuous must have their means before they can succeed.
Mì Zǐjiàn governed Dànfù,
fearing that the ruler of Lǔ would listen to slanderers
and prevent him from carrying out his methods.
When about to take his leave and depart,
he requested two close officials from the ruler of Lǔ
to accompany him to Dànfù.
When the district officials all came to court,
Mì Zǐjiàn ordered the two officials to write.
As the officials were about to write,
Mì Zǐjiàn from the side would periodically twitch and shake their elbows.
If the officials wrote poorly,
Mì Zǐjiàn would become angry with them.
The officials were greatly troubled by this,
and resigned, requesting to return.
Mì Zǐjiàn said:
"Your writing is very poor,
you may go home."
The two officials returned and reported to their lord,
saying:
"It is impossible to write for Mìzǐ."
The lord said:
"Why?"
The officials replied:
"Mìzǐ made us write,
and constantly twitched and shook our elbows.
When our writing was bad, he became very angry.
All the officials laughed at Mìzǐ,
this is why we resigned and left."
The ruler of Lǔ sighed deeply and exclaimed:
"Mìzǐ uses this to admonish my unworthiness.
My interference with Mìzǐ,
preventing him from carrying out his methods,
must have happened many times.
If not for these two men,
I would have almost erred."
He then dispatched his beloved official
to Dànfù,
and told Mìzǐ:
"From now on,
Dànfù is no longer mine,
it is yours.
Whatever is beneficial for Dànfù,
you are to decide and do it.
Report its essentials in five years."
Mìzǐ respectfully assented,
and thus was able to implement his methods in Dànfù.
Three years later,
Wūmǎ Qí, wearing short coarse clothes and a tattered fur robe,
went to observe the transformation in Dànfù.
He saw a night fisherman,
who, upon catching fish, would release them.
Wūmǎ Qí asked him,
saying:
"Fishermen fish to catch.
Now you catch and release them,
why is that?"
He replied:
"Mìzǐ does not want people to take small fish.
Those I release are small fish,
that is why I release them."
Wūmǎ Qí returned and told Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Mìzǐ's virtue is profound!
He makes the common people act in the dark
as if there were severe punishment nearby.
May I ask how Mìzǐ achieved this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I once told him:
'What is sincere here will be effective there.'
Mìzǐ must have applied this method in Dànfù."
Mìzǐ was able to implement this method
because the ruler of Lǔ understood it later.
The ruler of Lǔ understood it later
because Mìzǐ had prepared for it beforehand.
Having prepared for it beforehand,
was it necessarily sudden?
This was the wisdom of the ruler of Lǔ.
A three-month-old infant,
with splendid carriages and caps before it,
does not know to desire them;
with axes and battle-axes behind it,
does not know to fear them.
The love of a tender mother instructs it,
it is sincerity.
Therefore, sincerity with sincerity accords with emotion,
and essence with essence penetrates Heaven.
When it penetrates Heaven,
the natures of water, wood, and stone
can all be moved,
much less those with blood and *qì*?
Therefore, among all efforts in persuasion and governance, nothing is better than sincerity.
Hearing words of sorrow
is not as good as seeing one cry;
hearing words of anger
is not as good as seeing one fight.
If persuasion and governance are not sincere,
their power to move people's hearts is not divine.
19.1 《Lí Sú》
First says:
What the world lacks
is principle and righteousness;
what it has in excess
is recklessness and carelessness.
The nature of people
is to value what is lacking
and despise what is in excess.
Therefore, the conduct of a commoner official,
pure, upright, clean, and adhering to rules,
the poorer he gets, the more honored he becomes.
Even if he dies,
the world will hold him in higher esteem,
for he is what is lacking.
However, if one applies principle and righteousness to criticize,
even Shénnóng and Huángdì
still have aspects that can be criticized,
not to mention Shùn and Tāng.
Fēitù and Yāonìao,
ancient swift horses,
still had their shortcomings in ability.
Therefore, if one takes wood according to the carpenter's line,
then a palace cannot be completed.
Shùn ēn offered his throne to his friend Shíhù zhī Nóng.
Shíhù zhī Nóng said:
“The Lord is so gentle in his conduct,
a man of profound strength.”
He considered Shùn’s virtue to be insufficient,
so he and his wife,
carrying their child, went into the sea,
and never returned for the rest of their lives.
Shùn also offered his throne to his friend Běirén Wúzè.
Běirén Wúzè said:
“How strange is the Lord’s conduct!
He lived among the fields,
yet gained entrance to Yáo’s court.
Not only that,
he now wishes to defile me with his disgraceful acts.
I am ashamed of him.”
And he threw himself into the abyss of Cānglǐng.
Tāng was about to attack Jié,
and sought counsel from Biàn Suí.
Biàn Suí declined, saying:
“This is not my business.”
Tāng asked:
“Who then is suitable?”
Biàn Suí replied:
“I do not know.”
Tāng then sought counsel from Wù Guāng.
Wù Guāng said:
“This is not my business.”
Tāng asked:
“Who then is suitable?”
Wù Guāng replied:
“I do not know.”
Tāng asked:
“What about Yī Yǐn?”
Wù Guāng said:
“He is strong and capable of enduring reproaches.
I know nothing else about him.”
Tāng then consulted with Yī Yǐn about attacking Jié of Xià,
and vanquished him.
He then offered the throne to Biàn Suí.
Biàn Suí declined, saying:
“The Lord attacked Jié,
and consulted me,
surely thinking me a scoundrel.
Now he has vanquished Jié and offers the throne to me,
surely thinking me greedy.
I live in a chaotic age,
and this unprincipled man has come to reproach me again.
I cannot bear to hear of it repeatedly.”
He then threw himself into the Yǐngshǔi River and died.
Tāng also offered the throne to Wù Guāng, saying:
“The wise plan,
the brave execute,
the benevolent reside over the realm –
this is the ancient way.
Why does my lord not take this position?
Please let me serve my lord.”
Wù Guāng declined, saying:
“To depose a sovereign
is not righteous.
To kill people
is not benevolent.
For others to undertake the difficulty,
while I enjoy the benefits,
is not integrity.
I have heard:
‘If it is not righteous,
do not accept its benefits;
in a world without the Way,
do not tread its land.’
How much less so when it is offered to me with honor?
I cannot bear to see this for long.”
He then carried a stone and sank into the Mùshǔi River.
Therefore, men like Shíhù zhī Nóng,
Běirén Wúzè,
Biàn Suí, and Wù Guāng,
regarded the world as beyond the six directions,
something unknowable to others.
As for nobility and wealth,
if they could possibly avoid it,
they would certainly not rely on it.
With lofty principles and severe conduct,
they found joy in their own convictions,
and nothing could harm them.
They were not swayed by profit,
nor bound by office,
and were ashamed to dwell in a corrupt world.
These are the principles of these four gentlemen.
As for Shùn and Tāng,
they concealed and accommodated,
acting only out of necessity,
adapting to the times,
taking love and benefit as their foundation,
and the myriad people as their righteousness.
They are like a fisherman:
fish vary in size,
bait must be appropriate,
and feathers (on the line) have movements and stillness.
Qí and Jìn were at war.
A soldier from Píng’ā, having lost his halberd, obtained a spear.
He turned and left,
but was not pleased with himself.
He asked a passerby:
“Having lost a halberd and gained a spear,
may I return home?”
The passerby said:
“A halberd is a weapon,
a spear is also a weapon.
Having lost one weapon and gained another,
why can you not return home?”
He continued on,
still not pleased with himself.
He met Gāotáng zhī Gū Shú Wúsūn,
who stood before his horse and said:
“In today’s battle,
I lost a halberd and gained a spear.
May I return home?”
Shú Wúsūn said:
“A spear is not a halberd,
a halberd is not a spear.
Having lost a halberd and gained a spear,
how can this be considered a fair exchange?”
The soldier from Píng’ā said:
“Ah!
I must turn back and fight again,
and rush to catch up.”
He then fought and died.
Shú Wúsūn said:
“I have heard:
‘A noble person who saves others from distress
must share their difficulty.’”
He galloped quickly to follow him,
and also died without returning.
If this man were to lead an army,
he would certainly not retreat.
If this man were to stand beside a ruler,
he would certainly die for righteousness.
Now he is dead without great accomplishment;
his responsibility was minor.
Those with minor responsibilities
do not understand great matters.
How do we know there are no such men as the Píng’ā soldier and Shú Wúsūn in the world today?
Therefore, a ruler who desires to obtain men of integrity
must diligently seek them out.
During the time of Qí Zhuāng Gōng,
there was a gentleman named Bīn Bēijù.
He dreamed of a strong man
wearing a white silk headband,
a red brocade skirt,
a tunic of eastern cloth,
new white slippers,
and a black sword scabbard.
The man followed him and shouted at him,
and spat on his face.
He awoke with a start,
it was only a dream.
He sat up all night, displeased with himself.
The next day, he summoned his friends and told them:
“I have loved bravery since youth,
and at sixty years old, I have never been humiliated.
Last night I was humiliated.
I will seek out this figure;
if I find him, good,
if not, I shall die.”
Every morning, he and his friends stood together at the crossroads.
After three days, he did not find him,
so he retreated and took his own life.
To say this man truly understood his duty is not yet true.
However,
his heart’s unwillingness to be humiliated
is something that can be admired.
19.2 “Exalted Righteousness”
Second:
A noble person’s conduct,
when moving, must follow righteousness;
when acting, must truly embody righteousness.
Even if the world calls it failure,
it is success.
If conduct does not truly embody righteousness,
and actions do not follow righteousness,
even if the world calls it success,
it is failure.
Thus, the success or failure of a noble person
is different from that of the common world.
Therefore, one should receive rewards for merits,
and punishment for crimes.
If a reward is not due,
even if given, one must decline it.
If a punishment is truly due,
even if pardoned, one will not avoid it.
When considered in relation to the state,
it must be beneficial for the long term.
For the long-term benefit of the ruler,
it must be appropriate internally and not cause shame in one’s heart before acting.
Kǒngzǐ met with Qí Jǐnggōng.
Jǐnggōng offered Lǐnqiu as sustenance.
Kǒngzǐ declined and did not accept.
He went out and said to his disciples:
“I have heard that a gentleman receives emolument based on merit.
Now I have advised Jǐnggōng,
but Jǐnggōng has not yet acted on it, and he has already bestowed Lǐnqiu upon me.
His not understanding Qiū is indeed profound.”
He ordered his disciples to prepare the carriage quickly,
declined the offer, and departed.
Kǒngzǐ was a commoner,
yet his official position as Sīkòu in Lǔ
meant that a state of ten thousand chariots would find it difficult to equal his conduct;
the advisors of the Three Kings did not manifest such distinction.
His choices to accept or reject were not made casually!
Zǐ Mòzǐ traveled with Gōngshàng Guò in Yuè.
Gōngshàng Guò spoke of Mòzǐ's righteousness,
and the King of Yuè was pleased.
He said to Gōngshàng Guò:
“If your teacher would only consent to come to Yuè,
I ask to grant him the former lands of Wú,
the shores of Yinjiāng,
and three hundred households,
to enfeoff the Master.”
Gōngshàng Guò returned to Zǐ Mòzǐ.
Zǐ Mòzǐ said:
“From your observation of the King of Yuè,
can he listen to my words and employ my Way?”
Gōngshàng Guò said:
“He probably cannot.”
Mòzǐ said:
“Not only does the King of Yuè not understand Zhái’s intention,
but even you do not understand Zhái’s intention.
If the King of Yuè were to listen to my words and employ my Way,
Zhái would tailor his clothes to his body,
and measure his food to his stomach.
Compared to a guest or a refugee,
I would not dare to seek office.
If the King of Yuè does not listen to my words and does not employ my Way,
even if he were to give me the whole of Yuè,
I would have no use for it.
If the King of Yuè does not listen to my words and does not employ my Way,
and I accept his state,
this would be selling righteousness.
Why must I sell righteousness to Yuè?
Even in the Central States, it would be possible.”
One must not fail to scrutinize all people.
The country folk of Qín,
for the sake of small gains,
imprison their brothers,
and turn a blind eye to their relatives;
now, to be able to obtain a state,
yet fear diminishing one's righteousness and decline it—
this can be called being able to uphold one's conduct;
how far indeed he is from the country folk of Qín!
The people of Jīng and the people of Wú were about to do battle.
The Jīng army was few,
the Wú army was numerous.
The Jīng general Zǐnáng said:
“If I fight the people of Wú,
I will surely be defeated.
To defeat the king's army,
disgrace the king's name,
and diminish the territory—
a loyal minister cannot bear to do such things.”
He did not report back to the king but fled.
When he reached the outskirts,
he sent someone to report to the king, saying:
“Your minister requests to die.”
The king said:
“The general's flight
was for its benefit.
If it was truly beneficial,
why should the general die?”
Zǐnáng said:
“If those who flee are without fault,
then future ministers of the king
will all use the name of 'disadvantage' and imitate your minister's flight.
If this happens, the state of Jīng will ultimately be ruined by the world.”
Thereupon, he fell on his sword and died.
The king said:
“I accept the general's righteousness.”
So, he had a three-inch catalpa coffin made for him,
and placed an axe and a chopping block on it to display throughout the state.
The peril of a ruler
is to exist but not know why they exist,
and to perish but not know why they perish.
This is why existence and perishing frequently occur.
The vastness of É and Qí,
and the obedience of all states,
arose from this.
Jīng has been Jīng for forty-two generations.
It has experienced the chaos of Gānqī and Bái Gōng, and the refuge of Zhèng Xiùzhōuhóu,
yet today it is still a great state of ten thousand chariots.
Did it have ministers like Zǐnáng during those times?
Zǐnáng’s integrity
did not merely inspire the ministers of one generation.
During the time of Jīng Zhāowáng,
there was a scholar
named Shí Zhǔ.
He was a man
public-spirited, upright, and selfless.
The king appointed him to govern.
At that time, there was a murderer in the court.
Shí Zhǔ pursued him,
and it turned out to be his father.
He turned his carriage back and returned,
standing in the court and saying:
“The murderer
is my father.
To execute the law on my father
I cannot bear;
to cover up a crime
and abandon the state's law
is unacceptable.
To violate the law and submit to punishment
is the righteousness of a minister.”
Thereupon he laid himself on the axe and chopping block,
requesting to die before the king.
The king said:
“You pursued him but did not catch him,
why must you submit to punishment?
You should resume your duties.”
Shí Zhǔ declined, saying:
“Not to be partial to one's parent
cannot be called a filial son.
To serve the ruler by bending the law
cannot be called a loyal minister.
The king’s order to pardon
is the benevolence of the superior.
Not daring to abandon the law
is the conduct of a minister.”
He did not move from the axe and chopping block,
and died with his head upon them in the king’s court.
To uphold the law, one who bends it must die.
His father broke the law and he could not bear it,
the king pardoned him and he would not accept it.
Shí Zhǔ, as a minister,
can be called both loyal and filial.
19.3 《Shàng Dé》
Thirdly:
For the world and the state,
nothing is better than to use virtue,
nothing is better than to practice righteousness.
With virtue and righteousness,
the people are encouraged without reward,
and evil ceases without punishment.
This was the governance of Shénnóng and Huángdì.
With virtue and righteousness,
the vastness of the Four Seas,
the waters of the Jiāng and Hé,
cannot obstruct;
the height of Tàihuá,
the perilousness of Kuàijī,
cannot hinder;
the teachings of Hélǘ,
the armies of Sūn and Wú,
cannot withstand.
Thus, the ancient kings,
their virtue pervaded heaven and earth,
and spread serenely throughout the Four Seas,
east, west, south, north,
reaching as far as the sun and moon shine.
Heaven covered, earth supported,
love and hate were not concealed.
With emptiness and purity, they were impartial.
The common people all knew what they were doing but did not know how it came about.
This is called complying with Heaven.
They changed customs and altered traditions, yet no one knew from whom they received it.
This is called complying with human nature.
Therefore, the ancients,
their persons were obscure but their achievements were manifest,
their forms ceased but their names shone,
their teachings spread and transformations flourished,
benefits circulated throughout the world but the people were unaware.
Must they necessarily rely on severe punishments and generous rewards?
Severe punishments and generous rewards—
this is the governance of a decadent age.
The Sānmiáo did not submit.
Yǔ requested to attack them.
Shùn said:
“Virtue will suffice.”
He practiced virtue for three years,
and the Sānmiáo submitted.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it and said:
“If one comprehends the essence of virtue,
then Mèngmén and Tàiháng are not considered perilous.
Thus it is said, the speed of virtue
is swifter than transmitting commands by post.”
At the Zhōu Míngtáng,
metal was placed behind it,
which serves to show precedence of virtue over military might.
Was Shùn perhaps like this?
His virtue was as encompassing as that of Zhōu.
Jìn Xiàngōng, for Lìjī, alienated the crown prince.
Crown Prince Shēnshēng resided in Qǔwò,
Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr resided in Pú,
and Gōngzǐ Yíwú resided in Qū.
Lìjī said to the crown prince:
"Formerly, the lord dreamt of Jiāngshì."
The crown prince performed a sacrifice and presented a meal to the duke.
Lìjī tampered with it.
When the duke was about to taste the meal,
Lìjī said:
"It came from afar,
please have someone taste it first."
The taster died,
the food given to a dog caused the dog to die.
Therefore, the crown prince was executed.
The crown prince refused to exonerate himself,
saying:
"If the lord does not have Lìjī,
he will not rest peacefully,
nor eat with pleasure."
He then died by the sword.
Gōngzǐ Yíwú fled from Qū to Liáng.
Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr fled from Pú to Zhái.
Leaving Zhái, he passed through Wèi,
but Wèi Wéngōng treated him discourteously.
Passing through Wǔlù, he went to Qí,
but Qí Huángōng had died.
Leaving Qí, he went to Cáo,
Cáo Gònggōng observed his fused ribs,
and made him bare his torso to catch fish in a pond.
Leaving Cáo, he passed through Sòng,
Sòng Xiānggōng treated him with great courtesy.
He went to Zhèng,
Zhèng Wéngōng showed no respect.
Pī Zhān remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard that a wise ruler does not push the desperate to their limits.
Now, among the followers of the Jìn公子,
all are worthy men.
If Your Highness does not treat them with courtesy,
it would be better to kill them."
The lord of Zhèng did not listen.
Leaving Zhèng, he went to Jīng,
but Jīng Chéngwáng treated him with disdain.
Leaving Jīng, he went to Qín,
Qín Mùgōng welcomed him.
Once Jìn was settled,
it raised an army to attack Zhèng,
seeking Pī Zhān.
Pī Zhān said to the lord of Zhèng:
"It would be better to give your servant to them."
The lord of Zhèng said:
"This is my fault."
Pī Zhān said:
"To sacrifice your servant to save the state,
your servant wishes for it."
Pī Zhān entered the Jìn army,
Wéngōng was about to boil him.
Pī Zhān stood on the cauldron and cried out:
"All the soldiers of the three armies, listen to Zhān!
From now on,
let no one be loyal to their lord,
for those loyal to their lord will be boiled!"
Wéngōng apologized,
dismissed the army,
and sent him back to Zhèng.
Furthermore, Pī Zhān was loyal to his lord, and his lord was spared from the Jìn calamity;
he acted righteously in Zhèng, and was admired by Wéngōng.
Thus, the benefit of righteousness is extensive.
Mòzhe Jùzǐ Mèng Shèng
was on good terms with Yángchéng Jūn of Jīng.
Yángchéng Jūn ordered him to guard the state,
broke a jade *huáng* to make a tally,
and agreed, saying:
"If the tally matches, listen."
When the king of Jīng died,
the officials attacked Wú Qǐ,
fighting at the mourning place.
Yángchéng Jūn was involved in this,
and Jīng condemned him.
Yángchéng Jūn fled,
and Jīng confiscated his state.
Mèng Shèng said:
"I received a state from a person,
and was given a tally.
Now, I do not present the tally,
and am powerless to stop it;
yet I am unable to die—
this is unacceptable."
His disciple Xú Ruò admonished Mèng Shèng, saying:
"If dying benefits Yángchéng Jūn,
then dying is acceptable.
But if it is of no benefit,
and extinguishes the Mòzhě from the world,
then it is unacceptable."
Mèng Shèng said:
"Not so.
As for my relationship with Yángchéng Jūn,
if not a teacher, then a friend;
if not a friend, then a minister.
If I do not die,
from now on,
those seeking a strict teacher will certainly not seek among the Mòzhě;
those seeking a worthy friend will certainly not seek among the Mòzhě;
those seeking a good minister will certainly not seek among the Mòzhě.
My death is to uphold the righteousness of the Mòzhě and continue their legacy.
I will entrust the Jùzǐ position to Tián Xiāngzǐ of Sòng.
Tián Xiāngzǐ is a worthy man,
what need to worry about the Mòzhě being extinguished from the world?"
Xú Ruò said:
"If that is what our Master says,
then your servant requests to die first to clear the way."
He then struck his head forward and died.
Mèng Shèng then sent two men to convey the Jùzǐ position to Tián Xiāngzǐ.
Mèng Shèng died,
and one hundred and eighty disciples died with him.
The three men, having delivered the message to Tián Xiāngzǐ,
wished to return and die for Mèng Shèng in Jīng.
Tián Xiāngzǐ stopped them, saying:
"Mèngzǐ has already transmitted the Jùzǐ position to me;
you should obey."
Thereupon, they returned and died.
The Mòzhě considered it disrespectful to the Jùzǐ not to inquire.
Strict punishments and generous rewards
are insufficient to achieve this.
The present generation's discussions of governance
mostly rely on strict punishments and generous rewards,
which are like the temporary guests of ancient times.
19.4 "Employing the People"
Fourth:
In all cases of employing the people,
the supreme method is by righteousness;
next is by rewards and punishments.
If their righteousness is not worth dying for,
and rewards and punishments are not worth leaving or staying for,
yet one can still employ their people,
then such a case has never existed, ancient or modern.
People are not constantly useful,
nor are they constantly useless;
only by obtaining the right way can they be employed.
Hélú's army did not exceed thirty thousand,
Wú Qǐ's army did not exceed fifty thousand.
For a state of ten thousand chariots,
three to five thousand is still a large number.
Now, externally, it cannot repel enemies;
internally, it cannot defend the state.
It is not that the people cannot be employed,
but that the method of employing them has not been found.
If the method of employing them is not found,
though the state be large,
though its position be advantageous,
though its troops be numerous,
what benefit is there?
In ancient times, many possessed all under Heaven and perished,
because their people were not employed.
The discourse on employing the people
must be thoroughly understood.
A sword does not cut by itself,
a carriage does not move by itself;
someone makes them do it.
Indeed, if one plants wheat and gets wheat,
or plants millet and gets millet,
people are not surprised.
Employing the people also has its seeds;
if one does not examine its seeds,
and yet prays for the people to be useful,
there is no greater confusion.
In Yǔ's time,
there were ten thousand states under Heaven;
by Tāng's time, over three thousand states;
now none remain.
All were unable to employ their people.
The reason the people were not employed
was that rewards and punishments were insufficient.
Tāng and Wǔ relied on the people of Xià and Shāng,
and found the way to employ them.
Guǎn and Shāng also relied on the people of Qí and Qín,
and found the way to employ them.
There is a reason why people are employed;
if one understands that reason,
there are no people who cannot be employed.
Employing the people has its main threads and its guiding principles;
pull one of its main threads,
and all the strands will rise;
pull one of its guiding principles,
and all the meshes will spread.
What are the main threads and guiding principles for the people?
Desire and aversion.
What is desired? What is abhorred?
Desiring glory and gain,
abhorring disgrace and harm.
Disgrace and harm are the means by which punishments are fulfilled,
glory and gain are the means by which rewards are actualized.
If both rewards and punishments are fulfilled and actualized,
then the people will not fail to be utilized.
Hé Lǘ tested his people at Wǔhú.
Swords were all placed on shoulders,
blood flowed onto the ground almost unstoppably.
Gōujiàn tested his people in his sleeping palace.
The people vied to enter water and fire,
over a thousand died.
He hastily struck a gong to call them back.
Rewards and punishments were fulfilled.
Mòyé does not act for the brave nor change for the timid.
The brave use it skillfully,
the timid use it clumsily.
This is the difference between capability and incapability.
The people of Sùshā
attacked their own lord
and submitted to Shénnóng.
The people of Mìxū
bound their own ruler
and offered him to Wén Wáng.
Tāng and Wǔ not only could employ their own people,
but also could employ people who were not their own.
If one can employ people who are not their own,
though the state be small
and the troops few,
achievements and fame can still be established.
In ancient times, many commoners established a generation's order,
all by being able to employ what was not their own.
The heart that employs what is not its own
is a fundamental principle that cannot be overlooked.
The Way of the Three Dynasties is not twofold:
it takes trustworthiness as its guiding principle.
A man from Sòng was driving on the road.
His horse would not advance.
He beheaded it and threw it into the Xīshuǐ.
He then got another horse to drive. It would not advance.
He again beheaded it and threw it into the Xīshuǐ.
He did this three times.
Even Zàofù's method of aweing horses
would not exceed this.
Yet, without obtaining Zàofù's Way,
and merely obtaining his awe,
it is useless for driving.
An unworthy ruler
is similar to this.
Without obtaining the Way,
they merely multiply their awe.
The more awe,
the less the people are utilized.
Rulers of fallen states
often used excessive awe to command their people.
Therefore, awe is indispensable,
but it should not be solely relied upon.
It is like salt in flavoring.
The use of all salt
has something it depends on.
If it is not suitable, it spoils what it depends on and becomes inedible.
Awe is also like this;
it must have something it depends on
before it can be effective.
What does it depend on?
It depends on love and benefit.
When the principle of love and benefit is clear,
awe can then be effective.
If awe is too great, the principle of love and benefit ceases.
If the principle of love and benefit ceases and one merely pushes awe,
the person will certainly suffer calamity.
This is why Yīn and Xià were cut off.
The ruler, profit, and power are primary; the secondary official is next.
When in a secondary official position,
wielding profit and power,
one must not fail to scrutinize this.
Indeed, those who forbid without forbidding—
surely only those who deeply understand this principle can do so.
19.5 "Shì Wēi"
Fifthly:
The ancient kings, when employing their people,
were like driving good horses:
lightly loaded with new reins.
Wishing to run, but unable to,
thus reaching a thousand *lǐ*.
Those skilled at employing their people are also like this.
The people pray day and night to be used, but cannot get it.
If they are fortunate enough to be used by the superior,
the people will rush forward
like accumulated water bursting forth from a thousand-fathom ravine—
who could stop it?
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
"If the people are treated well, they are like livestock;
if not well, they are enemies."
To have many enemies
is worse than having none.
Lì Wáng was the Son of Heaven,
but had many enemies,
so he was exiled to Zhì,
and calamity reached his descendants.
Were it not for Zhào Gōng Hǔ, his lineage would have been cut off without heirs.
The rulers of today
mostly wish to have many people,
but do not know how to treat them well.
This is multiplying their enemies.
If not treated well, then they are not truly "had."
To "have" necessarily means to cherish them in one's heart.
Possessing their physical form cannot be called "having" them.
Shùn was a commoner yet possessed the world.
Jié was the Son of Heaven,
yet could not rest.
This is where it arises from.
The discussion of "having" and "not having"
must be thoroughly understood.
Tāng and Wǔ understood this principle,
thus their achievements and fame were established.
Ancient rulers of the people
governed them with benevolence and righteousness,
secured them with love and benefit,
and guided them with loyalty and trustworthiness.
They strove to remove their calamities,
and contemplated bringing them blessings.
Therefore, the people's relationship with their superiors
was like clay to a seal:
pressed with a square, it becomes square;
pressed with a circle, it becomes circular.
It was like the five grains to the earth:
they must respond according to their kind,
and multiply a hundredfold.
This is why the Five Emperors and Three Kings were unrivaled.
Their bodies had already passed,
yet later generations were transformed by them as if by spirits.
Their human endeavors were indeed profound.
When Wèi Wǔhóu resided in Zhōngshān,
he asked Lǐ Kè:
"Why did Wú perish?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Frequent battles and frequent victories."
Wǔhóu said:
"Frequent battles and frequent victories are
the fortune of the state.
Why did it alone perish
for this reason?"
He replied:
"Frequent battles exhaust the people,
frequent victories make the ruler arrogant.
If an arrogant ruler employs exhausted people,
there are few states in the world
that would not perish.
Arrogance leads to indulgence,
indulgence leads to exhausting things.
Exhaustion leads to resentment,
resentment leads to extreme deliberation.
When both superior and inferior are exhausted,
Wú's demise was still late.
This is why Fūchā buried himself at Gānsuì."
Dōngyě Jì was presented to Zhuāng Gōng for his charioteering skills.
His advances and retreats were perfectly aligned with the rope,
his turns left and right perfectly aligned with the compass.
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"Excellent!"
He believed that Zàofù could not surpass him,
and ordered him to make a hundred turns, but he fell short.
Yán Hé met him
and entered to see the Duke.
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"Did you meet Dōngyě Jì?"
He replied:
"Yes,
I met him.
His horses will certainly fail."
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"How will they fail?"
A moment later,
Dōngyě Jì's horses failed and returned.
Zhuāng Gōng summoned Yán Hé and asked him:
"How did you know they would fail?"
Yán Hé replied:
"His advances and retreats were perfectly aligned with the rope,
his turns left and right perfectly aligned with the compass.
Zàofù's charioteering
could not surpass him.
However, when I met him just now,
his horses' strength was already exhausted,
yet he was still pushing his horses.
This is how I knew they would fail."
Thus, when a disordered state employs its people,
it disregards human nature,
and does not reflect on human emotions.
It vexatiously issues teachings, but faults are not recognized.
It frequently issues commands, but wrongs are not followed.
When great dangers arise, people dare not commit crimes.
When heavy burdens are assigned, punishments are unbearable.
If the people advance, they desire rewards;
if they retreat, they fear punishment.
When they realize their abilities are insufficient,
they resort to deceit.
If they resort to deceit,
the ruler then punishes them again.
This is to invite punishment with punishment,
and the mutual enmity between superiors and subordinates
arises from this.
Therefore, if rituals are vexatious, there is no solemnity.
If tasks are vexatious and numerous, there is no achievement.
If commands are harsh, they are not heeded.
If prohibitions are many, they are not enforced.
The prohibitions of Jié and Zhòu
were countless,
thus the people were executed for them.
This was extreme,
unable to effectively use power.
Zǐyáng (子陽) was extremely fond of strictness.
A man who broke his bow by accident
feared certain death,
and so, like a rabid dog, he assassinated Zǐyáng (子陽). This was extreme.
There was a bronze tripod of Zhōu (周) with a winding pattern,
its shape very long,
curved both above and below,
indicating the failure of extremes.
19.6 On Desires
Six:
If the people have no desires,
even if the ruler is worthy, he cannot employ them.
Indeed, for those without desires,
their view of being the Son of Heaven is the same as being a mere servant;
their view of possessing the world is the same as having no place to stand an awl;
their view of living as long as Péngzǔ (彭祖) is the same as being a child who died young.
The Son of Heaven is the most noble;
possessing the world is the greatest wealth;
Péngzǔ (彭祖) lived the longest.
If one truly has no desires, these three are not enough to motivate.
A servant is the most lowly;
having no place to stand an awl is the greatest poverty;
a child who died young is the most short-lived.
If one truly has no desires, these three are not enough to prohibit.
If there is even one desire,
then from the Great Xià (大夏) in the north,
to Běihù (北戶) in the south,
to Sānwēi (三危) in the west,
to Fúmù (扶木) in the east,
no one would dare to cause disorder;
they would brave sharp blades,
face flying arrows,
and rush into fire and water,
without daring to retreat;
they would wake early in the morning,
diligently cultivate the land with urgent labor,
and endure toil and humiliation,
without daring to rest.
Therefore, the more desires people have,
the more they can be employed;
the fewer desires people have,
the less they can be employed;
those without desires
cannot be employed at all.
Even if people have many desires,
if the ruler has no means to command them,
even if people satisfy their desires,
they still cannot be employed.
The way to enable people to satisfy their desires
must be carefully considered.
A good ruler
can enable people to satisfy infinite desires,
thus the extent to which people can be employed is also infinite.
In countries of barbarians with "reversed tongues," strange customs, and different habits,
their clothes, caps, and belts,
palaces and dwellings,
boats, carriages, and tools,
sounds, colors, and flavors are all different,
but their motivation for desire is one.
The Three Kings could not change this;
that they could not change it yet achieved success
was because they followed its natural course.
Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂) could not detach from this;
that they could not detach from it yet their states perished
was because they went against its natural course.
To go against it and not know one is going against it
is to be deeply mired in customs.
If one is deeply mired for a long time and does not depart, it becomes like nature.
That which is like nature but is not nature
must be carefully examined.
Those who have not heard the Way,
how can they remove that which is not nature?
Without means to remove that which is not nature,
desires have never been rectified.
If desires are not rectified,
using them to govern oneself leads to an early death,
and using them to govern a state leads to ruin.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings
carefully followed their natural course and acted upon desires,
then the people were all obedient,
and achievements were all established.
The sage kings upheld the One,
and the four Yi (夷) all came to them;
this is what is meant by that.
To uphold the One is to be most noble.
The most noble has no enemies.
The sage king relies on having no enemies,
thus the lives of the people are bound to the enemy.
When a pack of dogs lived together,
they were all quiet and without contention.
Throw them roasted chicken,
and they will contend with each other.
Some will break bones,
some will tear tendons;
the art of contention exists.
If the art of contention exists, it leads to contention;
if the art of non-contention exists, it leads to non-contention.
Take the art of non-contention and contend with each other,
and no state among the myriad will achieve it.
Generally, a well-governed state makes its people contend to practice righteousness;
a disordered state makes its people contend to commit unrighteousness.
A strong state makes its people contend to delight in being employed;
a weak state makes its people contend to delight in not being employed.
The difference between contending to practice righteousness and delighting in being employed versus contending to commit unrighteousness and delighting in not being employed—
this is the source of fortune and misfortune,
which Heaven cannot cover,
and Earth cannot carry.
Jìn Wéngōng (晉文公) attacked Yuán (原),
and promised his soldiers seven days.
After seven days, Yuán (原) did not fall,
so he ordered a retreat.
His advisor spoke, saying:
"Yuán (原) is about to fall."
The army officer said:
"Please wait for it."
The Duke said:
"Trustworthiness is the treasure of the state.
To gain Yuán (原) and lose treasure,
I will not do it."
So he departed.
The next year, he attacked it again,
promising his soldiers they would surely take Yuán (原) before returning.
When the people of Yuán (原) heard this, they surrendered.
When the people of Wèi (衛) heard this,
they considered Wéngōng's (文公) trustworthiness supreme,
and thus pledged allegiance to Wéngōng (文公).
Therefore, it is said that "attacking Yuán (原) gained Wèi (衛)";
this is what it refers to.
Wéngōng (文公) did not not want to gain Yuán (原);
but to gain Yuán (原) through untrustworthiness
was worse than not gaining it.
He must truly gain it through trustworthiness,
and those who returned to him were not only Wèi (衛).
Wéngōng (文公) can be said to have known how to seek desires.
19.7 Valuing Trustworthiness
Seven:
All rulers must be trustworthy.
Trustworthy again and again,
who would not be close?
Therefore, the Shū (書) of Zhōu (周) says:
"Indeed, indeed!"
This means that without trustworthiness, a hundred affairs will not be fulfilled.
Thus, the merit of trustworthiness is great.
If trustworthiness is established, even empty words can be rewarded.
If empty words can be rewarded,
then everything within the six directions will become one's own treasury.
Wherever trustworthiness reaches,
it controls everything.
To control it but not use it
is for others to possess;
to control it and use it
is for oneself to possess.
If one possesses it,
then all things in Heaven and Earth will be utilized.
If a ruler comprehends this doctrine,
his reign will not be short;
if a minister understands this doctrine,
he can serve as an assistant to a king.
If Heaven's movements are not trustworthy,
it cannot complete the year;
if Earth's movements are not trustworthy,
grass and trees will not grow large.
The virtue of spring is wind.
If the wind is not trustworthy,
its blossoms will not be luxuriant.
If the blossoms are not luxuriant, then fruits will not be produced.
The virtue of summer is heat.
If the heat is not trustworthy,
its soil will not be fertile.
If the soil is not fertile, then growth will not be vigorous.
The virtue of autumn is rain.
If the rain is not trustworthy,
its grains will not be firm.
If the grains are not firm, then the five kinds of seeds will not mature.
The virtue of winter is cold.
If the cold is not trustworthy,
its ground will not be hard.
If the ground is not hard, then freezing and sealing will not be thorough.
The vastness of Heaven and Earth,
the transformations of the four seasons—
even they cannot accomplish things without trustworthiness.
How much more so for human affairs?
If ruler and ministers are not trustworthy,
then the common people will slander,
and the altars of soil and grain will not be at peace.
If officials are not trustworthy,
then the young will not fear the old,
and the noble and humble will despise each other.
If rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
then the people will easily violate laws
and cannot be commanded.
If friends are not trustworthy in their associations,
then they will scatter with resentment,
unable to be close to each other.
If artisans are not trustworthy,
then tools and machinery will be poorly made and deceptive,
and paints, lacquers, and dyes will not be genuine.
Indeed, that which allows one to begin,
to finish,
to share honor and success,
and to share lowliness and distress—
is it not trustworthiness alone?
Trustworthiness, and then more trustworthiness,
repeatedly cultivated in one's person,
will then reach up to Heaven.
If one governs people with this,
then rich rains and sweet dew will descend,
and the cold and heat of the four seasons will be appropriate.
Qí Huán Gōng attacked Lǔ.
The people of Lǔ did not dare to fight lightly.
Qí Huán Gōng withdrew fifty *lǐ* from the state of Lǔ and offered a fief.
Lǔ requested to be treated like a noble within the passes to comply.
Huán Gōng agreed to this.
Cáo Huì said to Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng:
"Would you rather die again and again,
or would you rather live again and again?"
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"What do you mean?"
Cáo Huì said:
"If you listen to your servant's words,
your state will certainly expand and be great,
and your person will certainly be safe and joyful.
This is to live again and again.
If you do not listen to your servant's words,
your state will certainly be destroyed,
and your person will certainly be in danger and disgrace.
This is to die again and again."
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"I will follow."
So, the next day, when they were about to make an alliance,
Zhuāng Gōng and Cáo Huì both carried swords and went to the altar.
Zhuāng Gōng grabbed Huán Gōng with his left hand,
drew his sword with his right hand to hold himself up,
and said:
"The state of Lǔ is several hundred *lǐ* from its border.
Now it is fifty *lǐ* from the border,
and there is no longer any hope of survival.
If I must die,
I will be executed before your majesty."
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū advanced.
Cáo Huì pressed his sword between the two steps and said:
"Let the two lords reconsider their plans.
Let no one advance."
Zhuāng Gōng said:
"If it is enfeoffed in Wèn, then it is acceptable.
Otherwise, I request to die."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Land is used to protect the ruler, not the ruler to protect land.
Your majesty should agree to this."
So,
Lǔ was then enfeoffed south of Wèn,
and they made an alliance.
Upon returning, Huán Gōng wanted to renege.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You cannot.
If someone merely coerced you but you did not make the alliance,
and you did not realize this,
you cannot be called wise.
If, facing difficulty, you could not avoid complying,
you cannot be called brave.
If you promised but did not deliver,
you cannot be called trustworthy.
Without wisdom, without courage, and without trustworthiness,
possessing these three,
you cannot establish meritorious fame.
Give it to them.
Even if you lose land, you will gain trustworthiness.
To gain the trust of the world with four hundred *lǐ* of land,
your majesty still profits."
Zhuāng Gōng was an enemy,
and Cáo Huì was a bandit.
If one is trustworthy towards enemies and bandits,
how much more so towards those who are not enemies or bandits?
That Qí Huán Gōng was able to unite the lords nine times
and correct the world once and be obeyed—
it originated from this trustworthiness.
Guǎn Zhòng can be called skilled at adapting to circumstances.
Turning disgrace into honor,
and hardship into success;
though there was a loss in the beginning,
it can be said that he gained it in the end.
Things truly cannot be perfect.
19.8 *Jǔ Nán*
Eight:
It is indeed difficult to judge a person based on perfection,
this is the nature of things.
People criticize Yáo with the name of being unkind,
Shùn with the title of demeaning his father,
Yǔ with the intention of being greedy for his position,
Tāng and Wǔ with the plot of banishing and regicide,
and the Five Hegemons with acts of invasion and usurpation.
From this perspective,
how can anything be perfect?
Therefore, a *jūnzǐ* judges others as human,
but judges himself by righteousness.
Judging others as human makes it easy to be satisfied,
and being easily satisfied means gaining people.
Judging oneself by righteousness makes it difficult to do wrong,
and making it difficult to do wrong adorns one's conduct.
Thus, one can take on the whole world and still have plenty.
An unworthy person is not like this:
he judges others by righteousness,
but judges himself as human.
Judging others by righteousness makes it difficult to meet expectations,
and making it difficult to meet expectations means losing close relations.
Judging oneself as human makes it easy to act,
and acting easily means one's conduct is negligent.
Thus, even the vastness of the world cannot tolerate him,
he brings danger upon himself and destruction upon his state.
These are the actions of Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
A foot of wood must have knots,
an inch of jade must have flaws.
The ancient kings knew that things cannot necessarily be perfect,
thus they chose essentials and valued taking one thing.
Jì Sūn Shì coerced the ducal house.
Kǒng Zǐ wanted to explain his principles but was seen as an outsider.
So, he accepted support and spoke conveniently,
and the state of Lǔ gained wealth.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"The dragon feeds in the clear and swims in the clear.
The *chī* feeds in the clear and swims in the turbid.
Fish feed in the turbid and swim in the turbid.
Now, I, Qiū, am not as high as a dragon
nor as low as a fish;
I must be a *chī*."
Indeed, one who wishes to establish meritorious deeds,
how can he always act perfectly according to the rules?
One who saves a drowning person gets wet,
one who pursues a fugitive hurries.
Wèi Wén Hóu had a younger brother named Jì Chéng,
and a friend named Zhái Huáng.
Wén Hóu wanted to appoint one of them as prime minister but could not decide,
so he asked Lǐ Kè.
Lǐ Kè replied:
"If your majesty wishes to appoint a prime minister,
then ask whether Lè Téng or Wáng Sūn Gǒu Duān is more worthy?"
Wén Hóu said:
"Good."
Because Wáng Sūn Gǒu Duān was unworthy,
Zhái Huáng recommended him.
Because Lè Téng was worthy,
Jì Chéng recommended him.
Therefore, Jì Chéng was appointed prime minister.
Whenever one listens to a lord,
one must be cautious in speaking about people.
Jì Chéng was his younger brother,
Zhái Huáng was his friend,
yet he still could not know them.
How then could he know Lè Téng and Wáng Sūn Gǒu Duān?
The distant and humble are known,
the close and familiar are not known—
this reasoning is not naturally so.
If one judges by natural inclinations alone, then errors will occur.
Lǐ Kè's reply to Wén Hóu was also erroneous.
Although both are erroneous,
it is like comparing gold and wood;
gold, though soft, is still harder than wood.
Mèngcháng Jūn asked Bái Guī, saying:
"Wèi Wénhóu's reputation surpassed that of Huán Gōng,
yet his achievements did not equal those of the Five Hegemons. Why was this?"
Bái Guī replied:
"Wénhóu took Zǐxià as his teacher,
befriended Tián Zǐfāng,
and respected Duàn Gānmù.
This is why his reputation surpassed Huán Gōng.
When selecting a chancellor, he would ask:
'Which is preferable, Chéng or Huáng?'
This is why his achievements did not equal those of the Five Hegemons.
A chancellor
is the head of all officials.
One should choose them broadly.
Now, if one chooses but cannot exclude two individuals,
it is far from using one's enemy.
Moreover, teachers and friends
are for the public good;
relatives and loved ones
are for private comfort.
To let private interest override public interest
is the policy of a declining state.
Nevertheless, his reputation and glory were prominent
because the three scholars supported him."
Níng Qī desired to gain an audience with Qí Huán Gōng,
but was poor and had no means to present himself.
So he became a merchant, driving a cart loaded with goods, and arrived in Qí.
At dusk, he lodged outside the city gate.
Huán Gōng was going out to welcome guests,
the city gates were opened at night,
carts were moved aside,
the torches were very bright,
and the followers were very numerous.
Níng Qī, while feeding his ox beneath his cart,
looked at Huán Gōng and became sorrowful,
striking his ox's horn and singing loudly.
Huán Gōng heard this
and patted his charioteer's hand, saying:
"How extraordinary!
This singer is no ordinary man."
He ordered that Níng Qī be taken in the carriage that followed.
When Huán Gōng returned
and arrived,
his followers requested an audience for Níng Qī.
Huán Gōng bestowed upon him robes and a cap
and prepared to meet him.
When Níng Qī met him,
he persuaded Huán Gōng on how to govern his territory.
The next day, he met him again
and persuaded Huán Gōng on how to rule all under Heaven.
Huán Gōng was greatly pleased
and intended to appoint him.
The ministers contended, saying:
"This visitor is from Wèi.
Wèi is not far from Qí.
Would it not be better, my lord, to send someone to inquire about him?
If he is truly worthy,
it will not be too late to employ him."
Huán Gōng said:
"No, that is not right.
If I inquire about him,
I fear he may have some minor flaws.
To discard a man's great virtue
because of his minor flaws
is how rulers lose the士 of all under Heaven."
All listening must have a reason.
Now, to listen and not inquire further
is in line with its reason.
Moreover, it is indeed difficult for a person to be perfect;
one must weigh and use their strengths.
When it comes to making appointments,
Huán Gōng succeeded in this.
20.1 《Shì Jūn》
One says:
By nature, humans
do not have claws and teeth sufficient to defend themselves,
nor skin and flesh sufficient to withstand cold and heat,
nor sinews and bones sufficient to pursue advantage and avoid harm,
nor courage and bravery sufficient to repel fierce animals and deter violent people.
Yet, they still regulate all things,
control birds and beasts,
subdue cunning insects.
Cold, heat, dryness, and dampness cannot harm them.
Is this not because they first had provisions,
and because they gathered in groups?
That groups can be gathered
is because they mutually benefit from it.
That benefit comes from groups
is because the way of the ruler is established.
Therefore, when the way of the ruler is established, benefit comes from groups,
and human provisions can be completed.
In ancient times, there were once no rulers.
The people lived in scattered groups,
knowing their mothers but not their fathers,
without distinctions between relatives, siblings, spouses, male and female;
without the ways of high and low, old and young;
without the rites of advance, retreat, and deference;
without the conveniences of clothes, shoes, belts, palaces, and stored provisions;
without the preparations of tools, boats, carts, city walls, and dangerous barriers.
These were the troubles of having no ruler.
Therefore, the righteousness between ruler and minister
must not be unclear.
Since ancient times,
many states under Heaven have perished,
but the way of the ruler has not been abolished
because all under Heaven find it beneficial.
Therefore, they abolish those who are not true rulers
and establish those who practice the way of the ruler.
What is the way of the ruler?
It is to benefit, and to make the benefit of things manifest.
East of Fēibīn,
in the lands of Yí and Huì,
where Dàjiě, Língyú, Qí, Lùyě, Yáoshān, Yángdǎo, and the Dàrén reside,
many have no ruler; south of Yáng and Hàn,
in the regions of the Bǎiyuè,
in the lands of Bìkǎizhū, Fūfēng, and Yúmí,
in the states of Fúlóu, Yángyú, and Huāndōu,
many have no ruler; west of Dī, Qiāng, Hútáng, and Líshuǐ,
in the rivers of Bó Rén, Yě Rén, and Piānzuó,
in the lands of Zhōu Rén, Sònglóng, and Tū Rén,
many have no ruler; north of Yànmén,
in the states of Yīngsǔn, Suǒzhì, and Xūkuī,
in the lands of Tāotiè and Qióngqí,
in the abode of Shūnì,
in the dwellings of Dāněr,
many have no ruler. These are the rulerless peoples of the four quarters.
Their people are like deer and wild beasts;
the young exploit the old,
the old fear the strong,
the powerful are esteemed,
the arrogant and violent are respected,
day and night they mutually harm each other,
without rest,
until their kind is exhausted.
The Sages deeply foresaw this calamity.
Therefore, for the long-term benefit of all under Heaven,
there is nothing better than to establish a Son of Heaven;
for the long-term benefit of a state,
there is nothing better than to establish a ruler.
To establish a ruler is not to flatter the ruler;
to establish a Son of Heaven is not to flatter the Son of Heaven;
to establish officials is not to flatter the officials.
When virtue declines and the world is chaotic,
then the Son of Heaven benefits All under Heaven,
the state ruler benefits the state,
and officials benefit their offices.
This is why states alternately rise and fall,
and why chaos and difficulties sometimes arise.
Therefore, loyal ministers and incorruptible scholars,
internally, remonstrate with their ruler about his faults,
and externally, die for the righteousness of a minister.
Yù Ràng desired to assassinate Zhào Xiāngzǐ.
He plucked out his beard and eyebrows,
mutilated himself to change his appearance,
became a beggar, and went to beg at his wife's place.
His wife said:
"His appearance is not like my husband's,
but why is his voice so similar to my husband's?"
He then swallowed charcoal to make himself mute
to change his voice.
His friend said to him:
"What you are doing is very difficult and fruitless.
To say you have ambition, that is true,
but to say you have wisdom, that is not.
With your talent, if you sought to serve Xiāngzǐ,
Xiāngzǐ would surely favor you.
You could then get close and carry out your desire.
This would be very easy and surely succeed."
Yù Ràng smiled and replied:
"That would be to repay the former knowing with the later knowing,
to harm the new ruler for the sake of the former ruler.
Those who greatly disrupt the righteousness between ruler and minister do not do this;
I would lose the very reason for my actions.
All that I do this for
is to clarify the righteousness between ruler and minister,
not to follow the easy path."
Zhù Lìshū served Jǔ Áogōng.
Believing he was not recognized,
he left and lived by the sea,
eating water chestnuts and gorgon nuts in summer,
and acorns and chestnuts in winter.
When Jǔ Áogōng encountered difficulties,
Zhù Lìshū bade farewell to his friends and went to die for him.
His friend said:
"You left because you believed you were not recognized.
Now you go to die for him.
This means there is no difference between being recognized and not recognized."
Zhù Lìshū
said, “No,
he thought himself ignorant, and therefore he departed.
Now, if he dies and I do not go die with him,
this would truly show he understood me.
I will die for him to shame later generations of rulers who fail to understand their ministers,
thereby inspiring the conduct of those who govern others
and sharpening the integrity of rulers.
With inspired conduct and sharpened integrity,
loyal ministers will be fortunate enough to be recognized.
When loyal ministers are recognized, the way of the ruler will be secure.”
20.2 “Chánglì”
Secondly, it is said:
Those who are truly scholars of the world
consider the long-term benefits for the world
and firmly secure them with their lives.
Though a benefit may be twice as great today
but inconvenient for the future,
they will not pursue it.
Though security may last long,
if it is to privatize it for their descendants,
they will not act on it.
From this perspective,
Chén Wúyǔ’s shame is indeed grave.
Compared to Bóchéng Zǐgāo,
Zhōu Gōngdàn, and Róng Yí,
though their forms are similar, the difference in what they chose to take and reject
is indeed vast!
When Yáo governed the world,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo was enfeoffed as a feudal lord.
When Yáo yielded the throne to Shùn,
and Shùn to Yǔ,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo resigned his position as a feudal lord and took to farming.
Yǔ went to see him,
and found him farming in the fields.
Yǔ hurried to him, stood downwind, and asked him,
saying:
“When Yáo governed the world,
you, sir, were established as a feudal lord.
Now that it has come to me, you have resigned.
What is the reason for this?”
Bóchéng Zǐgāo said:
“In Yáo’s time,
the people were industrious without being rewarded,
and feared without being punished.
The people knew no resentment
and no joy;
they were as pleased as infants.
Now, rewards and punishments are very numerous,
yet the people scramble for profit and remain disobedient.
Virtue has declined from this,
and self-interest has arisen from this.
The chaos of later generations will begin from this.
Why do you not leave, sir?
Do not worry about my farming.”
He hoed and covered the seeds,
and never looked back.
To be a feudal lord,
one’s name is prominent and glorious,
one’s substance is leisurely and joyful,
and one’s descendants all receive its benefits.
Bóchéng Zǐgāo knew this without needing to be asked.
Yet he resigned from being a feudal lord
to prevent the chaos of later generations.
Xīn Kuān saw Lǔ Mùgōng and said:
“From now on, I realize that our former sovereign, Zhōu Gōng, was not as wise in his enfeoffment as Tài Gōngwàng.
In the past, Tài Gōngwàng was enfeoffed in Yíngqiū,
a land fortified by the sea and high, perilous mountains.
Therefore, his territory daily expanded,
and his descendants became increasingly prominent.
Our former sovereign, Zhōu Gōng, was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
a place without the dangers of mountains, forests, valleys, and streams,
and where feudal lords had access from all four sides.
Therefore, his territory daily dwindled,
and his descendants became increasingly diminished.”
When Xīn Kuān left,
Nángōng Kuò entered to see the Duke.
The Duke said:
“Just now, Kuān spoke ill of Zhōu Gōng,”
his words were like this.
Nángōng Kuò replied:
“Kuān is young,
he does not understand.
Have you not heard the explanation of Chéngwáng’s establishment of Chéngzhōu?
His words were:
‘Only I, the sole ruler,
reside in Chéngzhōu.
Only I, the sole ruler,
can easily see good deeds
and easily punish evil deeds.’
Therefore, it is said:
The good gain, and the bad lose;
this is the ancient way.
Would a worthy person desire their descendants to rely on the dangers of mountains and forests to perpetuate unrighteousness?
Kuān is a petty person!
If one were to make sparrows and swallows consider the concerns of swans and phoenixes,
they would certainly fail.
What they seek
are the gaps between tiles
and the shadows of the eaves;
whereas one flight for a swan or phoenix carries the ambition of a thousand *lǐ*,
and if their virtue is not profound and their righteousness not great, they will not even reach their outskirts.
The foolish and base common people,
when they consider matters for the worthy,
are just like this.
They simply slander and defame;
is this not lamentable?”
Róng Yí left Qí for Lǔ.
It was extremely cold, and he arrived late at the gate.
He and one disciple spent the night outside the city wall.
As the cold intensified,
he said to his disciple:
“If you give me your clothes,
I will live;
if I give you my clothes,
you will live.
I am a man of national importance.
The world would regret my death;
you are an unworthy person,
not worth cherishing.
Give me your clothes.”
The disciple said:
“As an unworthy person,
how can I give clothes to a man of national importance?”
Róng Yí sighed deeply and said:
“Alas!
The Way cannot be fulfilled!”
He took off his clothes and gave them to his disciple.
He died in the middle of the night,
and his disciple lived.
To say that Róng Yí was able to bring stability to an entire generation
is not something we know;
but as for his desire to benefit others,
nothing could surpass it.
He had achieved insight into the distinction of benevolence and love,
and thus was able to demonstrate his righteousness through certain death.
20.3 “Zhīfēn”
Thirdly, it is said:
A person of broad understanding
understands the distinction between life and death.
When one understands the distinction between life and death,
then gain and harm, existence and destruction, cannot confuse them.
Therefore, Yànzǐ, when swearing an oath with Cuī Zhù in the face of death, did not waver from his righteousness;
Yánlíng Jìzǐ, though the people of Wú wanted to make him king, would not consent;
Sūn Shú'áo, who became Prime Minister three times without joy,
and resigned as Prime Minister three times without sorrow;
all had achieved such understanding.
When one has achieved such understanding, external things cannot confuse them.
In Jīng, there was a man named Cìfēi.
He obtained a precious sword at Gànsuí.
Returning and crossing the Jiāng River,
when he reached mid-stream,
two蛟dragons coiled around his boat.
Cìfēi said to the boatman:
“Have you ever seen two蛟dragons coiled around a boat, yet both survived?”
The boatman said:
“I have never seen that.”
Cìfēi bared his arm, pushed up his sleeve, and drew his precious sword, saying:
“These are but rotten flesh and decaying bones in the river.
If I abandon my sword to save myself,
what do I cherish about it?”
Thereupon, he plunged into the river and stabbed the蛟dragons,
killed them, and returned to the boat.
All the people in the boat were saved.
When Jīngwáng heard of it,
he appointed him to a high office.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it and said:
“Indeed, how excellent!
Not abandoning one’s sword for rotten flesh and decaying bones—
is this not what Cìfēi exemplifies?”
When Yǔ journeyed south to inspect the regions,
and crossed the Jiāng River,
a yellow dragon carried his boat on its back.
The people in the boat
were overcome with fear.
Yǔ looked up at the sky and
smiled, saying:
“I received my mandate from Heaven
to exert my strength in nurturing the people.
Life is innate nature,
death is fate.
What concern do I have for the dragon?”
The dragon lowered its ears and dropped its tail, and departed.
Thus, Yǔ understood the distinction between life and death and the principles of gain and harm.
All human beings
are transformations of Yīn and Yáng.
Yīn and Yáng
are formed by Heaven.
Heaven inherently has decline, deficiency, abandonment, and concealment,
as well as abundance, fullness, growth, and cessation;
humans also have distress, poverty, constraint, and scarcity,
as well as fulfillment, prosperity, and success.
These are all the capacities of Heaven and the principles of things,
and they are unavoidable occurrences.
The ancient sages did not allow these to grieve their private feelings or wound their spirits,
but rather calmly accepted them.
Yàn Zǐ and Cuī Zhù swore an oath.
Its words were:
“He who does not side with the Cuī clan but sides with the Gōngsūn clan shall suffer misfortune.”
Yàn Zǐ bent down and drank the blood,
then looked up and called to Heaven, saying:
“He who does not side with the Gōngsūn clan but sides with the Cuī clan shall suffer this misfortune.”
Cuī Zhù was displeased.
He pointed a weapon at Yàn Zǐ’s chest
and hooked a weapon around his neck,
saying to Yàn Zǐ:
“If you change your words,
then I will share the state of Qí with you;
if you do not change your words,
then this is the end for you now.”
Yàn Zǐ said:
“Master Cuī!
Are you not familiar with the ‘Shī’ (Odes)?
The ‘Shī’ says:
‘Luxuriant are the kudzu vines,
spreading over the tips of the branches.
A gentle and amiable gentleman,
seeks blessings without deviating.’
How can Yīng possibly deviate to seek blessings?
You (only) reflect upon it.”
Cuī Zhù said:
“This is a worthy person;
he cannot be killed.”
He withdrew his weapons and left.
Yàn Zǐ (took) the handrail and mounted his carriage.
His charioteer was about to gallop,
but Yàn Zǐ (gently) patted his charioteer's hand, saying:
“Calm down!
Do not lose composure.
Speed does not necessarily mean life,
nor does slowness necessarily mean death.
A deer is born in the mountains but its fate hangs in the kitchen.
Now Yīng’s life
has something it depends on.”
Yàn Zǐ can be said to have known fate.
Fate,
is that which happens without knowing why it happens;
human affairs, wisdom, and clever contrivances cannot interfere with it.
Therefore, fate
is not gained by seeking it,
nor is it lost by forsaking it.
A true patriot knows this to be the case,
and so makes his decisions based on righteousness and rests in peace.
Bái Guī asked Zōu Gōngzǐ Xiàhòu Qǐ:
“The integrity of Jiànshéng,
the aspirations of Sìshàng,
and the affairs of the Sān Jìn;
these are the heroes and prominent figures of the world.
While living in Jìn,
I have frequently heard about the affairs of Jìn.
But I have never heard of the integrity of Jiànshéng or the aspirations of Sìshàng.
I wish to hear about them.”
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
“I am a humble person;
how am I worthy of being asked?”
Bái Guī said:
“I wish, my lord, that you would not decline.”
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
“If one believes something can be done,
one does it;
once it is done,
the world cannot stop it.
If one believes something cannot be done,
one abandons it;
once it is abandoned,
the world cannot compel one to do it.”
Bái Guī said:
“Can profit not compel one?
Can power not stop one?”
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
“If life is not enough to compel one,
then how can profit be enough to compel one?
If death is not enough to stop one,
then how can harm be enough to stop one?”
Bái Guī had no reply.
Xiàhòu Qǐ excused himself and left.
In general, employing the worthy and the unworthy differs;
the unworthy are employed with rewards and punishments,
the worthy are employed with righteousness.
Therefore, a worthy ruler, when employing his subordinates, must use righteousness,
and must carefully administer rewards and punishments.
Only then can both the worthy and the unworthy be fully utilized.
20.4 “Zhàolèi”
Fourth:
Like kinds summon each other,
like dispositions combine,
like sounds resonate.
Thus, beating the gōng note makes the gōng note respond,
and beating the jiǎo note makes the jiǎo note move;
dragons are used to bring rain,
and forms are used to pursue shadows.
The origin of fortune and misfortune,
the common people consider it fate,
how can they know its source?
(They do not know its origin).
Therefore, a state in disorder is not disordered merely on its own;
it will inevitably invite invaders.
Disorder alone may not lead to ruin,
but inviting invaders leaves no means of survival.
The use of arms
is for benefit
and for righteousness.
Attacking the disordered leads to their submission;
submission benefits the attacker.
Attacking the disordered is righteous;
righteousness brings honor to the attacker.
With both honor and benefit,
even a mediocre ruler would do it,
how much more so a worthy ruler?
Therefore, ceding land, offering precious vessels, spears and swords, humble words, and submission
are not enough to stop an attack;
only good governance is sufficient.
If there is good governance, those who seek benefit will not attack,
and those who seek fame will not invade.
Whenever people attack or invade,
it is either for benefit or for fame.
If neither fame nor substance can be gained,
even if a state is strong and great,
there will be no reason to attack it.
The origin of military action is ancient:
Yáo fought by the banks of Dānshuǐ
to subdue the Southern Mán;
Shùn repelled the Miáo people,
changing their customs;
Yǔ attacked Cáo and Wèi,
and subdued Ào and Yǒuhù,
to implement his teachings;
from the Three Sovereigns upwards,
they all certainly used military force.
When there is disorder, arms are used;
when there is order, they cease.
To attack when there is order,
there is no greater misfortune;
to fail to suppress when there is disorder,
there is no greater harm to the people.
This is the transformation of order and disorder,
the source from which wén (civil) and wǔ (military) arise.
Wén is the sign of love,
wǔ is the expression of hate.
Love and hate follow righteousness;
wén and wǔ have constancy,
which is the origin of the sage.
It is like the sequence of cold and heat,
when the time comes, events arise.
The sage cannot create the seasons,
but can adapt actions to the seasons.
Those whose actions are appropriate to the season achieve great success.
Shìyǐn Chí was an envoy from Jīng to Sòng.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn hosted him.
The wall of the southern house
was cluttered in front and not straight;
the sewage from the western house
ran through his palace without stopping.
Shìyǐn Chí asked the reason.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said:
“The southern house belongs to a craftsman,
one who makes drumheads.
I was going to move him.
His father said:
‘I have relied on making drumheads to feed three generations.
If I move now,
those in the state of Sòng who seek drumheads will not know my location.
I will not eat.
I hope that Your Excellency will be concerned about my not eating.’
For this reason,
I did not move him.
The western house is high,
my palace is low.
The overflow of water through my palace is beneficial,
so I do not forbid it.”
Shì Yǐn Chǐ (士尹池) returned to Jīng (荊).
The king of Jīng (荊) was about to raise an army to attack Sòng (宋).
Shì Yǐn Chǐ (士尹池) remonstrated with the king of Jīng (荊), saying:
“Sòng (宋) cannot be attacked.
Its ruler is virtuous,
and its prime minister is benevolent.
The virtuous can win the people,
and the benevolent can employ men.
If Jīng (荊) attacks it,
will it not gain no merit and become a laughingstock to the world?”
Therefore, he released Sòng (宋) and attacked Zhèng (鄭).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) heard of this and said:
“As for those who cultivate themselves in the imperial court, and yet repel the enemy a thousand lí (里) away,
is that not a description of Sīchéng Zǐhǎn (司城子罕)?”
Sòng (宋) was situated between three states of ten thousand chariots.
During Zǐhǎn’s (子罕) time,
there was no mutual invasion,
and the borders increased on all four sides.
He assisted Duke Píng (平公), Duke Yuán (元公), and Duke Jǐng (景公) until the end of his life.
Was it not solely due to his benevolence and moderation?
Therefore, the achievement of benevolence and moderation is great.
Thus, the Bright Hall had thatched roofs and Artemisia columns,
and earthen steps of three grades,
to demonstrate frugality.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子) was about to raid Wèi (衛),
and sent Shǐ Mò (史默) to observe it.
He set a one-month deadline,
but Shǐ Mò (史默) returned six months later.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子) said:
“Why such a long time?”
Shǐ Mò (史默) said:
“To scheme for profit and obtain harm,
is it because one did not investigate?
Now Qú Bóyù (蘧伯玉) is the prime minister,
Shǐ Qiū (史鰌) assists him,
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) is a guest,
and Zǐgòng (子貢) transmits orders before the ruler,
who listens intently.
The Yì (易) says:
‘Disperse their groups,
primordial good fortune.’
‘Disperse’ means ‘virtuous,’
‘groups’ means ‘the multitude,’
‘primordial’ means ‘the beginning of good fortune’;
‘Disperse their groups, primordial good fortune’ means
their assistants are mostly virtuous.”
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子) held his troops and did not move.
All schemes involve doubt.
When in doubt, decide matters based on righteousness.
When matters are decided based on righteousness, the scheme will not fail.
When the scheme does not fail, fame and reality will follow.
When a wise ruler acts,
must he wait until banners fall and generals perish before knowing victory or defeat?
Examine the principles, and gain or loss, glory or disgrace, will be determined.
Therefore, what the Three Dynasties valued
was nothing like virtue.
20.5 Dáyù (達鬱)
The fifth says:
All humans have three hundred and sixty joints,
nine orifices, five zàng (臟) organs, and six fǔ (腑) organs.
The muscles and skin desire to be compact,
the blood vessels desire to be open,
the tendons and bones desire to be firm,
the heart and mind desire to be harmonious,
the essence and vital energy desire to flow.
If this is so, then illness will have no place to reside and evil will have no way to arise.
The retention of illness and the generation of evil
are due to the stagnation of essence and vital energy.
Thus, if water stagnates, it becomes foul;
if a tree stagnates, it becomes worm-eaten;
if grass stagnates, it becomes diseased.
A state also has stagnation.
If the ruler's virtue does not flow,
and the people's desires are not met,
this is the stagnation of the state.
When the stagnation of a state persists for long,
then all evils will arise simultaneously,
and myriad disasters will gather.
The mutual endurance of superiors and inferiors
arises from this.
Therefore, the sage kings valued eminent scholars and loyal officials,
because they dared to speak frankly and resolve stagnation and obstruction.
King Lì of Zhōu (周厲王) oppressed the people,
and all the people of the state slandered him.
Zhào Gōng (召公) reported this, saying:
“The people can no longer endure the commands.”
The king sent a wizard from Wèi (衛) to monitor those who slandered;
if caught, they were killed.
The people of the state dared not speak,
and communicated on the roads with their eyes.
The king was pleased,
and reported to Zhào Gōng (召公), saying:
“I can now stop slander.”
Zhào Gōng (召公) said:
“This is obstructing it,
not stopping it.
Blocking the mouths of the people
is worse than blocking a river;
