when a river is dammed and then bursts,
many people will be harmed.
The people are just like this.
Therefore, those who manage rivers clear them to guide the flow,
and those who govern the people encourage them to speak.
Thus, when the Son of Heaven listens to government,
he has dukes, ministers, and ranked officials offer upright remonstrance,
those fond of learning and widely read offer poems,
blind musicians chant,
common people transmit words,
close ministers give full counsel,
and relatives supplement and inspect,
and only then does the king deliberate.
Thus, below, no good deeds are overlooked,
and above, no errors are committed.
Now, the king blocks the mouths of those below,
and thereby perpetuates the errors of those above,
which I fear will be a concern for the altars of soil and grain.”
The king did not listen.
Three years later,
the people of the state exiled the king to Zhì (彘).
This is the failure of stagnation.
Stagnation
is not bright.
The Zhōu (周) tripod depicted a rat,
ordering a horse to trample it,
because it was not bright.
Not being bright
is the custom of a perishing state.
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) entertained Duke Huán (桓公) with wine.
As dusk fell,
Duke Huán (桓公) enjoyed it and asked for candles.
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) said:
“Your minister planned for the day,
but not for the night.
Your Highness can now depart.”
The Duke was displeased,
and said:
“Zhòngfù (仲父) is old.
How much longer will I, the solitary man, enjoy pleasure with Zhòngfù (仲父)?
Please let us continue into the night.”
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) said:
“Your Highness is mistaken.
Those who are extravagant in taste are meager in virtue;
those who are immersed in pleasure revert to sorrow.
To be strong yet lazy is to lose opportunity;
to be old yet lax is to have no name.
Your minister is now about to strive for Your Highness;
how can you be immersed in wine?”
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) can be said to have been able to establish his conduct.
All conduct is corrupted by pleasure,
but now he was pleased yet became more circumspect;
conduct is ruined by power,
but now the ruler wished him to stay and he did not permit it.
Extending his will and carrying out principles,
unswayed by power or pleasure,
he served his ruler.
This is why Duke Huán (桓公) became hegemon.
Lièjīng Zǐgāo (列精子高) listened to the conduct of King Mǐn of Qí (齊湣王).
He wore fine Eastern coarse cloth,
a white silk gauze cap,
and shoes pushed up at the forehead,
and specially went to the hall at dawn in a light rain, walking down the steps,
and asked his attendant:
“How am I?”
The attendant said:
“Your Excellency is handsome and beautiful.”
Lièjīng Zǐgāo (列精子高) then walked and peeked into a well,
and saw a bright, ugly face of a man,
and sighed profoundly, saying:
“My attendant speaks to me about the conduct of the King of Qí (齊),
but why does he flatter?
How much more so when speaking of the conduct of a ruler of ten thousand chariots!
People's flattery of him is also excessive,
and he has no mirror.
His downfall and ruin are imminent.
Who should be the proper mirror?
Only scholars, perhaps!
Everyone knows to be pleased by a mirror that reflects himself clearly,
yet detests a scholar who reflects himself clearly.
The merit of a mirror reflecting oneself is small,
but the merit of a scholar reflecting oneself is great.
To obtain the small
and lose the great
is simply not knowing the proper category.”
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子) said:
“Jué (厥) loves me,
but Duó (鐸) does not love me.
When Jué (厥) remonstrates with me,
it is always in a place where no one else is present;
when Duó (鐸) remonstrates with me,
he likes to confront me in front of the multitude,
and invariably makes me look bad.”
Yǐn Duó
replied, "Jué
loved the shame of his lord,
but not the faults of his lord.
Duó
loved the faults of his lord,
but not the shame of his lord.
I once heard from a master who read people that those with thick faces and sallow complexions endure shame.
I did not present my lord among men,
fearing that my lord would not change."
This is the sagacity of Jiǎn Zǐ.
If a ruler is sagacious, his ministers' words are sharp.
If Jiǎn Zǐ
were not sagacious, Duó
would not have remained in the land of Zhào
in the end,
let alone by Jiǎn Zǐ's
side!
20.6 On Conduct
Six says:
The conduct of a ruler differs from that of a commoner.
When circumstances are not advantageous,
and the times are not favorable,
he must serve an enemy to survive.
Holding the lives of the people,
holding the lives of the people,
is a heavy responsibility;
one cannot make quick gratification the reason.
Therefore, if a commoner acts thus,
he is condemned by the state
and not tolerated in the countryside.
Yáo
ceded the empire to Shùn.
Gǔn,
as a feudal lord,
angrily said to Yáo:
"He who obtains the Way of Heaven becomes emperor;
he who obtains the Way of Earth becomes a Grand Minister.
Now I have obtained the Way of Earth,
yet you do not make me a Grand Minister."
He considered Yáo's
decision wrong
and desired to become a Grand Minister.
He was greatly angered, like a fierce beast,
wishing to cause chaos.
Its horns could form a wall;
its tail, when raised,
could be a banner.
When summoned, it would not come,
loitering in the wilderness to trouble the emperor.
Thereupon, Shùn
executed him at Yǔ Shān
and severed him with a Wú
knife.
Yǔ
dared not resent it,
but instead served him,
was appointed Sī Kōng,
to clear waterways,
his face became dark and sallow,
his steps did not cross each other,
his breath did not flow freely,
thus pleasing the emperor's heart.
In the past, Zhòu
was without principle,
killed Méi Bó
and minced him,
killed Guǐ Hóu
and made him into dried meat,
to present to the feudal lords in the temple.
Wén Wáng
wept profusely and sighed over it.
Zhòu
feared his rebellion,
wishing to kill Wén Wáng
and destroy Zhōu.
Wén Wáng
said:
"Even if a father is without principle,
how dare a son not serve his father?
Even if a lord is not benevolent,
how dare a minister not serve his lord?
Who is the king that can be rebelled against?"
Zhòu
then pardoned him.
The whole empire heard of it,
and considered Wén Wáng
to fear superiors and pity inferiors.
The Odes say:
"This Wén Wáng,
cautious and wary,
reverently served the Lord on High,
thus embracing many blessings."
Qí
attacked Sòng.
The King of Yān
sent Zhāng Kuí
to lead Yān
troops to follow.
The King of Qí
killed him.
The King of Yān
heard of it,
and tears streamed down his face in several lines.
He summoned his officials and informed them, saying:
"I initiated this affair, and Qí
killed my envoy.
I request to raise an army to attack Qí."
The envoy received the command.
Fán Yáo
came forward to be seen,
and argued, saying:
"A wise king would wish for a minister.
Now, if the King is not a wise ruler,
I wish to resign and not be a minister."
Zhāo Wáng
said:
"What is this?"
He replied:
"During the chaos of Sōng Xià,
the late king, being unsettled,
abandoned his ministers.
That Your Majesty endured the pain and served Qí
was because his strength was insufficient.
Now that Kuí
is dead, and Your Majesty attacks Qí,
this means you regard Kuí
as more worthy than the late king."
The King said:
"Agreed."
"I ask the King to halt the troops."
The King said:
"If so, what should be done?"
Fán Yáo
replied:
"I ask the King to wear plain white clothes,
move his residence to the suburbs,
send an envoy to Qí,
and act as a guest to apologize,
saying:
'This is all the fault of this humble person.
Your Majesty is a wise ruler,
how could you kill all the envoys of feudal lords?
Yet Yān's
envoy alone died;
this is because our humble state was not careful in selecting people.
We wish to make a change and beg for punishment.'"
The envoy traveled to Qí.
The King of Qí
was then feasting grandly,
his officials and retainers filling the hall,
and many charioteers.
He then ordered the envoy to report.
The envoy reported that the King of Yān
was very fearful and begged for punishment.
After finishing,
he repeated it,
to show off to his officials and retainers.
Then he dispatched a minor envoy to order the King of Yān
to return to his residence.
This is why Jì Shàng
was defeated,
and the state of Qí
was emptied.
Seventy cities,
had it not been for Tián Dān,
they would have barely been recovered.
Mǐn Wáng
was arrogant and cruel with the greatness of Qí;
Tián Dān
established his功at the city of Jì Mó.
The Odes say:
"If you wish to destroy it,
you must first pile it high;
if you wish to overthrow it,
you must first lift it high."
Is this what they mean?
Piled high but not destroyed,
lifted high but not overthrown—
is that only possible for those who possess the Way?
King Zhuāng
of Chǔ
sent Wén Wú Wèi
to Qí.
Passing through Sòng,
he did not first request passage.
Upon his return,
Chapter Seven:
The ruler of a ruined state
is invariably arrogant,
invariably considers himself wise,
and invariably treats things lightly.
Arrogance leads to slighting scholars;
self-professed wisdom leads to acting alone;
treating things lightly leads to unpreparedness.
Unpreparedness invites disaster,
acting alone endangers one's position,
and slighting scholars causes obstruction.
To avoid obstruction, one must treat scholars with respect;
to prevent one's position from being endangered, one must win over the populace;
to avoid inviting disaster, one must be fully prepared.
These three are the great principles for a ruler.
Jìn Lìgōng (晉厲公) was extravagant and licentious,
fond of listening to slanderers,
and wished to remove all his high officials to elevate his close associates.
Xū Tóng (胥童) said to Lìgōng:
"You must first kill the three Qī (郄).
Their clans are large and many resent them;
removing a great clan will not cause coercion."
The Duke said:
"Good."
Then he ordered Chángyú Jiǎo (長魚矯) to kill Qī Chōu (郄犨), Qī Qí (郄錡), and Qī Zhì (郄至于) at court and display their bodies.
Afterward, Lìgōng was enjoying himself at the Jiànglìshì (匠麗氏) residence,
when Luán Shū (欒書) and Zhōngháng Yǎn (中行偃) seized and imprisoned him.
The feudal lords did not come to his rescue,
the common people did not mourn him,
and he was killed three months later.
The trouble with a ruler
lies in knowing how to harm others,
but not knowing that harming others is improper and will ultimately revert to oneself.
Why is this so?
Because of short-sightedness.
Short-sightedness leads to not understanding transformation;
those who do not understand transformation invariably endanger themselves.
Wèi Wǔhóu (魏武侯) once planned an affair successfully,
and flexing his arms, he exclaimed loudly in the court:
"No official's deliberation is as good as mine!"
After a short while,
he repeated it two or three times.
Lǐ Kuí (李悝) hastened forward and said:
"Formerly, Chǔ Zhuāngwáng (楚莊王) planned an affair successfully,
achieved great merit,
but returned from court with a look of worry.
His attendants asked:
'Your Majesty has achieved great merit,
yet returns from court with a look of worry.
May we ask why?'
The King replied:
'Zhònghuī (仲虺) once said something that I appreciate.
He said:
"Among the feudal lords,
those whose virtue
enables them to seek out their own teachers will become kings;
those who can seek out their own friends will survive;
but those who choose [associates] and find none to be their equal will perish."
Now, I, though unworthy,
find that among all my ministers' plans, none can surpass mine.
Shall I then perish?
This is why I worry.' "
He continued:
"This is what a hegemonic king worries about,
yet Your Lord alone boasts about it.
How can this be acceptable?"
Wǔhóu said:
"Excellent."
The trouble with a ruler
is not in underestimating oneself,
but in overestimating oneself.
Overestimating oneself leads to refusing [good advice or help];
refusing leads to the exhaustion of resources.
Lǐ Kuí can be said to have been able to admonish his lord effectively,
as with a single utterance he made Wǔhóu better understand the way of a ruler.
Qí Xuānwáng (齊宣王) was building a grand palace (太室),
whose size exceeded a hundred *mǔ*,
and the main hall alone had three hundred households.
Despite the size of Qí (齊), after three years of preparation, it was still unfinished.
No official dared to admonish the King.
Chūn Jū (春居) asked Xuānwáng:
"Jīngwáng (荊王) abandoned the rituals and music of the former kings and delighted in trivialities.
May I ask if Jīng (荊) has a ruler?"
The King said:
"It has no ruler."
"With thousands of worthy ministers, none dared to admonish him.
May I ask if Jīng has ministers?"
The King said:
"It has no ministers."
"Now Your Majesty is building a grand palace,
whose size exceeds a hundred *mǔ*,
and the main hall alone has three hundred households.
Despite the size of Qí,
after three years of preparation, it cannot be finished.
No official dares to admonish you.
May I ask if Your Majesty has ministers?"
The King said:
"It has no ministers."
Chūn Jū said:
"I request to withdraw."
He hurried out.
The King said:
"Master Chūn!
Master Chūn, come back!
Why is your admonition to me so late?
I ask to stop it now."
He immediately summoned the scribe and said:
"Record this:
I, though unworthy,
was fond of building a grand palace,
and Master Chūn stopped me."
Vigilant admonition must not be neglected.
Those who dared not admonish
were not unwilling to do so.
The reason Chūn Jū wished to admonish was the same as others',
but the way he presented it was different from others'.
Had Xuānwáng (宣王) not had Chūn Jū,
he would have almost become a laughingstock of the world.
Judging from this,
rulers who lose their states
are often like Xuānwáng,
but their trouble lies in having no Chūn Jū.
Therefore, the admonitions of loyal ministers,
and how they are presented,
must not be treated carelessly;
this is the foundation of success and failure.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子) drowned Luán Jiǎo (鸞徼) in the river,
saying:
"I once liked music and beauty,
and Luán Jiǎo procured them.
I once liked palaces and pavilions,
and Luán Jiǎo built them.
I once liked good horses and skilled charioteers,
and Luán Jiǎo brought them.
Now I have liked scholars for six years,
yet Luán Jiǎo has never presented a single one.
This is extending my faults and diminishing my virtues."
Thus, a man like Jiǎnzǐ
was able later to supervise and demand accountability from his ministers with reason.
If one supervises and demands accountability from one's ministers with reason,
then the ruler can do good with them,
but cannot do wrong with them;
can be upright with them,
but cannot be crooked with them;
this was the flourishing teaching of the Three Dynasties.
20.8 *Guān Biǎo* (觀表)
Chapter Eight:
In all discussions of human nature,
observing events and transmissions,
one must be thorough,
one must be profound.
Heaven is high,
yet the sun, moon, stars, clouds, vapor, rain, and dew never cease;
Earth is vast,
yet springs, plants, feathered creatures, and scaled creatures never rest.
Among all things residing between heaven and earth,
within the six directions,
those striving for mutual peace and benefit
are countless,
while those causing mutual harm and danger are innumerable.
Human affairs are all like this.
Actions follow the heart,
the heart follows desires.
Those whose desires have no measure,
their hearts have no measure;
those whose hearts have no measure,
then their actions become unpredictable.
The human heart is hidden and difficult to see,
deep and difficult to fathom.
Therefore, the sages paid attention to it in affairs.
The reason sages surpass others in foreknowledge
is that foreknowledge requires careful examination of signs and indicators.
Without signs and indicators, if one wishes to possess foreknowledge,
then Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) would be no different from ordinary people.
Although signs may be easy,
and indicators difficult,
sages cannot be swayed by them;
while ordinary people have no way to reach [such insight].
Without a way to reach it, they consider it divine,
or luck.
It is neither divine nor luck;
it is simply the inevitable outcome of the method.
Hòu Chéngzǐ (郈成子) and Wú Qǐ (吳起) were close to this.
Hòu Chéngzǐ (郈成子) was dispatched by Lǔ (魯) to Jìn (晉) as an envoy.
Passing through Wèi (衛),
Yòuzǎi Gǔchén (右宰穀臣) stopped him and offered him wine,
displayed music but Hòu Chéngzǐ did not enjoy it.
When the wine was in full swing, Gǔchén sent him off with a jade disc.
Hòu Chéngzǐ returned [to Wèi],
passed by without taking his leave,
whereupon his servant said:
"Just now, Yòuzǎi Gǔchén entertained you with such joy,
yet you casually passed by without taking your leave?"
Hóu Chéngzǐ said:
“When they stopped and offered me wine,
they were delighting me.
When they arranged music but did not enjoy it,
they were telling me of their sorrow.
When the wine was flowing freely and they saw me off with a *bì* jade,
they were entrusting something to me.
If we view it from this perspective,
will Wèi perhaps experience chaos?”
Thirty *lǐ* away from Wèi,
he heard that the rebellion of Níng Xǐ had broken out,
and Yòuzǎi Gǔchén had died.
He turned his carriage back and observed,
made three gestures of mourning, and then returned.
Upon arrival,
he sent someone to welcome Gǔchén’s wife and children,
separated their residence by providing a different house,
shared his emoluments to feed them,
and when Gǔchén’s son grew up, he returned the *bì* jade to him.
Confucius heard of this and said:
“He who possesses wisdom to devise subtle plans and benevolence to be entrusted with wealth,
surely that refers to Hóu Chéngzǐ!”
Hóu Chéngzǐ’s observation of Yòuzǎi Gǔchén
was profound and subtle.
He did not observe his actions, but observed his intentions,
which can be called being skilled at observing people.
Wú Qǐ governed the region beyond Xīhé.
Wáng Cuò slandered him to Wèi Wǔhóu.
Wǔhóu sent someone to summon him.
Wú Qǐ arrived at Ànmén,
stopped his carriage and rested.
Looking towards Xīhé,
tears streamed down in several lines.
His servant said to him:
“I have observed your intentions, sir,
and you seem to regard abandoning the world as casting off a sandal.
Why do you weep now upon leaving Xīhé?”
Wú Qǐ, wiping away tears, replied:
“You do not understand.
If the lord truly knew me
and allowed me to fully utilize my abilities,
Qín could certainly be destroyed,
and Xīhé could become a royal domain.
Now the lord listens to the counsel of slanderers
and does not understand me.
Xīhé’s falling to Qín will not be long in coming,
and the state of Wèi will henceforth be weakened.”
Wú Qǐ indeed left Wèi and entered Jīng.
After a while, Xīhé entirely fell to Qín,
Wèi grew weaker day by day,
and Qín grew stronger day by day.
This is why Wú Qǐ foresaw this and wept.
Among those in antiquity skilled at judging horses were:
Hán Fēng judged the mouth and teeth;
Má Zhāo judged the cheeks;
Zǐnǚ Lì judged the eyes;
Wèi Jì judged the whiskers;
Xǔ Bǐ judged the hooves;
Tóufá Hè judged the chest and ribs;
Guǎn Qīng judged the belly and flanks;
Chén Bēi judged the thighs and legs;
Qín Yá judged the front;
Zàn Jūn judged the rear.
All these ten people
were excellent artisans of the world.
Their methods of judging differed,
yet seeing one sign of a horse,
they could know the height or lowness of its joints,
the smoothness or rough movement of its legs,
the firmness or brittleness of its constitution,
and the extent of its capabilities.
It is not only with judging horses that this is true;
people also have signs,
and events and states all have signs.
Sages know a thousand years into the past
and a thousand years into the future.
This is not mere conjecture;
there are indeed signs from which to derive it.
The Green Charts and the Flying Banners
originated from this.
21.1 *Kāichūn*
It is said:
When spring begins with thunder, the hibernating insects stir.
When seasonal rain falls, plants and trees grow.
When food, drink, dwelling, and rest are appropriate, the nine orifices, hundred joints, and thousand脉 all flow freely.
When a king accumulates virtue
and gathers many good deeds,
phoenixes and sages all come.
When Gòng Bó Hé cultivated his conduct
and favored the worthy and benevolent,
all within the four seas came to him for guidance.
During the calamity of Zhōu Lì,
when the Son of Heaven was absent and cut off,
everyone in the world came to him for counsel.
This illustrates how things correspond to each other.
Therefore, it is said: action is accomplishment.
A skilled persuader is also like this;
when his words fully articulate the principle, gain and loss, benefit and harm are determined.
How could he speak for just one person?
Wèi Huìwáng died,
and the day for his burial was set.
There was a heavy snowfall,
reaching up to the eyes of oxen.
Many ministers advised the crown prince,
saying:
“The snow is so heavy,
if we proceed with the burial,
the people will surely resent it greatly,
and the official expenses might not be sufficient.
Please postpone the date and set a new one.”
The crown prince said:
“As a son,
to not carry out the burial of the former king
due to the labor of the people and official expenses
is unrighteous.
Do not speak of it again.”
All the ministers dared not advise him further
and reported it to Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu said:
“I have no way to persuade him.
Is this not a matter for Huìgōng?
Please report it to Huìgōng.”
Huìgōng said:
“Agreed.”
He drove to see the crown prince and said:
“The burial date is set.”
The crown prince said:
“That is so.”
Huìgōng said:
“In ancient times, Wáng Jìlì was buried at the foot of Wō Shān.
The Luán River eroded his tomb,
exposing the front panel of his coffin.
Wénwáng said:
‘Alas!
My late lord surely wished to have one last look at his ministers and the common people,
thus he caused the Luán River to reveal him.’
Thereupon, he went out and arranged an audience for him,
all the common people saw him,
and after three days, he was reburied.
This was the righteousness of Wénwáng.
Now, the burial date is set,
but the snow is heavy,
reaching the eyes of oxen,
making it difficult to proceed.
Is the crown prince, for the sake of meeting the date,
perhaps suspected of wishing to bury him too quickly?
I wish for the crown prince to change the date.
The former king surely wished to stay a little longer to soothe the state and settle the populace,
thus he caused the heavy snowfall.
By postponing the date and setting a new one,
this would be the righteousness of Wénwáng.
If you do not do this,
do you perhaps feel ashamed to emulate Wénwáng?”
The crown prince said:
“Excellent.
I respectfully postpone the date
and will choose a new burial day.”
Huìzǐ did not merely put forward his argument;
he also allowed the Wèi crown prince, before burying his former lord, to thereby have a discourse on the righteousness of Wénwáng.
To expound the righteousness of Wénwáng to show to the world,
how could that be a small achievement!
The Hán clan was building Xīnchéng,
with a deadline of fifteen days for completion.
Duàn Qiáo was the Sīkōng.
One county was two days behind schedule,
so Duàn Qiáo seized its official and imprisoned him.
The prisoner’s son ran to tell Fēngrén Zǐgāo, saying:
“Only you, master, can save my father from death.
I wish to entrust this to you, master.”
Fēngrén Zǐgāo said:
“Agreed.”
Thereupon, he went to see Duàn Qiáo
and, leaning on him, ascended the city wall.
Fēngrén Zǐgāo looked left and right and said:
“What a magnificent city!
A great achievement!
You will surely receive a generous reward!
From antiquity to the present,
there has never been anyone whose achievement was so great
and yet was able to escape punishment or execution.”
When Fēngrén Zǐgāo left,
Duàn Qiáo sent someone at night to untie and release his official.
Therefore, it is said that Fēngrén Zǐgāo spoke on his behalf
and concealed his own effort to act;
Duàn Qiáo listened and acted on it,
concealing his own action in acting.
The execution of the persuasion was so subtle.
Fēngrén Zǐgāo can be called a skilled persuader.
Shū Xiàng’s younger brother, Yángshé Hǔ, was close to Luán Yíng.
Luán Yíng committed a crime against Jìn.
Jìn executed Yángshé Hǔ.
Shū Xiàng was enslaved because of this and suffered indignities.
Qí Xī said:
“I have heard that when a petty person gains a position,
it is inauspicious not to contend for it;
when a gentleman is in distress,
it is inauspicious not to rescue him.”
So he went to see Fàn Xuānzǐ and spoke to him,
saying:
“I have heard that those who govern a state well,
their rewards are not excessive and their punishments are not lenient.
If rewards are excessive, one fears they may reach licentious people;
if punishments are lenient, one fears they may reach gentlemen.
Rather than mistakenly erring in that way,
it is better to err by rewarding licentious people,
than to err by punishing gentlemen.
Therefore, Yáo’s punishment
was to exile Gǔn to Yú but employ Yǔ;
Zhōu’s punishment
was to execute Guǎn and Cài but appoint Zhōu Gōng as prime minister;
these were not lenient punishments.”
Xuānzǐ then ordered his officials to release Shū Xiàng.
When one rescues others from calamity,
one undergoes danger and hardship, without avoiding annoyance or humiliation,
yet still might not escape.
Now Qí Xī discussed the virtues of the former kings,
and Shū Xiàng was able to be spared.
How can learning ever be stopped?
Many such examples exist.
21.2 “Examining the Worthy”
Second, it says:
If there were a skilled physician here,
who treated ten people and cured nine,
he would be sought after by ten thousand.
Therefore, the achievement of fame and merit by worthy people
is certainly like that of a skilled physician,
yet rulers do not know to eagerly seek them,
is this not a great fault?
Now, in a contest,
bravery, strength, auspicious times, divination, and prayer are of no avail;
the skilled will certainly win.
Achieving fame and merit is also like this;
the key lies in obtaining worthy people.
Wèi Wénhóu made Bǔ Zǐxià his teacher,
befriended Tián Zǐfāng,
and treated Duàn Gānmù with respect;
his state was well-governed and he lived in ease.
How could the worthy rulers of the world
necessarily suffer physical hardship and mental worry?
They merely grasped the essential points.
When snow, frost, rain, and dew arrive on time,
then all things grow,
the people flourish,
and diseases and calamities depart.
Therefore, it is said that Yáo’s appearance was as if he were merely wearing clothes and furs,
meaning he had few duties.
Mì Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù.
He played the zither,
and did not descend from his hall, yet Dānfù was well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī went out by starlight
and returned by starlight,
never resting day or night,
personally attending to everything,
and Dānfù was also well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī asked Mì Zǐ the reason.
Mì Zǐ said:
“I am called one who relies on others,
you are called one who relies on effort.
He who relies on effort is therefore toilsome;
he who relies on others is therefore at ease.”
People said Mì Zǐ was a gentleman,
who rested his four limbs,
preserved his ears and eyes,
calmed his mind and spirit,
and all officials managed affairs well.
He merely relied on the proper method.
Wūmǎ Qī, on the other hand,
exhausted his life and strained his spirit,
wearied his hands and feet,
and bothered people with instructions;
though it was well-governed, it had not reached the ultimate.
21.3 “Seeking the Worthy”
Third, it says:
Now, when one lures cicadas with fire,
the key lies in making the fire bright
and shaking the tree.
If the fire is not bright,
though one shakes the tree,
what good is it?
Making the fire bright does not solely depend on the fire itself,
but on the darkness.
In the present age, it is very dark.
If a ruler can make his virtue shine brightly,
then the scholars of the world
will flock to him
like cicadas rushing towards a bright fire.
No state is secure by itself,
no fame becomes prominent by itself;
one must acquire worthy scholars.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was at leisure during the day,
and sighed deeply, saying:
“How strange!
I have wanted to attack Wèi for ten years,
but Wèi has not been attacked.”
A attendant said:
“Given Zhào’s greatness
and Wèi’s smallness,
if Your Lord does not wish to, then it is fine.
If Your Lord wishes to,
please order the attack.”
Jiǎnzǐ said:
“It is not as you say.
Wèi has ten scholars in my service.
If I were to attack it now,
those ten people would say it is unjust,
and if I attack it,
that would make me unjust.”
Thus, in Jiǎnzǐ’s time,
Wèi relied on those ten people to hold back Zhào’s army
for Jiǎnzǐ’s entire life.
Wèi can be said to have known how to employ people,
by merely having ten scholars wander about, the state gained peace.
Jiǎnzǐ can be said to have been good at following advice,
by listening to ten scholars, he avoided the reputation of invading the small and seizing from the weak.
Wèi Wénhóu passed by Duàn Gānmù’s neighborhood and bowed respectfully over his chariot rail.
His servant said:
“Why did Your Lord bow?”
He said:
“Is this not Duàn Gānmù’s neighborhood?
Duàn Gānmù is indeed a worthy person;
how dare I not bow respectfully?
Moreover, I have heard that Duàn Gānmù has never been willing to exchange himself for me;
how dare I be arrogant towards him?
Duàn Gānmù shines with virtue,
I shine with territory;
Duàn Gānmù is rich in righteousness,
I am rich in wealth.”
His servant said:
“If so, why does Your Lord not appoint him as prime minister?”
Thereupon, the ruler invited him to be prime minister,
but Duàn Gānmù refused to accept.
Then the ruler offered him a salary of a million,
and visited him regularly.
At this, all the people of the state rejoiced,
and chanted to each other:
“Our ruler loves righteousness,
thus he respects Duàn Gānmù;
our ruler loves loyalty,
thus he elevates Duàn Gānmù.”
Not long after,
Qín raised an army to attack Wèi.
Sīmǎ Táng admonished the Qín ruler, saying:
“Duàn Gānmù is a worthy person,
and Wèi treats him with respect;
everyone under Heaven has heard of this.
Surely, we cannot wage war against them!”
The Qín ruler considered it true,
so he halted his troops,
and refrained from daring to attack them.
Wèi Wénhóu can be said to have been skilled in military strategy.
It is often said that when a gentleman wages war,
their form is not seen,
yet their achievement is already made;
this is what that refers to.
When a common person wages war,
the drum sounds like thunder,
shouts shake the earth,
dust fills the sky,
flying arrows fall like rain,
the wounded are supported, the dead carried away,
people walk over intestines and wade through blood,
and the number of innocent people who die is as vast as a marsh,
yet the survival of the state and the life or death of the ruler are still unknown,
and they are far removed from benevolence and righteousness.
21.4 “Examining What Is Done”
Fourth, it says:
The body is that which acts,
the world is that for which one acts;
if one examines what one acts for and by what means, then the proper priorities are understood.
Now, if there were a person here
who cut off his head to exchange it for a cap,
or killed himself to exchange for clothes,
the world would certainly be bewildered by him.
Why is this?
A cap is for adorning the head;
clothes are for adorning the body.
If one now destroys that which adorns and seeks that by which one is adorned,
then one does not know what one is doing.
The world’s pursuit of gain
is similar to this.
To endanger one’s person, harm one’s life, sever one’s neck, and cut off one’s head in pursuit of gain,
then one also does not know what one is doing.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù lived in Bīn.
The Dí people attacked him.
He served them with animal hides and silks, but they would not accept;
he served them with pearls and jade, but they would not consent.
What the Dí people sought was land.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù said:
“To live with one person’s elder brother and kill his younger brother,
to live with one person’s father and kill his son,
I cannot bear to do.
All of you should strive to settle.
What is the difference between being my subject and being a Dí subject?
Moreover, I have heard this:
Do not harm that which is nourished by that which nourishes it.”
He took up his staff and departed.
The people followed him, connecting one to another,
and thus a state was formed at the foot of Qíshān.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù can be said to have been able to revere life.
One who can revere life,
though noble and wealthy, does not harm their body for the sake of sustenance;
though poor and lowly, does not burden their form for the sake of gain.
Now, if one receives the rank and emoluments of one’s ancestors,
then one must consider it grievous to lose them.
Life, from where it comes, has been long;
to lightly lose it,
is this not delusion?
Hán and Wèi contended with each other, encroaching on territory.
Zǐhuázi saw Zhāolízóu.
Zhāolízóu had a worried expression.
Zǐhuázi said:
“Now, suppose someone inscribed a message before Your Lordship,
and the message said:
‘If you grasp it with your left hand, your right hand will be crippled;
if you grasp it with your right hand, your left hand will be crippled;
yet whoever grasps it will surely possess the world.’
Will Your Lordship grasp it?
Or will you not?”
Zhāolízóu said:
“I, the lonely one, will not grasp it.”
Zǐhuázi said:
“Very good.
From this perspective,
two arms are weightier than the world,
and the body is even weightier than two arms.
Hán is far lighter than the world;
what you are now contending for
is even far lighter than Hán.
Why should Your Lordship trouble your body and harm your life to worry over it and suffer discontent?”
Zhāolízóu said:
“Good.
Many have instructed me, the lonely one,
but I have never heard such words.”
Zǐhuázi can be said to have understood relative importance.
Understanding relative importance,
therefore his judgment was never mistaken.
Zhōngshān Gōngzǐ Móu said to Zhānzi:
“My body is among the rivers and seas,
but my heart resides beneath the Wèiquè.
What is to be done?”
Zhānzi said:
“Value life.
If you value life, you will lightly regard gain.”
Zhōngshān Gōngzǐ Móu said:
“Although I know this,
I still cannot overcome myself.”
Zhānzi said:
“If you cannot overcome yourself, then let yourself go.
There is nothing evil in the spirit.
One who cannot overcome oneself but insists on not letting go
is what is called ‘heavy injury.’
Those with heavy injury are not among the long-lived.”
21.5 On Loving One's Kind
Fifthly:
To be benevolent to other things
but not benevolent to humans
cannot be called benevolence;
to be not benevolent to other things
but exclusively benevolent to humans
can still be called benevolence.
Benevolence
is benevolence towards one’s own kind.
Therefore, when a benevolent person deals with the common people,
if it can benefit them,
there is nothing they will not do.
The teachings of Shénnóng say:
“If there is a man in his prime who does not plow,
then somewhere in the world, someone will suffer hunger;
if there is a woman in her prime who does not weave,
then somewhere in the world, someone will suffer cold.”
Therefore, he personally plowed,
and his wife personally wove,
which served to demonstrate the bringing of benefit to the people.
Worthy individuals do not shun the roads across the seas,
and they often come and go to the courts of kings and dukes,
not to seek gain,
but because they make the people their business.
If a ruler can make the people their business,
then the world will return to them.
A king is not necessarily one with strong armor, sharp weapons, elite soldiers, and trained warriors;
nor is it necessarily one who demolishes others’ city walls and kills others’ people.
There were many kings in ancient times,
and their deeds all differed.
What was common was their response to the urgencies of their time, their concern for the people’s benefit, and their removal of harm from the people.
Gōngshū Bān made a high cloud ladder,
intending to attack Sòng.
Mòzǐ heard of it,
and traveled from Lǔ,
tearing his robe to wrap his feet,
without rest day or night,
and arrived at Yǐng after ten days and ten nights.
He met the King of Jīng and said:
“I am a humble person from the North.
I heard that Your Great Majesty intends to attack Sòng.
Is this truly so?”
The King said:
“It is.”
Mòzǐ said:
“Will you attack only if you are certain to take Sòng? Or will you attack even if you cannot take Sòng and it is unjust?”
The King said:
“If I am certain not to take Sòng,
and moreover it would be unjust,
then why would I attack it?”
Mòzǐ said:
“Very good.
I believe Sòng certainly cannot be taken.”
The King said: “Gōngshū Bān,
the most skilled artisan in the world,
has already built the siege engines for attacking Sòng.”
Mòzǐ said:
“Please allow Gōngshū Bān to try attacking,
and I will try defending.”
Thereupon, Gōngshū Bān set up his siege engines for attacking Sòng,
and Mòzǐ set up his defenses for Sòng.
Gōngshū Bān attacked nine times,
Mòzǐ repelled him nine times.
He could not enter,
and so Jīng ceased its attack on Sòng.
That Mòzǐ could use his skill to deter Jīng and avert the disaster for Sòng,
this is what is referred to.
No sagely king or accomplished scholar ever acted without benefiting the people.
In ancient times, before Lóngmén was opened,
and Lǘliáng was not cleared,
the Yellow River emerged from Mèngmén,
overflowed greatly, and flowed upstream,
wiping out all hills, fertile plains, level lands, and high mounds,
destroying them entirely.
It was called Hóngshuǐ.
Yǔ then dredged the Yellow River and cleared the Jiāng,
created the barrier of Pénglǐ,
and dried the eastern lands.
Those he saved were eighteen hundred states.
This was Yǔ’s accomplishment.
Working diligently for the people,
no one suffered more than Yǔ.
Kuāng Zhāng said to Huìzi:
“Your teaching rejects reverence (for rulers),
yet now you serve Qí Wáng.
How contradictory!”
Huìzi said:
“Suppose there is a person here
who is determined to strike the head of their beloved child.
A stone can substitute for it.”
Kuāng Zhāng said:
“Would you take the stone to substitute,
or not?”
“One would offer the stone as a substitute.
The child’s head is weighty;
the stone is light.
To strike that which is light to save that which is weighty,
how can this not be done?”
Kuāng Zhāng said:
“The reason Qí Wáng employs troops incessantly and attacks people ceaselessly,
what is it?” Huìzi said:
“If great, he can become a king;
second to that, he can become a hegemon.
Now, if one can make Qí Wáng a king and prolong the lives of the common people,
saving the people from death,
this is like substituting a stone for a beloved child’s head.
Why should it not be done?
When people are cold, they desire fire;
when hot, they desire ice;
when dry, they desire wetness;
when wet, they desire dryness.
Cold, heat, dryness, and wetness are opposite,
but in benefiting the people, they are one.
How can benefiting the people be a single path?
It is simply a matter of adapting to the times.”
21.6 《Guì Zú》
Sixthly, it says:
Strength values a sudden attack,
wisdom values swiftness.
When both are achieved, swiftness is superior;
when both are achieved in victory, delay is inferior.
The reason a swift horse (jì) is valued
is because it can cover a thousand *lǐ* in a single day.
If it takes ten days to achieve,
it is no different from an inferior, tired horse (nú tái).
The reason a sharp arrow (zú shǐ) is valued
is because it arrives at the sound.
If it takes all day to arrive,
then it is as good as not arriving at all.
Wú Qǐ said to King Jīng:
"What Jīng has in abundance is land,
what it lacks is people.
Now Your Majesty is using what is lacking to augment what is abundant.
I cannot undertake this."
Thereupon, he ordered nobles to go and populate the vast, empty lands,
all of whom suffered greatly.
When King Jīng died,
all the nobles returned.
While the corpse lay in the hall,
the nobles shot arrows at Wú Qǐ.
Wú Qǐ cried out:
"I will show you how I employ troops!"
He pulled out the arrows and fled,
then inserted them into the King's corpse and quickly said:
"The ministers are in rebellion against the King!"
Wú Qǐ died.
Moreover, by the laws of Jīng,
anyone who left weapons on the King's corpse
would be subjected to severe punishment,
extending to their three clans.
Wú Qǐ's wisdom
can be said to have been swift.
When Duke Xiāng of Qí ascended the throne,
he hated Gōngsūn Wúzhī
and confiscated his emolument.
Wúzhī was displeased
and killed Duke Xiāng.
Prince Jiū fled to Lǔ,
Prince Xiǎobái fled to Jǔ.
Afterwards, the people of the state killed Wúzhī,
and there was no ruler.
Prince Jiū and Prince Xiǎobái both returned.
Upon their simultaneous arrival,
they competed to enter the ducal palace first.
Guǎn Zhòng drew his bow and shot Prince Xiǎobái,
hitting his belt hook.
Bào Shú was driving the chariot,
and Prince Xiǎobái feigned collapse.
Guǎn Zǐ thought Xiǎobái was dead,
and told Prince Jiū:
"Rest assured.
Prince Xiǎobái is dead."
Bào Shú then drove quickly ahead and entered first,
thus Prince Xiǎobái was able to become the ruler.
Bào Shú's wisdom, in responding to the shot by having Prince Xiǎobái feign collapse,
was like a sharp arrow.
King Wǔ of Zhōu sent someone to assassinate Líng Kuī in Eastern Zhōu.
Líng Kuī feigned collapse,
and ordered his son to quickly cry out:
"Who assassinated my father?!"
The assassin heard this
and thought he was dead.
Zhōu considered this untrustworthy
and consequently punished him severely.
The Zhào clan attacked Zhōngshān.
Among the strong men of Zhōngshān was Wúqiū Yù.
He wore iron armor and wielded an iron staff in battle,
and whatever he struck was shattered,
whatever he charged into was breached.
He threw chariots at chariots,
and men at men,
nearly reaching the general's position before he died.
22.1 《Shèn Xíng》
First, it says:
One's actions must not be imprudent.
If imprudent,
it is like leaping into a deep ravine;
even regret will be too late.
The *jūnzǐ* plans actions considering righteousness,
the petty person plans actions considering their own profit,
and consequently suffers disadvantage.
If one knows the disadvantage in a seeming advantage,
then one can discuss principles with them.
King Píng of Jīng had a minister named Fèi Wújí,
who harbored malice towards Crown Prince Jiàn
and wished to remove him.
The King took a beautiful wife for Jiàn from Qín,
but Wújí persuaded the King to take her for himself.
After the King took her,
he alienated the Crown Prince.
Wújí then convinced the King, saying:
"Jìn's hegemony
is close to the various Xià states,
while Jīng is remote,
thus it cannot compete with them.
It would be better to build a large city at Chéngfù and place the Crown Prince there
to seek the north, while Your Majesty secures the south;
this way, you will gain the entire realm."
The King was pleased
and sent the Crown Prince to reside in Chéngfù.
After a year,
he slandered him, saying:
"Jiàn and Lián Yǐn are planning to revolt from outside Fāngchéng."
The King said:
"He is already my son,
what more could he seek?"
He replied:
"He resents you over the matter of his wife.
Moreover, he considers himself like Sòng,
and with Qí and Jìn assisting him,
he intends to harm Jīng.
The plot is already set."
The King believed him
and ordered Lián Yǐn to be arrested.
Crown Prince Jiàn fled.
Zuǒ Yǐn Xī Wǎn
was popular among the people of the state.
Wújí again wished to kill him,
and said to Prime Minister Zǐcháng:
"Xī Wǎn wishes to invite you, the Prime Minister, for a drink."
Then he told Xī Wǎn:
"The Prime Minister wishes to drink at your home."
Xī Wǎn said:
"I am a humble man,
not worthy of the Prime Minister's presence.
If the Prime Minister must condescend to come,
how shall I receive him?"
Wújí said:
"The Prime Minister likes armor and weapons.
You should bring them out and place them by the gate.
When the Prime Minister arrives,
he will surely examine them.
Afterward,
you can use them as a toast."
On the day of the feast,
Xī Wǎn placed armor and weapons on both sides of his gate.
Wújí then said to the Prime Minister:
"I almost brought disaster upon you, Prime Minister!
Xī Wǎn intends to kill you;
the armor is at his gate."
The Prime Minister sent someone to check,
and believing it,
attacked Xī Wǎn
and killed him.
The people of the state were greatly resentful;
everyone who acted spoke ill of the Prime Minister.
Shěn Yǐn Shù said to the Prime Minister:
"Fèi Wújí is a slanderer of Jīng.
He caused the flight of Crown Prince Jiàn,
killed Lián Yǐn Shē,
and blocked the King's ears and eyes.
Now Your Excellency uses him again,
killing many innocent people,
thereby creating great calumny.
Calamity is likely to reach Your Excellency."
Prime Minister Zǐcháng said:
"This is my fault.
I dare not plan poorly again."
Thereupon he killed Fèi Wújí
and exterminated his entire clan
to appease his state.
Acting without considering its righteousness,
knowing how to harm others but not knowing that others would harm him,
leading to the extermination of his clan—
this describes Fèi Wújí!
Cuī Zhù and Qìng Fēng conspired to kill Duke Zhuāng of Qí.
After Duke Zhuāng died,
Duke Jǐng was enthroned instead,
and Cuī Zhù became his prime minister.
Qìng Fēng then wanted to kill Cuī Zhù and take his place as prime minister.
Thereupon, he instigated Cuī Zhù's sons
to dispute over the succession.
Cuī Zhù's sons privately fought among themselves.
Cuī Zhù went to see Qìng Fēng and reported this.
Qìng Fēng said to Cuī Zhù:
"Stay for a moment,
I will raise troops to kill them."
He then ordered Lú Mǎn Wùbiē to raise troops to execute them,
killing all of Cuī Zhù's wives, children, and collateral relatives,
and burning his houses.
He reported back to Cuī Zhù:
"I have already executed them."
Cuī Zhù returned to find nowhere to go
and consequently hanged himself.
Qìng Fēng served as Prime Minister to Duke Jǐng,
and Duke Jǐng resented him.
When Qìng Fēng went hunting,
Duke Jǐng, along with Chén Wúyǔ, Gōngsūn Zào, and Gōngsūn Chài, executed Fēng.
Qìng Fēng fought with his retainers,
but did not win,
and fled to Lǔ.
The Qí people found this objectionable,
so he left Lǔ and went to Wú.
The King gave him Zhūfāng.
King Líng of Jīng heard of this,
led the feudal lords to attack Wú,
besieged Zhūfāng,
captured it,
and seized Qìng Fēng.
He had him bound to an axe and block,
and paraded him through the armies of the feudal lords,
then ordered him to shout:
"Let no one be like Qìng Fēng of Qí,
who murdered his lord and weakened his orphaned son,
thereby losing his position as a high official!"
Then he killed him.
The eminent Huángdì died,
the virtuous Yáo and Shùn died,
the brave Mèng Bēn died;
indeed, all people die.
A man like Qìng Fēng
can be said to have died a double death.
His body was disgraced,
his family members could not remain intact,
all because of his malicious deeds.
Whenever people commit acts of chaos,
they initially help each other,
but later they are bound to hate each other.
Those who act righteously are not like this:
they begin by associating with each other,
over time they trust each other,
and in the end they cherish each other,
and future generations take them as a model.
22.2 《Wú Yì》
Second, it states:
The Former Kings were exhaustive in their deliberations;
thus, righteousness is the beginning of all affairs,
the foundation of all benefits,
and beyond the reach of those of mediocre wisdom.
If it is beyond reach, then one does not understand it,
and one does not know how to pursue benefits.
Pursuing benefits cannot be guaranteed,
as exemplified by Gōngsūn Yāng, Zhèng Píng, Xù Jīng, and Gōngsūn Jié.
If one acts with righteousness, there will be no unfulfilled tasks.
When ministers conspire with other ministers to commit treachery,
there are still some who will support it.
How much more so when a ruler conspires with his ministers to act righteously—
who would not support him?
It is not only his ministers,
but the entire world will support him.
Gōngsūn Yāng, in relation to Qín,
was not a father or elder brother,
nor was there any prior connection;
it was because he was capable of being employed.
Wishing to shoulder the responsibility of stemming [the tide],
there was no way without attacking.
Thereupon, he became a general for Qín and attacked Wèi.
Wèi sent Prince Yáng as general to oppose him.
When Gōngsūn Yāng was in Wèi,
he had always been on good terms with Prince Yáng.
He sent someone to tell Prince Yáng:
"All that I did while traveling and wishing for eminence
was for the sake of Your Highness.
Now Qín has ordered me to be general,
and Wèi has ordered Your Highness to oppose me.
How could we bear to fight each other?
Your Highness should speak to your lord,
and I also ask to speak to my lord,
so that both armies may withdraw."
Thereupon, he was about to return.
He sent someone to tell the Prince:
"There will be no opportunity to see each other upon returning.
I wish to sit with Your Highness and bid farewell."
The Prince said,
"Very well."
Wèi officials protested, saying,
"This is not permissible."
The Prince did not listen,
and so they sat together.
Gōngsūn Yāng then ambushed him with soldiers, chariots, and cavalry, and captured Prince Yáng.
When Duke Xiào of Qín died,
King Huì ascended the throne,
and on account of this doubted Gōngsūn Yāng's conduct,
wishing to punish him.
Gōngsūn Yāng, with his private retainers and mother, returned to Wèi.
Xiāng Cī did not accept him,
saying:
"Because of your betrayal of Prince Yáng,
I have no way of knowing you."
Therefore, an officer's actions must be undertaken with great caution.
Zhèng Píng was a minister to the King of Qín,
and an associate of Marquis Yìng.
He deceived his associate and betrayed his lord,
for the sake of personal gain.
When he was a Qín general,
there was nothing the world held in high esteem that he did not possess;
he was respected.
What is gained by respect
will certainly be lost by disrespect.
Leaving his position as Qín general,
and entering Zhào and Wèi,
there was nothing the world despised that he did not possess;
there was nothing shameful that he did not possess.
When his conduct was contemptible and shameful,
and he lacked the prestige of a Qín general,
what else awaited him but ruin?
Zhào urgently sought Lǐ Kài.
Lǐ said that Xù Jīng would accompany him to Wèi,
to meet Gōngsūn Yǔ.
Gōngsūn Yǔ met them and let them in.
Xù Jīng then informed the Wèi officials to arrest Lǐ.
Xù Jīng thus became a Fifth Grand Master in Zhào.
No one would serve in the same court with him,
and his descendants could not make friends.
Gōngsūn Jié was involved in the affair with Lord Yīn,
and then reported it to Chancellor Chūlǐ,
thereby becoming a Fifth Grand Master in Qín.
His achievement was not small,
yet he was not permitted to enter the three capitals.
How much more so for one without such achievement, yet with such conduct?
22.3 《Yísì》
Third, it states:
What causes people great confusion
must be things that are similar.
What troubles the jade worker
is stone that resembles jade;
what troubles the sword connoisseur
is swords that resemble Wúgān;
what troubles the wise ruler
is people who are widely learned and eloquent, yet merely seem to be insightful.
The ruler of a ruined state seems wise,
and the minister of a ruined state seems loyal.
Similar things
are a great source of confusion for the ignorant,
but a matter of serious concern for the sages.
Therefore, Mòzǐ wept when he saw diverging paths.
When Zhōu settled in Fēng and Hào, it was near the Róng people.
They made a covenant with the feudal lords:
high signal towers were erected along the royal road,
with drums placed on top,
so that signals could be heard far and near.
If Róng invaders arrived,
the drums would be beaten to signal,
and the armies of the feudal lords would all come to the aid of the Son of Heaven.
Once, Róng invaders did arrive.
King Yōu beat the drum,
the armies of the feudal lords all arrived,
and BāoSì was greatly pleased,
and rejoiced.
King Yōu, wishing BāoSì to laugh,
repeatedly beat the drum.
The armies of the feudal lords repeatedly arrived, but there were no invaders.
Later, when Róng invaders truly arrived,
King Yōu beat the drum,
but the armies of the feudal lords did not arrive.
King Yōu himself
died at the foot of Mount Lì,
becoming a laughingstock for all under Heaven.
This is indeed a case of losing true invaders by means of false invaders.
A worthy person may have small faults that lead to great evils.
BāoSì's downfall
led King Yōu to indulge in trivial pleasures, which resulted in great destruction.
Thus, bodies were separated,
the Three Ducal Ministers and Nine Chief Ministers fled,
this was the cause of BāoSì's death,
and why King Píng moved east,
and why Qín Xiāng and Jìn Wén exerted themselves for the King and were granted land.
North of Liáng, there was the Lígqiū district,
where there was a strange ghost
that was good at imitating the appearance of people's sons, nephews, and siblings.
An old man from the town, returning drunk from the market,
was imitated by the ghost of Lígqiū in the form of his son,
who helped him along the way but tormented him.
When the old man returned,
sobering up, he scolded his son,
saying:
"I am your father,
how could you say I am not loving?
I was drunk,
and you tormented me on the way.
Why?"
His son wept and prostrated himself, saying:
"This is a disaster!
No such thing happened.
You can ask the person from the East Village whom I visited earlier."
His father believed him,
and said:
"Alas!
This must be a strange ghost;
I have indeed heard of it before."
The next day, Duān again drank in the market,
hoping to encounter and stab the ghost to death.
The next morning he went to the market and got drunk.
His true son, fearing that his father would not be able to return,
went to meet him.
The old man saw his true son,
drew his sword, and stabbed him.
The old man's judgment was confused by the one who resembled his son,
and he killed his true son.
To be confused by those who resemble worthies and thus lose true worthies,
this is the wisdom of the old man of Líqiū.
The traces of suspicion and resemblance
must not be left unexamined.
To examine them, one must look to the person himself.
Shùn acted as charioteer,
Yáo sat on the left,
Yǔ sat on the right,
and upon entering a marsh, they asked a herdsboy;
upon entering a body of water, they asked a fisherman.
Why was this?
Because their knowledge was thorough.
When people's sons resemble each other,
their mothers always recognize them,
for their knowledge is thorough.
22.4 The Yīxíng
Fourthly, it is said:
Of what the former kings disliked,
none was more disliked than unknowability.
If unknowable, then the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brothers, friends, and husband and wife are ruined.
If all ten relationships are ruined,
no chaos is greater.
All human relationships depend on the ten relationships for security.
If the ten relationships are abandoned, there is no difference from elk, deer, tigers, and wolves,
and those with more courage will simply dominate.
If unknowable, then there is no secure ruler, no joyful parents,
no honored elder brothers, no close friends, and no respected husband.
The strong and powerful do not necessarily rule as king,
but a king must be strong and powerful.
What does a king rely on to achieve this?
He relies on his prestige and his benefit.
If not strong and powerful, his prestige is not prestigious, and his benefit is not beneficial.
If his prestige is not prestigious, it is insufficient to prohibit;
if his benefit is not beneficial, it is insufficient to encourage.
Therefore, a worthy ruler must make his prestige and benefit unrivaled,
so that when he prohibits, it will surely stop,
and when he encourages, it will surely be done.
With unrivaled prestige and benefit,
if one cares for the people and acts predictably, one becomes king.
With unrivaled prestige and benefit,
if one acts unpredictably, one perishes.
If one is small and weak and unpredictable,
the strong and powerful will suspect them.
It is human nature not to love what one suspects;
if small and weak and greatly unloved, there is no way to survive.
Therefore, the way of unknowability:
a king who practices it fails,
the strong and powerful who practice it are endangered,
and the small and weak who practice it are destroyed.
Today, travelers, seeing a large tree,
will surely take off their clothes, hang their hats, lean their swords, and sleep beneath it.
A large tree is not a person's close relative, intimate friend, or acquaintance,
yet they feel secure like this.
This is trust.
A giant tree on a hill,
people take it as a landmark,
because it is easily recognizable.
How much more so for a worthy!
A worthy's righteousness is recognizable,
thus trust in them is certain.
How much more so for a powerful state!
If a powerful state is truly recognizable,
then its ruler will not have difficulty.
The reason people ride on boats
is because they can float and not sink.
The reason the world esteems noble individuals
is because they can practice righteousness and cannot practice evil and depravity.
Kǒngzǐ divined
and obtained the hexagram Bì.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is not auspicious."
Zǐgòng said:
"But Bì is also beautiful;
why do you say it is not auspicious?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If white is white,
and black is black,
what beauty is there in Bì?"
Therefore, what the worthy dislike in things
is nothing more than having no place [for itself, i.e., being without clear definition or distinction].
Of what the world dislikes,
nothing is more disliked than unknowability.
If unknowable,
thieves will not make appointments with you,
and villains will not conspire with you.
Thieves and villains are great scoundrels,
yet they still find companions.
How much more so if one wishes to achieve great accomplishments?
If one wishes to achieve great accomplishments,
and make all under heaven lightly encouraged to assist them,
then one must be a recognizable worthy.
22.5 The Qiúrén
Fifthly, it is said:
If one's person is stable,
the state secure,
and all under heaven well-governed,
it must be due to worthy individuals.
Of those who ruled all under heaven in antiquity,
seventy-one were sages.
Looking at the Chūnqiū,
from Lǔ Yǐngōng to Āigōng, for twelve generations,
the means by which they gained and lost [power],
their methods were one.
If worthy individuals are obtained,
no state is insecure,
no reputation is not glorious.
If worthy individuals are lost,
no state is not endangered,
no reputation is not disgraced.
The former kings spared no effort in seeking worthy individuals,
descending to the lowest and most humble,
traveling the furthest and enduring the greatest toil.
Yú employed the words of Gōngzhīqí, and Wú employed those of Wǔzǐxū.
If these two states [had listened],
they could have survived even until today.
Thus, a state can have a long life.
If there is one who can increase a person's lifespan,
then no one would not desire it.
Now there is a way to prolong the life of a state,
yet those who rule over people do not seek it.
This is a mistake.
Yáo transmitted all under heaven to Shùn,
treated him with the rites of a feudal lord,
gave him his two daughters as wives,
and his ten sons as ministers.
He personally requested to face north and pay court to him,
which was the utmost humility.
Yīyǐn was a kitchen servant,
Fù Yuè was a bondsman of Yīn.
Both ascended to be prime ministers to the Son of Heaven,
which was the utmost lowliness.
Yǔ went east to the land of Fúmù,
where the sun rises, the nine shoals, the wilderness of Qīngqiāng,
the place of gathered trees,
the mountains that touch the sky,
the valleys of birds, the region of Qīngqiū,
and the land of black teeth.
South to the lands of Jiāozhǐ, Sūnpú, and Xùmán,
the cinnabar grains, lacquer trees, boiling waters, surging currents, and nine yang mountains,
the abode of winged people and naked people,
and the land of immortality.
West to the land of Sānwēi,
below Wūshān,
the people who drink dew and inhale qi,
the mountains of accumulated gold,
and the regions of joined arms, single arms, and three faces.
North to the land of Rénzhèng,
the extremity of the summer sea,
above Héngshān,
the land of Quǎnrónɡ,
the wilderness of Kuāfù,
the abode of Yúqiáng,
and the mountains of accumulated water and accumulated stones.
He did not slacken or grow weary,
worrying about his common people,
his complexion dark and sallow,
his orifices and internal organs obstructed,
his steps never failing to meet,
to seek worthy individuals,
desiring to fully utilize the land's benefits,
which was the utmost toil.
He obtained Táo, Huàyì, Zhēnkuī, Hénggé, and Zhījiāo, five men to assist Yǔ,
hence his accomplishments are inscribed on metal and stone, and recorded on bronze vessels.
In the past, Yáo paid court to Xǔ Yóu in the middle of the Péizé marsh,
saying:
"Ten suns have risen, yet the scorching fire does not cease,
is this not tiresome?
You, Master, are to be the Son of Heaven,
and all under heaven is already governed.
I request to entrust all under heaven to you, Master."
Xǔ Yóu辞曰：
“Is it that the world is not well governed?
But it is already well governed.
Is it for myself?
A chirping bird nesting in the forest,
does not take more than one branch;
a timid mouse drinking from the river,
does not drink more than its fill.
Return it to Your Lordship!
What use is the world to me?”
Thereupon he went to the foot of Jīshān,
on the sunny side of the Yǐngshuǐ River,
plowed and ate,
and to the end of his life showed no desire to rule the world.
Therefore, for a sagacious ruler with regard to sagacious men,
nothing obstructs them;
kinship, affection, habit, and old customs,
are not used to harm them;
thus sagacious men gather there.
Where sagacious men gather,
heaven and earth do not destroy,
ghosts and spirits do not harm,
human affairs do not conspire,
this is the fundamental principle of the five constants.
Gāo Zǐ众疑 took the state,
summoned Nángōng Qián and Kǒng Bóchǎn, and they stopped him with their unanimous objections.
The people of Jìn wanted to attack Zhèng,
and ordered Shū Xiàng to go there as an envoy,
to see if it had capable men or not.
Zǐchǎn composed a poem for him, saying:
“If you think of me with kindness,
I will lift my skirt and cross the Wěi River;
if you do not think of me,
is there no other gentleman?”
Shū Xiàng returned and said:
“Zhèng has capable men;
Zǐchǎn is there,
it cannot be attacked.
Qín and Jīng are nearby,
their poetry shows a different intention,
it cannot be attacked.”
The people of Jìn then ceased their attack on Zhèng.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The 《Shī》 says:
‘There is no rivalry but for men.’
Zǐchǎn spoke once and the state of Zhèng was spared.”
22.6 《Chá Zhuàn》
Sixth says:
One must not fail to scrutinize hearsay,
for after several transmissions, white becomes black,
and black becomes white.
Thus a dog resembles a monkey-like animal (jué),
a jué resembles a macaque (mǔhóu),
a macaque resembles a human,
but a human and a dog are far apart.
This is why the foolish make great errors.
If one hears and verifies, it will be a blessing;
if one hears and does not verify,
it is better not to have heard.
Qí Huán Gōng heard about Guǎnzǐ from Bào Shú,
Chǔ Zhuāng heard about Sūn Shú'áo from Shěn Yǐn Shì,
they verified it,
and thus their states became hegemons among the feudal lords.
King Wú heard about King Yuè Gōujiàn from Tàizǎi Pǐ,
Zhì Bó heard about Zhào Xiāngzǐ from Zhāng Wǔ,
they did not verify,
and thus their states perished and their bodies died.
Whenever one hears words, one must thoroughly deliberate them,
and with regard to people, one must test them with reason.
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
“I heard that Yuèzhèng Kuí had one foot,
is this true?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“In the past, Shùn wished to spread education throughout the world with music,
so he ordered Zhòng Lí to raise Kuí from the wilds and present him,
and Shùn made him Music Master (Yuèzhèng).
Kuí then rectified the six pitches,
harmonized the five sounds,
to communicate with the eight winds,
and the world was greatly submissive.
Zhòng Lí further wished to seek more people,
Shùn said:
‘Music is the essence of heaven and earth,
the measure of gains and losses,
thus only a sage can harmonize the fundamental principles of music.
Kuí is able to harmonize it,
to bring peace to the world.
One such as Kuí is sufficient.’
Therefore it is said Kuí ‘one-foot’,
not that he literally had one foot.”
The Dīng family of Sòng,
having no well at home, went out to draw water,
and always kept one person outside.
When their family dug a well,
they told people:
“We dug a well and gained one person.”
Someone heard it and transmitted it, saying:
“The Dīng family dug a well and gained one person.”
The people of the state repeated it,
and it reached the ear of the Lord of Sòng.
The Lord of Sòng sent someone to ask the Dīng family,
and the Dīng family replied:
“We gained the service of one person,
not that we obtained one person from inside the well.”
Seeking knowledge like this,
it is better not to have heard.
Zǐ Xià went to Jìn,
passing through Wèi,
he heard someone reading a historical record, saying:
“The Jìn army, three pigs (sān shǐ), crossed the river.”
Zǐ Xià said:
“That is incorrect,
it is jì hài.
Indeed ‘jǐ’ and ‘sān’ are similar,
and ‘shǐ’ and ‘hài’ are similar.”
When he arrived in Jìn and inquired about it,
it was indeed said “The Jìn army, jì hài, crossed the river.”
Many words resemble what is wrong but are right,
many resemble what is right but are wrong.
The principles of right and wrong,
must not be left undivided,
this is what the sages are cautious about.
So then, how to be cautious?
By following the nature of things and the nature of humans to judge what is heard, one will succeed.
23.1 《Guì Zhí》
First says:
Among those valued by a sagacious ruler, none are like scholars.
The reason scholars are valued
is for their ability to speak straightforwardly.
If words are straightforward, then the crooked will be revealed.
The trouble with rulers of men
is that they wish to hear of wrongdoing but dislike straightforward words.
This is like blocking its source yet desiring its water,
how can the water arrive?
This is like disparaging what one desires and valuing what one dislikes,
how can what one desires come?
Néng Yì met Qí Xuān Wáng.
King Xuān said:
“I heard that you like to be straightforward,
is that so?”
He replied:
“How can Yì be straightforward?
Yì heard that gentlemen who like to be straightforward
do not reside in chaotic states,
and do not meet corrupt rulers.
Now my person is able to meet the King,
and my home is in Qí,
how can Yì be straightforward?”
King Xuān angrily said:
“He is a rustic fellow!”
and intended to punish him.
Néng Yì said:
“Your servant was fond of good things when young,
and practiced them when grown.
Why can't the King treat a rustic fellow well,
will you thereby proclaim what you like?”
The King then released him.
If someone like Néng Yì were careful in discussing beside the ruler,
he would certainly not flatter the ruler.
If he does not flatter the ruler,
how small would the ruler’s gains be?
This is what sagacious rulers seek,
but what unworthy rulers dislike.
Hú Yuán persuaded Qí Mǐn Wáng, saying:
“The tripods of Yīn are displayed in the court of Zhōu,
its altar covered by the screen of Zhōu,
the sounds of its shields and axes,
are heard in people’s entertainment.
The music of a vanquished state,
must not reach the temple;
the altar of a vanquished state,
must not be seen by heaven;
the vessels of a vanquished state are displayed in the court,
to serve as a warning.
Your Majesty must strive diligently.
Do not let the Grand Bell (Dà Lǚ) of Qí be displayed in the court,
do not let the altar of Tàigōng be covered by a screen,
do not let Qí music fill people’s entertainment.”
The King of Qí did not accept.
Hú Yuán left and cried for the state for three days,
his words were:
“Those who leave first,
wear fine ramie garments;
those who leave later,
fill the prisons.
I now see the people drifting eastward, unaware of where they belong.”
King Qí asked his official,
“What is the law for weeping for the state?”
The official replied,
“Beheading.”
The King said,
“Execute the law.”
The official set up an axe and a block at the eastern gate,
not wishing to kill [Hú Yuán],
but wanting him to leave.
Hú Yuán heard of it and rushed there, passing by.
The official said,
“The law for weeping for the state is beheading.
Is the Master old or confused?”
Hú Yuán said,
“How can I be confused?”
Thereupon he said,
“There was a man who came from the south,
a gudgeon entered and a giant salamander dwelled there, causing the people's court to become wasteland and the state a ruin.
Yīn had Bǐgān,
Wú had Zǐxū,
Qí has Hú Yuán.
If you do not use his words,
and moreover behead him at the eastern gate,
each beheader will compare me to those two men!”
Hú Yuán did not enjoy being beheaded;
the state was already in chaos,
the ruler was already perverse,
and he pitied the altars of soil and grain and the people,
hence he uttered such words.
Uttering such words was not a calm discussion,
but intended to avert disaster,
thus it was certainly close to danger.
This is why Chù Zǐ left,
and why Dá Zǐ died for it.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ attacked Wèi at Fùguō,
personally leading the troops.
When it came to battle,
he stood far away,
and moreover positioned himself behind rhinoceros-hide shields and defensive screens.
He beat the drums, but the soldiers did not advance.
Jiǎnzǐ threw down his drumstick and sighed,
“Alas!
Are the soldiers so quickly exhausted, just like this?”
The officer Xíngrén Zhúguò removed his helmet, held his spear horizontally, and advanced, saying,
“I have heard that
it is also because of the ruler's incompetence,
what exhaustion do the soldiers have?”
Jiǎnzǐ flushed with anger and said,
“If I, the lonely one, had no one to command,
and you personally led this multitude,
and you directly called me incompetent—
if you have an explanation, it is acceptable;
if not, then death.”
He replied,
“In the past, our former ruler Xiàngōng ascended the throne for five years,
annexed nineteen states,
using these very soldiers.
Huìgōng ascended the throne for two years,
indulged in lust and was arrogant and disrespectful,
personally fond of beautiful women;
the Qín people attacked us,
and we retreated seventy *li* from Jiàng,
using these very soldiers.
Wéngōng ascended the throne for two years,
established them with bravery,
thus in three years the soldiers were all resolute and daring;
in the Battle of Chéngpú,
they defeated the Jīng people five times;
they besieged Wèi and took Cáo,
and captured Shíshè;
they established the Son of Heaven's position,
and achieved a respected name throughout the world;
using these very soldiers.
It is also because the ruler cannot manage them;
what exhaustion do the soldiers have?”
Jiǎnzǐ then removed the rhinoceros-hide shields and defensive screens and stood where arrows and stones could reach.
With one drumbeat, all the soldiers charged.
Jiǎnzǐ said,
“To obtain a thousand chariots
is not as good as hearing a single word from Xíngrén Zhúguò.”
Xíngrén Zhúguò can be said to have been able to admonish his ruler.
In the midst of battle,
while drumsticks and drums were being used,
without increasing rewards,
without increasing punishments,
with a single word, all the soldiers were willing to die for their ruler.
23.2 *Zhí Jiàn* (Direct Admonition)
Second:
When words are too extreme, anger arises;
when anger arises, the speaker is in danger.
Who but a worthy person would be willing to risk danger?
If not a worthy person,
they will be seeking personal gain.
What benefit is there for someone seeking gain to risk danger?
Therefore, an unworthy ruler has no worthy people.
Without worthy people, extreme words are not heard;
without hearing extreme words, treacherous people form cliques, and all kinds of evil arise.
If this is the case, there is no way to survive.
The survival of any state,
and the security of any ruler,
must have a reason.
If one does not know the reason,
though it may exist, it will surely perish;
though it may be secure, it will surely be endangered.
Therefore, it must be discussed.
Qí Huángōng, Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shū, and Níng Qī were drinking together.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Huángōng said to Bào Shū,
“Why don't you stand up and offer a toast to me?”
Bào Shū held up his cup and advanced, saying,
“May the Duke not forget his exile in Jǔ.
May Guǎn Zhòng not forget being bound and held in Lǔ.
May Níng Qī not forget his ox-herding and living beneath a cart.”
Huángōng left his mat and bowed twice, saying,
“If I and the Grand Masters can all remember the Master's words,
then the altars of soil and grain of the state of Qí will fortunately be free from danger.”
At this time,
Huángōng could be spoken to with extreme words.
Because he could be spoken to with extreme words,
he could become a hegemon.
Jīng Wénwáng obtained the hound Rúhuáng and the feathered arrow Wǎnlù,
and hunted in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months.
He obtained the consort Dān,
and indulged in lust,
not attending court for a full year.
Bǎo Shēn said,
“The former king divined and appointed me as his tutor;
it was auspicious.
Now the King has obtained the hound Rúhuáng and the feathered arrow Wǎnlù,
hunted in Yúnmèng,
and not returned for three months.
He obtained the consort Dān,
and indulged in lust,
and not attended court for a full year.
The King's crime deserves a caning.”
The King said,
“I, the unworthy one, put aside swaddling clothes and was ranked among the feudal lords;
I wish to request a change, and not be caned.”
Bǎo Shēn said,
“Your servant carries out the former king's command,
and dare not abandon it.
If the King does not receive the caning,
it is abandoning the former king's command.
Your servant would rather be punished by the King,
than be punished by the former king.”
The King said,
“I respectfully obey.”
Then he pulled away his mat,
and the King lay prostrate.
Bǎo Shēn tied fifty fine thorny branches,
knelt and applied them to the King's back.
He did this twice,
and said to the King, “Rise.”
The King said,
“The name of caning is one.
Let it be completed.”
Bǎo Shēn said,
“Your servant has heard that a gentleman is ashamed of it,
a petty man feels pain from it.
If shame does not lead to change,
what good is pain?”
Bǎo Shēn quickly left,
wishing to throw himself into the abyss,
begging for death for his offense.
Wénwáng said,
“This is my, the unworthy one's, fault.
What crime has Bǎo Shēn committed?”
The King then changed his conduct,
summoned Bǎo Shēn,
killed the hound Rúhuáng,
broke the feathered arrow Wǎnlù,
and dismissed the consort Dān.
Afterward, the state of Jīng annexed thirty-nine states.
That the state of Jīng became vast and extensive to this degree
was due to Bǎo Shēn's strength and the merit of his extreme words.
23.3 *Zhī Huà* (Knowing Transformation)
Third:
Indeed, those who serve a ruler with courage do so with their lives.
To speak of death before dying
is not discussed;
with death, whether one knows or does not know is the same.
The value of wisdom,
is in knowing transformation.
Confused rulers, however, are not like this.
When transformation has not yet arrived, they do not know;
when transformation has already arrived, whether they know or do not know is all the same.
There are things that can be overlooked,
and there are things that cannot be overlooked.
When one's person dies and the state perishes,
how can this be overlooked?
This is what wise rulers value,
and what deluded rulers take lightly.
When something is taken lightly,
how can the state avoid peril?
How can one avoid distress?
The path to peril and distress,
to one's death and the state's ruin,
lies in not foreseeing change.
King Fūchā of Wú exemplifies this.
Zǐxū was not ignorant of impending change;
he remonstrated but was not heeded,
hence Wú became ruins,
and disaster reached Hélǘ.
When King Fūchā of Wú was about to attack Qí,
Zǐxū said:
"Impossible.
As for Qí and Wú,
their customs are different,
their languages are not mutually intelligible.
If we gain their territory, we cannot settle it;
if we gain their people, we cannot command them.
As for Wú and Yuè,
their lands adjoin, their territories are linked and connected,
their customs are the same,
their languages are mutually intelligible.
If we gain their territory, we can settle it;
if we gain their people, we can command them.
Yuè's situation regarding us is also thus.
The power of Wú and Yuè cannot coexist.
Yuè to Wú
is like a disease of the heart and abdomen;
though it may not be active,
its wound is deep and internal.
As for Qí to Wú,
it is like a scabies or ringworm,
it does not cause much suffering even if it is there,
and besides, it causes no serious harm.
Now, to release Yuè and attack Qí
is like fearing a tiger yet stabbing a wild boar;
even if you defeat it,
the future trouble will be unending."
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"Impossible.
The reason the King's commands are not obeyed by the great states
is Qí and Jìn.
If the King attacks Qí and defeats it,
then moves his troops to confront Jìn,
Jìn will certainly obey his orders.
Thus, the King will conquer two states with one action,
and the King's commands will certainly be obeyed by the great states."
Fūchā thought this was right,
did not listen to Zǐxū's words,
and adopted Grand Steward Pǐ's strategy.
Zǐxū said:
"Heaven intends to destroy Wú,
thus it will let the King win battles.
If Heaven did not intend to destroy Wú,
it would let the King lose battles."
Fūchā did not listen.
Zǐxū pulled up both his sleeves, strode high, and exited the court,
saying:
"Alas!
The Wú court will surely grow thorns."
Fūchā raised an army to attack Qí,
fought at Àilíng,
greatly defeated the Qí army,
and upon his return, executed Zǐxū.
As Zǐxū was about to die, he said:
"Ah!
How can I get one eye to see the Yuè people enter Wú?"
Then he committed suicide.
Fūchā then took his body and cast it into the river,
gouged out his eyes,
and hung them on the East Gate,
saying:
"Why do you watch the Yuè people enter my land?"
A few years later,
Yuè retaliated against Wú,
destroyed its state,
extinguished its lineage,
demolished its altars of soil and grain,
leveled its ancestral temples,
and Fūchā himself was captured.
As Fūchā was about to die, he said:
"If the dead have knowledge,
how can I face Zǐxū in the underworld?"
Then he covered his face with a funerary cloth and died.
When calamity has not arrived,
it cannot be spoken of;
when calamity has already arrived,
even knowing it is too late.
Therefore, Fūchā's shame at knowing Zǐxū's prophecy
was worse than not knowing it.
Fourthly:
The rulers of doomed states are all alike;
though the times may differ,
and their affairs may vary,
the reason for their ruin is the same:
improper delight.
If delight is improper, the state cannot survive.
A hill of dregs, a pond of wine,
a meat forest used as a rack,
carved pillars and (handcuffing) fettering the feudal lords—
this is improper.
Executing the daughter of Guǐhóu and taking her treasures,
cutting open the shins of those crossing the ford to examine their marrow,
killing Méibó and sending his pickled flesh to King Wén—
this is improper.
King Wén feigned acceptance and reported it to the feudal lords.
Building a house of jade,
constructing a vast palace,
dissecting pregnant women to observe the fetus's development,
killing Bǐgān to examine his heart—
this is improper.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"If his apertures had been clear, Bǐgān would not have died."
This is why Xià and Shāng perished.
Duke Líng of Jìn was without principle,
shooting people from his terrace with pellets and watching them dodge;
he ordered his cook to stew a bear's paw poorly,
killed him,
and had women carry his remains past the court to display his power—
this is improper.
Zhào Dùn repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded.
The Duke resented him
and sent Jǔ Mí to assassinate him.
Jǔ Mí saw him,
could not bear to assassinate him,
and said:
"He never forgets respect,
he is the lord of the people.
To assassinate the lord of the people is disloyal;
to disregard the ruler's command is faithless.
Rather than choose between these two, it is better to die."
Then he struck the locust tree in the courtyard and died.
King Mǐn of Qí, when he fled and resided in Wèi,
