said to Gōng Yùdān:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
Yùdān replied:
"Your Majesty is a wise ruler.
I have heard of ancient men who renounced the world without a trace of resentment;
I have heard of their reputation
and seen their reality in Your Majesty.
Your Majesty is named 'Eastern Emperor,'
and truly distinguishes throughout the world.
Having left your state and residing in Wèi,
your countenance is full,
your complexion radiant,
without any thought of the burden of the state."
The King said:
"Excellent!
Dān understands me.
Since I left my state and resided in Wèi,
my belt has increased by three measures."
King Sòng built an altar as a 'God of Disaster,'
poured blood into a leather sack,
hung it high,
shot arrows at it while wearing armor,
from below,
and the blood fell and flowed onto the ground.
Those around him all congratulated him, saying:
"Your Majesty's wisdom surpasses that of Tāng and Wǔ!
Tāng and Wǔ conquered men,
but now Your Majesty conquers Heaven;
no one can be wiser."
King Sòng was greatly pleased
and drank wine.
Inside the chamber, someone shouted "Long live!",
and everyone in the hall responded.
After those in the hall responded,
everyone downstairs responded.
When those outside the gate and in the courtyard heard it,
none dared not to respond—
this is improper.
Fifthly:
The kings of doomed states
cannot tolerate direct speech.
If direct speech is not tolerated,
then mistakes are not heard,
and good things do not come naturally.
When good things do not come naturally, there is obstruction.
During the time of Duke Mù of Qín,
the Róng were powerful.
Duke Mù of Qín sent them sixteen singing girls and a good steward.
The King of Róng was greatly pleased,
and because of this,
he frequently feasted, day and night without rest.
When his attendants spoke of the Qín invasion,
he would grab his bow and shoot them.
The Qín bandits indeed arrived,
but the Róng King was drunk and lying beneath a wine vessel.
His soldiers were captured (bound) and seized him.
Before he was captured, it could not be known;
once captured, it was no longer unknown.
Even those skilled at persuasion are like this.
Why?
Qí attacked Sòng.
The Sòng King sent someone to scout the whereabouts of the Qí bandits.
The envoy returned
and said:
"The Qí bandits are near,
and the people of the state are afraid."
His attendants all said to the Sòng King:
"This is what is called 'meat inviting maggots.'
With Sòng's strength
and Qí's army's weakness,
how could it be like this?"
The Sòng King, in a rage, had him killed in disgrace.
He again sent someone to observe the Qí bandits.
The envoy reported the same as before,
and the Sòng King again angrily had him killed in disgrace.
This happened three times.
Afterward, he again sent someone to observe:
"The Qí bandits are near,
and the people of the state are afraid."
The envoy met his elder brother.
He said:
"The state is in great danger,
where are you going?"
His younger brother said:
"I am observing the Qí bandits for the King,
not expecting them to be so close,
and the people of the state to be so afraid.
Now I privately worry about those who previously scouted the Qí bandits
all died for reporting that the bandits were near.
Now, if I report the truth,
I die;
if I don't report the truth,
I also fear death;
what should I do?"
His elder brother said:
"If you report the truth,
some will die earlier than their predecessors,
and some will perish earlier than their predecessors."
So, he reported to the King, saying:
"I have absolutely no idea where the Qí bandits are.
The people of the state are very peaceful."
The King was greatly pleased.
His attendants all said:
"Those who died previously deserved it."
The King amply rewarded him with gold.
When the bandits arrived,
the King himself jumped into a chariot and fled,
and this man was able to become rich in another state.
Indeed, when one climbs a mountain and looks down, cattle appear like sheep,
and sheep appear like piglets.
The nature of cattle is not like sheep,
nor is the nature of sheep like piglets;
it is because the vantage point from which one views them is too high,
and then one gets angry at the smallness of the cattle and sheep;
this is the greatest foolishness.
To be foolish and yet dispense rewards and punishments,
this is why the Dài family was wiped out.
Qí Wáng wished to appoint Chúnyú Kūn as tutor to the crown prince.
Kūn declined, saying:
"Your minister is unworthy,
not sufficient to undertake this great responsibility.
It would be better for Your Majesty to choose an elder of the state and appoint him."
Qí Wáng said:
"Sir, do not decline.
How could I expect you to make the crown prince necessarily like me?
I was naturally born with it.
Will you make the crown prince like Yáo for me?
Or like Shùn?"
In all acts of persuasion,
one leads the unwise to listen to the wise,
and makes those who are wrong accept what is right.
If one now considers oneself superior to Yáo and Shùn,
how can one listen to persuasion?
Persuasion will surely not be accepted.
Not hearing means the ruler cannot be preserved.
Qí Xuān Wáng was fond of archery,
and liked people to say he could use strong bows.
The bow he actually used never exceeded three stones,
which he would show to his attendants.
His attendants all tried to draw it,
stopping at the midpoint,
and all said:
"This is no less than nine stones;
who but Your Majesty could use it?"
Xuān Wáng's actual strength
allowed him to use no more than three stones,
yet he believed throughout his life that he used nine stones;
isn't this tragic?
Who but an upright scholar would not flatter the ruler?
Upright scholars in the world,
their scarcity compared to the multitude
is a matter of course.
Therefore, for the ruler of a chaotic state,
the calamity lies in treating three stones as nine stones.
23.6 "Yuán Luàn"
Sixth:
Chaos must have stages.
Great chaos has five,
minor chaos three,
subtle chaos three.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Do not pass through the gate of chaos,"
which is why one keeps far from it.
When considering blessings, one falls short;
when considering misfortune, one exceeds.
This is why one seeks to preserve oneself completely.
Wǔ Wáng gained the world through military might,
and sustained it through civil virtues.
He inverted his spears and unstrung his bows,
showing the world that he would not use military force.
This is how he preserved it.
Jìn Xiàn Gōng established Lí Jī as his consort,
and made Xī Qí the crown prince.
Lì Kè led the people of the state to attack and kill them.
Xún Xī then established his younger brother, Gōngzǐ Zhuó.
After the burial,
Lì Kè again led the people of the state to attack and kill him.
Consequently, Jìn had no ruler.
Gōngzǐ Yí Wú heavily bribed Qín with territory to seek entry.
Qín Mù Gōng led his army to escort him in.
The people of Jìn established him as their ruler;
this was Huì Gōng.
After Huì Gōng was established in Jìn,
he betrayed Qín's favor and did not give the territory.
Qín Mù Gōng led his army to attack Jìn.
Jìn Huì Gōng met him,
and fought with the Qín people at Hán Yuán.
The Jìn army was greatly defeated,
Qín captured Huì Gōng and returned,
imprisoning him at Líng Tái.
In the tenth month,
an agreement was made with Jìn,
Huì Gōng was returned, and the crown prince Yǔ was held as a hostage.
Crown Prince Yǔ escaped and returned.
When Huì Gōng died,
Yǔ was established as ruler;
this was Huái Gōng.
Qín Mù Gōng was angry at his escape and return,
so he raised and supported Gōngzǐ Chóng Ěr to attack Huái Gōng,
killed him at Gāo Liáng,
and established Chóng Ěr;
this was Wén Gōng.
Wén Gōng distributed relief,
revived the neglected and stranded,
aided the poor and distressed,
rescued those in calamity and suffering,
prohibited impropriety and wickedness,
lightened taxes and levies,
pardoned crimes and offenses,
economized on tools and supplies,
employed the people according to the seasons,
defeated the Jīng people at Chéng Pú,
pacified Xiāng Wáng,
lifted the siege of Sòng,
released the garrison at Gǔ,
and both internal and external (affairs) were submissive.
Only then did the chaos in Jìn cease.
Therefore, Xiàn Gōng listened to Lí Jī,
befriended Liáng Wǔ and Yōu Shī,
and killed Crown Prince Shēn Shēng;
subsequently, five great calamities followed,
three rulers died (in confinement),
one ruler was captured,
and ministers and high officials who died numbered in the hundreds,
with twenty years of calamity and suffering.
Since ancient times,
chaos has never been simple,
yet those who worry about chaos
all say it is merely one thing.
In this matter, their deliberations do not align with the truth.
When deliberations do not align with the truth,
their minds are divergent.
Therefore, for all those who incite chaos,
misfortune rarely fails to befall them personally.
24.1 "Bù Gǒu"
First:
The actions of a worthy person,
though noble, are not done lightly;
though listened to, he does not flatter himself.
He must conform to principle before acting,
and must accord with righteousness before moving.
This is the conduct of a loyal minister.
A wise ruler is pleased by this,
and even if an unworthy ruler is unworthy, his pleasure
is not because he dislikes the sound.
Although a ruler may be unworthy,
his pleasure in the voice of a loyal minister is the same as that of a worthy ruler,
but his actual conduct differs from that of a worthy ruler.
Because of this difference, his achievements, fame, misfortune, and fortune also differ.
Because of this difference, Zǐ Xū was appreciated by Hé Lǘ but disliked by Fū Chā,
and Bǐ Gān was disliked by Shāng during his life, but appreciated by Zhōu after his death.
King Wǔ arrived at the outskirts of Yīn.
His harness fell off.
Five men were attending in front of him,
but none of them would pick it up for him.
They said:
"The reason we serve our lord is not to pick up harnesses."
King Wǔ released the white feathers from his left hand,
released the yellow battle-axe from his right hand,
and laboriously picked up the harness himself.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"These five men are the kind who assist a true king,
but incompetent rulers would not feel comfortable with them."
Therefore, there are Son of Heavens who cannot overcome the common people,
and there are those in the world who cannot overcome a state with a thousand chariots.
Qín Mùgōng saw Róng Yóuyú,
was pleased, and wished to retain him,
but Yóuyú refused.
Mùgōng told Jiǎn Shū about this.
Jiǎn Shū said:
"My lord, tell Nèishǐ Liào."
Nèishǐ Liào replied:
"The Róng people are not sophisticated regarding the five tones and the five flavors.
My lord, why not send him a gift?"
Mùgōng sent him sixteen female musicians and an excellent chef as a gift.
The Róng king was delighted,
became utterly confused and disordered,
and drank alcohol
day and night without rest.
Yóuyú frequently remonstrated but was not heeded,
so he became angry and returned to Mùgōng.
Jiǎn Shū was not incapable of doing what Nèishǐ Liào did,
but his sense of righteousness prevented it.
Mùgōng was able to have his ministers always uphold their righteous principles,
thus he avenged the disgrace of Xiáo,
and extended his territory westward to Hé Yōng.
Qín Mùgōng appointed Bǎilǐ Xī as prime minister.
Jìn sent Shú Hǔ, and Qí sent Dōngguō Jiǎn to Qín.
Gōngsūn Zhī requested an audience with them.
The Duke said:
"You wish to see the guests,
is this your business?"
He replied:
"No."
"Did the prime minister send you?"
He replied:
"No."
The Duke said:
"In that case, your business is not your business.
The state of Qín is remote and backward.
Even with the Róng and Yí submitting to us,
and each person attending to their own duties,
we still fear being ridiculed by the other feudal lords.
Now you meddle in business that is not yours.
Withdraw, and I will discuss your punishment."
Gōngsūn Zhī exited,
and positioned himself before Bǎilǐ's residence.
Bǎilǐ Xī pleaded for him.
The Duke said:
"Is this what you heard from the prime minister?
If Zhī is innocent, why do you plead for him?
If he is guilty, why do you plead for him?"
Bǎilǐ Xī returned,
and excused Gōngsūn Zhī.
Gōngsūn Zhī moved,
and positioned himself in the street.
Bǎilǐ Xī ordered his official to carry out the punishment.
To establish clear divisions of official duties —
this is how the ancients created laws.
Now Mùgōng embraced this.
Was it not fitting that he dominated the western Róng?
Jìn Wéngōng was about to attack Yè.
Zhào Shuāi spoke of the method to defeat Yè.
Wéngōng used it,
and indeed defeated Yè.
Upon returning,
he was about to bestow rewards.
Shuāi said:
"Does Your Lord wish to reward the source
or the minor contributors?
If you reward the minor contributors, then only the charioteers and horsemen will be accounted for.
If you reward the source, then your minister heard it from Xì Zǐhǔ."
Wéngōng summoned Xì Zǐhǔ and said:
"Shuāi spoke of the method to defeat Yè.
Now that Yè is defeated,
I am about to reward him.
He said:
'I heard it from Zǐhǔ,
I request that Zǐhǔ be rewarded.'"
Zǐhǔ said:
"Speaking is easy,
acting is difficult.
I was merely the one who spoke."
The Duke said:
"You must not decline."
Xì Zǐhǔ dared not firmly decline,
so he accepted the reward.
In general, when bestowing rewards, one desires them to be broad,
for broadness brings much assistance.
Now Zǐhǔ was not the one who personally spoke,
yet the reward still reached him.
This is why even those far removed will exert their full wisdom.
Jìn Wéngōng was exiled for a long time,
returned, and took advantage of the aftermath of great chaos,
yet was still able to become a hegemon.
Was it not due to this?
24.2 "Praise for Ability"
Second, it says:
The worthy and good employ people by their character,
the mediocre by their deeds,
and the unworthy by their wealth.
To obtain ten excellent horses
is not as good as obtaining one Bólè;
to obtain ten excellent swords
is not as good as obtaining one Ōuyě;
to obtain a thousand li of land
is not as good as obtaining one sage.
Shùn obtained Gāoyáo and Shùn received the empire;
Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn and possessed the people of Xià;
King Wén obtained Lǚ Wàng and subjugated the Yīn-Shāng.
Indeed, in obtaining a sage,
how can it be measured in mere li?
Guǎnzǐ was imprisoned in Lǔ.
Huángōng wished to appoint Bào Shú as prime minister.
Bào Shú said:
"If our lord wishes to be a hegemon,
then Guǎn Yíwú is over there,
and your minister is not his equal."
Huángōng said:
"Yíwú is my enemy,
he shot me.
It is not acceptable."
Bào Shú said:
"Yíwú shot at a person for his lord.
If Your Lord can obtain him and make him your minister,
then he will also shoot at people for Your Lord."
Huángōng did not listen,
and forcibly appointed Bào Shú as prime minister.
Bào Shú firmly declined the appointment,
and Huángōng finally listened to him.
Thereupon, he sent someone to inform Lǔ, saying:
"Guǎn Yíwú is my enemy.
I wish to obtain him and personally lay hands on him."
The Lord of Lǔ agreed,
and then ordered officials to skin his fists,
glue his eyes shut,
put him in a leather bag,
and place him in a carriage.
Upon reaching the border of Qí,
Huángōng sent someone to welcome him with a court carriage,
purified him with a burning torch,
and smeared him with the blood of a boar sacrifice.
He brought him into the state alive,
and ordered the relevant official to remove the mats and tables from the ancestral temple and present him there,
saying:
"Since I, the Orphan, heard Yíwú's words,
my eyes have become brighter,
my ears more acute.
I, the Orphan, dare not keep this for myself;
I dare to report it to my ancestors."
Then he turned and commanded Guǎnzǐ, saying:
"Yíwú, assist me."
Guǎn Zhòng quickly withdrew,
bowed twice and kowtowed,
received the order and exited.
Guǎnzǐ governed the state of Qí,
and every undertaking was successful.
Huángōng would always reward Bào Shú first,
saying:
"The one who enabled the state of Qí to obtain Guǎnzǐ
was Bào Shú."
Huángōng can be said to have known how to bestow rewards.
In general, when bestowing rewards, one desires to reward the source,
for if the source is rewarded, then mistakes will have no way to arise.
Sūnshū Áo and Shěnyǐn Jīng were friends.
Shū Áo traveled in Yǐng for three years,
but his reputation was unknown,
and his conduct was unheard of.
Shěnyǐn Jīng said to Sūnshū Áo:
"To explain righteousness to be heard,
to act faithfully according to methods,
to be able to enable a ruler to reach the level of a king,
or at least a hegemon —
I am not as good as you.
But to adapt to the times and conform to customs,
to explain righteousness in a moderate way,
so as to suit the ruler's mind —
you are not as good as I am.
Why do you not return home to farm?
I will travel on your behalf."
Shěn Yǐnjīng (沈尹莖) sojourned in Yǐng (郢) for five years.
King Jīng (荊) wished to appoint him as Lingyǐn (令尹).
Shěn Yǐnjīng (沈尹莖) declined, saying:
"Among the humble people of Qīsī (期思) there is a Sūn Shū'áo (孫叔敖),
who is a sage.
If Your Majesty must employ someone,
I am not his equal."
King Jīng (荊) thereupon sent someone with the royal carriage to welcome Sūn Shū'áo (孫叔敖) and made him Lingyǐn (令尹).
Twelve years later, King Zhuāng (莊王) achieved hegemony.
This was due to Shěn Yǐnjīng's (沈尹莖) effort.
No merit is greater than advancing the worthy.
24.3 Self-Knowledge
Thirdly, it says:
To know what is level and straight,
one must use a plumb line and a chalk line;
to know what is square and round,
one must use a compass and a square.
If a ruler wishes to know himself,
he must have upright officials.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven appoints辅弼 (fǔbì) (advisors)
and establishes师保 (shībǎo) (tutors),
to point out his faults.
Indeed, people cannot know themselves;
a ruler is no different.
Survival and demise, safety and danger,
do not seek them externally;
the crucial thing is self-knowledge.
Yáo (堯) had a drum for those wishing to admonish him,
Shùn (舜) had a "slander post" (诽谤之木),
Tāng (湯) had upright officials who pointed out his faults,
King Wǔ (武王) had a warning drum (戒慎之鞀),
yet they still feared they could not know themselves.
Now, if one is not as sagely as Yáo (堯), Shùn (舜), Tāng (湯), or Wǔ (武),
and yet has means of concealment,
how can one know oneself?
Jīng Chéng (荊成) and Qí Zhuāng (齊莊) did not know themselves and were killed;
King Wú (吳王) and Zhì Bó (智伯) did not know themselves and perished;
Sòng (宋) and Zhōngshān (中山) did not know themselves and were annihilated;
Jìn Huì Gōng (晉惠公) and Zhào Kuò (趙括) did not know themselves and were captured;
Zuān Tú (鑽荼), Páng Juān (龐涓), and Prince Shēn (太子申) did not know themselves and died.
Therefore, no defeat is greater than not knowing oneself.
When the Fàn (范) clan perished,
there was a commoner who obtained one of their bells.
He wanted to carry it off,
but the bell was too large to carry.
He tried to smash it with a hammer.
The bell gave a resounding ring.
Fearing that others would hear it and take it from him,
he hastily covered his ears.
It is understandable to not want others to hear it,
but it is perverse not to want oneself to hear it.
For a ruler to not want to hear his faults,
is this not similar?
Not wanting others to hear his faults is still somewhat understandable.
(Not wanting oneself to hear one's own faults is perverse.)
Wèi Wén Hóu (魏文侯) was feasting,
and he ordered all the grandees to discuss him.
Some praised his wisdom.
When it came to Rèn Zuò (任座),
Rèn Zuò (任座) said:
"Your Lordship is an unworthy ruler.
You obtained Zhōngshān (中山) but did not enfeoff your younger brother with it,
instead enfeoffing your son.
This is how I know Your Lordship is unworthy."
Wén Hóu (文侯) was displeased,
which showed in his countenance.
Rèn Zuò (任座) hurried out.
Next was Zhái Huáng (翟黃).
Zhái Huáng (翟黃) said:
"Your Lordship is a worthy ruler.
I have heard that when a lord is worthy,
his officials speak straightforwardly.
Today, Rèn Zuò's (任座) words were straightforward;
this is how I know Your Lordship is worthy."
Wén Hóu (文侯) rejoiced and said:
"Can he be brought back?"
Zhái Huáng (翟黃) replied:
"Why not?
I have heard that loyal officials complete their loyalty
and dare not shrink from death.
Rèn Zuò (任座) is probably still at the gate."
Zhái Huáng (翟黃) went to look for him;
Rèn Zuò (任座) was indeed at the gate.
He summoned him with the lord's command.
Rèn Zuò (任座) entered.
Wén Hóu (文侯) descended the steps to welcome him
and throughout the banquet treated him as an honored guest.
If Wén Hóu (文侯) had not had Zhái Huáng (翟黃),
he would nearly have lost a loyal official.
To conform to the lord's wishes and thereby highlight the worthy,
was that not Zhái Huáng (翟黃)?
24.4 On Rewards
Fourthly, it says:
People have no way of directly knowing Heaven;
people know Heaven by the movements of the four seasons, cold and heat, sun, moon, and stars.
When the movements of the four seasons, cold and heat, sun, moon, and stars are proper,
then all living creatures with blood and breath will find their proper place and live in peace.
Similarly, officials have no way of directly knowing their lord;
officials know their lord by where rewards, punishments, titles, and emoluments are bestowed.
When the lord's bestowal of rewards, punishments, titles, and emoluments is appropriate,
then relatives and strangers, distant and near, worthy and unworthy, will all exert their full strength and be put to use.
When Jìn Wén Gōng (晉文公) returned to his state,
he rewarded those who had followed him in exile,
but Táo Hú (陶狐) was not included.
His attendants said:
"Your Lordship has returned to your state,
titles and emoluments have been distributed three times,
yet Táo Hú (陶狐) has not been included.
May we ask why?"
Wén Gōng (文公) said:
"Those who aided me with righteousness and guided me with ritual,
I consider them for the highest rewards.
Those who taught me goodness and urged me towards worthiness,
I consider them for the second-tier rewards.
Those who thwarted my desires and frequently pointed out my faults,
I consider them for the lowest rewards.
These three categories are for rewarding meritorious officials.
If I were to reward the laborers of Tángguó (唐國),
then Táo Hú (陶狐) would be first among them."
Zhōu Nèi Shǐ Xīng (周內史興) heard this and said:
"Jìn Gōng (晉公) will surely achieve hegemony!
In ancient times, the sagely kings prioritized virtue over strength,
and Jìn Gōng (晉公) is now aligning with that."
The young Lord's wife of Qín (秦) used a eunuch to seize power (奄變).
All worthy men were displeased and went into hiding,
while the common people harbored resentment and criticized the authorities.
Gōngzǐ Lián (公子連), who had fled to Wèi (魏),
heard of this
and wished to return. He then led his officials and people to the pass at Zhèngsuǒ (鄭所).
Yòu Zhǔrán (右主然) was guarding the pass
and did not allow him to enter,
saying:
"I have integrity;
I serve not two lords.
Prince, please leave."
Gōngzǐ Lián (公子連) left,
entered Dí (翟),
and approached the pass at Yānshì (焉氏).
Jūn Gǎi (菌改) let him in.
The wife heard of this
and was greatly alarmed.
She ordered officials to raise troops,
issuing a command that said:
"There are bandits on the border."
When the troops and officials first set out,
they all said "we are going to attack bandits."
Midway, they changed their tune, saying:
"We are not attacking bandits;
we are welcoming our lord."
Gōngzǐ Lián (公子連) then came with the troops.
Upon arriving at Yōng (雍),
they surrounded the wife,
and she committed suicide.
Gōngzǐ Lián (公子連) was enthroned;
he became Xiàn Gōng (獻公).
He resented Yòu Zhǔrán (右主然) and intended to severely punish him,
but favored Jūn Gǎi (菌改) and wished to richly reward him.
Jiān Tū (監突) argued against this, saying:
"This is unacceptable.
There are many Qín (秦) princes in exile.
If you do this, officials will compete to bring back exiled princes.
This is not beneficial to the lord."
Xiàn Gōng (獻公) considered this to be true.
Therefore, he pardoned Yòu Zhǔrán's (右主然) offense,
and bestowed Jūn Gǎi (菌改) with the title of Grandee (官大夫),
and gave the pass-guards twenty *shi* (石) of rice each.
Xiàn Gōng (獻公) can be said to have been skilled in using rewards and punishments.
In general, rewards are not given out of love,
and punishments are not inflicted out of hatred;
they are used to observe what people will incline towards.
If what they incline towards is good,
they are rewarded even if disliked;
if what they incline towards is not good,
they are punished even if loved.
This is how the former kings brought order to chaos and ensured safety in peril.
24.5 Concentrating Will
Fifthly, it says:
The former kings had great undertakings,
and they removed those who hindered them.
Thus, what they desired was surely obtained,
and what they detested was surely eliminated.
This is how their achievements and fame were established.
Common rulers, however, are not like this.
They have great undertakings but cannot remove those who hinder them.
This is why they achieve nothing.
Indeed, whether one removes hindering factors or cannot remove them,
this is where the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy lies.
If deer run swiftly,
horses cannot catch up.
If one later obtains them,
it is because of their momentary pause.
A *jì* (fine steed) can travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day
if its carriage is light;
if it carries a heavy load, it cannot go even a few *lǐ*,
because its burden is heavy.
When a worthy person undertakes a task,
it is not heard that they fail to achieve results;
yet, if their fame is not widely established, and their benefits do not reach the world,
it is because the foolish and unworthy are tasked with implementing it.
Winter and summer cannot both inflict their extremes,
weeds and crops cannot both flourish,
new grain ripens and old grain diminishes,
all horned creatures lack upper incisors,
trees that bear abundant fruit must be short,
those whose wisdom is narrow will achieve no lasting success—
these are the laws of Heaven.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven does not occupy the state of completeness,
does not occupy the state of extremity,
does not occupy the state of overflowing.
For complete things will surely diminish,
extreme things will surely reverse,
and overflowing things will surely dwindle.
The former kings knew that things cannot both be great,
thus they chose their tasks,
and positioned themselves appropriately.
Kǒng, Mò, and Níng Yuè
were all commoners,
who deliberated for the world,
believing that there was no better method than that of the former kings,
and so they studied it day and night.
If something was beneficial to learning,
they would do it without fail;
if something was not beneficial to learning,
they would never do it.
It is said that Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí,
during the day, recited and practiced their studies,
and at night personally saw Wén Wáng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn and questioned them.
With such refined dedication,
what task would not be achieved?
What endeavor would not be completed?
Therefore, it is said: refine and master it,
and spirits will tell you.
It is not spirits telling you,
but the refinement and mastery itself.
Now, if there is a precious sword and a fine horse here,
one admires them without satiety,
looks at them without weariness.
If one values good conduct and a good path,
yet deviates from it and never returns,
desiring the body's security,
and the name's prominence,
is this not difficult?
Níng Yuè, a commoner from Zhōngmóu,
suffered from the toil of farming,
and said to his friend:
"What can one do to be free from this suffering?"
His friend replied:
"Nothing is better than learning.
If you study for thirty years, you can achieve success."
Níng Yuè said:
"Please allow me fifteen years.
When others rest,
I will not dare to rest;
when others sleep,
I will not dare to sleep."
After fifteen years, Zhōu Wēi Gōng made him his teacher.
An arrow's speed, though swift, does not exceed two *lǐ*,
then it stops;
a step's slowness, though slow, can reach a hundred *shè*,
if it does not stop.
Now, with Níng Yuè's talent, and never stopping,
is it not fitting
that he should be a teacher to the feudal lords?
Yǎng Yóujī and Yǐn Rú
were both masters of the six arts.
In the court of Jīng, there was once a divine white ape.
None of Jīng's expert archers could hit it.
The King of Jīng asked Yǎng Yóujī to shoot it.
Yǎng Yóujī bent his bow, grasped an arrow, and went.
Before he shot it, he had already anticipated where to hit it;
when he released the arrow, the ape responded to the arrow and fell.
Thus, Yǎng Yóujī had the ability to anticipate the target before hitting it.
Yǐn Rú studied charioteering for three years and could not master it.
He suffered greatly from this frustration.
One night, he dreamt he was taught "autumn driving" by his master.
The next morning, when he went to pay his respects,
his master looked at him and said:
"It is not that I begrudge teaching you the Way,
but I feared you were not yet ready to receive it.
Today I shall teach you autumn driving."
Yǐn Rú walked backwards,
knelt facing north, and bowed twice, saying:
"Just last night, your servant dreamt of receiving it."
He first told his master his dream,
and what he dreamt was indeed autumn driving.
(Above) These two gentlemen can be said to have been able to learn,
and can be said to have been free from harm.
This is why they serve as models for later generations.
24.6 "Valuing What is Appropriate"
Sixth:
Great fame and reputation
cannot be strenuously sought;
they must follow their proper course.
One who governs things does not focus on things but on people;
one who governs people does not focus on affairs but on the ruler;
one who governs the ruler does not focus on the ruler but on the Son of Heaven;
one who governs the Son of Heaven does not focus on the Son of Heaven but on desires;
one who governs desires does not focus on desires but on nature (*xìng*).
Nature is the root of all things;
it cannot be lengthened,
it cannot be shortened.
Let it be as it naturally is.
This is the law of Heaven and Earth.
When red meat is exposed, crows and magpies gather;
when a wildcat is in the hall, all rats scatter;
when mourning attire is displayed, people know it is a funeral;
when *yú* and *sè* are displayed, people know it is music.
Tāng and Wǔ cultivated their conduct and the world followed;
Jié and Zhòu neglected their conduct and the world rebelled.
Why await their words?
A *jūnzǐ* examines only what is within himself.
In Jīng, there was a skilled physiognomist,
whose predictions never missed,
and he was renowned throughout the state.
Zhuāng Wáng met him and asked.
He replied:
"I am not skilled at physiognomy,
but I can observe a person's friends.
When I observe a commoner,
if all his friends are filial, fraternal, pure, cautious, and obedient,
then such a person's family
will surely prosper daily,
and his person will surely be honored daily.
This is what is called an auspicious person.
When I observe one who serves a ruler,
if all his friends are sincere, trustworthy, active in good deeds, and fond of virtue,
then such a person
will daily advance in serving the ruler,
and his official position will daily progress.
This is what is called an auspicious minister.
When I observe a ruler,
if his court officials are mostly worthy,
and his attendants are mostly loyal,
and if the ruler makes a mistake,
they all contend and strongly admonish him,
then such a ruler's state
will daily be secure,
the ruler will daily be honored,
and the world will daily submit.
This is what is called an auspicious ruler.
I am not skilled at physiognomy,
but I can observe a person's friends."
Zhuāng Wáng approved of this,
and thereupon eagerly gathered scholars,
working day and night without ceasing,
and eventually dominated the world.
Therefore, when a worthy ruler sees people of literary and artistic talent,
it is not merely to possess them,
but to accomplish great undertakings.
Indeed, matters, whether great or small,
are inherently interconnected.
Hunting and chasing,
shooting birds and running dogs—
worthy people do engage in these,
and doing so, their wisdom daily increases.
Unworthy rulers engage in these, and their wisdom daily becomes more confused.
The *Zhì* says:
"For affairs of arrogance and delusion,
what else but ruin can await?"
There was a lord who was fond of hunting.
He spent many days and long periods but could not catch any beasts.
When he returned, he was ashamed before his family,
and when he went out, he was ashamed before his friends and neighbors.
The reason he could not catch anything
was that his dogs were bad.
He wanted good dogs,
but his family was poor and had no means.
So he returned and diligently farmed.
With diligent farming, his family became wealthy.
With wealth, he had the means to seek good dogs.
With good dogs, he frequently caught beasts,
and his hunting gains always surpassed others.
This is true not only for hunting,
but for all matters.
There has never been a hegemonic king in ancient or modern times
who became a hegemonic king without first farming.
This is the difference between the worthy and the unworthy.
What the worthy and unworthy desire is the same as what other people desire;
Yáo, Jié, Yōu, and Lì were all like this.
It is their method of achieving it that differs.
Therefore, a wise ruler examines this,
considers it infeasible,
and does not do it;
considers it feasible,
and therefore does it.
To do it, one must follow its Way.
Nothing can harm it.
This is why achievements differ by a factor of ten thousand.
25.1 《Sìshùn》
One says:
Many matters appear perverse but are actually顺,
and many appear 顺 but are actually perverse.
One who knows what appears 顺 to be perverse, and what appears perverse to be 顺,
can be spoken with about transformation.
The utmost long becomes short,
the utmost short becomes long—
this is the Way of Heaven.
Jīng Zhuāngwáng (King Zhuāng of Jīng) wanted to attack Chén (陳),
and sent someone to scout it.
The envoy said:
“Chén cannot be attacked.”
King Zhuāng said:
“Why?”
He replied:
“Its city walls are high,
its moats are deep,
and its stores are abundant.”
Níngguó (寧國) said:
“Chén can be attacked.
Chén is a small state,
yet its stores are abundant,
meaning its taxes are heavy.
Then the people resent their superiors.
Its city walls are high,
and its moats are deep,
meaning the people’s strength is exhausted.
If we raise an army to attack it,
Chén can be taken.”
King Zhuāng listened to him, and consequently took Chén.
The reason Tián Chéngzǐ (田成子) obtained the state and held it until now,
was that he had an elder brother named Wánzǐ (完子),
who was benevolent and brave.
The Yuè (越) people raised an army to punish Tián Chéngzǐ, saying:
“Why did you kill your lord and seize the state?”
Tián Chéngzǐ was troubled by this.
Wánzǐ requested to lead the officers and common people to resist the Yuè (越) army,
requested to surely fight,
requested to surely be defeated in battle,
and requested to surely die in defeat.
Tián Chéngzǐ said:
“It is acceptable to surely fight the Yuè (越).
To be surely defeated in battle,
and to surely die in defeat,
this寡人 doubts.”
Wánzǐ said:
“Your having the state,
the common people resent their superiors,
and the worthy and good ones die for it, while your servant bears the shame.
From your servant Wán’s (完) observation,
the state is already fearful.
Now the Yuè (越) people have raised an army.
Your servant will fight them.
If we fight and are defeated, all the worthy and good will die.
Those who do not die will not dare to enter the state.
Your Lord will remain in the state with the orphans.
From your servant’s observation,
the state will surely be secure.”
Wánzǐ set off.
Tián Chéngzǐ wept as he saw him off.
Now death and defeat
are what people hate,
yet they were considered a means to security.
How can this be the same Way?
Therefore, rulers who listen and scholars who learn
must be broad-minded.
Yǐn Duó (尹鐸) was the governor of Jìnyáng (晉陽).
He had a request from Zhào Jiǎnzǐ (趙簡子).
Jiǎnzǐ said:
“Go and level those ramparts.
I will be coming.
If I come and see the ramparts,
it will be like Zhōngháng Yín (中行寅) and Fàn Jíshè (范吉射).”
Duó went and increased them instead.
Jiǎnzǐ arrived at Jìnyáng,
saw the ramparts from a distance, and angrily said:
“Alas!
Duó (鐸) has deceived me.”
Thereupon, he encamped in the suburbs,
intending to send men to execute Duó (鐸).
Sūn Míng (孫明) advanced and remonstrated, saying:
“From your servant’s private view,
Duó (鐸) should be rewarded.
Duó’s (鐸) words indeed said:
‘When one sees pleasure, one becomes extravagant and indulgent.
When one sees worry, one becomes [諍] orderly and governs well.
This is the way of people.
Now, when you see the ramparts, you think of worries and troubles.
How much more so for your ministers and people?
If it benefits the state and is advantageous to the ruler,
even if it involves wrongdoing,
Duó (鐸) will do it.
As for those who follow orders to gain favor,
the multitude can do that,
how much more so Duó (鐸)?’
Please consider this.”
Jiǎnzǐ said:
“Without your words,
寡人 would have almost erred.”
Thereupon, he rewarded Yǐn Duó (尹鐸) with the reward for escaping calamity.
For a ruler,
the best is to always act according to principle in joy and anger.
Next best is not to act according to principle,
but to frequently change.
Even if one does not reach the level of a great sage,
this is still sufficient to cover a corrupt age.
Jiǎnzǐ was of this kind.
The trouble with worldly rulers
is being ashamed of not knowing but prideful in self-reliance,
liking to repeat mistakes and disliking to hear remonstrance,
thus leading to danger.
There is no greater shame than danger.
25.2 《Biélèi》
Two says:
To know what one does not know is superior.
The trouble with erring people
is not knowing but believing oneself to know.
Many things appear to be one way but are not, hence endless failed states and humiliated people.
As for grasses, there is the shēn (莘) and the lěi (藟).
Eaten alone, they kill people;
eaten together, they prolong life.
Ten thousand kinds of aconite do not kill.
Lacquer is viscous, water is viscous.
If two viscous things are mixed, they become firm;
if moistened, they become dry.
Gold is soft, tin is soft.
If two soft things are mixed, they become hard;
if fired, they become soft.
Some become dry when wet,
some become soft when fired.
Similarities cannot necessarily be used for deduction.
A small square and a large square are of the same kind.
A small horse and a large horse are of the same kind.
Small wisdom and great wisdom are not of the same kind.
There was a man from Lǔ (魯) named Gōngsūn Chuò (公孫綽),
who told people:
“I can raise the dead.”
People asked him why.
He replied:
“I can cure paralysis.
Now, if I double the medicine I use for paralysis, I can raise the dead.”
Indeed, some things can be used for small amounts but not for large amounts,
can be used for a part but not for the whole.
A sword appraiser said:
“White is what makes it hard,
yellow is what makes it flexible.
If yellow and white are mixed, it will be both hard and flexible,
a good sword.”
A challenger said:
“White is what makes it inflexible,
yellow is what makes it not hard.
If yellow and white are mixed, it will be neither hard nor flexible.
Moreover, if it is soft, it will bend;
if it is hard, it will break.
A sword that breaks and bends,
how can it be considered a sharp sword?”
The nature of the sword has not changed,
yet some consider it good,
and some consider it bad.
It is the explanation that causes this.
Therefore, if one uses intelligence to listen to explanations, false explanations will cease.
If one does not use intelligence to listen to explanations, there will be no distinction between Yáo (堯) and Jié (桀).
This is what troubles loyal ministers,
and why worthy people are dismissed.
Righteousness: if done on a small scale, there is small fortune;
if done on a large scale, there is great fortune.
With misfortune, it is not so:
having a little is not as good as having none.
One who shoots at a target wants to hit the small center.
One who shoots at an animal wants to hit a large area.
Things are not necessarily fixed;
how can they be inferred?
Gāoyáng Yīng (高陽應) was about to build a house.
The carpenter replied:
“Not yet.
The wood is still green.
If plaster is applied to it,
it will surely bend.
If a house is built with green wood,
even if it seems good now,
it will surely fail later.”
Gāoyáng Yìng replied:
"No.
According to your words,
the house would not collapse.
For wood, the drier it gets, the stronger it becomes;
mortar, the drier it gets, the lighter it becomes.
To use stronger wood to bear lighter mortar means it will not collapse."
The craftsman had no words to reply,
accepted the order, and did as he was told.
When the house was first completed, it was good,
but afterward, it indeed collapsed.
Gāoyáng Yìng was fond of petty observations,
but did not comprehend the greater principles.
Jì'áo and Lǜ'ěr ran west with the sun at their backs,
but by evening, the sun was in front of them.
The eyes inherently have things they cannot see;
wisdom inherently has things it does not know;
calculations inherently have things they cannot reach.
Not knowing the explanation of why something is so,
the sage accordingly establishes systems,
without exerting his own mind.
25.3 Yǒudù
Thirdly, it says:
A sagacious ruler listens with measure,
thus he does not err.
When he listens with measure,
then he cannot be deceived,
cannot be alarmed,
cannot be frightened,
cannot be pleased.
With the understanding of ordinary people,
they are not confused by what they already know,
but confused by what they do not know.
Thus people are easily deceived,
can be alarmed,
can be frightened,
can be pleased.
Their knowledge is not discerning.
A guest asked Jìzǐ:
"How do you know the ability of Shùn?"
Jìzǐ replied:
"Yáo had already governed the world well;
Shùn spoke of governing the world, and his words matched Yáo's understanding.
Thus I knew his ability."
"Even if you know that,
how do you know he wasn't selfish?"
Jìzǐ replied:
"Those who are able to govern the world
must inherently comprehend the truths of human nature and destiny.
(Those who comprehend the truths of human nature and destiny)
will naturally be selfless.
In summer one does not wear furs;
it is not that one dislikes furs,
but that there is surplus warmth.
In winter one does not use a fan;
it is not that one dislikes a fan,
but that there is surplus coolness.
The sage's not being selfish
is not because he dislikes honor,
but because he restrains himself.
If one restrains oneself,
even a greedy and corrupt heart would stop,
how much more so a sage?"
Xǔ Yóu was not powerful;
he had comprehended something.
When one has comprehended something, then the benefits of greed and corruption are externalized.
The disciples and followers of Kǒng and Mò filled the world,
all teaching the methods of benevolence and righteousness throughout the world.
Yet they found no place to implement them.
If the teachers' methods could not be implemented,
how much less those who were taught?
Why is this?
Because the methods of benevolence and righteousness are external.
For the external to overcome the internal,
even an ordinary man on foot cannot achieve it,
how much less a ruler?
Only by comprehending the truths of human nature and destiny
will the methods of benevolence and righteousness be implemented spontaneously.
The former kings could not know everything,
yet by grasping one principle, all things were governed.
What prevents people from grasping one principle
is that things influence them.
Therefore it is said to clarify conflicting intentions,
resolve confused thoughts,
remove the burdens on virtue,
and unblock the obstacles to the Dao.
Nobility, wealth, prominence, authority, fame, and profit – these six
are what conflict with intentions.
Countenance, demeanor, expression, reasoning, temperament, and will – these six
are what confuse the mind.
Dislike, desire, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure – these six
are what burden virtue.
Wisdom, ability, departure, engagement, taking, and relinquishing – these six
are what obstruct the Dao.
If these four sets of six do not agitate the chest, then one is upright.
If upright, then tranquil;
if tranquil, then clear and bright;
if clear and bright, then empty;
if empty, then one acts without doing and yet nothing is left undone.
25.4 Fēnzhí
Fourthly, it says:
The former kings used what was not theirs
as if it were their own.
This is to comprehend the way of a ruler.
The ruler
resides in emptiness and simplicity, without wisdom,
thus he can make the multitude wise;
he is inherently without ability,
thus he can make the multitude able;
he maintains non-action,
thus he can make the multitude act.
Being without wisdom, without ability, without action –
these are what the ruler upholds.
What confuses rulers, however, is otherwise:
they assert their own wisdom,
assert their own ability,
assert their own actions.
This is to occupy the position of a minister.
To occupy the position of a minister and yet desire to avoid obstruction,
even Shùn could not do it.
King Wǔ had five assistants.
King Wǔ was incompetent in the affairs of these five men,
yet the world universally says:
"King Wǔ was the one who seized the world."
Thus King Wǔ used what was not his
as if it were his own,
having comprehended the way of a ruler.
Having comprehended the way of a ruler,
he can command the wise to plan,
can command the brave to be enraged,
can command the eloquent to speak.
As for horses,
Bólè assesses them,
Zàofù drives them,
a sagacious ruler rides them.
They travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day,
and the ruler gains their achievement without the toil of the driver or assessor.
Thus he knows how to ride.
Now, when a guest is invited,
and in the midst of wine,
singing, dancing, playing the *sè* and the *yú* occur,
the next day the guest does not bow to those who entertained him,
but bows to the host.
It is the host who made it happen.
The former kings' establishment of merits and fame
is similar to this.
By making the multitude able and the multitude sagacious,
great merits and fame were established in the world.
Credit is not given to their assistants,
but to their ruler,
for it was their ruler who made it happen.
It is like building a palace:
one must employ skilled craftsmen.
Why?
It is said:
"If the craftsman is not skilled, the palace will not be good."
Now, a state is a weighty matter;
if it is not good,
how can it be compared to mere palaces?
Skilled craftsmen build palaces:
to make a circle, they must use a compass;
to make a square, they must use a set square;
to make it level and straight, they must use a level and a plumb line.
When the work is completed,
one does not recognize the compass, set square, plumb line, and ink line,
but rewards the skilled craftsman.
When the palace is completed,
one does not recognize the skilled craftsmen,
but everyone says:
"Excellent!
This is the palace of such-and-such a lord, such-and-such a king."
This cannot be overlooked.
Rulers who do not comprehend the way of a ruler, however, are otherwise:
they try to do the work of others themselves and fail,
they dislike employing the sagacious,
and they consult with the unworthy.
This is why merits and fame are damaged,
and why the state is endangered.
Jujubes
belong to the thornbush;
fur coats
belong to the fox.
To eat the jujubes of the thornbush
and wear the skins of foxes,
the former kings indeed used what was not theirs,
and possessed it as their own.
Tāng and Wǔ in one day gained possession of all the people of Xià and Shāng,
gained possession of all the lands of Xià and Shāng,
gained possession of all the wealth of Xià and Shāng.
Because their people were at peace, no one in the world
dared to endanger them;
because their lands were bestowed, no one in the world dared to be displeased;
because their wealth was rewarded, everyone in the world eagerly encouraged it.
Without spending anything in Yì or Qízhōu,
the world praised them as greatly benevolent and greatly righteous,
understanding the use of what was not their own.
Bái Gōngshèng obtained the state of Jīng,
but could not distribute its treasury and granaries to the people.
Seven days later,
Shí Qǐ entered and said:
"Calamity is approaching!
If you cannot distribute it to the people, then burn it,
do not let others use it to harm us."
Bái Gōng was still unable to do so.
Nine days later,
Yè Gōng entered,
and then distributed the wealth from the grand treasury to the masses,
brought out weapons from the high arsenal to arm the people,
and consequently attacked him.
Nineteen days later, Bái Gōng died.
To desire to possess a state that is not one's own
can be called extreme greed;
to be unable to act for others,
and also unable to act for oneself,
can be called extreme foolishness.
Bái Gōng's stinginess
was like an owl's love for its young.
Wèi Línggōng was digging a pond in cold weather.
Wǎn Chūn remonstrated, saying:
"Starting a labor project in cold weather,
I fear it will harm the people."
The Duke said:
"Is it cold?"
Wǎn Chūn said:
"Your Lord wears a fox fur robe,
sits on a bear skin mat,
and has stoves in the corners;
therefore you are not cold.
But now the people's clothes are tattered and not mended,
their shoes are torn and not repaired.
You are not cold,
but the people are cold."
The Duke said:
"Excellent!"
And ordered the work stopped.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"Your Lord was digging a pond,
not knowing the coldness of the weather,
but Chūn knew it.
Because Chūn knew it and persuaded you to stop,
fortune will go to Chūn,
and resentment will go to Your Lord."
The Duke said:
"Not so.
Chūn
is a common man of the state of Lǔ,
and I promoted him.
The people have not yet seen this.
Now I will let the people see it through this.
Moreover, if Chūn possesses goodness,
is Chūn's goodness not my goodness?"
Línggōng's discussion of Wǎn Chūn
can be called understanding the way of a ruler.
A ruler fundamentally has no specific duties,
but accepts duties through appointments.
Skill and clumsiness are for subordinates,
rewards and punishments are for the law;
what does the ruler do?
If this is the case, those who receive rewards will have no self-congratulation,
and those who suffer punishment will have no resentment,
people will merely reflect on themselves.
This is the ultimate in governance.
25.5 《Chǔfēn》
Fifth:
All governance must first establish distinctions.
When ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife—
these six roles are in their proper places—
then subordinates will not overstep their bounds and superiors will not act arbitrarily,
the young will not be unruly and the old will not be disrespectful.
Metal and wood have different functions,
water and fire have distinct tasks,
yin and yang are not the same,
yet their benefit to the people is one.
Therefore, distinction is what brings peace to commonality,
and commonality is what endangers distinction.
The distinction between commonality and difference,
the separation of noble and humble,
the righteousness of elder and younger—
these were carefully considered by the former kings,
and are the principles of order and disorder.
Now, an archer measures a hair but misses the wall;
a painter measures a hair but alters the appearance.
This speaks of carefully examining the root.
If the root is not carefully examined,
even Yáo and Shùn could not bring order.
Therefore, all disorder
must begin from what is near and then reach far,
must begin from the root and then reach the branches.
Order is also like this.
Thus, Bǎi Lǐxī was in Yú and Yú perished;
he was in Qín and Qín dominated.
Xiàng Zhì was in Shāng and Shāng was destroyed;
he was in Zhōu and Zhōu became king.
When Bǎi Lǐxī was in Yú,
his wisdom was not foolish;
when Xiàng Zhì was in Shāng,
his principles were not bad;
it was because there was no root.
When he was in Qín,
his wisdom was not increased;
when he was in Zhōu,
his principles were not improved;
it was because there was a root.
That root
means establishing distinctions.
Qí ordered Zhāng Zǐjiāng to lead troops and attack Jīng with Hán and Wèi.
Jīng ordered Táng Miè to lead troops to resist him.
The armies faced each other,
for six months without fighting.
Qí ordered Zhōu Zuì to urge Zhāng Zǐ to fight quickly,
his words were very harsh.
Zhāng Zǐ replied to Zhōu Zuì:
"Kill me, dismiss me,
ruin my family;
the King can demand this of your servant.
But to fight when it is not opportune to fight,
or not to fight when it is opportune to fight—
the King cannot demand this of your servant."
He camped opposite the Jīng army across the Cǐ River.
Zhāng Zǐ sent men to scout the river for crossing points.
The Jīng men shot at them,
making it impossible to get close to the water.
A grass-cutter by the water's edge
reported to the Qí scout,
saying:
"The depth of the water is easy to know.
Where the Jīng people heavily guard
is all the shallow parts;
where they lightly guard
is all the deep parts."
The scout brought the grass-cutter to see Zhāng Zǐ.
Zhāng Zǐ was very pleased,
and then trained his troops to attack by night the heavily guarded positions of the Jīng army,
and indeed killed Táng Miè.
Zhāng Zǐ can be called someone who understood the distinction of a general's role.
Hán Zhāolíhóu went out hunting with falcons.
A rein was too loose.
Zhāolíhóu was in the carriage
and said to his driver:
"Isn't the rein too loose?"
His driver said:
"Yes."
When they arrived at the lodge,
Zhāolíhóu shot a bird,
and his right-hand man adjusted one of the reins
to the proper tension.
After Zhāolíhóu finished shooting,
he hitched the carriage and returned.
When he got into the carriage,
he waited for a moment and
said:
"Earlier the rein was loose,
now it's adjusted.
What happened?"
His right-hand man replied from behind:
"This time your servant adjusted it."
When Zhāolíhóu arrived back,
he questioned the carriage officer.
Each was dismissed.
Therefore, even if the method of unauthorized action and arbitrary judgment is correct,
a wise ruler does not follow it.
Now, if there is a person here
who, by acting unilaterally, can avert national disaster,
who, by manipulating weights, is as accurate as scales and steelyards,
who, by drawing squares and circles, is as precise as compasses and rulers—
this person is indeed skillful and ingenious,
but not to be emulated.
The law is what everyone agrees upon,
what allows the worthy and the unworthy to exert their strength.
Plans that cannot be put into common use,
and actions that cannot be commonly approved,
these were abandoned by the former kings.
25.6 《Shènxiǎo》
Sixth:
The superior is honored, and the inferior is humble.
If humble, one cannot view the superior from a small perspective.
If honored, one is unrestrained;
if unrestrained, one belittles small things;
if one belittles small things, the superior has no means to understand the inferior.
The inferior has no means to understand the superior.
If superior and inferior do not understand each other,
then the superior will disapprove of the inferior,
and the inferior will resent the superior.
It is the nature of a subject
not to act for one whom they resent;
it is the nature of a ruler
not to love one whom they disapprove of.
This is a great divergence in the ways of superior and inferior.
Therefore, a wise ruler carefully attends to small matters to discern likes and dislikes.
A great dike can hold a mole,
yet flood a city and kill people;
a crack can leak a wisp of smoke,
yet burn down palaces and stores;
a general can lose one command,
and his army is shattered and he himself dies;
a ruler can err in one word,
and his state is ruined, his name disgraced,
and he becomes a laughingstock for future generations.
Wèi Xiàn Gōng cautioned Sūn Línfù and Níng Zhí about their meal.
When wild geese gathered in the imperial park,
the park ranger reported it.
The Duke went to the park to shoot geese.
The two ministers waited for the ruler,
but it grew late,
and the Duke did not return.
When he did return, he did not remove his leather cap before seeing the two ministers.
The two ministers were displeased,
and they banished Xiàn Gōng,
establishing Gōngzǐ Qiān.
When Wèi Zhuāng Gōng was enthroned,
he wished to banish Shí Pǔ.
He ascended a tower to look out,
saw Róngzhōu, and asked:
“What is that place?”
An attendant replied:
“It is Róngzhōu.”
Zhuāng Gōng said:
“I am of the Jī surname.
How dare the Róng people reside in my state?”
He ordered their dwellings to be seized
and their district destroyed.
When the Jìn people later attacked Wèi,
the Róngzhōu people consequently joined Shí Pǔ in killing Zhuāng Gōng,
and established Gōngzǐ Qǐ.
These were failures to attend to small matters.
It is human nature not to stumble over a mountain,
but to stumble over an anthill.
When Qí Huán Gōng ascended the throne,
in three years, with three declarations,
the world praised him as wise,
and all his ministers were pleased.
He eliminated the beasts that ate meat,
the birds that ate grain,
and the nets made of silk.
Wú Qǐ governed Xīhé.
Wishing to demonstrate his trustworthiness to the people,
he erected a pole outside the south gate at night,
and issued an order throughout the city saying:
“Tomorrow, whoever can knock down the pole outside the south gate
will be appointed a senior grand master.”
The next day, it grew late,
but no one had knocked down the pole.
The people said to each other:
“This must not be true.”
One man said:
“Let’s try going to knock down the pole.
Even if we don’t get the reward,
what harm is there?”
He went and knocked down the pole,
then came to report to Wú Qǐ.
Wú Qǐ personally came out to see him
and appointed him a senior grand master.
That night, he again erected a pole
and issued the same order throughout the city as before.
The city people guarded the gate and competed for the pole,
but the pole was more firmly planted,
and they did not obtain the reward.
From then on,
the people trusted Wú Qǐ’s rewards and punishments.
If rewards and punishments are trusted by the people,
what undertaking cannot be accomplished?
Why just military affairs?
26.1 *Shì Róng*
First:
A scholar is neither partisan nor biased,
gentle yet firm,
empty yet substantial.
His demeanor is bright and not frivolous,
as if he has lost something.
He scorns small things but his ambition belongs to the great;
he seems fearless yet cannot be intimidated or bullied;
his resolve is steadfast, bold, and he cannot be insulted or harmed;
when facing trouble or hardship, he adheres to righteousness without deviating;
he faces south and claims to be solitary, yet is not extravagant or boastful;
today he rules the people and wishes to subdue those beyond the seas;
he values things highly, yet does not rely on petty gains;
his ears and eyes ignore common customs, yet he can bring peace to the world;
he does not seek wealth and honor, nor is he deterred by poverty and lowliness;
his virtue and conduct respect principle, and he is ashamed to use clever defenses;
he is tolerant and not critical, yet his inner heart is very severe;
he is difficult to sway by external things, but will certainly not yield improperly.
This is the demeanor of a national scholar.
In Qí, there was a man skilled in judging dogs.
His neighbor borrowed from him a dog for catching rats,
and after a year, he obtained it,
saying:
“This is a good dog.”
His neighbor kept it for several years,
but it did not catch rats,
so he informed the judge.
The judge said:
“This is a good dog.
Its ambition is for deer, elk, boars, and stags,
not for rats.
If you want it to catch rats, then hobble it.”
His neighbor hobbled its hind legs,
and the dog then caught rats.
Indeed, the spirit of a fine steed,
the ambition of a swan or wild goose,
there is a sincerity that communicates to people’s hearts.
People are also like this.
If there is sincerity, it will evoke a response in others.
How can mere words be sufficient to convey it?
This is called unspoken words.
A guest visited Tián Pián,
whose attire was proper,
whose movements were orderly,
whose walking and strolling were graceful and elegant,
and whose speech was modest and quick-witted.
Tián Pián listened to all of it and then bid him farewell.
As the guest left,
Tián Pián watched him with his eyes.
A disciple said to Tián Pián:
“Was that guest a scholar?”
Tián Pián said:
“Probably not a scholar.
What the guest just now concealed,
a scholar displays;
what a scholar conceals,
the guest displays.
The guest is probably not a scholar.”
Thus, if a lamp illuminates only one corner,
the room will be partially dark;
if bones and joints form too early,
and the orifices are underdeveloped,
the body will certainly not grow tall;
if the multitude lacks strategic planning,
and focuses only on cautious observation,
many troubles will arise;
if one’s ambition is not impartial,
one cannot achieve great deeds;
if one loves to receive and hates to give,
even if the state is large, it will not become a kingdom;
calamities will arrive daily.
Therefore, the demeanor of a noble person
is pure, like the jade of Zhōngshān,
and unyielding, like the trees on a mound.
He is sincerely and diligently cautious and reverent toward transformation,
and unwilling to be self-satisfied;
he is diligently and sincerely unwavering in acceptance and rejection,
and his heart is utterly simple and unadorned.
Táng Shàng, at the same age, became a historian.
His old friend told Táng Shàng that he wished for him to be one,
and then conveyed this to Táng Shàng.
Táng Shàng said:
“It is not that I could not become a historian,
but I was ashamed to do so.”
His old friend did not believe him.
When Wèi besieged Hándān,
Táng Shàng persuaded Huì Wáng and lifted the siege,
giving the credit to Bóyáng.
Then his old friend believed that he was ashamed to be a historian.
After some time,
his old friend requested something on behalf of his brother.
Táng Shàng said:
“When the ruler of Wèi dies,
I will have your brother replace him.”
His old friend then got up, bowed twice, and believed him.
Indeed, to trust when it is not trustworthy,
and not to trust when it is trustworthy,
this is the misfortune of the foolish.
Those who understand human nature
cannot avoid harming themselves.
If such a person becomes a ruler,
what benefit is there, even if they possess the whole world?
Therefore, no failure is greater than folly.
The danger of folly
lies in always being self-willed.
If one is self-willed, then foolish and base people will follow and congratulate them.
To have a state like this
is worse than having none at all.
The ancients' praise of the worthy
arises from this.
It is not that they detest their descendants,
nor that they seek to boast of their own names;
rather, it is the reversal of the truth.
26.2 《Wùdà》
Second, it says:
Try to observe the intentions of those above:
the assistants of the Sān Wáng,
their names were all glorious,
and their substance was all secure,
because their achievements were great.
The assistants of vulgar rulers,
their desire for name and substance was the same as that of the assistants of the Sān Wáng,
yet their names were all disgraced,
and their substance was all imperiled,
because they had no achievements.
All worried that their own persons were not honored in their state,
but did not worry that their ruler was not honored in the world.
This is why those who desired glory became more disgraced,
and those who desired security became more imperiled.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Swallows and sparrows contend for the best dwelling place under one roof.
Mothers and children feed each other,
and they take petty joy in each other,
believing themselves to be secure.
When the chimney cracks,
and the beams above burn,
the swallows and sparrows' expressions do not change.
Why is this?
They do not know that disaster is about to befall them.
Is this not foolish!
Few are those who, as ministers, are free from the intelligence of swallows and sparrows.
Those who are ministers
advance their official positions, salaries, wealth, and honor.
Fathers, sons, and brothers band together and form cliques in one state,
taking petty joy in each other,
but thereby endangering their altars of soil and grain.
This is close to the chimney burning,
yet they never realize it.
Their intelligence is no different from that of swallows and sparrows.
Therefore, it is said:
'When the world is in great chaos,
no state is secure;
when a state is entirely in chaos,
no family is secure;
when a family is entirely in chaos,
no person is secure.'
This is what is meant.
Therefore, the security of the small
must depend on the great;
the security of the great
must depend on the small.
The small and the great, the lowly and the noble,
mutually assist each other,
and then all can obtain what they enjoy."
Bó Yí advised Wèi Sìjūn with the art of kingship.
Sìjūn replied:
"What I possess is a thousand chariots;
I wish to receive instruction on this."
Bó Yí responded:
"Wū Huò (Fèng) can lift a thousand jūn,
how much more so a single jīn?"
Dù Hè persuaded Zhōu Zhāowénjūn to pacify the world.
Zhāowénjūn said to Dù Hè:
"I wish to learn how to pacify Zhōu."
Dù Hè replied:
"If what your minister says is not feasible,
then Zhōu cannot be pacified;
if what your minister says is feasible,
then Zhōu will pacify itself."
This is what is called pacifying through non-pacification.
The ruler of Zhèng asked Bèi Zhān:
"I heard your principles, Sir,
that you do not die for your ruler,
and do not lose your ruler.
Is this truly so?"
Bèi Zhān replied:
"It is so.
If one's words are not listened to,
and one's Way is not practiced,
then one simply does not serve the ruler.
If one's words are listened to and one's Way is practiced,
then how can there be death or loss?"
Therefore, Bèi Zhān's not dying or losing
was more worthy than those who died or lost.
In the past, Shùn wanted to subdue the lands beyond the seas but did not succeed,
yet he was already sufficient to become an Emperor.
Yǔ wanted to become Emperor but did not succeed,
yet he was already sufficient to rule within the seas.
Tāng and Wǔ wanted to succeed Yǔ but did not succeed,
yet they were already sufficient to rule the well-connected lands.
The Wǔ Bó wanted to succeed Tāng and Wǔ but did not succeed,
yet they were already sufficient to be chiefs of the feudal lords.
Kǒng and Mò wanted to practice the Great Way in the world but did not succeed,
yet they were already sufficient to achieve prominence and honor.
The non-achievement of the great Way
already implies some achievement,
therefore one must strive to accomplish great things.
26.3 《Shàng Nóng》
Third, it says:
The reason why the ancient sage kings guided their people
was to prioritize agriculture.
People engaging in agriculture is not merely for the benefit of the land;
it is to value their will.
When people farm, they are simple;
when simple, they are easy to employ;
when easy to employ, the borders are secure,
and the ruler's position is honored.
When people farm, they are steadfast;
when steadfast, they have few private notions of righteousness;
when they have few private notions of righteousness, public law is established,
and their efforts are focused and unified.
When people farm, their produce returns;
when their produce returns, they are reluctant to move;
when they are reluctant to move, they die in their place without second thoughts.
If people abandon the root and pursue the branch, they will not be orderly;
if not orderly, they cannot guard,
and cannot fight.
If people abandon the root and pursue the branch, their produce will be scarce;
if their produce is scarce, they will easily move;
if they easily move,
then when the state faces trouble,
all will have distant ambitions,
and no settled heart.
If people abandon the root and pursue the branch, they will love cleverness;
if they love cleverness, they will be deceitful;
if deceitful, they will skillfully manipulate laws,
taking right for wrong,
and wrong for right.
Hòujì said:
"The reason for prioritizing plowing and weaving
is to make it the fundamental teaching."
Therefore, the Son of Heaven personally led the feudal lords to plow the imperial fields,
and the grandees and scholars all had meritorious tasks.
Therefore, at that time,
farmers were not seen in the capital,
to teach the people to respect agricultural produce.
The empress and concubines led the nine concubines to rear silkworms in the suburbs,
and planted mulberries in the public fields.
Thus, in spring, autumn, winter, and summer, there were achievements in flax, hemp, silk, and cocoons,
to exert the teaching for women.
Therefore, men wore clothes without weaving,
and women ate without plowing.
Men and women exchanged efforts,
to prolong life;
this was the system of the sages.
Therefore, they respected the seasons and cherished the days,
not resting unless old,
not ceasing unless ill,
not giving up unless dead.
On superior land,
one man feeds nine people.
On inferior land,
one man feeds five people.
This can be increased,
but cannot be decreased.
One person manages it,
ten people eat from it,
and the six livestock are all included in it.
This is the great way of utilizing the land.
Therefore, at that time,
no great earthworks were undertaken,
no armies were raised.
Commoners did not wear caps or crowns, marry wives, give daughters in marriage, or offer sacrifices.
They did not gather crowds for alcoholic beverages.
Farmers were not reported to the authorities,
and dared not privately record their earnings,
as this would be detrimental to the season.
After this, field restrictions were established:
if not of the same clan,
farmers were not to go out to meet,
and women were not to marry outside,
to secure the farmers.
There were five field restrictions:
If the land was not yet cleared,
one should not handle hemp,
nor spread manure.
When teeth and years are not yet mature,
one dares not establish parks and orchards.
When strength is insufficient,
one dares not channel the land and plow.
Farmers dare not engage in trade,
and dare not undertake diverse tasks.
This is to harm the season.
Thereafter, seasonal prohibitions are established:
on mountains, one dares not cut down timber or lower branches;
marsh dwellers dare not burn vegetation;
snares, nets, and traps dare not be taken out of the gate;
large fishing nets dare not enter the deep waters.
In marshes, if one is not a boatman,
one dares not claim a share,
for this harms its season.
If the people do not exert themselves in farming,
and Mo (墨) becomes a household practice,
the state will be difficult to govern,
and the three doubts will reach their extreme.
This is called abandoning the root and defying the rule,
destroying one's state.
All common people from seven *chǐ* (尺) and above,
are assigned to the three officials.
Farmers focus on grain,
artisans on tools,
merchants on goods.
If seasonal tasks are not mutually observed,
this is called a great misfortune.
To take from them for military service,
this is called *jī* (稽),
then worries and grief will not cease,
and their grain will surely be lost.
To take from them for water conservation projects,
this is called *yuè* (籥),
then loss will follow joy,
and the four neighbors will come to empty (their coffers).
To take from them for military affairs,
this is called *lì* (厲),
then disaster will follow year after year,
and sickles and scythes will not be raised.
Repeatedly depriving the people of their time,
a great famine will then come.
There will be abandoned plows in the fields,
some talking, some singing,
day becoming night,
and much grain will be lost.
Everyone knows the superficial,
but no one knows the fundamental truth.
26.4 *Rèndì* (任地)
Fourthly, it says:
Hòujì (后稷) said:
Can you make the hollow a mound?
Can you conceal its flaws and greet it with shade?
Can you make our soil tranquil and allow the furrows to bathe the soil?
Can you make it so that the moist land is stable and settled?
Can you make it so that the weeds do not spread rampantly?
Can you make your fields entirely covered with cool breezes?
Can you make the stalks have many joints and sturdy stems?
Can you make the ears of grain large, firm, and even?
Can you make the grains round and with thin husks?
Can you make the rice abundant and nourishing, and strengthen the body when eaten?
If not, what then?
The general principles of farming are:
the strong desire softness,
the soft desire strength.
The resting desire labor,
the laborious desire rest.
The barren desire fertility,
the fertile desire barrenness.
The urgent desire slowness,
the slow desire urgency.
The wet desire dryness,
the dry desire wetness.
In upper fields, abandon the ridges;
in lower fields, abandon the furrows.
Plow and weed five times,
always carefully and thoroughly.
The depth of planting should be such that
the Yin (陰) soil is reached,
no large weeds grow,
and there are no insect pests.
This year's wheat crop will be good,
next year's barley crop will be good.
Therefore, a six-*chǐ* (尺) plow
is used to form the ridges;
its width is eight *cùn* (寸),
used to form the furrows;
the hoe handle is one *chǐ* (尺),
this is its measure;
the hoe blade is six *cùn* (寸),
used to space the crops.
Land can be made fertile,
and also made barren.
When people cultivate fertile land, they must do so in damp conditions,
to make the seedlings strong and the soil loose;
when people weed, they must do so in dry conditions,
to make the soil fertile and soft.
Weeds grow large in the major months.
Fifty-seven days after the winter solstice,
the sweet flag begins to grow.
The sweet flag is the first of all grasses to grow,
and at this time, plowing begins.
In the evening of early summer,
three leaves are killed and barley is harvested.
When the solstice arrives,
bitter greens die and other plants emerge,
and one plants hemp and beans.
This tells the people that the earth's treasures have died.
When all grasses grow and are stored, then emerge from the sunlight,
and *xīshǒu* (狶首) grows while wheat has no leaves,
and one engages in storing and hoarding,
this tells the people of their ultimate destiny.
When life is seen in the five seasons, plants are planted;
when death is seen, the dead are harvested.
Heaven determines the seasons,
earth produces wealth,
without consulting the people.
In fruitful years, bury soil;
in unfruitful years, bury soil.
Do not miss the people's time;
do not make them govern.
The common people know how to profit from poverty and wealth,
all beginning their work when the time comes,
and stopping when they are weary.
Thus, the strength of the old and weak can be fully utilized;
their daily use
can double their achievements.
Those who do not understand the tasks
go against the time before it arrives,
and long for it after it has passed,
and disparage it when it is present,
making their people withdraw.
Once the people have withdrawn,
they then long for the good time.
This is the lowest level of engaging in tasks.
When managing affairs causes suffering,
and one does not know the high and low,
the people then move away.
Planting early grain does not make it early,
planting late grain does not make it late,
thus the grain is scarce and the effort is lost.
26.5 *Biàntǔ* (辯土)
Fifthly, it says:
The way of farming:
it must begin with hard, rocky soil,
because it has little moisture and later withers;
it must be thickened and followed by soft soil,
because only by thickening and following does it reach;
loosen that which is tangled,
plow that which is firm,
moisten its deep soil and then follow it;
for upper fields, cover their locations;
for lower fields, exhaust their filth.
Do not allow three thieves to manage the land:
If the four seasons are stimulated unevenly,
with large furrows and small ridges,
like fish stealing from the sides,
and the seedlings are like directly hunted prey,
then the land steals it;
if, after planting, there are no rows,
and plowing does not lead to growth,
then the seedlings steal from each other;
if not weeded, it becomes overgrown;
if weeded, it becomes sparse;
then the weeds steal it.
Therefore, only by getting rid of these three thieves
can the grain be abundant.
What is called the present-day farming,
which involves labor without gain:
those who are early are before their time,
those who are late are behind their time,
the cold and heat are not regulated,
and crops suffer many disasters
and realities.
Its becoming dark means:
if it is high and precarious, moisture is stolen;
if it is sloped, it becomes ridged;
if exposed to wind, it is battered;
if mounded high, it is pulled up;
if cold, it withers;
if hot, it dries up;
five or six die in one season,
thus it cannot provide for the future.
They do not sprout together and die together.
Sparse crops die first,
then the numerous thieves pilfer.
When viewed from afar, there seems to be an abundance,
but upon approach, it is empty.
The farmer knows his field is easy to cultivate,
but does not know that his crops are sparse and unsuitable;
he knows the boundaries of his field are cleared,
but does not know that his crops occupy the land sparsely;
if not cleared, it becomes wild,
if cleared, it becomes empty;
this is what harms the matter.
Therefore, the field (mǔ) should be broad and flat,
the furrows (quán) should be small, deep, and clear;
below, they receive yin,
above, they receive yang,
and only then do all things grow.
Crops desire to grow from dust,
and to be planted in firm ground.
Be careful with their seeds,
do not make them too dense,
nor too sparse.
When applying soil to them,
do not let it be insufficient,
nor let there be too much.
When harrowing (yōu) them,
be sure to mound the earth around them (péi).
When they are harrowed (yōu) upright,
those that are upright will certainly sprout first.
When the soil is applied evenly,
those that are even will certainly grow strong.
Thus, if the field (mǔ) is broad and flat,
the main stalks will not be lost;
those that grow from the ground,
divide them by five parts of the ground.
Stems grow in rows,
hence they grow quickly;
the weak do not harm each other,
hence they grow large quickly.
Horizontal rows must be achieved,
vertical rows must be skillfully managed.
Straighten their rows,
allow wind to pass through them,
clear the center of the heart (kuài xīn zhōng yāng),
to lead in cool breezes.
When seedlings are weak, they desire to be solitary;
when they grow, they desire to be together;
when they mature, they desire to support each other.
Therefore, when three make a cluster (zú),
then there will be much grain (sù).
The common problem with grains (hé) is
that they do not sprout together and die together.
Therefore, those that sprout first produce fine rice,
those that sprout later become husks (pǐ).
Hence, when weeding (nòu),
leave the elder and remove the younger.
If the trees are fertile, do not let them be too sparse;
if the trees are barren, they should not grow alone, but in clusters (zú).
If fertile and sparse, there will be many husks (pǐ);
if barren and growing alone, many will die.
Those who do not understand crops:
when they weed (nòu), they remove the elder and nurture the younger,
they do not harvest the grain (sù) but harvest the husks (pǐ).
If neither above nor below is at peace,
then many grains (hé) will die.
If the soil is thick, the shoots (niè) will not penetrate and develop;
if the soil is thin, they will grow luxuriantly (fán fán) but not sprout.
Hard, sticky, dark soil (lú zhí míng sè),
hard soil with soft seeds,
avoid tilling, kill hidden pests,
so that farm work succeeds.
26.6 《Shěn Shí》
Sixth, it says:
In all methods of farming,
abundance (hòu) is considered precious:
if trees are cut at the wrong time,
they will not break but will sprout;
if crops ripen but are not harvested,
they will certainly encounter natural disasters (tiān zāi).
Indeed, crops are made by humans (rén),
grown by the earth (dì),
and nurtured by heaven (tiān).
Therefore, for human cultivation, there should be enough room for the feet;
for weeding (nòu), enough room for the hoe (nòu);
for grasping, enough room for the hand.
This is called the Way of Cultivation (Gēng Dào).
Thus, grains (hé) that are planted at the right time,
